title: מבנה הסוגיות – Nedarim
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Kinnuyim are like vows
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Kinnuyim are like vows
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that all euphemisms (kinnuyim) for vows are legally equivalent to vows, and similarly for dedications (charamim), oaths (shevu'ot), and nazirite vows (nezirut). This establishes that indirect or substitute language can create binding prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that all euphemisms (kinnuyim) for vows, dedications, oaths, and nazirite vows are legally equivalent to the actual terms.
The mishnah lists specific euphemistic phrases that render a person forbidden from benefiting from another.
The mishnah notes that regarding the phrase 'I am excommunicated from you', Rabbi Akiva was inclined to be stringent.

items.text: List of prohibited formulations
items.text_en: List of prohibited formulations
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists specific phrases that, when said to another person, render the speaker prohibited from eating or tasting anything of the other: 'muddrani mimakh', 'mufreshani mimakh', 'meruchakani mimakh', 'she'ani okhel lakh', and 'she'ani to'em lakh'.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists five specific formulations that, when spoken to another person, render the speaker prohibited from eating or tasting anything of that person.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's stringency regarding 'menudeh ani lach'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's stringency regarding 'menudeh ani lach'
items.desc_en: The mishnah notes that regarding the phrase 'menudeh ani lach' (I am ostracized from you), Rabbi Akiva would treat it stringently, implying he considers it a valid vow, unlike the Sages who may disagree.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah reports that regarding the phrase 'menudeh ani lach' (I am ostracized from you), Rabbi Akiva would treat it stringently, implying he considers it a valid vow.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists all euphemisms for vows but not for naziriteship, and answers that since vow and oath are written together, the Mishnah teaches both categories, and therefore lists all euphemisms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah in Nedarim lists all euphemisms for vows, dedications, oaths, and nazirite vows, whereas the Mishnah in Nazir does not list all of them.
The Gemara answers that because vow and oath are written together in the Torah, the Mishnah teaches both categories, and once it teaches two, it teaches all of them.

items.text: Objection and resolution about order
items.text_en: Objection and resolution about order
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that oaths should be taught after vows, but resolves that vows and herem are similar in forbidding an object, unlike oaths which forbid the person from the object.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishna should have taught substitutes for oaths immediately after substitutes for vows.
The Gemara resolves that vows and dedications are taught together because both forbid an object, unlike oaths which forbid the person from the object.

items.text: Question about handles and resolution
items.text_en: Question about handles and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah begins with euphemisms but then explains handles, and answers that the Mishnah is incomplete and actually teaches: all euphemisms of vows are like vows, and handles of vows are like vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah opens with euphemisms (כינויים) but then explains handles (ידות), which are a different category.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is incomplete and actually teaches: all euphemisms of vows are like vows, and handles of vows are like vows.

items.text: Question about explaining euphemisms first and proof from other mishnayot
items.text_en: Question about explaining euphemisms first and proof from other mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah doesn't explain euphemisms first, and answers that the topic it opened with is explained first, citing examples from other mishnayot where the opening topic is explained first, except when the opening is a general list that is then detailed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not explain the euphemisms (כינויים) first, before the handles (ידות).
The Gemara answers that the topic which the Mishnah opened with is explained first, citing the example of 'במה מדליקין' (with what may one light) where the opening prohibition is detailed first.
The Gemara objects by citing mishnayot (e.g., 'יש נוחלין', 'יש מותרות', 'יש טעונות', 'יש בכור') where the opening general list is not explained first, but rather the detailed cases follow.
The Gemara resolves that those mishnayot are exceptions because they are general lists (אוושו ליה), so the opening topic is still explained first, but the list format requires detailing all items.

items.text: Counterexample and conclusion
items.text_en: Counterexample and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a counterexample where the opening topic is not explained first, but concludes that the rule holds except when the opening is a general list that is then detailed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah 'במה בהמה יוצאת' (with what may an animal go out) does not have a general opening list, yet it still explains the opening topic first.
The Gemara concludes that the rule holds except when the opening is a general list that is then detailed, as in the case of 'במה בהמה יוצאת' where the opening is not a general list.

items.text: Explaining the order of the Mishnah: kinnuyim before yadot
items.text_en: Explaining the order of the Mishnah: kinnuyim before yadot
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two explanations for why the Mishnah lists kinnuyim before yadot: either the Tanna sometimes specifies the last-mentioned item first, or because yadot are derived from a drasha, they are explained first. It then asks why the Tanna didn't simply open with yadot, and answers that he opened with Torah-based kinnuyim first and then explained the derasha-derived yadot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers two explanations for why the Mishnah lists קינואים (substitutes) before ידות (intimations): either the Tanna is not particular about order, or because ידות are derived from a דרשה (exposition), they are cherished and explained first.
The Gemara asks: If so, why not open the Mishnah with ידות (intimations) first?
The Gemara answers: The Tanna opens with קינואים (substitutes) which are Torah-based, and then explains ידות (intimations) which are derived from a דרשה (exposition).

items.text: Challenge based on the nature of kinnuyim
items.text_en: Challenge based on the nature of kinnuyim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer based on the dispute about kinnuyim: according to the view that kinnuyim are foreign words, the answer works, but according to the view that they are words invented by the Sages, what can be said?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer: according to the view that kinnuyim are foreign words, the answer works, but according to the view that they are words invented by the Sages, what can be said?

items.text: Reconstructing the Mishnah's text
items.text_en: Reconstructing the Mishnah's text
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it should have first taught 'All handles of vows are like vows' and then 'All euphemisms of vows are like vows', and then listed examples of both. This resolves the order issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does the Mishnah actually teach yadot? It then reconstructs the Mishnah as including both yadot and kinnuyim in the proper order.
The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah should have first taught 'All handles of vows are like vows' and then 'All euphemisms of vows are like vows', listing examples of both, resolving the order issue.

items.text: Deriving yadot for nezirut and nedarim from the verse
items.text_en: Deriving yadot for nezirut and nedarim from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives yadot for nezirut from the double expression 'nazir lehazir', and then uses a hekesh (analogy) between nedarim and nezirut to extend yadot to nedarim. It also derives other laws: that nedarim and nezirut share the prohibitions of bal yachel and bal te'acher, and the laws of annulment by father or husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah are yadot (verbal handles) derived, and cites the verse 'איש כי יפליא לנדר נדר נזיר להזיר לה׳'.
A baraita is cited, teaching that the double expression 'נזיר להזיר' serves to make both kinuyei nezirut (substitute terms) and yadot nezirut (verbal handles) effective like actual nezirut.
The Gemara asks: this derivation applies only to nezirut; from where do we derive yadot for nedarim (vows)?
The Gemara answers: the verse itself juxtaposes nedarim and nezirut (היקש), teaching that just as nezirut has yadot, so too nedarim have yadot.

The Gemara extends the היקש (analogy) to derive additional laws: that nezirut shares with nedarim the prohibitions of בל יחל (violating one's word) and בל תאחר (delaying fulfillment), and the laws of annulment by father or husband.

items.text: Questioning the need for a hekesh
items.text_en: Questioning the need for a hekesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a hekesh is needed for nedarim, since the verse also has a double expression 'lindor neder'. It answers that the Torah wrote 'lindor neder' in the language of people (dibrah Torah kileshon bnei adam), not as a drasha, so the hekesh is necessary to derive yadot for nedarim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a hekesh is needed for nedarim, since the verse also has a double expression 'lindor neder'.
The Gemara answers that the Torah wrote 'lindor neder' in the language of people (דיברה תורה כלשון בני אדם), not as a drasha, so the hekesh is necessary to derive yadot for nedarim.

items.text: Alternative view: dibrah Torah kileshon bnei adam rejected
items.text_en: Alternative view: dibrah Torah kileshon bnei adam rejected
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the view that rejects 'dibrah Torah kileshon bnei adam'. According to this view, the double expression 'lindor neder' is used to derive yadot for nedarim, and then nezirut is compared to nedarim via hekesh. The section ends mid-derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: this works for the opinion that the Torah speaks in human language, but for the opinion that does not hold this, what does he do with the phrase 'לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר'?

The Gemara answers: he interprets 'לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר' to make yadot nedarim like nedarim, and 'נָזִיר לְהַזִּיר' to teach that kinnuyei nezirut and yadot nezirut are like nezirut, and then makes a היקש between nezirut and nedarim.

items.text: Opening statement: Nazirite vow takes effect on another nazirite vow
items.text_en: Opening statement: Nazirite vow takes effect on another nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that a nazirite vow can take effect upon an existing nazirite vow, setting up the discussion that follows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a nazirite vow can take effect upon an existing nazirite vow.

items.text: Gemara's question: Source for nazirite vow on nazirite vow
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Source for nazirite vow on nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the principle that a nazirite vow can take effect on another nazirite vow, considering the opinion that the Torah speaks in human language and that the phrase 'nazir lehazir' is expounded to make verbal handles like the vow itself. It offers an answer from the extra word 'lehazir' implying two things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the opinion that the Torah speaks in human language and that 'nazir lehazir' is expounded to make verbal handles like the vow itself, what is the source that nazirite vow takes effect on another nazirite vow?

The Gemara answers: the verse could have said 'lizor' (to be a nazirite), but instead says 'lehazir' (to cause to be a nazirite), implying two things — that nazirite vow takes effect on another nazirite vow.

items.text: Alternative sources for verbal handles
items.text_en: Alternative sources for verbal handles
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in the West they say there is a Tanna who derives verbal handles from the phrase 'to vow a vow' and another Tanna who derives them from 'as all that proceeds from his mouth he shall do'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that in the West they say there are two Tannaim: one derives verbal handles from the phrase 'לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר' (to vow a vow) and the other from 'כְּכׇל הַיֹּצֵא מִפִּיו יַעֲשֶׂה' (as all that proceeds from his mouth he shall do).

items.text: Discussion of 'bal yachel' for nazirite vows
items.text_en: Discussion of 'bal yachel' for nazirite vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how the prohibition of 'bal yachel' applies to nazirite vows. It explains that for vows, one violates 'bal yachel' if he says he will eat a loaf and does not. For nazirite vows, since saying 'I am a nazirite' makes him a nazirite, eating or drinking violates other prohibitions. Rava says the violation of 'bal yachel' comes in addition to those.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that for vows, one violates the prohibitions of 'bal yachel' and 'bal te'acher', and explains that 'bal yachel' applies when one says he will eat a loaf and does not.

The Gemara asks how the prohibition of 'bal yachel' applies to nazirite vows, since saying 'I am a nazirite' immediately makes one a nazirite, and eating or drinking already violates other prohibitions.
Rava answers that the violation of 'bal yachel' comes in addition to the other prohibitions, so that one violates two prohibitions simultaneously.

items.text: Discussion of 'bal te'acher' for nazirite vows
items.text_en: Discussion of 'bal te'acher' for nazirite vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines how 'bal te'acher' applies to nazirite vows. It considers a case where one says 'when I want, I will be a nazirite', but that does not involve a delay. Rava explains a case where one says 'I will not depart from the world until I am a nazirite', which immediately makes him a nazirite because we assume he might die at any moment, analogous to a get given conditionally on death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the prohibition of 'bal te'acher' (delaying fulfillment of vows) applies to nazirite vows, and suggests a case where one says 'when I want, I will be a nazirite'.
The Gemara objects that if one says 'when I want', there is no delay and thus no violation of 'bal te'acher'.

Rava explains that the case is where one says 'I will not depart from the world until I am a nazirite', which immediately makes him a nazirite because we assume he might die at any moment, analogous to a conditional get given before death.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's case of a nazirite in a cemetery
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's case of a nazirite in a cemetery
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov presents a case where one vows to be a nazirite while in a cemetery, raising the question of whether 'bal te'acher' applies if the vow does not take effect immediately.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov presents a case where one vows to be a nazirite while in a cemetery, to illustrate a scenario where the vow does not take effect immediately.

The Gemara objects that this case only works for the opinion that nazirite status does not take effect immediately, but according to Mar bar Rav Ashi who says it takes effect immediately, there is no 'bal te'acher' issue.
The Gemara resolves that even if nazirite status takes effect immediately, the person still violates 'bal te'acher' because he delays the pure nazirite period that would follow his purification.
Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika states that the nazirite violates 'bal te'acher' regarding his shaving (תגלחת).
The Gemara clarifies that this applies even according to the opinion that shaving does not block the completion of the nazirite period, because the mitzvah of shaving itself is not fulfilled.
Mar Zutra brei d'Rav Mari states that the nazirite violates 'bal te'acher' regarding his offerings (קרבנותיו).
The Gemara objects that this ruling is already derived from the verse 'כי דרוש ידרשנו' which includes sin-offerings and guilt-offerings.
The Gemara answers that the ruling is needed because one might think the nazirite is a novelty (חידוש) that the Torah introduced, and therefore might not be subject to 'bal te'acher'.

The Gemara objects: what is the novelty? If it is that the sin-offering of a nazirite is not subject to a vow, the same applies to a sin-offering for eating forbidden fat, which also is not subject to a vow yet one violates 'bal te'acher'.

The Gemara explains the novelty: one might think that since a nazirite from grape pits is a full nazirite, the Torah would not apply 'bal te'acher' to his offerings, but the verse teaches that it does.

The Gemara objects that this explanation works only for the opinion that a nazirite from grape pits is a full nazirite, but according to Rabbi Shimon who requires abstention from all grape products, what can be said? Moreover, this novelty is a stringency (לחומרא), not a leniency.
The Gemara begins to offer another explanation of the novelty, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does 'bal te'acher' apply if nazirite status takes effect immediately?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does 'bal te'acher' apply if nazirite status takes effect immediately?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case based on the dispute about whether nazirite status takes effect immediately. For those who say it does, there is no delay, and Mar bar Rav Ashi's view that the dispute is about lashes is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the applicability of 'בל תאחר' (the prohibition against delaying vows) for those who hold that nazirite status takes effect immediately, citing Mar bar Rav Ashi's view that the dispute is about lashes.

items.text: Answer: 'Bal te'acher' applies due to delaying pure naziriteship
items.text_en: Answer: 'Bal te'acher' applies due to delaying pure naziriteship
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even if nazirite status takes effect immediately, one still violates 'bal te'acher' because he delays the pure naziriteship that will follow his impurity. Rav Ashi extends this to a nazirite who deliberately defiles himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even if nazirite status takes effect immediately, one still violates 'bal te'acher' because he delays the pure naziriteship that will follow his impurity.
Rav Ashi extends the principle: a nazirite who deliberately defiles himself also violates 'bal te'acher' regarding his pure naziriteship.

items.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika: Violation for delaying shaving
items.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika: Violation for delaying shaving
items.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika argues that the violation of 'bal te'acher' applies to delaying the shaving (taglachat) of the nazirite, even if shaving is not essential for atonement, as the mitzvah of shaving is not fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika states that one violates the prohibition of 'bal te'acher' (delaying) regarding the shaving of the nazirite.
The Gemara explains that this applies even according to the view that shaving does not impede atonement, because the mitzvah of shaving is still not fulfilled.

items.text: Mar Zutra brei d'Rav Mari: Violation for delaying offerings
items.text_en: Mar Zutra brei d'Rav Mari: Violation for delaying offerings
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra brei d'Rav Mari states that the violation of 'bal te'acher' applies to delaying the nazirite's offerings (korbanot).

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra brei d'Rav Mari states that the violation of 'bal te'acher' applies to delaying the nazirite's offerings.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Source from elsewhere
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Source from elsewhere
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the source for delaying offerings is already derived from the verse 'כי דרוש ידרשנו' referring to sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, so why is a new derivation needed for nazirite offerings?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the source for delaying offerings is already derived from the verse 'כי דרוש ידרשנו' referring to sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, so why is a new derivation needed for nazirite offerings?

items.text: Gemara's resolution: The novelty of nazirite offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: The novelty of nazirite offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the novelty is that one might think nazirite offerings are exempt from 'bal te'acher' due to the unique leniency that a nazirite vow can be taken even from grape pits, or due to Rabbi Shimon's view that naziriteship requires abstaining from all grape products. The Gemara concludes that the novelty is actually a stringency, not a leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the possibility that nazirite offerings are a novel institution (חידוש) of the Torah, which might exempt them from the prohibition of 'בל תאחר' (delaying fulfillment of vows).
The Gemara asks what the novelty is, suggesting it might be that the sin-offering of a nazirite (חטאת נזיר) is not subject to the vow's binding force (תפיסה).
The Gemara rejects this, noting that the sin-offering for consuming forbidden fat (חטאת חלב) is also not subject to the vow's binding force, yet one still violates 'בל תאחר' for it.

The Gemara proposes that the novelty is that one might think that since a nazirite vow can be fulfilled even with grape pits (חרצן), the offerings should be exempt from 'בל תאחר', but the Torah teaches otherwise.

The Gemara objects that this explanation works only for the opinion that a nazirite vow from grape pits makes one a full nazirite, but not for Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one is not a nazirite unless one abstains from all grape products.
The Gemara adds that this novelty is actually a stringency (לחומרא), not a leniency, undermining the initial premise that the novelty would exempt from 'בל תאחר'.
The Gemara begins to propose a different explanation for the novelty, but the text is cut off at this point.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya: the novelty of the nazirite case
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya: the novelty of the nazirite case
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's statement about a nazirite who shaved for one of three korbanot teaches that he does not violate 'bal te'acher' (delay), even though he could have brought them earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's statement about a nazirite who shaved for one of three korbanot teaches that he does not violate 'bal te'acher' (delay), even though he could have brought them earlier.

items.text: Alternative explanation and objection regarding nazirite sin-offering
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and objection regarding nazirite sin-offering
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the novelty is that the vow is not subject to annulment. The Gemara objects that a sin-offering for forbidden fat comes for atonement, but a nazirite's sin-offering has no such purpose. The Gemara counters with the example of a yoledet's sin-offering, which also does not come for atonement but still incurs 'bal te'acher'; however, that offering permits her to eat sacred food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the novelty of the Mishnah's case is that the vow is not subject to annulment.
The Gemara objects that a sin-offering for forbidden fat comes for atonement, but a nazirite's sin-offering has no such purpose.
The Gemara counters with the example of a yoledet's sin-offering, which also does not come for atonement but still incurs 'bal te'acher'; however, that offering permits her to eat sacred food.

items.text: The need for a hekesh to compare nazirite vows to regular vows
items.text_en: The need for a hekesh to compare nazirite vows to regular vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a hekesh (analogy) is needed to teach that a father or husband can annul a nazirite vow, since it could be derived via a 'mah matzinu' (what we find) from regular vows. The answer is that regular vows have no fixed duration, whereas nazirite vows have a fixed term (30 days), so one might think they cannot be annulled; the hekesh teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a hekesh (analogy) is needed to teach that a father or husband can annul a nazirite vow, since it could be derived via a 'mah matzinu' (what we find) from regular vows.
The Gemara answers that regular vows have no fixed duration, whereas nazirite vows have a fixed term (30 days), so one might think they cannot be annulled; the hekesh teaches otherwise.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on the required language for a vow
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the required language for a vow
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that for all the expressions listed in the Mishnah (e.g., 'mudar ani mimcha'), the prohibition only takes effect if the speaker adds 'she'ani ochel lach' or 'she'ani to'eim lach'.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that in all these cases, the prohibition applies only when one says 'that I eat from you' or 'that I taste from you'.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists 'she'ani ochel lach' as one of the expressions that make one forbidden, implying it is not a necessary addition. The Gemara resolves that the baraita should be read as: 'In what case are these words said? When he says she'ani ochel lach.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists 'I am forbidden from you' and similar phrases as effective, and also lists 'that I eat from you' as effective, implying both are valid.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita should be read as: 'In what case are these words said? When he says she'ani ochel lach.'

items.text: Second objection and Shmuel's final clarification
items.text_en: Second objection and Shmuel's final clarification
items.desc_en: Another baraita is cited that reverses the order, listing 'she'ani ochel lach' first as forbidden. The Gemara attempts to reinterpret it, but notes that this would make it identical to the first clause and questions the repetition of 'asur'. Finally, Shmuel clarifies: the point is that when one says 'she'ani ochel lach', he is forbidden but his friend is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that reverses the order, listing 'she'ani ochel lach' first as forbidden.
The Gemara attempts to reinterpret the baraita by inserting the phrase 'and already said mudrani' to align it with Shmuel's view.
The Gemara questions that this reinterpretation makes the baraita identical to the first clause and asks why the word 'asur' is repeated.
Shmuel clarifies that the point is that when one says 'she'ani ochel lach', he is forbidden but his friend is permitted.

items.text: Opening statement on 'mudrani heimakh'
items.text_en: Opening statement on 'mudrani heimakh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that saying 'mudrani heimakh' (I am vowed from you) prohibits both parties, unlike other formulations.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces the rule that saying 'mudrani heimakh' alone makes both parties forbidden, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.

items.text: Mishna: 'harei aleicha herem' vs 'at alai herem'
items.text_en: Mishna: 'harei aleicha herem' vs 'at alai herem'
items.desc_en: The Mishna teaches that saying 'harei aleicha herem' (a ban upon you) prohibits the subject, but not the speaker; while 'at alai herem' (you are upon me a ban) prohibits the speaker, not the subject. This is clarified by explicit phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishna teaches that saying 'הֲרֵינִי עָלֶיךָ חֵרֶם' (I am hereby to you like an item dedicated to the Temple) prohibits the subject, but the speaker is permitted, when he specifies 'וְאַתְּ עֲלַי לָא' (and you are not upon me).

The Mishna further teaches that saying 'אַתְּ עָלַי חֵרֶם' (you are to me like an item dedicated to the Temple) prohibits the speaker, but the subject is permitted, when he specifies 'וַאֲנָא עֲלָךְ לָא' (and I am not upon you).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishna's default
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishna's default
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In the Mishna's default (without explicit clarification), are both parties prohibited? The Mishna's seifa (second clause) says 'harei aleicha ve'at alai' — both prohibited, implying the reisha (first clause) only prohibits one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In the Mishna's default (without explicit clarification), are both parties prohibited? The Mishna's seifa (second clause) says 'הֲרֵינִי עָלֶיךָ וְאַתְּ עָלַי' (I am hereby to you and you are to me) — both prohibited, implying the reisha (first clause) only prohibits one.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's alternative ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's alternative ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina distinguishes: 'mudar ani lakh' (I am vowed to you) prohibits both; 'mudrani heimakh' (I am vowed from you) prohibits only the speaker.

sub.desc_en: The gemara corrects the earlier citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina, stating that the phrase 'mudar ani lakh' (I am vowed to you) prohibits both parties, while 'mudrani heimakh' (I am vowed from you) prohibits only the speaker.

items.text: Mishna's 'heimakh' clause and Samuel's interpretation
items.text_en: Mishna's 'heimakh' clause and Samuel's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Mishna's clause 'heimakh' is interpreted by Samuel: in all cases until the speaker says 'she'ani to'eim lakh' or 'she'ani ochel lakh', only the speaker is prohibited; but with 'mudrani heimakh', both are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishna's clause 'הֵימָךְ' and notes that it was interpreted according to Samuel's view.
Samuel explains that in all cases until the speaker says 'שֶׁאֲנִי טוֹעֵם לָךְ' or 'שֶׁאֲנִי אוֹכֵל לָךְ', only the speaker is prohibited; but with 'מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ', both are prohibited.

items.text: Samuel's original teaching on eating/tasting vows
items.text_en: Samuel's original teaching on eating/tasting vows
items.desc_en: Samuel originally taught that saying 'she'ani ochel lakh' or 'she'ani to'eim lakh' only prohibits eating/tasting, not benefit; but 'mudrani mimakh' prohibits even benefit.

sub.text: Stam's resolution of Samuel's original teaching
sub.text_en: Stam's resolution of Samuel's original teaching
sub.desc_en: The Stam resolves that Samuel's original teaching was that 'she'ani ochel lakh' and 'she'ani to'eim lakh' only prohibit eating, but 'mudrani mimkha' prohibits even benefit.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Samuel's statement contradicts Mishna
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Samuel's statement contradicts Mishna
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If Samuel says only eating/tasting is prohibited, then saying 'she'ani ochel lakh' or 'she'ani to'eim lakh' should only prohibit eating, not benefit — but the Mishna says both are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If Samuel's statement is as understood, then saying only 'she'ani ochel lakh' or 'she'ani to'eim lakh' should prohibit only eating, but the Mishna implies both are prohibited.

items.text: Resolution: Samuel's actual position
items.text_en: Resolution: Samuel's actual position
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: Samuel's actual teaching is that saying 'she'ani ochel lakh' or 'she'ani to'eim lakh' indeed prohibits only eating; but 'mudrani heimakh' means 'I am distanced from you' and prohibits all benefit, consistent with the Mishna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Samuel's actual teaching is that 'she'ani ochel lakh' and 'she'ani to'eim lakh' prohibit only eating, while 'mudrani heimakh' and similar phrases imply a general distancing and prohibit all benefit.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about Shmuel's view
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about Shmuel's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Shmuel holds that 'hands that do not prove intent' are not valid, and answers that Shmuel interprets the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yehuda, who requires explicit intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Shmuel holds that 'hands that do not prove intent' (ידים שאין מוכיחות) are not valid.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel interprets the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yehuda, who requires explicit intent.

items.text: Support from a baraita and challenge to Shmuel
items.text_en: Support from a baraita and challenge to Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires additional wording in a get, supporting the need for explicit intent. It then challenges Shmuel: why not interpret the Mishnah according to the Rabbis, who do not require explicit intent?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires additional wording in a get (bill of divorce), supporting the need for explicit intent.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel: why not interpret the Mishnah according to the Rabbis, who do not require explicit intent?

items.text: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah's phrasing forces the interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah's phrasing forces the interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's specific wording—'that I eat for you'—implies a need for explicit intent, as it could have simply said 'that I eat.' This forces Shmuel to interpret it according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the Mishnah's specific wording—'that I eat for you' instead of simply 'that I eat'—forces the interpretation that we require יָדַיִם מוֹכִיחוֹת (explicitly indicative expressions).

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the principle
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the general dispute: Abaye holds that 'hands that do not prove intent' are valid, while Rava holds they are not. Rava supports his view with a scriptural analogy from nazirite vows, requiring explicit intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general dispute: Abaye holds that 'hands that do not prove intent' are valid, while Rava holds they are not.
Rava supports his view with a scriptural analogy from nazirite vows, requiring explicit intent (הפלאה).

items.text: Attempt to align the dispute with Tannaic views
items.text_en: Attempt to align the dispute with Tannaic views
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Abaye and Rava's dispute corresponds to the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda's views on divorce documents, with Abaye following the Rabbis and Rava following Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Abaye and Rava's dispute about whether non-indicative expressions of intent (ידים שאין מוכיחות) are valid corresponds to the Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding the required formula in a bill of divorce (גט).

Abaye rejects the alignment, arguing that his position (that non-indicative expressions are valid) holds even according to Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda's requirement for indicative language (ידים מוכיחות) applies only to a bill of divorce (גט) where a complete severance (כריתות) is needed, not to other contexts.

Rava similarly rejects the alignment, arguing that his position (that non-indicative expressions are invalid) holds even according to the Rabbis, because the Rabbis' leniency regarding non-indicative expressions applies only to a bill of divorce (גט), not to other contexts.

items.text: Abaye and Rava reject the alignment, each claiming broader applicability
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava reject the alignment, each claiming broader applicability
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree in non-divorce contexts, while Rava argues that even the Rabbis would require explicit intent in divorce due to the need for 'cutting off' (כריתות).

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that his position (ambiguous intimations are valid) holds even according to Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda requires explicit intimations only in the context of a גט (bill of divorce) due to the need for כריתות (complete severance), not in general contexts.

Rava argues that his position (ambiguous intimations are not valid) holds even according to the Rabbis, because the Rabbis dispense with explicit intimations only in the context of a גט (bill of divorce), not in general contexts.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge to Abaye
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge to Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abaye's view that a 'yad' (verbal indication) requires explicit context, arguing that in general, people do not divorce their friend's wife, but elsewhere do we require such explicit indication?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's view that a 'yad' (verbal indication) requires explicit context, arguing that while in divorce one assumes a man does not divorce his friend's wife, elsewhere do we require such explicit indication?

items.text: First refutation of Abaye from a baraita
items.text_en: First refutation of Abaye from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: 'Harei hu alai' and 'Harei zeh alai' are forbidden because it is a 'yad' for a korban. This implies that only when saying 'alai' is it forbidden, but without 'alai' it is not, contradicting Abaye's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about vow formulations ('הרי הוא עלי' — 'it is upon me') to challenge Abaye, concluding it is a refutation.

items.text: Abaye's response and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Abaye's response and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Abaye initially responds that the baraita means only 'alai' makes it forbidden, but 'harei hu' without 'alai' refers to hefker or tzedaka. The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'because it is a yad for a korban'. Abaye then revises: 'alai' makes only the speaker forbidden, while 'harei hu' makes both forbidden, as it might mean 'harei hu hekdesh'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye initially answers that the baraita's prohibition applies only when 'עלי' is said, while 'הרי הוא' without 'עלי' refers to hefker or tzedaka.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states the reason is 'because it is a yad for a korban', contradicting Abaye's interpretation.
Abaye revises his answer: 'עלי' makes only the speaker forbidden, while 'הרי הוא' makes both forbidden, as it might mean 'הרי הוא הקדש'.

items.text: Second refutation of Abaye from another baraita
items.text_en: Second refutation of Abaye from another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: If one says 'Harei zo chatat' or 'asham' without specifying 'shel li', it is invalid. Only if he says 'chatati' or 'ashami' and is obligated do his words stand. This contradicts Abaye's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita about designating a sin-offering or guilt-offering without explicit context, concluding it is a refutation of Abaye.

items.text: Abaye's retraction and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's retraction and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye initially deflects by saying the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, but the Gemara notes that Abaye himself had argued even according to Rabbi Yehuda. He then retracts his position.

sub.desc_en: Abaye deflects by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda, but the Gemara notes that Abaye himself had claimed to hold even according to Rabbi Yehuda, so he retracts.
The Gemara objects that Abaye himself had previously argued his position even according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara concludes that Abaye retracted his earlier position.

items.text: Rava's position and distinction
items.text_en: Rava's position and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rava holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but Rava responds that he holds even like the Rabbis. The Rabbis only require 'yadim mochichot' in the case of a get, because one does not divorce another's wife, but elsewhere they do require explicit indication.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rava's position aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view.

Rava responds that he holds even according to the Rabbis, who only require explicit indication (ידים מוכיחות) in the case of a get because one does not divorce another's wife, but elsewhere they do require such indication.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about betrothal
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether there is a 'hand' for betrothals, i.e., whether an incomplete statement can effect betrothal. He clarifies the case: if he says to one woman 'you are betrothed to me' and to another 'and you', is it considered as if he said 'and you too' so that betrothal takes effect, or did he mean 'and you see' so it does not?

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether there is a 'hand' (incomplete statement) for betrothals, presenting the case where he says to one woman 'you are betrothed to me' and to another 'and you', and questions whether the incomplete phrase is interpreted as 'and you too' (effecting betrothal) or 'and you see' (not effecting betrothal).

items.text: Gemara's objection: Rav Pappa already assumes yes
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Rav Pappa already assumes yes
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Does Rav Pappa really need to ask this? He himself said to Abaye 'Does Shmuel hold that inconclusive indications are considered indications?' implying that Rav Pappa himself holds that there is a 'hand' for betrothals. The Gemara answers: He was merely stating what Shmuel holds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Pappa's question seems unnecessary, since he previously asked Abaye whether Shmuel holds that 'hands without proof' are considered hands, implying that Rav Pappa himself holds that there is a 'hand' for betrothals; the Gemara resolves that Rav Pappa was merely asking based on Shmuel's position.
The Gemara answers that Rav Pappa was merely stating what Shmuel holds, not expressing his own view.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about pe'ah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about pe'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether there is a 'hand' for pe'ah. He clarifies the case: if one says 'this furrow shall be pe'ah, and this one too' that is clearly pe'ah. The question is when he says 'and this one' without saying 'too'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether there is a 'hand' for pe'ah (the corner of the field left for the poor), presenting the case where he says 'this furrow shall be pe'ah, and this one' without saying 'also', and questions whether the incomplete statement is effective.

items.text: Gemara's inference and support for making entire field pe'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and support for making entire field pe'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rav Pappa's question that if one says 'the entire field shall be pe'ah', it is indeed pe'ah. It supports this with a baraita: one can make his entire field pe'ah, as it says 'the corner of your field' (implying the entire field can be designated).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rav Pappa's question that if one says 'the entire field shall be pe'ah', it is indeed pe'ah.
The Gemara affirms and cites a baraita that one can make his entire field pe'ah, as the verse says 'the corner of your field' (implying the entire field can be designated).

items.text: Gemara's deliberation: analogy to offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's deliberation: analogy to offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether pe'ah has a 'hand' because it is juxtaposed to offerings (which have a 'hand'), or whether the juxtaposition is only for the prohibition of delaying. It begins to cite a baraita about the juxtaposition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether pe'ah has a 'hand' because it is juxtaposed to offerings (קרבנות) which have a 'hand', or whether the juxtaposition only applies to the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר), and asks where this juxtaposition is found, introducing a baraita.
The Gemara raises the alternative that the juxtaposition is only for the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר), not for the rule of 'hand'.
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita that demonstrates the juxtaposition, to clarify the context.

items.text: Opening citation from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening citation from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'me'imach' referring to gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'me'imach' as referring to gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

items.text: Question: Is there yad for charity?
items.text_en: Question: Is there yad for charity?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is a 'yad' (verbal extension) for charity, similar to that for vows. It considers a case where one says 'this coin for charity, and this one too' versus just 'and this one', and whether the analogy to sacrifices applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is a 'yad' (verbal extension) for charity, and presents a case where one says 'this coin' without specifying 'also' to test if it is considered a valid designation.

The Gemara considers whether charity is analogous to sacrifices (קרבנות) via the verse 'בפיך' (in your mouth) — this is charity — and thus has a 'yad', or whether the analogy is only for the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר).

items.text: Question: Is there yad for hefker?
items.text_en: Question: Is there yad for hefker?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is yad for ownerless property (hefker), and distinguishes it from charity because charity is only for the poor, while hefker is for both poor and rich.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is a yad (verbal handle) for hefker (ownerless property), and immediately notes that this is the same question as for charity.
The Gemara refines the question: assuming there is a yad for charity, it distinguishes charity (only for the poor) from hefker (for both poor and rich), leaving the matter unresolved.

items.text: Ravina's question: Is there yad for a toilet?
items.text_en: Ravina's question: Is there yad for a toilet?
items.desc_en: Ravina asks whether there is yad for designating a house as a toilet, similar to the previous cases.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks whether a latrine (בית הכסא) has 'yad', clarifying the scenario: if one says 'this house for a latrine, and this one too' it is a latrine, but if he says 'and this one' without 'too', the doubt is whether he meant 'and this one too for a latrine' or merely a trailing statement.

items.text: Clarification: Ravina's question about designation
items.text_en: Clarification: Ravina's question about designation
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Ravina's question actually depends on whether designation (zimmun) is effective for a toilet; if it is, then the question of yad arises.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Ravina's inquiry about yad for a toilet presupposes that he already resolved the issue of zimmun (designation) for a toilet, which itself is an unresolved question.
The Gemara resolves that Ravina's question about yad is contingent: he first asks whether zimmun is effective, and if it is, then the question of yad arises.

items.text: Discussion of 'menudeh ani lach'
items.text_en: Discussion of 'menudeh ani lach'
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rav Papa discuss the dispute about the formula 'menudeh ani lach' (I am excommunicated to you). Abaye notes that Rabbi Akiva would agree that one is not lashed, and Rav Papa distinguishes between different formulations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'menudeh ani lach' (I am excommunicated to you) as the starting point for discussion.
Abaye asserts that Rabbi Akiva would agree that one who says 'menudeh ani lach' is not lashed, because otherwise the Mishnah would have stated 'Rabbi Akiva is stringent'.

Rav Papa distinguishes between formulations: 'ndina minekh' (I am judged by you) is universally forbidden, 'meshamatna minekh' (I am excommunicated from you) is universally permitted, and the dispute is about 'menudeh ani lach'.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'menudeh ani lach' and 'meshamtna'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'menudeh ani lach' and 'meshamtna'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree about the phrase 'menudeh ani lach' (I am excommunicated to you): Rabbi Akiva considers it a language of nidui, while the Rabbis consider it a language of shamta. This dispute is illustrated by a story involving Rav Chisda, who ruled against Rabbi Akiva's opinion in a case where someone said 'meshamtna' regarding property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds that 'menudeh ani lach' is a language of nidui (excommunication), while the Rabbis hold it is a language of shamta (a curse).
The Gemara cites a story where a man said 'meshamtna' regarding property, and Rav Chisda ruled against Rabbi Akiva's opinion, holding that the dispute is specifically about the term 'meshamtna'.

items.text: Rav's ruling on releasing a nidui in person or absent
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on releasing a nidui in person or absent
items.desc_en: Rav, quoted by Rabbi Ila, rules that if one was excommunicated in his presence, he can only be released in his presence; if excommunicated in his absence, he can be released either in his presence or in his absence.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one excommunicated in his presence can only be released in his presence, but if excommunicated in his absence, he can be released either in his presence or in his absence.

items.text: Obligation to excommunicate one who utters God's name in vain
items.text_en: Obligation to excommunicate one who utters God's name in vain
items.desc_en: Rav, quoted by Rav Chanin, rules that one who hears a friend utter God's name in vain must excommunicate him; if he does not, he himself is under a ban. The Gemara supports this with a verse and a teaching that wherever the Sages direct their attention, there is either death or poverty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin in Rav's name rules that one who hears a friend utter God's name in vain must excommunicate him, and if he does not, he himself is under a ban, because wherever God's name is uttered in vain, poverty is found.
The Gemara supports the equation of poverty with death by citing a verse and a teaching that wherever the Sages direct their attention, there is either death or poverty.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's testimony about Rav Huna's actions
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's testimony about Rav Huna's actions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba recounts that he was standing before Rav Huna when a woman uttered God's name in vain; Rav Huna excommunicated her and immediately released her in her presence. From this, three halakhot are derived: the obligation to excommunicate, the rule about releasing in person, and that there is no interval between excommunication and release.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba recounts that he was standing before Rav Huna when a woman uttered God's name in vain, and Rav Huna excommunicated her and immediately released her in her presence.

The Gemara derives three halakhot from Rav Huna's actions: the obligation to excommunicate one who utters God's name in vain, the rule that excommunication in person requires release in person, and that there is no interval between excommunication and release.

items.text: A Torah scholar can excommunicate and release himself
items.text_en: A Torah scholar can excommunicate and release himself
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav that a Torah scholar can excommunicate himself and release himself. The Gemara questions the obviousness of this, but explains that it teaches that a prisoner cannot release himself from prison. The practice of Mar Zutra the Pious is cited as an example: he would first excommunicate himself before excommunicating a student, and upon entering his home, he would release himself first.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav that a Torah scholar can excommunicate himself and release himself.
The Gemara questions the obviousness of the ruling, asking why it needed to be stated.
The Gemara explains that the statement is necessary to counter the principle that a prisoner cannot release himself from prison.

sub.text: Example of Mar Zutra the Pious
sub.text_en: Example of Mar Zutra the Pious
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the practice of Mar Zutra the Pious, who would excommunicate himself before excommunicating a student and release himself before releasing the student.

items.text: Beginning of a new statement by Rav Giddel
items.text_en: Beginning of a new statement by Rav Giddel
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement by Rav Giddel quoting Rav, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel begins a new statement in the name of Rav, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Source for vowing to fulfill a mitzvah
items.text_en: Source for vowing to fulfill a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to prove that one may swear to fulfill a mitzvah, despite already being obligated from Sinai. It explains that the verse teaches it is permitted to spur oneself on.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source that one may swear to fulfill a mitzvah, given that one is already obligated from Sinai.
The Gemara answers that the verse teaches it is permitted for a person to spur himself on to fulfill the mitzvah.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement on vowing to study
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement on vowing to study
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says that one who says 'I will arise and study this chapter' has made a great vow. The Gemara questions how a vow can take effect when one is already obligated, and explains that since one could fulfill the obligation with minimal study, the vow adds a new obligation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav states that one who says 'I will arise and study this chapter' has made a great vow to the God of Israel.
The Gemara objects that one is already obligated from Sinai, so a vow cannot take effect on an existing obligation.
The Gemara resolves that this is the same as Rav Giddel's earlier teaching about spurring oneself on.
The Gemara resolves that since one could fulfill the obligation with minimal study (קריאת שמע שחרית וערבית), the vow adds a new obligation and therefore takes effect.

items.text: Rav Giddel on inviting a friend to study
items.text_en: Rav Giddel on inviting a friend to study
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says that one who says to another 'Let us arise and study this chapter' must arise early, as derived from a verse about Ezekiel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav rules that one who says to another 'Let us arise and study this chapter' must arise early, citing a verse about Ezekiel.

items.text: Excommunication in a dream
items.text_en: Excommunication in a dream
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that one who is excommunicated in a dream requires ten people to release him, but only if they are learned in halakha. If no such people are available, even those who have studied but are not experts suffice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that one who is excommunicated in a dream needs ten people to release him.
Rav Yosef specifies that the ten must be those who study halacha, but if none are available, even those who only recite Mishnah suffice.

items.text: Question about the excommunicator's identity
items.text_en: Question about the excommunicator's identity
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the excommunicated person can release himself if he knows who excommunicated him. Rav Ashi answers that the excommunicator was only appointed to excommunicate, not to release.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if one knows who excommunicated him, may that person release him?
Rav Ashi answers that the person was appointed as an agent only to excommunicate, not to release.

items.text: Question about release in a dream
items.text_en: Question about release in a dream
items.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi about one who was excommunicated and released in a dream. Rav Ashi begins to answer with a metaphor about straw.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi: if one was excommunicated and released in a dream, what is the law?
Rav Ashi answers with a parable: just as grain cannot exist without straw, so too the dream release is not effective without proper procedure.

items.text: Opening statement about dreams
items.text_en: Opening statement about dreams
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a dream cannot occur without some meaningless elements, providing a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general principle that a dream cannot occur without some meaningless elements.

items.text: Ravina's question about a husband as agent
items.text_en: Ravina's question about a husband as agent
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a husband can serve as an agent for his wife's regret (charatah) to annul her vow. Rav Ashi responds conditionally: if people are gathered, yes; if not, no.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a husband may serve as an agent for his wife's expression of regret (חרטה) to annul her vow.
Rav Ashi answers that if the husband gathers a court (מכניפין) he may act as agent; otherwise not.

items.text: Three inferences from Rav Ashi's response
items.text_en: Three inferences from Rav Ashi's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives three halakhot from Rav Ashi's statement: a husband can be an agent for his wife's regret, one should not dissolve a vow in the presence of one's teacher, and it is proper to gather people for the dissolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halachic conclusions from Rav Ashi's response: a husband can be an agent for חרטה, one should not annul a vow in the presence of one's teacher, and gathering a court is proper.
The Gemara infers that a husband can serve as an agent for his wife's regret (חרטה) to dissolve her vow.
The Gemara infers that one should not dissolve a vow in the presence of one's teacher.
The Gemara infers that it is proper to gather people for the dissolution of a vow.

items.text: Rule about excommunication
items.text_en: Rule about excommunication
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that excommunication (shamta) can be dissolved even in the presence of one's teacher, and an expert individual can dissolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds a digression that excommunication (שמתא) may be annulled even in the presence of one's teacher, and an expert individual may annul it.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about the sun of righteousness
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about the sun of righteousness
items.desc_en: A chain of tradition from Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai explains that the verse 'And a sun of righteousness shall shine for you who fear My name' refers to those who fear to utter God's name in vain. Abaye infers that the heat of the day heals.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Zevid citing a chain
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Zevid citing a chain
sub.desc_en: A chain of tradition from Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai interprets the verse 'וזרחה לכם יראי שמי' as referring to those who fear to utter God's name in vain.
Abaye infers from the verse that the heat of the day (חמץ) heals.

items.text: Dispute with Resh Lakish about Gehinnom
items.text_en: Dispute with Resh Lakish about Gehinnom
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Abaye's statement disagrees with Resh Lakish, who says there is no Gehinnom in the world to come; instead, God brings out the sun from its sheath, healing the righteous and punishing the wicked, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Abaye's statement disagrees with Resh Lakish.
Resh Lakish states that there is no Gehinnom in the world to come; instead, God brings out the sun from its sheath, healing the righteous and punishing the wicked.
Resh Lakish cites the verse 'וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי שֶׁמֶשׁ' to show the righteous are healed, and adds that they also delight, as per 'וִיצָאתֶם וּפִשְׁתֶּם כְּעֶגְלֵי מַרְבֵּק'.
Resh Lakish cites the verse 'הִנֵּה הַיּוֹם בָּא בֹּעֵר כַּתַּנּוּר' to show that the wicked are punished by the sun.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'like the vows of the wicked' and specifies nazirite, sacrifice, or oath, it is binding; if one says 'like the vows of the virtuous' it is meaningless; if one says 'like their freewill offerings' it is binding.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that saying 'like the vows of the wicked' with specification of nazirite, sacrifice, or oath is binding.
The Mishnah states that saying 'like the vows of the virtuous' is meaningless.
The Mishnah concludes that saying 'like their freewill offerings' is binding for nazirite and sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's question and Shmuel's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Shmuel's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase might mean 'I do not vow like the wicked,' and Shmuel explains that it refers to one who says 'like the vows of the wicked, I take upon myself and from it,' with each term specifying a different type of vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the speaker might have meant 'I do not vow like the vows of the wicked.'
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah refers to one who says 'like the vows of the wicked, הריני (I am upon myself) and from it,' where each phrase specifies a different obligation.

items.text: Clarification of 'hareini' for nazirite
items.text_en: Clarification of 'hareini' for nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'hareini' might refer to a fast, and Shmuel answers that it is when a nazirite was passing before him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'הריני' might refer to a fast rather than naziriteship.
Shmuel answers that the case is when a nazirite was passing before him, clarifying the reference.

items.text: Clarification of 'heimeno' for oath
items.text_en: Clarification of 'heimeno' for oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'heimeno' might mean 'I will eat,' and Rava explains that one says 'heimeno that I will not eat.' The Gemara then asks why this is necessary, and answers that it teaches that even though he does not explicitly utter the oath, it is still binding.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who distinguishes vow from freewill offering
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who distinguishes vow from freewill offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah distinguishes between 'vows of the virtuous' (non-binding) and 'their freewill offerings' (binding), and asks which Tanna holds this distinction, suggesting it is neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna distinguishes between a vow (נדר) and a freewill offering (נדבה).
The Gemara suggests that neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehuda could be the Tanna of the Mishnah.

items.text: Baraita on vowing vs. not vowing
items.text_en: Baraita on vowing vs. not vowing
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says it is better not to vow at all, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is better to vow and pay. The Gemara then concludes that even according to Rabbi Meir, the Mishnah's distinction can be explained.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says it is better not to vow at all, based on the verse 'טוֹב אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִדֹּר' (it is good that you do not vow).
Rabbi Yehuda argues that it is better to vow and pay, citing the same verse as supporting the practice of vowing and fulfilling.
The Gemara concludes that even according to Rabbi Meir, the Mishnah's distinction between 'נדרי כשרים' (vows of the righteous) and 'נדבותם' (their freewill offerings) can be explained.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's statement and textual emendation
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's statement and textual emendation
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Meir's statement applies only to vows (neder), not to freewill offerings (nedavah). It notes a contradiction from the Mishnah which includes both nazirite and sacrificial vows under 'their freewill offerings,' and resolves it by emending the text to read 'he offered freely' instead of 'he vowed.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Meir's statement applies only to vows (neder), not to freewill offerings (nedavah).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah includes both nazirite and sacrificial vows under 'their freewill offerings,' contradicting the distinction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the text to read 'he offered freely' (נדב) instead of 'he vowed' (נדר).

items.text: Question on the distinction between neder and nedavah
items.text_en: Question on the distinction between neder and nedavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why vows are discouraged due to potential stumbling, while freewill offerings are not similarly discouraged. It implies that both could lead to sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a neder (vow) is discouraged due to potential stumbling, while a nedavah (freewill offering) is not similarly discouraged, implying both could lead to sin.

items.text: Practice of Hillel the Elder regarding freewill offerings
items.text_en: Practice of Hillel the Elder regarding freewill offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Hillel the Elder, who ensured that no one misused consecrated property by bringing an animal as unconsecrated to the Temple courtyard, then consecrating it, leaning on it, and slaughtering it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing Hillel the Elder's practice of bringing an animal as unconsecrated (חוּלִּין) to the Temple courtyard, then consecrating it, leaning on it, and slaughtering it, to prevent misuse of consecrated property.

items.text: Application to nazirite freewill offerings and Shimon the Righteous
items.text_en: Application to nazirite freewill offerings and Shimon the Righteous
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this explanation works for sacrificial freewill offerings, but questions what applies to nazirite freewill offerings. It answers that Rabbi Meir holds like Shimon the Righteous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this explanation works for sacrificial freewill offerings, but what about nazirite freewill offerings?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Meir holds like Shimon the Righteous regarding nazirite offerings.

items.text: Story of Shimon the Righteous and a nazirite
items.text_en: Story of Shimon the Righteous and a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Shimon the Righteous recounts that he only ate one guilt offering of a nazirite who became impure. A handsome nazirite from the south explained that he took a nazirite vow to overcome his evil inclination after seeing his reflection. Shimon blessed him and cited the verse about making a nazirite vow for God.

sub.desc_en: Shimon the Righteous recounts that he only ate one guilt offering of a nazirite who became impure, and describes encountering a handsome nazirite from the south.
The nazirite explains that he took a nazirite vow to overcome his evil inclination after seeing his reflection and being tempted.
Shimon the Righteous blesses the nazirite and cites the verse about making a nazirite vow for God.

items.text: Objection by Rabbi Mani regarding guilt offerings
items.text_en: Objection by Rabbi Mani regarding guilt offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani objects: why did Shimon the Righteous only avoid eating the guilt offering of a nazirite who became impure? All guilt offerings come for sin, so he should avoid all of them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani objects: why did Shimon the Righteous only avoid eating the guilt offering of a nazirite who became impure? All guilt offerings come for sin, so he should avoid all of them.

items.text: Answer by Rabbi Yona and further clarification
items.text_en: Answer by Rabbi Yona and further clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona answers that the concern is specific to nazirites who vow impulsively (tohin), then become impure and regret it, leading to bringing unconsecrated animals to the Temple. The Gemara questions why this doesn't apply to a pure nazirite, and answers that a pure nazirite is assumed to be capable of fulfilling the vow.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona answers that the concern is specific to nazirites who vow impulsively (תוהין), then become impure and regret it, leading to bringing unconsecrated animals to the Temple.
The Gemara questions why the same concern does not apply to a pure nazirite.
The Gemara answers that a pure nazirite is assumed to be capable of fulfilling the vow, so the concern does not apply.

items.text: Alternative explanation introduced
items.text_en: Alternative explanation introduced
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation (iba'it eima) for the matter, though the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation (איב

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda's statement about vowing applies only to voluntary offerings (nedavah), not to vows (neder). It then addresses the apparent contradiction from the verse 'better than both is one who vows and fulfills,' emending it to 'pledges and fulfills.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda's statement about vowing applies only to voluntary offerings (נדבה), not to vows (נדר).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says 'better than both is one who vows (נודר) and fulfills,' contradicting the suggestion.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the baraita to read 'pledges (נודב) and fulfills' instead of 'vows (נודר) and fulfills.'

items.text: Question on the distinction between neder and nedavah
items.text_en: Question on the distinction between neder and nedavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why vowing (neder) is prohibited due to potential stumbling, while pledging (nedavah) is not, since both could lead to sin. It answers that Rabbi Yehuda holds his consistent view that one can bring a voluntary animal offering to the Temple without prior consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why vowing (neder) is prohibited due to potential stumbling, while pledging (nedavah) is not, since both could lead to sin.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda holds his consistent view that one can bring a voluntary animal offering to the Temple without prior consecration.

items.text: Applying Rabbi Yehuda's principle to nazirite pledges
items.text_en: Applying Rabbi Yehuda's principle to nazirite pledges
items.desc_en: The Gemara extends the question to voluntary nazirite offerings, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda's view is consistent with a baraita where the early pious ones would voluntarily accept naziriteship to bring a sin offering, as God does not bring calamity through them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view works for voluntary offerings, but what about voluntary nazirite pledges?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda's view is consistent with a baraita where the early pious ones voluntarily accepted naziriteship to bring a sin offering, as God does not bring calamity through them.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's opposing view on nazirite pledges
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's opposing view on nazirite pledges
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the early pious ones did not volunteer for naziriteship, but only for burnt offerings, peace offerings, and thanks offerings, to avoid being called sinners, as the verse says 'and he shall atone for him for having sinned regarding the soul.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that the early pious ones did not volunteer for naziriteship, but only for burnt offerings, peace offerings, and thanks offerings, to avoid being called sinners, citing the verse 'and he shall atone for him for having sinned regarding the soul.'

items.text: Abaye's unification of views that a nazirite is a sinner
items.text_en: Abaye's unification of views that a nazirite is a sinner
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Shimon HaTzaddik, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar all share the view that a nazirite is a sinner. He cites Rabbi Elazar's kal vachomer that one who abstains only from wine is called a sinner, all the more so one who abstains from everything, and addresses the objection that the verse refers to a contaminated nazirite.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by asserting that Shimon HaTzaddik, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar all share the view that a nazirite is a sinner.

sub.text: Citation of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's baraita
sub.text_en: Citation of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's baraita
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar HaKappar derives from a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) that one who abstains from wine is called a sinner, and all the more so one who abstains from everything.
The Gemara objects that the verse cited by Rabbi Elazar HaKappar refers specifically to a contaminated nazirite (נזיר טמא), not a general nazirite.
The Gemara resolves that the contaminated nazirite is called a sinner because he sinned by becoming contaminated, not because of the nazirite vow itself.

items.text: Mishnah: Euphemisms for vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Euphemisms for vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists euphemisms (kinnuyim) for korban, cherem, nezirut, and shevuah, such as 'konam,' 'konach,' 'konas' for korban, and 'herek,' 'herech,' 'heref' for cherem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists euphemisms (kinnuyim) for korban, cherem, nezirut, and shevuah.

items.text: Debate on the origin of kinnuyim
items.text_en: Debate on the origin of kinnuyim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says kinnuyim are foreign languages, while Reish Lakish says they are terms invented by the Sages. The Gemara explains the reason for instituting euphemisms: to avoid saying 'korban' directly, which might lead to saying 'korban laHashem' or uttering God's name in vain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says kinnuyim (euphemisms for vows) are foreign languages.
Reish Lakish argues that kinnuyim are terms invented by the Sages for use in vows.
Reish Lakish cites a verse using the root 'בדא' (invented from his heart) to support his view.
The Gemara asks: why did the Sages institute kinnuyim at all?
The Gemara answers: to avoid saying 'korban' directly, lest one say 'korban laHashem'.
The Gemara objects: why not just say 'korban laHashem'? It answers: one might say only 'laHashem' without 'korban'.
The Gemara concludes: uttering God's name alone would be a vain utterance, so kinnuyim prevent that.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita with Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita with Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita quoting Rabbi Shimon, which continues the discussion on euphemisms or related topics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita quoting Rabbi Shimon, which continues the discussion on euphemisms or related topics.

items.text: Scriptural derivation against mentioning God's name in vain with offerings
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation against mentioning God's name in vain with offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'korban laHashem' that one may not say 'laHashem olah' etc., and uses a kal vachomer argument: if the Torah requires the word 'korban' even when intending to mention God's name over a sacrifice, how much more so is it forbidden to mention God's name in vain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a scriptural derivation that one may not say 'laHashem olah' etc., because the Torah says 'korban laHashem'.

The Gemara applies a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if the Torah requires the word 'korban' even when intending to mention God's name over a sacrifice, then mentioning God's name in vain is certainly forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding kinnuyei kinnuyim
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding kinnuyei kinnuyim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about kinnuyei kinnuyim (secondary euphemisms) corresponds to a tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai (forbid) and Beit Hillel (permit). Two explanations are offered: one based on whether these are actual foreign languages, and another based on whether we decree against them because of primary kinnuyim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute about kinnuyei kinnuyim (secondary euphemisms) corresponds to a tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai (forbid) and Beit Hillel (permit).
The Gemara infers that Beit Shammai holds kinnuyei kinnuyim are actual foreign languages, while Beit Hillel holds they are artificial terms coined by the Sages.
The Gemara rejects the inference and explains that all agree kinnuyim are foreign languages; the dispute is whether these specific terms are actually used by those nations.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Beit Shammai decrees against kinnuyei kinnuyim because of primary kinnuyim, while Beit Hillel does not.

items.text: Examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for vows, herem, and nazirite vows
items.text_en: Examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for vows, herem, and nazirite vows
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and a baraita provide examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim: for vows (maknenmana, maknachna, maknesna), for herem (charakim, charachim, charafim), and for nazirite vows (machzekna, manzachna, mapichna).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim (secondary substitutes) for vows.
Rav Yosef teaches a baraita listing three examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for vows: 'מקנמנא', 'מקנחנא', 'מקנסנא'.
The Gemara asks for examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for herem (devoted property).
A baraita taught by Mafshaya lists three examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for herem: 'חראקים', 'חראכים', 'חראפים'.
The Gemara asks for examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for nazirite vows.
Rav Yosef teaches a baraita listing three examples of kinnuyei kinnuyim for nazirite vows: 'מחזקנא', 'מנזחנא', 'מפיחנא'.

items.text: Unresolved queries about specific terms for kinnuyei kinnuyim
items.text_en: Unresolved queries about specific terms for kinnuyei kinnuyim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions about whether certain terms (mipchazna, mitchazna, mit'azna, kinma, kina) are valid kinnuyei kinnuyim or refer to other things like cinnamon or a chicken coop.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved queries about whether the terms mipchazna, mitchazna, and mit'azna are valid kinnuyei kinnuyim for nezirut.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the term kinma refers to a kinnui for a vow (konam) or to cinnamon spice.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Chiyya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Chiyya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Chiyya asks Rav Ashi whether the term kina refers to a chicken coop or is a language of konam (vow).
The Gemara concludes that these queries remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Kinnuyei kinnuyim for oaths and the term 'bemohi'
items.text_en: Kinnuyei kinnuyim for oaths and the term 'bemohi'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses kinnuyei kinnuyim for oaths (shevuel, shevutiel, shekukael) and notes that 'shevuel' is ambiguous. Shmuel rules that certain terms like 'ashivta' are meaningless. A baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that 'bemohi' alone is invalid, but 'bemomata da'amar mohi' is a valid kinnui for an oath.
