sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the latter clause of the Mishnah to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, who holds that cherem in the Galilee is forbidden, while the first clause follows Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows made with ambiguous intent
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows made with ambiguous intent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a person makes a vow using terms like 'herem' or 'korban' but then claims they meant something else (e.g., a fisherman's net, kings' gifts). Rabbi Meir rules that such people are not asked for absolution, and if they ask, they are punished and treated stringently. The Sages disagree and say we open a different path for them and teach them, so they do not treat vows lightly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a person makes a vow using terms like 'herem' or 'korban' but claims they meant something else (e.g., a fisherman's net, kings' gifts).
Rabbi Meir rules that such people are not asked for absolution, and if they ask, they are punished and treated stringently.
The Sages disagree and say we open a different path for them and teach them, so they do not treat vows lightly.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: first it says 'they are not asked,' then it says 'if they asked, they are punished.' Rav Yehuda resolves this by explaining that the Mishnah means that Torah scholars do not need to ask, but an ignoramus who comes to ask is punished and treated stringently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: first it says 'they are not asked,' then it says 'if they asked, they are punished.'
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah means Torah scholars do not need to ask, but an ignoramus who comes to ask is punished and treated stringently.

items.text: Clarification of the punishment and a baraita on nazirites
items.text_en: Clarification of the punishment and a baraita on nazirites
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the punishment entails. It cites a baraita about a nazirite who violated his vow: Rabbi Yehuda says he must observe the prohibition for as many days as he observed the permit, and Rabbi Yosei limits this to a short nazirite period. Rav Yosef then rules that a court that gets involved with such a person does not act properly, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says we excommunicate him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: it is understandable that they are stringent (מחמירין) by not opening with regret, but what does the punishment (עונשין) actually entail?

The Gemara cites a baraita: one who became a nazirite and violated his vow — we do not attend to him until he observes the prohibition for as many days as he observed the permit (Rabbi Yehuda), and Rabbi Yosei limits this to a short nazirite period, but for a long period thirty days suffice.
Rav Yosef rules: since the rabbis said we do not attend to him, a court that does attend to him does not act properly.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds: we excommunicate him (משמתינן ליה).

items.text: Tanna on the Sages' ruling and warnings against bad habits
items.text_en: Tanna on the Sages' ruling and warnings against bad habits
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that one should not become accustomed to vows, as it leads to misuse of oaths, and warns against frequenting an ignoramus, a priest who is an ignoramus, or excessive conversation with women, as these lead to sin.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches a series of warnings: not to become accustomed to vows (lest one misuse oaths), not to frequent an ignoramus (lest one be fed טבלים (untithed produce)), not to frequent a priest who is an ignoramus (lest one be fed תרומה (priestly portion)), and not to converse excessively with women (lest one come to adultery).

items.text: Rabbi Acha and Resh Lakish on gazing at women
items.text_en: Rabbi Acha and Resh Lakish on gazing at women
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiya says that anyone who gazes at women will eventually sin, and looking at a woman's heel leads to unworthy children. Rav Yosef specifies this applies even to one's wife when she is a niddah. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies the 'heel' as the place of filth opposite the heel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiya states that anyone who gazes at women will eventually sin, and looking at a woman's heel leads to unworthy children.
Rav Yosef specifies that the prohibition applies even to one's wife when she is a niddah (menstruant).
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies the 'heel' as the place of filth (טינופת) opposite the heel.

items.text: Baraita on shame and fear of sin
items.text_en: Baraita on shame and fear of sin
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'that His fear may be before you' as referring to shame, teaching that shame leads to fear of sin. It states that a bashful person is a good sign and does not sin quickly, while one without shame shows that his ancestors did not stand at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'that His fear may be before you' and identifies it as referring to shame.
The baraita expounds the continuation of the verse to teach that shame leads to fear of sin.
The baraita derives that a bashful person is a good sign.
Others state that a bashful person does not sin quickly.
The baraita concludes that one without shame shows that his ancestors did not stand at Sinai.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai on angelic teachings and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai on angelic teachings and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai reports four things the ministering angels told him: crippled children come from overturning the table, mute from kissing that place, deaf from talking during intercourse, and blind from looking at that place. The Gemara then raises a contradiction from a question asked of Imma Shalom, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai reports four angelic teachings about the causes of birth defects: crippled children from overturning the table, mute from kissing that place, deaf from talking during intercourse, and blind from looking at that place.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a question asked of Imma Shalom, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Story of the pious man's conduct
items.text_en: Story of the pious man's conduct
items.desc_en: A woman praises her sons' beauty and explains that her husband only speaks with her at midnight, revealing and covering a handbreadth, as if compelled by a demon. She asked him why, and he said it was to prevent him from looking at other women, lest his children become mamzerim.

sub.desc_en: A woman describes her husband's unusual conduct: he only speaks with her at midnight, revealing and covering a handbreadth, as if compelled by a demon.
The woman asked her husband why he acts this way, and he replied that he does so to avoid looking at other women, lest his children become mamzerim.

items.text: Distinction between speech and intercourse
items.text_en: Distinction between speech and intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a potential contradiction: the pious man's conduct regarding speech (conversation) is different from conduct regarding intercourse itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between matters of intercourse (תשמיש) and other matters of conversation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan rejects the pious man's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan rejects the pious man's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the earlier story reflects the view of Yochanan ben Dahavai, but the Sages say the halakha is not like him; rather, a man may do whatever he wants with his wife, like meat from the butcher or fish from the fisherman.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the earlier story reflects the view of Yochanan ben Dahavai, but the halakha does not follow him.
The Sages rule that a man may do whatever he wants with his wife, using the analogy of meat from the butcher or fish from the fisherman.

items.text: Amemar identifies the ministering angels
items.text_en: Amemar identifies the ministering angels
items.desc_en: Amemar explains that the 'ministering angels' in the earlier story refer to the Sages, not actual angels, because if they were angels, why would Rabbi Yochanan reject their view? They are called ministering angels because they are distinguished like angels.

sub.desc_en: Amemar opens by identifying the 'ministering angels' as the Sages, not actual angels.
The gemara objects that if they were actual angels, Rabbi Yochanan would not reject their view, since angels are more knowledgeable about fetal formation.
Amemar answers that they are called 'ministering angels' because they are distinguished like angels.

items.text: Stories of women who complained about their husbands
items.text_en: Stories of women who complained about their husbands
items.desc_en: Two women came before Rabbi and Rav, each saying she prepared a table for her husband and he overturned it. Rabbi said the Torah permitted her, and he can do nothing. Rav asked what is different from a fish (i.e., the husband may do as he pleases).

sub.desc_en: A woman comes before Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) complaining that she prepared a table for her husband and he overturned it, and Rabbi responds that the Torah has permitted her and he can do nothing.
A second woman comes before Rav with the same complaint, and Rav asks what is different from a fish (i.e., the husband may do as he pleases with his wife).

items.text: Prohibition of looking at another woman
items.text_en: Prohibition of looking at another woman
items.desc_en: From the verse 'Do not follow your hearts,' Rabbi derives that a man should not drink from one cup and look at another. Ravina adds that this applies even to his two wives.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi derives from the verse 'Do not follow your hearts' that a man should not drink from one cup and look at another woman.
Ravina adds that this prohibition applies even to a man's two wives.

items.text: Children of nine measures
items.text_en: Children of nine measures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi interprets the verse 'I will purge the rebels from you' as referring to children of nine specific improper unions, listed as acronyms and then detailed: children of fear, rape, hated woman, etc.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi interprets the verse 'I will purge the rebels from you' as referring to children of nine specific improper unions, listed as an acronym.
Rabbi Levi details the nine categories: children of fear, rape, hated woman, excommunication, exchange, strife, drunkenness, divorce of the heart, confusion, and insolence.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding children of a desiring wife
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding children of a desiring wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that a man whose wife initiates relations will have children as great as those in Moses' generation. The Gemara questions this from the previous list, and resolves that the list refers to a wife who is overly insistent (maratziah artzuyei), not one who merely initiates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in Rabbi Yonatan's name said that a man whose wife initiates relations will have children as great as those in Moses' generation, which seems to conflict with the list of bad children.
The Gemara cites verses about Issachar's wisdom to support the claim that children of a desiring wife can be exceptionally wise.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the list refers to a wife who is overly insistent (מרציא ארצויי), not one who merely initiates relations.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.desc_en: The mishnah begins the chapter on permitted vows, listing four types of vows that the Sages permit: vows of exaggeration, vows of urgency, vows of error, and vows of coercion. It gives an example of a vow of exaggeration regarding a seller and buyer.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens the new chapter by listing four types of vows that the Sages permit (vows of exaggeration, urgency, error, and coercion) and gives an example of a vow of exaggeration between a seller and buyer.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when both parties agree on a price of three dinars, the vow is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when both parties agree on a price of three dinars, the vow is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Abba bar Memel's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Abba bar Memel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who taught the Mishnah of four vows. Rabbi Abba bar Memel reports in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia that it is Rabbi Yehuda, who said in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that neither becomes a nazir because nazirite vows require explicit articulation.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks Rabbi Ami about the identity of the Tanna who taught the rule of four vows, citing a tradition from Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a that it is Rabbi Yehuda who says in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that neither party ever becomes a nazirite because nazirite vows require explicit declaration.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel reporting Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel reporting Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel tells Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia that the Tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, who said in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that neither becomes a nazir because nazirite vows require explicit articulation (להפלאה).

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even if the Tanna is the Rabbis, the Mishnah says 'they want' (present tense), not 'they wanted', implying ongoing willingness, which aligns with the Rabbis' view.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that even if you say the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, the Mishnah uses the present tense 'רוֹצִין' (they want) rather than the past tense 'רָצוּ' (they wanted), implying ongoing willingness.

items.text: Ravina's question to Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Ravina's question to Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a case where one says 'more than a sela' and the other says 'less than a shekel' constitutes a vow or mere exaggeration.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether a case where one says 'more than a sela' and the other says 'less than a shekel' constitutes a vow (נִדְרָא) or mere encouragement (זֵרוּזִין).

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer with a proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer with a proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita about a person who refuses to eat with his friend and says 'konam your house I enter' or 'a drop of cold water I taste' — such statements are permitted because they are only meant as exaggeration. Similarly, here it is exaggeration.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita about a person who refuses to eat with his friend and says 'קונם (konam) your house I enter' or 'a drop of cold water I taste' — such statements are permitted because they were only meant for the sake of eating and drinking, i.e., exaggeration.
The Gemara objects: why is it permitted? He explicitly said 'a drop of cold water' — that sounds like a real vow!
The baraita resolves: rather, a person speaks in exaggeration (משתעי אינש הכי), so the vow is not real.
Rav Ashi concludes: here too, a person speaks in exaggeration, so the vow is not binding.

items.text: Unfinished response
items.text_en: Unfinished response
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a response but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rav Ashi said to Ravina (the continuation is implied but not fully quoted here).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's four vows
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's four vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the four vows are truly permitted or require examination, comparing them to the righteous who say little but do much. It raises a doubt: perhaps the speaker meant less than a sela and more than a shekel, making it a matter of zeal, or perhaps he meant precisely, making it a vow. The issue remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the four vows are truly permitted, comparing them to the righteous who say little but do much.
The Gemara raises an unresolved doubt: perhaps the speaker meant less than a sela and more than a shekel, making it a matter of zeal, or perhaps he meant precisely, making it a vow.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Asi's statement and Shmuel's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Asi's statement and Shmuel's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi says these four vows require a sage's inquiry. When Rav Yehuda reported this before Shmuel, Shmuel objected: the Tanna teaches 'the sages permitted four vows,' but you say they require inquiry? Rav Yosef then taught the tradition in a different version: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi said that a sage may only permit vows similar to these four, because they hold that one does not open with regret.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi states that these four vows require a sage's inquiry (שאלה לחכם).
When Rav Yehuda reported this before Shmuel, Shmuel objects: the Tanna teaches 'the sages permitted four vows,' but you say they require inquiry?

Rav Yosef teaches the tradition in a different version: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi said that a sage may only permit vows similar to these four, because they hold that one does not open with regret (אין פותחין בחרטה).

items.text: Stories of Rav Huna and Rabba bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Stories of Rav Huna and Rabba bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Two cases illustrate methods of opening vows: a man came before Rav Huna, who asked 'Is your heart upon you?' The man said no, and Rav Huna permitted him. Another came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who asked 'If ten people had appeased you at that time, would you have vowed?' The man said no, and he permitted him.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rav Huna, who asked 'Is your heart upon you?' The man said no, and Rav Huna permitted him.

sub.text: Narrator's story of Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Narrator's story of Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Another man came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who asked 'If ten people had appeased you at that time, would you have vowed?' The man said no, and he permitted him.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi
items.desc_en: A baraita records two opinions: Rabbi Yehuda says we ask a person 'Is this heart upon you?' If he says no, we permit him. Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi in his father's name says we ask 'If ten people had appeased you at that time, would you have vowed?' If he says no, we permit him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: we ask the person 'Is this heart upon you?' and if he says no, we permit him.
Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi in his father's name says we ask 'If ten people had appeased you at that time, would you have vowed?' and if he says no, we permit him.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic device for the following stories: Asi and Elazar, Yochanan and Yannai.

items.text: Additional stories with Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Additional stories with Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A man came before Rabbi Asi, who asked 'Were you confused?' He said no, and Rabbi Asi permitted him. Another came before Rabbi Elazar, who asked 'Did you want to vow?' The man said 'If they hadn't angered me, I wouldn't have wanted anything.' Rabbi Elazar said 'Let it be as you wish.' A woman who had vowed against her daughter came before Rabbi Yochanan, who asked her if she had known that her neighbors would speak ill of her daughter.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rabbi Asi, who asked him if he was confused; the man said no, and Rabbi Asi dissolved the vow.
A man came before Rabbi Elazar, who asked if he wanted to vow; the man said he would not have wanted anything if not angered, and Rabbi Elazar said 'Let it be as you wish,' dissolving the vow.
A woman who vowed against her daughter came before Rabbi Yochanan, who asked if she had known that her neighbors would speak ill of her daughter.

items.text: Two precedents for opening vows based on hypothetical regret
items.text_en: Two precedents for opening vows based on hypothetical regret
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts two stories: one where a woman's mother spoke ill of her, leading the Sage to ask if she would have vowed knowing that, and another where Rabbi Yannai asked a man if he would have vowed knowing his deeds would be examined. In both cases, the vow was released.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where a Sage asked a woman if she would have vowed knowing her mother would speak ill of her, and released her vow when she said no.
Rabbi Yannai asked his great-grandson if he would have vowed knowing his deeds would be examined, and released the vow when he said no.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's scriptural support and ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's scriptural support and ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba cites the verse 'And after vows, to inquire' (Proverbs 20:25) as support for opening vows. He notes that although Rabbi Yannai opened with this, we do not open with this reason.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba cites the verse 'וְאַחַר נְדָרִים לְבַקֵּר' (Proverbs 20:25) as scriptural support for opening vows, but notes that despite Rabbi Yannai's precedent, we do not open with this reason.

items.text: Second opening: Rabban Gamliel's teaching
items.text_en: Second opening: Rabban Gamliel's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another opening used by Rabban Gamliel, based on the verse 'There is one who speaks rashly like the thrusts of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing' (Proverbs 12:18), implying that one who speaks rashly deserves to be stabbed. We do not open with this either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not open with this other opening either.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabban Gamliel opened with the verse 'There is one who speaks rashly like the thrusts of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing' (Proverbs 12:18), implying that one who speaks rashly deserves to be stabbed.

items.text: Third opening: Rabbi Nathan's statement and dispute
items.text_en: Third opening: Rabbi Nathan's statement and dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rabbi Nathan's statement that a vow is like building a high place and fulfilling it is like offering a sacrifice. There is a dispute between Abaye and Rava about whether we open with the first part (building a high place) or the second part (offering a sacrifice). The halakha is that we do not open with either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a third opening statement from a baraita: Rabbi Nathan says that one who vows is like one who builds a high place (בָּמָה), and one who fulfills it is like one who offers a sacrifice upon it.

The Gemara frames a dispute: regarding the first part of Rabbi Nathan's statement (building a high place) we open with it; regarding the second part (offering a sacrifice), Abaye says we open with it, Rava says we do not.

sub.text: Stam (anonymous Gemara) citing Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous Gemara) citing Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei
sub.desc_en: The Gemara records two versions of the dispute: Rav Kahana teaches the version where the dispute is on the second part, while Rav Tavyomei teaches that the dispute is on the first part, and the halakha (הִלְכְתָא) is that we do not open with either the first or the second part.

items.text: Fourth opening: Shmuel's teaching that a fulfiller is called wicked
items.text_en: Fourth opening: Shmuel's teaching that a fulfiller is called wicked
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's statement that even one who fulfills a vow is called wicked, supported by a verse. We do not open with this either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not open with Shmuel's teaching either.
Shmuel teaches that even one who fulfills a vow is called wicked.
Rabbi Avahu supports Shmuel by citing a verse and a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) linking 'חדל' (refraining from vowing) to 'חדלו' (the wicked cease their anger).

items.text: Support from a Mishnah: vows of the wicked
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah: vows of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef brings support from a Mishnah that distinguishes between the vows of the righteous (invalid) and the wicked (valid for nazirite, sacrifice, and oath), implying that vowing is characteristic of the wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between the vows of the righteous (invalid) and the wicked (valid for nazirite, sacrifice, and oath), implying that vowing is characteristic of the wicked.

items.text: The severity of anger: Gehinnam and physical afflictions
items.text_en: The severity of anger: Gehinnam and physical afflictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that an angry person is subject to all types of Gehinnam and that lower bodily afflictions (like eye-wasting and soul-saddening) rule over him, citing verses.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that an angry person is subject to all types of Gehinnam, citing the verse 'והסר כעס מלבך והעבר רעה מבשרך' and interpreting 'רעה' as Gehinnam.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan (continued)
sub.desc_en: He adds that lower bodily afflictions (eye-wasting and soul-saddening) rule over the angry person, citing the verse 'ונתן ה' לך שם לב רגז וכליון עינים ודאבון נפש' and identifying these as the lower afflictions.

items.text: Story of Ulla and the murderous bandits
items.text_en: Story of Ulla and the murderous bandits
items.desc_en: Ulla, traveling to Eretz Yisrael, witnesses one bandit kill another and asks if he did well. Ulla initially affirms, then Rabbi Yochanan questions whether he supported transgressors. Ulla explains he saved his own life. Rabbi Yochanan then wonders about the verse 'God gave you a trembling heart' in Babylon.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Ulla traveling to Eretz Yisrael with two bandits, one of whom kills the other and asks Ulla if he acted properly.
Ulla affirms the bandit's action and even shows him the proper spot for slaughter.
Rabbi Yochanan asks Ulla whether he inadvertently supported transgressors by his affirmation.
Ulla explains that he only acted to save his own life from the bandit.
Rabbi Yochanan wonders how the verse about a trembling heart applies in Babylon, given the context of the bandits.
Ulla responds that the verse refers to that specific time of danger.

items.text: Opening statement: a travel restriction
items.text_en: Opening statement: a travel restriction
items.desc_en: A brief statement that one should not cross the Jordan River (perhaps in anger or under certain circumstances).

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a statement that one should not cross the Jordan River (perhaps in anger or under certain circumstances).

items.text: Three Amoraic teachings on the effects of anger
items.text_en: Three Amoraic teachings on the effects of anger
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna, Rabbi Yirmeya, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each teach that anger causes the Shekhinah to disregard the angry person, forgetfulness of Torah and increased foolishness, or reveals that one's sins outweigh merits. Rav Adda bar Rabbi Chanina adds that had Israel not sinned, they would have received only the Five Books of Moses and the Book of Joshua, because anger increases with wisdom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna teaches that an angry person is disregarded even by the Shekhinah, citing the verse 'רשע כגובה אפו בל ידרוש אין אלהים כל מזמותיו'.
Rabbi Yirmeya teaches that anger causes forgetfulness of Torah and increased foolishness, citing the verses 'כי כעס בחיק כסילים ינוח' and 'וכסיל יפרש אולת'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak teaches that anger reveals that one's sins outweigh merits, citing the verse 'ובעל חמה רב פשע'.

Rav Adda bar Rabbi Chanina teaches that had Israel not sinned, they would have received only the Five Books of Moses and the Book of Joshua, because anger increases with wisdom, citing the verse 'כי ברוב חכמה רב כעס'.

items.text: Rule about opening with 'Elokhei Yisrael' and a case
items.text_en: Rule about opening with 'Elokhei Yisrael' and a case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi states that one does not open an inquiry for a vow made with 'Elokhei Yisrael' except in cases of theft or assault. A woman came before him who vowed with that phrase, and he refused to open for her because she did not use a euphemism.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rules that one does not open an inquiry for a vow made with 'Elokhei Yisrael' except in cases of theft or assault, where it is known the accusation was false.
A woman came before Rabbi Asi who vowed with 'Elokhei Yisrael', and he refused to open for her because she did not use a euphemism.

items.text: Story of Rav Kahana and Rav Yosef: the phrase 'Marei Kol'a'
items.text_en: Story of Rav Kahana and Rav Yosef: the phrase 'Marei Kol'a'
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana visited Rav Yosef and was invited to eat. Rav Kahana refused using the phrase 'Marei Kol'a' (Master of the Universe). Rav Yosef repeated the phrase, and the Gemara explains that Rav Yosef was quoting Rav Kahana's words, not vowing himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Kahana visited Rav Yosef, who invited him to eat, and Rav Kahana refused using the phrase 'לָא מָרֵי כּוֹלָּא' (Master of the Universe, I will not taste it).
The Gemara notes that Rav Yosef repeated the phrase 'לָא מָרֵי כּוֹלָּא' and questions why Rav Yosef said it, since he was not the one vowing.
The Gemara explains that Rav Yosef was merely quoting Rav Kahana's words, saying 'It is 'Master of the Universe' that you said, therefore you will not taste it.'

items.text: Halakhic ruling: opening with regret and 'Elokhei Yisrael'
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling: opening with regret and 'Elokhei Yisrael'
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman rules that one opens an inquiry for a vow through regret, and one does engage with a vow made with 'Elokhei Yisrael'.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman rules that one opens an inquiry for a vow through regret, and one does engage with a vow made with 'Elokhei Yisrael'.

items.text: Story of Rav Savora: releasing his own vow after Rav Nachman's anger
items.text_en: Story of Rav Savora: releasing his own vow after Rav Nachman's anger
items.desc_en: Rava praised Rav Savora to Rav Nachman. When Rav Savora came to Rav Nachman to release a vow, Rav Nachman repeatedly asked if he vowed with certain intentions, and Rav Savora answered yes each time. Rav Nachman became angry and dismissed him. Rav Savora then opened for himself, citing Rabbi's principle that the proper path is what is praiseworthy to God and people, and since Rav Nachman was angry, he did not intend to vow under that condition, so he released himself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rava praised Rav Savora to Rav Nachman, and when Rav Savora later came to Rav Nachman to release a vow, Rav Nachman questioned him repeatedly.
Rav Nachman repeatedly asks Rav Savora if he vowed with specific intentions, and Rav Savora answers yes each time.
Rav Nachman becomes angry and dismisses Rav Savora, telling him to go away.

Rav Savora opens for himself, citing Rabbi's principle that the proper path is what is praiseworthy to God and people, and since Rav Nachman was angry, he did not intend to vow under that condition, so he releases himself.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi: a similar case
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi: a similar case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi had a vow to release. The rabbis asked him repeatedly if he vowed with certain intentions, and he answered yes each time. The text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces a case where Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi had a vow to release, and the rabbis repeatedly asked him about his intentions, to which he answered yes each time.

items.text: First case: Batnit's son and the suffering rabbis
items.text_en: First case: Batnit's son and the suffering rabbis
items.desc_en: The rabbis were suffering from sun and shade. Batnit's son asked the noder if he had made his neder with knowledge of the rabbis' suffering. The noder said no, and they annulled the neder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: the rabbis were suffering from the sun and shade as they moved.
An alternative version reports that the noder initially affirmed he had the rabbis' suffering in mind, but after repeated questioning, the rabbis still suffered.
Batnit's son asked the noder if he had made his neder with knowledge of the rabbis' suffering; the noder said no, and they annulled the neder.

items.text: Second case: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the nolad debate
items.text_en: Second case: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the nolad debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei had a neder to annul. After repeatedly affirming his intent, a cutter struck him, and he annulled the neder himself. Rav Acha from Difti questioned whether this was a nolad (unforeseen event), which cannot be used for opening. Ravina replied it is not nolad because apikorsim who harass rabbis are common.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes how Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei, seeking annulment of his vow, repeatedly affirmed his intent before the rabbis, then saw a cutter strike him and annulled the vow himself.
Rav Acha from Difti questions Ravina whether this is a נולד (unforeseen event), which cannot be used as a basis for opening annulment.
Ravina answers that this is not a נולד (unforeseen event) because apikorsim who harass rabbis are common and thus foreseeable.

items.text: Third case: Abaye's wife and the daughter's marriage
items.text_en: Third case: Abaye's wife and the daughter's marriage
items.desc_en: Abaye's wife married their daughter to her relatives against Abaye's will, violating his neder. Rav Yosef asked if he would have made the neder knowing she would disobey; he said no, and Rav Yosef annulled it. The Gemara supports this with a similar case from Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces the case: Abaye's wife had a daughter, and Abaye vowed to forbid his benefit from her if she married the daughter to her own relatives.
Rav Yosef asks Abaye whether he would have made the neder (vow) had he known his wife would disobey him.
Abaye answers that he would not have made the neder, and Rav Yosef annuls it.
The Gemara objects: is such an annulment permitted in this case?
The Gemara answers yes, citing a baraita where a man vowed to prevent his wife from making the pilgrimage, she disobeyed, and Rabbi Yosei annulled the neder after asking the same question.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Conditional nullification of future nedarim
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Conditional nullification of future nedarim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who wants to ensure a friend will eat with him can say 'All nedarim I will make are null,' provided he remembers at the time of the neder. The Gemara questions: if he says this, won't the friend not listen and not come?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling: one who wants a friend to eat with him can say 'All nedarim I will make are null,' provided he remembers at the time of the neder.
The Gemara questions: if the host says all future nedarim are null, won't the friend not listen and not come to eat with him?

items.text: Opening Mishnah with missing clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah with missing clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: one who wants his friend to eat with him and the friend refuses, so he vows — these are 'vows of urging'. And one who wants his vows not to be fulfilled all year should stand on Rosh Hashanah and say: any vow I will make in the future shall be null, provided he remembers at the time of the vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: one who wants his friend to eat with him and the friend refuses, so he vows — these are 'vows of urging'. And one who wants his vows not to be fulfilled all year should stand on Rosh Hashanah and say: any vow I will make in the future shall be null, provided he remembers at the time of the vow.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if he remembers at the time of the vow, he uproots his condition and fulfills his vow! Abaye teaches that the Mishnah actually says: provided he is NOT remember at the time of the vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if he remembers the condition at the time of the vow, he uproots his condition and fulfills his vow, contradicting the Mishnah's implication.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by asserting that the Mishnah actually reads: provided he is NOT remember at the time of the vow.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava says the original text stands, but the case is where he made the condition on Rosh Hashanah but did not know what he conditioned. If he remembers and says 'I vow on the basis of the first intention', the vow has no substance; if he does not say that, he uproots his condition.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that the original text stands, and explains the case as one where the person made the condition on Rosh Hashanah but did not know what he conditioned; if he remembers and says 'על דעת הראשונה אני נודר' (I vow on the basis of the first intention), the vow has no substance, but if he does not say that, he uproots his condition and fulfills his vow.

items.text: Rava's objection to public teaching
items.text_en: Rava's objection to public teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana sought to teach this in public. Rava objected, saying the Tanna deliberately concealed it to prevent frivolity with vows, and you would teach it publicly?

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana intended to teach this halacha publicly in the study hall.
Rava objects, arguing that the Tanna deliberately concealed this teaching to prevent frivolity with vows, so Rav Huna bar Chinana should not teach it publicly.

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: do the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov or not? And if they disagree, is the halakha like him? It brings a Mishnah to resolve this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: do the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and if so, is the halakha (הלכה) like him?
The Gemara proposes to resolve the inquiry by citing a Mishnah that begins 'האומר לחבירו' (one who says to his fellow).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conditional vow that can be annulled without a sage
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conditional vow that can be annulled without a sage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one says 'Konam if I benefit from you unless you take a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine for your son.' The person can annul the vow without a sage by saying 'This is my honor,' implying the vow was only for honor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a conditional vow that can be annulled without a sage because the speaker can say the condition was only for honor.

items.text: Gemara's question: Who holds this view?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Who holds this view?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling depends on the phrase 'this is my honor'; otherwise it would be a vow. It asks whose opinion this is, suggesting it cannot be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who considers such vows as 'vows of urging' (נדרי זירוזין). Therefore, it must be that the Rabbis disagree with him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that without the annulment statement, the vow is binding, and asks whose opinion this follows.
The Gemara objects that if it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, it would be a vow of encouragement (נדרי זירוזין), so it must be that the Sages disagree with him.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must reflect the view of the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concedes here
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concedes here
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it could still be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who concedes in this case that it is a vow because the speaker implies 'I am not a dog that I benefit from you but you do not benefit from me,' indicating a genuine vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is indeed Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but he concedes this is a real vow because the beneficiary can say 'I am not a dog to benefit from you while you do not benefit from me.'

items.text: Second Mishnah: Similar case with different wording
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Similar case with different wording
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents another case: 'Konam that you benefit from me unless you give my son a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine.' Rabbi Meir says it is binding until he gives, while the Sages say he can annul it by saying 'I consider myself as if I received.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where one says a similar conditional vow, and Rabbi Meir says it is binding, while the Sages allow annulment without a sage.
The Sages respond that even this person can annul his vow without a sage, by saying 'I consider myself as if I received.'

items.text: Gemara's inference: Again supports Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Again supports Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that without the phrase 'I consider myself as if I received,' it would be a vow. It asks whose view this is, again suggesting it cannot be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, so it must be the Rabbis who disagree with him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that without the annulment statement, the vow is binding, and asks whose opinion this follows.
The Gemara objects that if it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, it would be a vow of encouragement, so it must be that the Sages disagree with him.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must be according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Second answer: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concedes here too
items.text_en: Second answer: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concedes here too
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is still Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who concedes here because the speaker implies 'Am I a king that I benefit you but you do not benefit me?' making it a genuine vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who concedes this is a real vow because the beneficiary can say 'Am I a king that I benefit you while you do not benefit me?'

items.text: Third proof: Vows of coercion (נדרי אונסין)
items.text_en: Third proof: Vows of coercion (נדרי אונסין)
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda cites a baraita about 'vows of coercion': if one was forced by illness or a river, it is not a vow. The Gemara infers that otherwise it would be a vow, again challenging Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view.

sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita about vows of coercion (נדרי אונסין), inferring that without the coercion, the vow is binding, and asking if this proves the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
The Gemara infers that without coercion the vow would be binding, and asks whose view this follows, concluding it must be the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rav Ashi answers that the baraita can still align with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, because here the host initiated the vow, not the guest, so it is a real vow of coercion, not a 'vow of urging'.

items.text: Third answer: Distinguishing the case of coercion
items.text_en: Third answer: Distinguishing the case of coercion
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is still Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but here the host imposed the vow on the guest, not the guest on himself. The guest asked to be invited, and the host made a vow, so when prevented by coercion, it is a vow of coercion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but the case is where the invitee initiated the vow, so it is a real vow of coercion, not encouragement.

items.text: Fourth proof: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's own statement
items.text_en: Fourth proof: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's own statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov explicitly says that certain vows are 'vows of urging' and the Sages did not agree. The Gemara asks what 'did not agree' means, implying a dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov classifies a similar vow as a vow of encouragement (נדרי זירוזין), and the Sages did not agree with him.
The Gemara asks what 'the Sages did not agree with him' means, implying a question about the scope of their disagreement.

items.text: Halakhah like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Halakhah like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from the previous discussion that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and then cites Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah who both rule that the halakhah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from the earlier discussion that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
The Gemara asks what the practical ruling is regarding the dispute.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah who both rule that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Mishnah: Nedarei Havai
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nedarei Havai
items.desc_en: The Mishnah gives examples of nedarei havai (exaggerated vows), such as saying 'Konam if I did not see on this road as many as those who left Egypt' or 'if I did not see a snake as thick as a beam of an olive press.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the category of nedarei havai (exaggerated vows) with examples: a vow that one saw as many people as those who left Egypt, or a snake as thick as an olive press beam.

items.text: Tanna: Vows permitted, oaths forbidden
items.text_en: Tanna: Vows permitted, oaths forbidden
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that nedarei havai (exaggerated vows) are permitted, but shevu'ot havai (exaggerated oaths) are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that nedarei havai (exaggerated vows) are permitted, but shevu'ot havai (exaggerated oaths) are forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Defining shevu'ot havai
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining shevu'ot havai
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes shevu'ot havai. Abaye suggests the oath is 'I swear that I saw,' but Rava objects that this is not analogous to the vow case. Rava instead explains that the oath is 'May the fruits of the world be forbidden to me by oath if I did not see on this road as many as those who left Egypt.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes an exaggerated oath, rejecting the possibility that it is a simple false oath.
Abaye answers that the oath is formulated as 'שבועה שראיתי' (an oath that I saw) — a false claim of having seen something.
Rava objects that Abaye's explanation is unnecessary and that the Mishnah's formulation requires the oath to be parallel to the vow.

Rava explains that the oath is formulated as 'יאסרו פירות העולם עלי בשבועה אם לא ראיתי בדרך הזה כעולי מצרים' (may the fruits of the world be forbidden to me by oath if I did not see on this road [as many people as] those who left Egypt).

items.text: Ravina's objection: Possible truthful oath
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: Possible truthful oath
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: perhaps this person actually saw a swarm of locusts and called them 'those who left Egypt,' so his oath is truthful and should be permitted?

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that perhaps the man actually saw a swarm of locusts and called them 'עולי מצרים' (those who left Egypt), making his oath truthful and not exaggerated.

items.text: Initial claim: oath is according to the court's intent
items.text_en: Initial claim: oath is according to the court's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that when one takes an oath, it is according to the intent of the court, and the court does not consider themselves as having intent regarding small matters like cumin seeds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that an oath is taken according to the court's intent, and the court does not consider itself as having intent regarding trivial matters like cumin seeds.

items.text: Challenge: Does a person take an oath based on their own intent?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does a person take an oath based on their own intent?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement by citing a baraita where the court tells the oath-taker that the oath is not based on his own condition but on the court's intent, implying that normally a person does take an oath based on his own intent. The Gemara initially suggests this excludes cases where the oath-taker had a mental reservation about a loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement by citing a baraita where the court tells the oath-taker that the oath is not based on his own condition but on the court's intent, implying that normally a person does take an oath based on his own intent, and initially suggests this excludes cases where the oath-taker had a mental reservation about a loan.
The Gemara infers from the baraita's wording that a person does indeed take an oath based on his own intent, confirming the challenge.

items.text: Rejection: The baraita refers to Rava's cane incident
items.text_en: Rejection: The baraita refers to Rava's cane incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous inference, explaining that the baraita's purpose is to exclude a case like Rava's cane, where a debtor hid coins in a cane and swore falsely, but the court's intent prevented the oath from being valid. This shows the court's intent is to prevent deception, not that people normally swear based on their own intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous inference, stating that the baraita's purpose is to exclude a case like Rava's cane.
The Gemara recounts the story of a debtor who hid coins in a cane and swore falsely, but the court's intent prevented the oath from being valid.
The creditor broke the cane, the coins spilled out, and it was discovered that the debtor had sworn truthfully, showing the court's intent to prevent deception.

items.text: Second challenge: Moses' oath at Arvot Moav
items.text_en: Second challenge: Moses' oath at Arvot Moav
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita about Moses swearing the Israelites at Arvot Moav, where Moses said the oath is not based on their intent but on his and God's. The Gemara infers that this implies a person normally swears based on their own intent, and suggests this excludes cases where they might have intended to swear by an idol as a god.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous rejection by asking: does a person not swear according to their own intent? It cites a baraita about Moses swearing the Israelites at Arvot Moav.
The baraita describes the court's practice of telling the swearer that the oath is based on the court's intent, not his own.
The Gemara asks what case the baraita excludes, and suggests it excludes a case where the swearer intended to refer to a different item (e.g., a bundle of reeds) but swore about coins.
The Gemara concludes that from the baraita's wording 'according to our intent,' it follows that a person normally swears according to their own intent.

items.text: Rejection: Idol is called a god, and Moses chose a simple matter
items.text_en: Rejection: Idol is called a god, and Moses chose a simple matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that an idol is called a god in Scripture, so the exclusion is unnecessary. Then the Gemara explores various possible interpretations of Moses' oath, concluding that Moses chose a simple matter (the oath about keeping the commandments) to avoid complexity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference that an idolater might call an idol a god, because Scripture itself calls an idol a god, so the exclusion is unnecessary.
The Gemara asks why Moses did not simply swear them to observe the commandments, and answers that 'commandments' might be understood as the king's decrees.
The Gemara asks why Moses did not swear them to observe all the commandments, and answers that 'all commandments' might be understood as the single commandment of ציצית (ritual fringes).

The Gemara asks why Moses did not swear them to observe the Torah, and answers that 'Torah' might be understood as one specific Torah, and 'Torot' might be understood as the various Torah portions for offerings.
The Gemara asks why Moses did not swear them to observe both 'Torot' and 'commandments', and answers that each term still has a narrow possible interpretation.

The Gemara asks why Moses did not swear them to observe the entire Torah, and answers that 'the entire Torah' might be understood as the prohibition of idolatry, which is equivalent to the whole Torah.
The Gemara asks why Moses did not swear them to observe idolatry and the entire Torah, or alternatively the 613 commandments.
The Gemara concludes that Moses chose a simple matter (the oath about keeping the commandments) to avoid complexity.

items.text: Digression: A snake as thick as a beam and its practical implication
items.text_en: Digression: A snake as thick as a beam and its practical implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a statement about a snake as thick as a beam of an olive press, questioning its veracity with a story about a snake in King Shapur's time. Shmuel explains that the beam is 'tarf' (split), and the Gemara concludes that this teaches a practical halakha: if one sells a beam of an olive press, it must be split to be valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement about a snake as thick as an olive press beam, and questions it with a story of a snake in King Shapur's time that swallowed thirteen bundles of straw.
Shmuel answers that the beam is 'tarf' (split), and all snakes are split, so the Gemara speaks of a snake as thick as the split beam.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not explicitly state 'tarf' (split) instead of implying it.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches incidentally that an olive press beam must be split, and this has a practical halakha: if one sells such a beam, it is valid only if it is split.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Inadvertent vows and the case of figs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Inadvertent vows and the case of figs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists examples of inadvertent vows that are permitted, including cases where one mistakenly thought they ate or drank, or where one vowed against his wife based on a false belief. It then presents a case where one saw people eating figs and declared them forbidden, but later discovered his father and brother among them; Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether all are permitted or only the relatives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing three types of inadvertent vows that are permitted: one who mistakenly thought he ate or drank, one who forgot and ate, and one who falsely accused his wife.
The Mishnah presents a case where one saw people eating figs and declared them forbidden, but later discovered his father and brother among them along with others.
Beit Shammai rules that the relatives are permitted but the others remain forbidden.
Beit Hillel rules that both the relatives and the others are all permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Inadvertent oaths are also permitted
items.text_en: Gemara: Inadvertent oaths are also permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that just as inadvertent vows are permitted, so too are inadvertent oaths. It gives an example involving Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, each swearing that Rav said something, but both being sincere in their belief.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that just as inadvertent vows are permitted, so too are inadvertent oaths permitted.
The Gemara asks for an example of an inadvertent oath.
The Gemara gives the example of Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, each swearing that Rav said a particular teaching, each relying on his own correct understanding.

items.text: Gemara: The principle of partial nullification
items.text_en: Gemara: The principle of partial nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related teaching from elsewhere: one may open (i.e., seek absolution for) vows on Shabbat and Festivals. Initially, it was said that only those days are permitted, but Rabbi Akiva taught that a vow which is partially permitted is entirely permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related Mishnah about opening vows on Shabbat and festivals, where initially they said those days are permitted but other days are forbidden.
Rabbi Akiva came and taught the principle that a vow which is partially permitted is entirely permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Rabba's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabba's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabba explains that all agree in a case where one says, 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said, 'All of you are forbidden except my father,'' then all are forbidden and the father is permitted. The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is only where one says, 'Had I known, I would have said, 'So-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted.''

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that everyone agrees that if the person said 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said all of you are forbidden except my father,' then all are forbidden and the father is permitted.
Rabbah explains that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is only when the person said 'Had I known, I would have said so-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted.'

items.text: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava states that all agree that if one said 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said so-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted,' all are permitted. The dispute is only when one said 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said all of you are forbidden except my father.' Beit Shammai follow Rabbi Meir's principle of 'grasp the first expression,' while Beit Hillel follow Rabbi Yosei's principle that a person is bound by the conclusion of his words.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that all agree that if one said 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said so-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted,' all are permitted.
Rava specifies that the dispute is only when one said 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said all of you are forbidden except my father.'
Rava explains that Beit Shammai follow Rabbi Meir's principle of 'grasp the first expression' (תפוס לשון ראשון).
Rava explains that Beit Hillel follow Rabbi Yosei's principle that a person is bound by the conclusion of his words (בגמר דבריו אדם נתפס).

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava by citing a baraita: How did Rabbi Akiva say a neder that was partially permitted is entirely permitted? If one said 'Konam that I do not benefit from all of you,' and one was permitted, all are permitted. If one said 'I do not benefit from this one and that one,' and the first was permitted, all are permitted; if the last was permitted, only the last is permitted and the rest are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava by citing the baraita of Rabbi Akiva's ruling on a partially permitted neder (נדר), demonstrating that the principle of 'partially permitted = fully permitted' applies only when the vow was phrased as a single prohibition, not as separate prohibitions.

items.text: Rava's response and the difficulty
items.text_en: Rava's response and the difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rabba, the first clause of the baraita is explained as referring to one who said 'to this and to that,' and the latter clause as referring to one who said 'to all of you.' But for Rava, the first clause can be explained as referring to one who said 'to all of you,' leaving the latter clause difficult.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rabba, the first clause of the baraita is easily explained as referring to one who said 'to this and to that' (לָזֶה וְלָזֶה).
The Gemara adds that the latter clause of the baraita is explained as referring to one who said 'to all of you' (לְכוּלְּכֶם).
The Gemara raises a difficulty for Rava: while the first clause can be explained as referring to one who said 'to all of you,' the latter clause remains unexplained.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's latter clause
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Akiva in the latter clause of the Mishnah, given the earlier assertion that all agree the vow is permitted when one says 'to this and to this'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Akiva in the latter clause of the Mishnah, given the earlier assertion that all agree the vow is permitted when one says 'to this and to this'.

items.text: Rava's objection regarding Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Rava's objection regarding Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the assumption that the latter clause fits Rabbi Akiva, asking how Rabbi Akiva could explain the case of 'to all of you' where no first or last person is specified.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to the assumption that the latter clause fits Rabbi Akiva, asking how Rabbi Akiva could explain the case of 'to all of you' where no first or last person is specified.

items.text: Resolution: distinguishing between two cases
items.text_en: Resolution: distinguishing between two cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves by distinguishing the Mishnah's first clause (where one says 'to all of you') from the latter clause (where the vows are linked). A supporting baraita is cited showing that when the middle person is released, those below are permitted but those above remain forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the first clause (where one says 'to all of you') from the latter clause (where the vows are linked in a chain).
A baraita is cited showing that when the middle person is released, those below are permitted but those above remain forbidden, confirming the distinction.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection from the onion vow
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection from the onion vow
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges Rava with a case where one vowed against onions thinking they were harmful, but was permitted for the 'kufri' onion. The Gemara infers that the person meant: had I known the kufri was good, I would have said all onions are forbidden and kufri permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects to Rava by citing a baraita where one vowed against onions thinking they were harmful, but was permitted for the kufri onion and all onions, with Rabbi Meir permitting all onions.
The Gemara infers that the person meant: had I known the kufri was good, I would have said all onions are forbidden and kufri permitted.

Rava answers that the person meant: had I known the kufri was good, I would have said specific onions are forbidden and kufri permitted, and Rabbi Meir's ruling aligns with both Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

items.text: Rejection: alternative interpretation of the vow
items.text_en: Rejection: alternative interpretation of the vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the person meant: had I known, I would have said specific onions are forbidden and kufri permitted. Rabbi Meir's ruling aligns with both Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the person meant: had I known, I would have said specific onions are forbidden and kufri permitted, and Rabbi Meir's ruling aligns with both Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

items.text: Ravina's objection from Rabbi Natan's ruling
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from Rabbi Natan's ruling
items.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rava with Rabbi Natan's statement that there is a vow partially permitted and partially forbidden, citing the example of a basket.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rava by citing Rabbi Natan's ruling that there is a vow partially permitted and partially forbidden, giving the example of a basket.

items.text: Interpretation of the Mishnah on partial permission
items.text_en: Interpretation of the Mishnah on partial permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case of figs and sycamore figs reflects Rabbi Akiva's view that a partially permitted vow is entirely permitted, or whether it is a case where the speaker explicitly distinguished between the two types. The Gemara resolves that the speaker said 'all the basket is forbidden, and the sycamore figs are permitted,' which aligns with the Rabbis' view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case of figs and sycamore figs reflects Rabbi Akiva's view that a partially permitted vow is entirely permitted, or whether it is a case where the speaker explicitly distinguished between the two types, and the Rabbis disagree.
The Gemara resolves that the speaker said 'all the basket is forbidden, and the sycamore figs are permitted,' which aligns with the Rabbis' view.

items.text: The Tanna of the baraita on multiple people
items.text_en: The Tanna of the baraita on multiple people
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a baraita about a vow involving five people: if one is permitted, all are permitted (like Rabbi Akiva), but if one is excluded, only that one is permitted (like the Rabbis). The Gemara notes that according to Rabbah, the first clause follows Rabbi Akiva and the latter clause is everyone's view; according to Rava, the latter clause follows the Rabbis and the first clause is everyone's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita about a vow involving five people, where if one is permitted all are permitted, but if one is excluded only that one is permitted.

The Gemara resolves the question by explaining that according to Rabbah the first clause follows Rabbi Akiva and the latter clause is everyone's view, while according to Rava the latter clause follows the Rabbis and the first clause is everyone's view.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows of duress
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows of duress
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vows made under duress, such as when a friend pressures someone to eat with him but the invitee falls ill or is delayed by a river, are not binding.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vows made under duress, such as when a friend pressures someone to eat with him but the invitee falls ill or is delayed by a river, are not binding.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rava debate duress in a court case
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rava debate duress in a court case
items.desc_en: A man deposited documents in court and vowed that if he did not return within 30 days, the documents would be void. He was prevented by duress and did not come. Rav Huna ruled the documents void, but Rava argued that duress exempts him, citing the verse 'to the young woman you shall do nothing' and the Mishnah on vows of duress.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case: a man deposited documents in court and vowed that if he did not return within 30 days, the documents would be void.
The man was prevented by duress and did not come; Rav Huna ruled the documents void.
Rava objects that the man is an אונס (one compelled by duress), and the Torah exempts him, citing the verse 'to the young woman you shall do nothing'.
The Gemara anticipates a possible distinction that the case of killing is different, and cites the Mishnah on vows of duress (נדרי אונסין) as support that duress exempts in all cases.

items.text: Rava's distinction from the case of a conditional get
items.text_en: Rava's distinction from the case of a conditional get
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's position by citing a mishnah where a man gives a conditional get if he does not return within twelve months, and he dies within that time—the get is valid despite duress. The Gemara suggests that perhaps the case of death is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's position by citing a mishnah where a conditional get is given and the husband dies within the term, yet the get is valid despite the duress of death.
The Gemara answers that perhaps the case of death is different from other forms of duress.

items.text: Distinguishing awareness of death from an uncertain condition
items.text_en: Distinguishing awareness of death from an uncertain condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the giver had known of the death he would have completed the divorce immediately, thus the condition was not true consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that if the giver had known of the death, he would have completed the divorce immediately, so the condition was not true consent.

items.text: Contrast with the case of a river barrier (הבא מכאן ועד תלתין יומין) and hidden vs. revealed coercion
items.text_en: Contrast with the case of a river barrier (הבא מכאן ועד תלתין יומין) and hidden vs. revealed coercion
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of a man who said his get should be valid if he does not return within 30 days, but was prevented by a river barrier, and ruled by Shmuel that the get is not valid. It answers that a revealed coercion like the barrier is different from the hidden coercion of sudden death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a case where a man conditioned his get on not returning within 30 days, was prevented by a river barrier, and Shmuel ruled the get is invalid, questioning why this differs from the current case.
The Gemara answers that a revealed coercion (like the river barrier) is different from the hidden coercion of sudden death, so the cases are not comparable.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection: asmachta does not acquire
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection: asmachta does not acquire
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rav Huna, who holds that asmachta does not effect acquisition, the earlier case would normally not be valid, but here it is different because the giver's rights are lost (mitpasin zechuyateih).

sub.text: Gemara's objection on behalf of Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection on behalf of Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rav Huna, who holds that אסמכתא (a conditional commitment) does not effect acquisition, the earlier case should not be valid.
The Gemara answers that this case is different because the giver's rights are lost (מיתפסן זכוותיה), making it not a standard אסמכתא.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah of partially repaying a debt
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah of partially repaying a debt
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even where rights are lost it is still asmachta, citing a Mishnah where if one deposits a shtar on a conditional payment and does not pay, Rabbi Yosi says it is valid while Rabbi Yehuda says it is not. Rav Nachman in the name of Rav rules against Rabbi Yosi, who holds that asmachta does acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even where rights are lost, the transaction should still be considered אסמכתא (a conditional commitment not fully binding), and cites a Mishnah about partial repayment of a debt.
The Mishnah states that if the debtor fails to pay by the deadline, Rabbi Yosi rules the creditor receives the document, while Rabbi Yehuda rules he does not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) does not follow Rabbi Yosi, who holds that אסמכתא (a conditional commitment) acquires.

items.text: Distinction: explicit annulment of rights (ליבטלין זכותיה)
items.text_en: Distinction: explicit annulment of rights (ליבטלין זכותיה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that here the condition explicitly stated that the rights would be annulled (libatlan zechuteih), making it different from the general asmachta case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that here the condition explicitly stated that the rights would be annulled (לִבַּטְלָן זָכְוָתֵיהּ), making it different from the general asmachta case.

items.text: Practical ruling on asmachta
items.text_en: Practical ruling on asmachta
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with the ruling that asmachta does acquire, provided there is no coercion and it was performed before an important court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues a final ruling that an asmachta (conditional commitment) does acquire, provided there is no coercion and it was performed before an important court (בית דין חשוב).

items.text: Beginning of new Mishnah: vowing to murderers, tax collectors, etc.
items.text_en: Beginning of new Mishnah: vowing to murderers, tax collectors, etc.
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may make vows to murderers, confiscators, and tax collectors, saying the produce is terumah even if it is not, or that it belongs to the king even if it does not. Beit Shammai says one may vow with any wording.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may make vows to murderers, confiscators, and tax collectors, declaring produce as תרומה (priestly portion) or as belonging to the king, even if it is not.
Beit Shammai adds that one may vow with any wording, expanding the leniency.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on vowing to evade a tax collector
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on vowing to evade a tax collector
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Beit Shammai says one may vow only except for an oath, while Beit Hillel permits even an oath. Beit Shammai further restricts that one may only open with a vow regarding what the tax collector demands, while Beit Hillel allows even what he does not demand. An example illustrates: if told to say 'konam my wife benefit from me' but he says 'konam my wife and children benefit from me', Beit Shammai permits the wife but forbids the children, while Beit Hillel permits both.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding vowing to evade a tax collector, including the example of a man who vows against his wife and children.

items.text: Gemara's question and first answer: The principle of dina d'malkhuta dina
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first answer: The principle of dina d'malkhuta dina
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can evade a tax collector through vows, given Shmuel's principle that 'the law of the kingdom is law'. Rav Chinana quoting Rav Kahana quoting Shmuel answers that this applies only to a tax collector who has no fixed rate. The school of Rabbi Yannai adds that it applies to a tax collector who appoints himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can evade a tax collector through a vow, given Shmuel's principle that the law of the land is binding (דינא דמלכותא דינא).

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana in the name of Shmuel answers that the Mishnah deals with a tax collector who has no fixed rate (אין לו קצבה), and the school of Rabbi Yannai adds that it refers to a self-appointed tax collector (עומד מאליו).
The school of Rabbi Yannai adds that the principle applies to a tax collector who appoints himself (מוכס העומד מאליו).

items.text: Clarifying the vow's formulation: 'today' in the heart
items.text_en: Clarifying the vow's formulation: 'today' in the heart
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the vow is formulated, since if he says 'let all the fruits of the world be forbidden to me if they are not of the king's house', all fruits become forbidden. Rav Amram quoting Rav answers that he says 'today' in his heart but expresses it generally with his lips. Although matters of the heart are not normally considered, regarding coercion it is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one can vow to evade a tax collector who collects for the king but is not authorized, given that the vow must be effective.

sub.text: Rav Amram in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Amram in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram in the name of Rav answers that the person says: 'May all the fruits of the world be forbidden to me if they are not of the king's house.'
The Gemara objects that if he says 'may they be forbidden,' all fruits become forbidden to him permanently, and if he says 'today,' the tax collector will not accept it.

The Gemara resolves that he intends 'today' in his heart but expresses it generally with his lips, and regarding coercion (אונסין) the principle that matters of the heart are not matters is different.

items.text: Repetition of Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Repetition of Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is repeated verbatim, likely as a citation for the subsequent discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah again, repeating the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the scope of the vow.

items.text: Resolving contradictions between Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions between Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a baraita where Beit Shammai says one may not open with an oath but may with a vow, contradicting the Mishnah where Beit Shammai says one may not open with a vow. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's tanna teaches about vows to show Beit Shammai's stringency, while the baraita's tanna teaches about oaths to show Beit Hillel's leniency.

sub.text: Rav Huna's teaching and Gemara's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's teaching and Gemara's question
