sub.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches a baraita where Beit Shammai says one may not open with an oath, and the Gemara questions this against the Mishnah which says Beit Shammai forbids opening with a vow and forbids vowing with an oath.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches about a vow to show the stringency of Beit Shammai, while the baraita teaches about an oath to show the leniency of Beit Hillel.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's tanna teaches about vows to show Beit Shammai's stringency, while the baraita's tanna teaches about oaths to show Beit Hillel's leniency.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: dispute about release from oaths
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: dispute about release from oaths
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a different version of the baraita: Beit Shammai says there is no release from an oath, while Beit Hillel says there is release. This resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers an alternative interpretation of the baraita: Beit Shammai says there is no release (שאלה) for an oath, while Beit Hillel says there is release.

items.text: New Mishnah: Vows conditional on destruction
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Vows conditional on destruction
items.desc_en: A new Mishnah begins: If one says 'these plantings are korban if they are not cut down' or 'this cloak is korban if it is not burned', they have redemption. If one says 'these plantings are korban until they are cut down' or 'this cloak is korban until it is burned'...

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new case: if one says 'these trees are a korban if not cut' or 'this cloak is a korban if not burned,' they have redemption; but if one says 'these trees are a korban until cut' or 'this cloak is a korban until burned,' the rule is different.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that certain items have no redemption.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that certain items have no redemption (פדיון).

items.text: Gemara's question on mishnah's formulation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on mishnah's formulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah did not use a more precise phrase, and answers that the tanna included the first clause for symmetry with the second.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: why does the mishnah not simply teach 'consecrated and not consecrated' instead of the double formulation?
The gemara answers: because the mishnah wanted to teach the latter clause 'they have no redemption', it also taught the former clause 'they have redemption'.

items.text: Explanation of the vow's circumstances
items.text_en: Explanation of the vow's circumstances
items.desc_en: Ameimar explains that the vow is made conditionally, and the Gemara clarifies that it is necessary even when there is a strong wind, as one might think the trees will not be saved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks under what circumstances the vow was made.
Ameimar explains that the vow is conditional: 'If they are not cut down today,' and the day passed without them being cut.
The Gemara objects that this scenario is obvious and asks why the Mishnah needed to state it.
The Gemara resolves that the case is necessary when there is a strong wind, making the outcome uncertain.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah also taught this case regarding a cloak, which is destined for burning, implying a different context.
The Gemara answers that the cloak case also involves a fire, making the outcome uncertain.
The Gemara resolves that here too, with a strong wind, one might think the vower assumes the trees will not be saved and vows accordingly, so the Mishnah teaches that the vow is still valid.

items.text: Debate on redemption after cutting
items.text_en: Debate on redemption after cutting
items.desc_en: Bar Pada holds that cut trees can be redeemed once, while Ulla argues that once cut they cannot be redeemed at all.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the mishnah's continuation: 'these saplings are a korban' etc.
The gemara asks: does the consecration last forever?
Bar Pada answers: if one redeems them, they return and become consecrated again, until they are cut down; once cut, one redeems them once and that suffices.
Ulla answers: once they are cut down, one may no longer redeem them.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's question
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's question
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks: if a consecrated animal is later redeemed, where does the original sanctity go? He compares it to a conditional divorce, arguing that just as a conditional divorce does not release a wife without a get, so sanctity should not simply vanish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks where the sanctity of a redeemed consecrated animal goes, comparing it to a conditional divorce that cannot release a wife without a גט (bill of divorce).

items.text: Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: Rava rejects the comparison, distinguishing between sanctity of the body (קדושת הגוף) which cannot lapse, and sanctity of monetary value (קדושת דמים) which can lapse without action.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes between קדושת דמים (sanctity of monetary value) which lapses easily, and קדושת הגוף (sanctity of the body) which does not, rejecting the analogy to divorce.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava by citing a baraita where an animal designated as an olah for thirty days and then a shelamim afterward shows that even sanctity of the body can lapse, as the animal's status changes automatically after thirty days.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraita where a consecrated animal designated as an עולה (burnt-offering) for thirty days and then a שלמים (peace-offering) afterwards shows that קדושת הגוף (body sanctity) can lapse without a new act.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: the baraita refers to monetary value
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: the baraita refers to monetary value
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where the person said 'for its value' (לדמי), meaning the sanctity is only of monetary value, not of the body, so it can lapse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the owner specified 'for its monetary value' (לדמי), meaning the sanctity was only monetary, not bodily.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the second clause
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if the baraita is about monetary value, then the second clause (where the animal is an olah after thirty days but a shelamim now) would mix sanctity of the body and monetary value, which is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the resolution applies, the second clause of the baraita (where the animal is an עולה after thirty days and a שלמים now) would mix both קדושת הגוף and קדושת דמים, which is problematic.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Tanna's two teachings
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Tanna's two teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Tanna needed to teach two cases: one might have thought that sanctity of the body does not lapse easily, while sanctity of value does, so both are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna needed to teach two cases because one might have thought that sanctity of the body (קדושת הגוף) does not lapse easily, while sanctity of value (קדושת דמים) does, so both teachings are necessary.

items.text: Challenge to the distinction between sanctities
items.text_en: Challenge to the distinction between sanctities
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if both cases involve sanctity of value, why teach both? Surely if sanctity lapses from a severe sanctity to a light one, it certainly lapses from a light to a severe one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if both cases involve sanctity of value, why teach both? Surely if sanctity lapses from a severe sanctity to a light one, it certainly lapses from a light to a severe one.

items.text: Proposed refutation of Bar Pada
items.text_en: Proposed refutation of Bar Pada
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that this is a refutation of Bar Pada, who said that sanctity does not lapse without action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's ruling refutes Bar Pada, who held that sanctity does not lapse without action.

items.text: Rav Pappa's defense of Bar Pada
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's defense of Bar Pada
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains Bar Pada's position: if one did not say 'from now' it becomes an elevation-offering after thirty days, analogous to betrothal after thirty days where the woman is betrothed even if the money was consumed.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's defense of Bar Pada
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's defense of Bar Pada
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains Bar Pada's position: if one did not say 'from now', the animal becomes an elevation-offering (עולה) after thirty days.
Rav Pappa draws an analogy to betrothal (קידושין) after thirty days, where the woman is betrothed even if the money was consumed.

items.text: Clarification of the analogy
items.text_en: Clarification of the analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether this is obvious, and clarifies that it is needed in a case where he retracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ruling is obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling is needed in a case where he retracted.

items.text: Challenge from the view that betrothal can be retracted
items.text_en: Challenge from the view that betrothal can be retracted
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for one who says betrothal cannot be retracted, but for one who says it can be retracted, what can be said? It answers that here it is different, because a declaration to Heaven is like delivery to a commoner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that the previous resolution works only for the view that betrothal cannot be retracted, but for the view that it can be retracted, what can be said?

The Gemara answers that even for the view that betrothal can be retracted, here it is different because a declaration to Heaven (אמירה לגבוה) is like delivery to a commoner (מסירה להדיוט), so it cannot be retracted.

items.text: Discussion between Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Discussion between Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yitzchak, sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya who was dozing, discuss Bar Pada's view that redeemed animals return and become consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yitzchak sit before a dozing Rabbi Yirmeya and discuss Bar Pada's view that redeemed animals return and become consecrated.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's question about sequential kiddushin
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's question about sequential kiddushin
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether giving a woman two prutot with the stipulation that one is for immediate kiddushin and the other for after divorce creates valid kiddushin. The Gemara suggests this is analogous to the case of redeeming a firstborn animal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether giving a woman two prutot with the stipulation that one is for immediate kiddushin and the other for after divorce creates valid kiddushin, and the Gemara suggests this is analogous to the case of redeeming a firstborn animal.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yochanan's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yochanan's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to the analogy, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if the owner himself redeems a firstborn animal, it can become sanctified again; if others redeem it, it cannot. A woman is like others redeeming her, so sequential kiddushin is invalid. Rabbi Ami confirms this tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to the analogy between redeeming saplings and sequential kiddushin, citing Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: if the owner redeems, the saplings become consecrated again; if others redeem, they do not. A woman after divorce is like others redeeming her, so the second betrothal is invalid.
Rabbi Ami confirms Rabbi Yochanan's tradition: the ruling that saplings become consecrated again applies only when the owner himself redeems them, but not when others redeem them.

items.text: Mishnah: Vowing from seafarers vs. land-dwellers
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vowing from seafarers vs. land-dwellers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who vows from 'seafarers' is permitted to land-dwellers, but if he vows from 'land-dwellers' he is forbidden from seafarers, since seafarers are included in land-dwellers. The term 'seafarers' refers only to those who regularly sail, not occasional travelers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who vows from seafarers is permitted to land-dwellers, but if he vows from land-dwellers he is forbidden from seafarers, since seafarers are included in land-dwellers; the term 'seafarers' refers only to those who regularly sail, not occasional travelers.

items.text: Dispute over Mishnah's phrasing
items.text_en: Dispute over Mishnah's phrasing
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika disagree on how to teach the Mishnah: one teaches the first clause (reisha) and the other the latter clause (seifa). The one who teaches the reisha interprets it as forbidding seafarers entirely, with the exception of occasional travelers.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Pappa and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika disagree on how to teach the Mishnah: one teaches the first clause (reisha) and the other the latter clause (seifa).

sub.text: Stam's explanation of the first position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of the first position
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the one who teaches the reisha interprets it as forbidding seafarers entirely, with the exception of occasional travelers.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier mishnah about travelers from Acco to Jaffa
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier mishnah about travelers from Acco to Jaffa
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains two versions of the mishnah's teaching: one that permits those traveling from Acco to Jaffa because they are land-dwellers, and another that prohibits them because they eventually go to sea, but includes all who customarily go to sea since they ultimately return to land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first version of the mishnah: those traveling from Acco to Jaffa are considered land-dwellers, so the vow is permitted.
The Gemara presents the second version: one who vows from land-dwellers is forbidden even those who customarily go to sea, since they ultimately return to land.

items.text: Mishnah: Vowing from 'those who see the sun'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vowing from 'those who see the sun'
items.desc_en: The mishnah rules that one who vows from 'those who see the sun' is also prohibited from blind people, because the intent is those whom the sun sees. The Gemara explains the reasoning: since he did not say 'from the seers', it excludes fish and fetuses.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states: one who vows from 'those who see the sun' is forbidden even blind people, because the intent is those whom the sun sees.
The Gemara asks the reason for this ruling, and answers: because the phrase is 'from those who see the sun' (רואי החמה) not 'from the seers' (מן הרואים).
The Gemara concludes that the formulation excludes fish and fetuses, which are not seen by the sun.

items.text: Mishnah: Vowing from 'black-haired ones'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vowing from 'black-haired ones'
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who vows from 'black-haired ones' is prohibited from bald and gray-haired men but permitted with women and children, since only men are called 'black-haired ones'. The Gemara explains the reasoning: because he did not say 'from those with hair', and women always cover their hair while children always have it uncovered.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states: one who vows from 'black-haired ones' is forbidden bald men and gray-haired men, but permitted women and children, since only men are called 'black-haired ones'.
The Gemara asks the reason for this ruling, and answers: because the phrase is 'black-haired ones' (שחורי הראש) not 'owners of hair' (בעלי שער).
The Gemara explains that women always cover their heads and children always uncover theirs, so they are not called 'black-haired ones'.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Vowing from 'the born' or 'the yet-to-be-born'
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Vowing from 'the born' or 'the yet-to-be-born'
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a dispute: one who vows from 'the born' is permitted with the yet-to-be-born, but from 'the yet-to-be-born' is prohibited from the born; Rabbi Meir permits even the born, and the Sages say the intent is only those who are destined to be born. The Gemara clarifies Rabbi Meir's position by emending the mishnah, and Rav Pappa questions Abaye about the meaning of 'noladim', concluding that in vows we follow common language, excluding fish and birds.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the dispute: one who vows from 'the born' (ילודים) is permitted 'the yet-to-be-born' (נולדים); one who vows from 'the yet-to-be-born' is forbidden 'the born'; Rabbi Meir permits even 'the born'; the Sages say the intent is only those who are destined to be born.
The Gemara questions: according to Rabbi Meir, if he permits even 'the yet-to-be-born', from whom is he forbidden?

The Gemara resolves that the mishnah is missing a clause: Rabbi Meir says that one who vows from 'the yet-to-be-born' is also permitted 'the born', just as one who vows from 'the born' is permitted 'the yet-to-be-born'.

Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: does 'נולדים' (the yet-to-be-born) really mean those who will be born? If so, the verse 'your two sons who were born to you in Egypt' would also refer to future birth, which is impossible.
The Gemara rejects the objection: the word 'נולדים' is ambiguous, meaning both 'already born' and 'yet to be born', and in vows we follow common usage.
The Gemara concludes that the Sages' statement excludes fish and birds, which are not destined to be born in the usual human sense.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows regarding Sabbath observers, garlic eaters, and Jerusalem pilgrims
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows regarding Sabbath observers, garlic eaters, and Jerusalem pilgrims
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from 'Sabbath observers' is forbidden both Israelites and Samaritans; similarly for 'garlic eaters'; but one who vows from 'Jerusalem pilgrims' is forbidden Israelites but permitted Samaritans.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for one who vows from Sabbath observers, garlic eaters, and Jerusalem pilgrims.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's distinctions
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's distinctions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'Sabbath observers' and why Samaritans are included but not Gentiles. Abaye resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah refers to those who are commanded and perform: Israelites and Samaritans are commanded and perform, while Gentiles are not commanded; regarding Jerusalem pilgrimage, Samaritans are commanded but do not perform.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Sabbath observers' means, rejecting the literal interpretation and concluding it refers to those commanded about the Sabbath.
The Gemara objects that if the criterion is being commanded, then Samaritans should also be forbidden regarding Jerusalem pilgrimage, but the Mishnah permits them.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah refers to those who are both commanded and actually perform the practice: Israelites and Samaritans observe the Sabbath and eat garlic, but Samaritans do not go up to Jerusalem.

Abaye resolves that the Mishnah refers to those who are commanded and perform: Israelites and Samaritans are commanded and perform regarding Sabbath and garlic, but regarding Jerusalem pilgrimage, Samaritans are commanded yet do not perform.

items.text: Mishnah: Vow from 'sons of Noah'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vow from 'sons of Noah'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who vows not to benefit from 'sons of Noah' is permitted with Israelites but forbidden with other nations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows not to benefit from 'sons of Noah' is permitted with Israelites but forbidden with other nations.

items.text: Gemara: Why Israelites are excluded from 'sons of Noah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Why Israelites are excluded from 'sons of Noah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that since Abraham was sanctified, Israelites are called by his name and thus not included in the term 'sons of Noah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Israelites are excluded from the category of 'sons of Noah', and answers that since Abraham was sanctified, they are called by his name.
The Gemara answers that since Abraham was sanctified, Israelites are called by his name and thus excluded from the general category of 'בני נח (Noahides)'.

items.text: Mishnah: Vow from 'seed of Abraham'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vow from 'seed of Abraham'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows not to benefit from 'seed of Abraham' is forbidden with Israelites but permitted with other nations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows not to benefit from 'the seed of Abraham' is forbidden with Israelites but permitted with other nations.

items.text: Gemara: Excluding Ishmael and Esau from 'seed of Abraham'
items.text_en: Gemara: Excluding Ishmael and Esau from 'seed of Abraham'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Ishmael and Esau are included in 'seed of Abraham', and answers with verses: 'For in Isaac shall your seed be called' and 'in Isaac, but not all Isaac'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about Ishmael and Esau, and answers with the verse 'for in Isaac shall your seed be called' and the exclusion 'in Isaac, but not all Isaac'.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע' (for through Isaac shall your seed be called) excludes Ishmael.
The Gemara further objects that Esau is also Isaac's seed, so the vow should include him.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'ביצחק' (in Isaac), not 'all of Isaac', thereby excluding Esau.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows regarding benefit from Israelites
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows regarding benefit from Israelites
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the rules for one who vows not to benefit from Israelites: he may buy at a higher price and sell at a lower price; if he vows that Israelites may benefit from him, he buys at a lower price and sells at a higher price, but we do not listen to him; if he vows both, he may benefit from other nations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah details the rules for one who vows not to benefit from Israelites, including buying at a higher price and selling at a lower price, and the reverse.

items.text: Gemara: Analyzing Shmuel's principle and the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara: Analyzing Shmuel's principle and the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to inspect it and it is damaged is liable, indicating that the benefit of the buyer is considered. The Gemara challenges this with the Mishnah's cases, and resolves by distinguishing between a forced sale (זבינא דרמי על אפיה) and a desirable sale (זבינא חריפא).

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to inspect it and it is damaged is liable, indicating that the benefit of the buyer is considered a benefit.
The Gemara objects that if the buyer's benefit is considered a benefit, then even selling at an equal price should be forbidden, and resolves that the Mishnah deals with a forced sale.
The Gemara objects further that if the Mishnah deals with a forced sale, then even buying at a higher price should be permitted at an equal price, and similarly for the reverse case.
The Gemara resolves that the latter clause deals with a desirable sale, but then questions why buying at a lower price is not permitted even at an equal price, leaving the discussion incomplete.
The Gemara resolves that the latter clause of the Mishnah deals with a desirable sale (זבינא חריפא), where the buyer's benefit is fully recognized, and the objection is left unresolved.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding the liability of a bailee who transports goods for sale. Rav holds the bailee is a paid watchman, while Shmuel considers him a borrower.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rav holds the bailee is a paid watchman (בִּזְבִינָא מִיצְעָא), while Shmuel considers him a borrower (בִּזְבִינָא חֲרִיפָא).

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's view: a person who takes vessels from a merchant to send to his father-in-law, with a conditional agreement, is liable for accidents on the way there but exempt on the return, as the return is considered a paid service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Shmuel: one who takes vessels from a merchant to send to his father-in-law, with a conditional sale, is liable for accidents on the outward journey but exempt on the return, because the return is like a paid watchman.
The baraita rules that the person is liable for accidents on the way there but exempt on the return, because the return is considered a paid service.

items.text: Case of the agent and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the agent and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that an agent who took a donkey to sell and it was injured on the return must pay, because for an agent, the return is considered part of the journey. Rava objects based on the baraita, but Rav Nachman explains that an agent's return is like going, as he would sell even at his doorstep.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case of an agent who took a donkey to sell, it was not sold, and on the return it was injured; Rav Nachman ruled he must pay.
Rava objects to Rav Nachman's ruling by citing the baraita that distinguishes between liability during the going and exemption during the return.
Rav Nachman explains that for an agent, the return is considered like going, because he would sell even at his doorstep.

items.text: New Mishnah: Vows using 'arel'
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Vows using 'arel'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a vow prohibiting benefit from 'arel' (uncircumcised). It rules that 'arel' refers to the uncircumcised of the nations, not Jewish uncircumcised, and provides scriptural proofs that 'arel' is a term for gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a rule: one who vows not to benefit from 'uncircumcised' is permitted with Jewish uncircumcised but forbidden with circumcised gentiles; the reverse applies for 'circumcised'; and it cites verses showing 'uncircumcision' is only attributed to gentiles.
The Mishnah provides three scriptural proofs that 'arel' is a term exclusively for gentiles, citing verses from Jeremiah, Samuel, and Psalms.

items.text: Tannaitic homilies on the greatness of circumcision
items.text_en: Tannaitic homilies on the greatness of circumcision
items.desc_en: Several Tannaim expound on the greatness of circumcision: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says it is despised, Rabbi Yishmael says it is great because 13 covenants were made, Rabbi Yosi says it overrides Shabbat, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says Moses was not spared for neglecting it, Rabbi Nechemya says it overrides leprosy, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says Abraham was not called perfect until circumcised, and another statement says the world was created for circumcision.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya states that the foreskin (ערלה) is despised, as the wicked are disgraced by it, citing the verse 'כי כל הגוים ערלים'.
Rabbi Yishmael says circumcision is great because thirteen covenants were made concerning it.
Rabbi Yosi says circumcision is great because it overrides the stringent Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says circumcision is great because Moses the righteous was not granted even a full hour's delay for neglecting it.
Rabbi Nechemya says circumcision is great because it overrides the laws of leprosy (נגעים).
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says circumcision is great because Abraham our father was not called perfect (תמים) until he was circumcised, citing the verse 'התהלך לפני והיה תמים'.
An additional statement declares circumcision great because without it the Holy One, blessed be He, would not have created the world, citing the verse 'אם לא בריתי יומם ולילה חקות שמים וארץ לא שמתי'.

items.text: Gemara: Moses' delay in circumcision
items.text_en: Gemara: Moses' delay in circumcision
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says Moses was punished for neglecting circumcision. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects, explaining that Moses had valid reasons: he could not circumcise immediately due to danger, nor delay three days because God told him to go to Egypt. The Gemara then asks why Moses was punished.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha states that circumcision is so great that all of Moses' merits did not protect him when he neglected it, as the verse says God sought to kill him.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects, arguing that Moses had valid reasons for delaying: circumcising immediately was dangerous, and waiting three days would have delayed God's command to return to Egypt.
The Gemara asks: if Moses had valid reasons, why was he punished at all?

items.text: The incident of Moses and the angel at the inn
items.text_en: The incident of Moses and the angel at the inn
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why an angel sought to kill Moses, with different opinions: because Moses delayed at the inn, or because the angel sought to kill the child. Rabbi Yehuda bar Bizna describes how 'Af' and 'Cheima' swallowed Moses, leaving only his legs, until Zipporah circumcised their son. Moses then sought to kill them, and a dispute arises about whether he killed Cheima.

items.text: The greatness of circumcision
items.text_en: The greatness of circumcision
items.desc_en: Rabbi teaches that circumcision is great because Abraham was only called 'tamim' (perfect) on account of it, and it is equivalent to all the commandments. Another teaching states that without circumcision, heaven and earth would not endure.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's dispute: Torah is greater
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's dispute: Torah is greater
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that Torah is greater than circumcision, as without Torah, heaven and earth would not endure, citing the same verse but interpreting 'beriti' as Torah.

items.text: Abraham's fear and the promise of circumcision
items.text_en: Abraham's fear and the promise of circumcision
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav relates that when God told Abraham 'walk before Me and be perfect', Abraham trembled, fearing he had a blemish. God reassured him by saying 'I will give My covenant between Me and you'. Then God took Abraham outside and told him to abandon astrology, as Israel is not subject to fate.

items.text: Teachings on being 'tamim'
items.text_en: Teachings on being 'tamim'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that one who makes themselves perfect (tamim), God is perfect with them. Rabbi Hoshaya teaches that one who makes themselves perfect will have a favorable hour, as Abraham was promised to become a father of many nations.

items.text: On divination and its opposite
items.text_en: On divination and its opposite
items.desc_en: Rabbi teaches that one who practices divination will have divination befall them, citing 'there is no divination in Jacob'. The Gemara clarifies that the verse is written with a lamed-alef (lo) meaning 'no', but it is read as 'lo' meaning 'to him', implying measure for measure. Tanei Ahava bar Rabbi Zeira teaches that one who does not practice divination enters a partition that even ministering angels cannot enter.

items.text: Why Abraham's descendants were enslaved in Egypt
items.text_en: Why Abraham's descendants were enslaved in Egypt
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar states that Abraham was punished and his descendants enslaved for 210 years because he conscripted Torah scholars for war. Shmuel says it was because he questioned God's attributes. Rabbi Yochanan says it was because he prevented people from entering under the wings of the Shechinah.

items.text: Interpretations of Abraham's armed men and his age
items.text_en: Interpretations of Abraham's armed men and his age
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the meaning of 'vayarek' (he armed): Rav says he made them shine with Torah, Shmuel says with gold. Rabbi Ami bar Abba says Eliezer alone was equal to all 318 men, or that Eliezer's name's numerical value is 318. He also states that Abraham recognized his Creator at age three, based on the numerical value of 'eikev' (172).

items.text: Gematria of Satan and Avraham's name change
items.text_en: Gematria of Satan and Avraham's name change
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba notes that the gematria of 'Satan' is 364, and explains that initially God made Avraham rule over 243 limbs, and later over 248, listing the additional five: two eyes, two ears, and the head of the body.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba notes that the gematria of 'Satan' is 364, and explains that initially God made Avraham rule over 243 limbs, and later over 248.
Rami bar Abba lists the five additional limbs: two eyes, two ears, and the head of the body.

items.text: Allegory of the small city
items.text_en: Allegory of the small city
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba interprets the verse about the small city as an allegory: the body is the city, the few men are the limbs, the great king is the evil inclination, the siege works are sins, the poor wise man is the good inclination, and his wisdom is repentance and good deeds, but when the evil inclination prevails, no one remembers the good inclination.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba interprets the verse about a small city as an allegory for the body, its limbs, the evil inclination, and sins.

Rami bar Abba continues the allegory, identifying the poor wise man as the good inclination, his wisdom as repentance and good deeds, and notes that in times of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination.

items.text: Wisdom prevails over ten rulers
items.text_en: Wisdom prevails over ten rulers
items.desc_en: The verse 'Wisdom is stronger for the wise than ten rulers' is interpreted: wisdom is repentance and good deeds, and the ten rulers are the two eyes, two ears, two hands, two feet, the head of the body, and the mouth.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites and interprets the verse 'Wisdom strengthens the wise more than ten rulers', identifying wisdom as repentance and good deeds, and the ten rulers as the two eyes, two ears, two hands, two feet, the head of the body, and the mouth.

items.text: Priesthood taken from Shem and given to Avraham
items.text_en: Priesthood taken from Shem and given to Avraham
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya in the name of Rabbi Yishmael says that God wanted to bring forth the priesthood from Shem, but because Shem blessed Avraham before blessing God, the priesthood was taken from him and given to Avraham, as indicated by the verse 'He is a priest to God Most High' — he is a priest, but not his descendants.

sub.text: Rabbi Zecharya in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zecharya in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya in the name of Rabbi Yishmael states that God wanted to bring forth the priesthood from Shem, but because Shem blessed Avraham before blessing God, the priesthood was taken from Shem and given to Avraham.

The gemara cites the verse where Shem blessed Avraham before blessing God, and Avraham's objection that one does not precede a servant's blessing over the Master's, leading God to immediately transfer the priesthood to Avraham.
The gemara cites a verse from Psalms indicating that the priesthood was given to Avraham because of the speech of Malchizedek (Shem).
The gemara concludes that the verse 'He is a priest to God Most High' means that Shem himself is a priest, but his descendants are not priests.

items.text: Mishnah: Difference between מודר הנאה and מודר מאכל
items.text_en: Mishnah: Difference between מודר הנאה and מודר מאכל
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the only difference between one who is forbidden all benefit from his friend and one who is forbidden only food is the right to step on his property and use vessels not used for food preparation. The one forbidden food may not borrow a sieve, mill, or oven, but may borrow a cloak, ring, or earrings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the only difference between one forbidden all benefit and one forbidden only food is the right to step on property and use vessels not for food preparation.
The Mishnah specifies that one forbidden food may not borrow a sieve, mill, or oven, but may borrow a cloak, ring, or earrings.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that even a trivial benefit is forbidden to one who is under a vow of general benefit. The Gemara then cites the Mishnah's ruling about not lending a sieve, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the author of the Mishnah.
Rav Adda bar Ahava identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that even a trivial benefit (ויתור) is forbidden to one who is under a vow of general benefit.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's continuation
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's continuation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling about not lending a sieve, etc., as the continuation of the discussion.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and answers on the vow's scope
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and answers on the vow's scope
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a vow prohibiting food can include non-food items, and Resh Lakish and Rava offer interpretations: the vow is phrased as 'benefit of your food upon me' or 'benefit that leads to food upon me'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the vow was only about food, so how can it prohibit non-food items like a sack or donkey?
Resh Lakish explains that the vow was phrased as 'the benefit of your food is forbidden upon me', which includes any benefit derived from food.
The Gemara objects that even under Resh Lakish's formulation, one could still chew wheat and apply it to a wound, which is a non-food use of food.
Rava answers that the vow was phrased as 'benefit that leads to food is forbidden upon me', which includes items used to acquire or prepare food.

items.text: Rav Pappa's examples and query
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's examples and query
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that a sack for fruit, a donkey for fruit, and even a basket are considered 'benefit that leads to food', but he questions whether a horse for riding or a ring for display is included.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a sack for fruit, a donkey for fruit, and even a basket are considered 'benefit that leads to food'.
Rav Pappa questions whether a horse for riding or a ring for display is included in the prohibition.

items.text: Attempted proof from the Mishnah and rejection
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the Mishnah and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one may lend items for display, but concludes that the Mishnah refers to items not used for display, and the structure is merely contrasting the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one may lend items for display, since the Mishnah permits lending a cloak, garment, earrings, and rings without qualification.
The Gemara rejects the proof, concluding that the Mishnah refers to items not used for display, and the structure merely contrasts the first clause.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on items not used for food
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on items not used for food
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any item not used for food is forbidden where such items are rented out. The Gemara infers that in the first clause, even where they are not rented out, it is forbidden, and identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that any item not used for food is forbidden where such items are rented out.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that in the first clause, even where items are not rented out, it is forbidden, and asks who the Tanna is.
Rav Adda bar Ahava answers that the Tanna is Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Mishnah on returning lost items and Gemara's rationale
items.text_en: Mishnah on returning lost items and Gemara's rationale
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who is forbidden benefit from a friend may still pay his temple tax, repay his debt, and return his lost item; where payment is taken, the benefit goes to the Temple. The Gemara explains that returning a lost item is merely avoiding a loss, which is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who is forbidden benefit from a friend may still pay his temple tax, repay his debt, and return his lost item; where payment is taken, the benefit goes to the Temple.
The Gemara explains that returning a lost item is merely avoiding a loss (אברוחי ארי בעלמא), which is permitted.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to identify the Tanna of the Mishnah about returning lost items, with Rav Hoshaya starting to speak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah about returning lost items.
Rav Hoshaya begins to identify the Tanna, but the text cuts off before completing the identification.

items.text: Rava's initial claim
items.text_en: Rava's initial claim
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that the Mishnah's ruling can be explained even according to the Sages, not only Ḥanan, because the giver gives on condition that the recipient not repay.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the Mishnah's ruling follows Ḥanan's opinion.
Rava argues that the Mishnah can be explained even according to the Sages, because the giver gives on condition that the recipient not repay.
The gemara cites the Mishnah of Ḥanan: one who supported a woman whose husband went overseas loses his money.

sub.text: Continuation of the baraita with dissenting opinions
sub.text_en: Continuation of the baraita with dissenting opinions
sub.desc_en: The baraita records that the high priests' sons disagreed, Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas agreed with them, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai praised Ḥanan's ruling.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of Rava and Rav Hoshaya
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rava and Rav Hoshaya
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rava and Rav Hoshaya disagree: Rava does not adopt Rav Hoshaya's position that the Mishnah is universally applicable, while Rav Hoshaya rejects Rava's concern about a decree against repayment.

sub.text: Gemara's question about returning a lost object
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about returning a lost object
sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about returning a lost object when the owner is forbidden from benefit.

sub.text: First opinion of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: First opinion of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: One opinion holds that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the finder's property is forbidden to the owner, because the finder returns his own property, but not when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, due to the concern of Rabbi Yosef's coin.

sub.text: Second opinion of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Second opinion of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: The other opinion holds that even when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, the finder returns it, because the concern of Rabbi Yosef's coin is uncommon.

items.text: Explanation of Ḥanan's view
items.text_en: Explanation of Ḥanan's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains who Ḥanan is by citing a Mishnah where Ḥanan says a man who supported another's wife in his absence loses his money, while the Sages and Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas disagree, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai praises Ḥanan.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that even according to all opinions, the Mishnah's case involves a מודר הנאה (one forbidden from benefit) who gives on condition of not being repaid.
The Gemara asks who Ḥanan is, seeking to identify the source of his view.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Ḥanan rules that a man who supported another's wife in his absence loses his money.
The baraita records that the Sages and Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas disagree with Ḥanan, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai praises Ḥanan's ruling.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Rav Hoshaya
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Rav Hoshaya
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rava and Rav Hoshaya disagree: Rava does not accept Rav Hoshaya's interpretation that the Mishnah is universal, while Rav Hoshaya rejects Rava's concern about a decree preventing repayment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the disagreement between Rava and Rav Hoshaya: Rava rejects Rav Hoshaya's universal interpretation of the Mishnah, while Rav Hoshaya rejects Rava's concern about a decree preventing repayment.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi argue about the scope of returning a lost object: one limits it to when the finder's property is forbidden to the owner, the other extends it even when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, dismissing concern for the peruta of Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi regarding the scope of returning a lost object.

One opinion (Rabbi Ammi) limits the allowance to return the lost object to cases where the finder's property is forbidden to the owner, because returning the object is merely returning the finder's own property; but if the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, returning would benefit the finder via the peruta of Rav Yosef (the small coin the finder would otherwise have to pay for return).

The other opinion (Rabbi Assi) permits returning the lost object even when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, because the concern for the peruta of Rav Yosef (the small coin) is not common.

items.text: First version: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: First version: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that in a place where one takes a fee for returning a lost object, the benefit falls to hekdesh. It notes that according to the view that even when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, the finder still returns it, the Mishnah is consistent. But according to the view that the finder does not return it, why does the Mishnah say the benefit falls to hekdesh? The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is dealing with a single case (the owner's property is forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that in a place where one takes a fee for returning a lost object, the benefit falls to hekdesh.
The Gemara notes that according to the view that even when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, the finder still returns it, the Mishnah is consistent.
The Gemara asks: according to the view that the finder does not return it when the owner's property is forbidden, why does the Mishnah say the benefit falls to hekdesh?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is dealing with a single case (the owner's property is forbidden).

items.text: Second version: Dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.text_en: Second version: Dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.desc_en: There is an alternative formulation of the dispute: one says the Mishnah only applies when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, due to the rare coin of Rav Yosef, but if the finder's property is forbidden to the owner, the finder does not return it because he benefits the owner. The other says even if the finder's property is forbidden, it is permitted because he is returning his own property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute, attributed to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi.

Rabbi Ami holds that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the owner's property is forbidden to the finder, due to the rare case of Rabbi Yosef's coin, but not when the finder's property is forbidden to the owner.
Rabbi Asi holds that even when the finder's property is forbidden to the owner, returning the lost object is permitted because the finder is returning his own property.

items.text: Challenge to the second version from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to the second version from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara again cites the Mishnah and notes that according to the view that even when the finder's property is forbidden he returns it, the Mishnah is resolved. But according to the view that when the finder's property is forbidden he does not return it, how is the Mishnah resolved? This remains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara again cites the Mishnah's ruling about the benefit falling to hekdesh.
The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Asi's view, the Mishnah is consistent.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Ami's view that the finder does not return it when his own property is forbidden, how does he explain the Mishnah? This remains a difficulty.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a hekdesh loaf
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a hekdesh loaf
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one declares a hefker loaf as hekdesh, taking it to eat causes misuse of the entire loaf, but taking it to bequeath to his children causes misuse only according to the benefit value.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one declares a hefker loaf as hekdesh, taking it to eat causes misuse of the entire loaf, but taking it to bequeath to his children causes misuse only according to the benefit value.

items.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin's question about a vow after gifting
items.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin's question about a vow after gifting
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin asks Rava: if one says 'my loaf upon you' and then gives it as a gift, is it still forbidden? The question is whether the prohibition depends on the loaf being in the speaker's possession or on the vow's effect on the recipient.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin asks Rava whether a loaf declared forbidden by vow ('my loaf upon you') remains forbidden after the speaker gives it to the recipient as a gift, posing two possible interpretations: the prohibition depends on the loaf being in the speaker's possession, or the vow creates a sanctity-like status on the recipient.

items.text: Rava's answer and clarification
items.text_en: Rava's answer and clarification
items.desc_en: Rava responds that it is obvious the loaf remains forbidden even after being given as a gift. He then clarifies that the phrase 'my loaf upon you' serves to exclude cases where the loaf was stolen or where the recipient was invited to eat it.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that it is obvious (פשיטא) that even if the recipient gave the loaf as a gift, it remains forbidden.
Rava asks rhetorically what the phrase 'my loaf upon you' then serves to exclude.
Rava suggests that the phrase excludes a case where the loaf was stolen from the recipient.
Rav Chiya bar Avin rejects Rava's suggestion and clarifies that the phrase excludes a case where the recipient invited the owner to eat the loaf.

items.text: Opening baraita on a vow of prohibition
items.text_en: Opening baraita on a vow of prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that presents cases where one says a konam vow regarding a cow or ax, and then it is found that he does have that item. During his lifetime it is forbidden, but if he dies or gives it as a gift, it becomes permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita presenting cases of konam vows regarding a cow or ax, where the item is found to exist: during the vow-maker's lifetime it is forbidden, but after his death or if given as a gift it becomes permitted.

items.text: Clarification of the gift's nature
items.text_en: Clarification of the gift's nature
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika specifies that the gift must be given through another person. Rav Ashi supports this by noting the baraita uses passive language 'was given' rather than active 'he gave'.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's specification
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's specification
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika specifies that the gift mentioned in the baraita must be given through another person, not directly by the original owner.

Rav Ashi supports this by noting that the baraita uses the passive form 'שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה לוֹ' (was given to him) rather than the active 'שֶׁנְּתָנָהּ לוֹ' (he gave it to him), implying the gift was through an intermediary.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about me'ilah in konamot
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about me'ilah in konamot
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether the laws of me'ilah apply to konamot. Rav Nachman responds that they have already learned from a source: just as with hekdesh there is me'ilah, so too with konamot there is me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether the laws of me'ilah apply to konamot.
Rav Nachman responds that they have already learned from a source: just as with hekdesh there is me'ilah, so too with konamot there is me'ilah.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on me'ilah in konamot
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on me'ilah in konamot
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a konam vow phrased as 'hekdesh' (which has me'ilah and redemption) and 'upon me to hekdesh' (where only the vower is liable). The Sages rule that in all cases there is no me'ilah in konamot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a konam vow phrased as 'hekdesh' (which has me'ilah and redemption) and 'upon me to hekdesh' (where only the vower is liable).
The Sages rule that in all cases there is no me'ilah in konamot.

items.text: Case of a gift and me'ilah
items.text_en: Case of a gift and me'ilah
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi about a case where one says 'my loaf is upon you' and then gives it as a gift: who is liable for me'ilah? Rav Ashi answers that the recipient is liable when he spends it, by analogy to one who spends hekdesh money thinking it is non-sacred.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi about a case where one says 'my loaf is upon you' and then gives it as a gift: who, if anyone, commits מעילה?
Rav Ashi answers that the recipient commits מעילה when he spends the money, by analogy to one who spends consecrated money thinking it is unconsecrated.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions a person prohibited from benefit may still do for the one who vowed, including offering sacrifices and teaching midrash, but not teaching Scripture.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions a person prohibited from benefit may still do for the one who vowed, including offering sacrifices and teaching midrash, but not teaching Scripture.

items.text: Gemara's question: Are priests agents of the person or of Heaven?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Are priests agents of the person or of Heaven?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether priests who offer sacrifices for a person prohibited from benefit are considered the person's agents (making it forbidden) or Heaven's agents (permitting it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether priests who offer sacrifices for a person are considered agents of the person or agents of Heaven, which affects whether a person prohibited from benefit may receive their service.

items.text: First attempt: proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First attempt: proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that priests are Heaven's agents, since the Mishnah permits offering sacrifices for the one who vowed, implying no benefit is conferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that priests are agents of Heaven, since otherwise the Mishnah would be permitting forbidden benefit.

items.text: Rejection: those lacking atonement are different
items.text_en: Rejection: those lacking atonement are different
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that the Mishnah deals with those lacking atonement, who do not require consent, as Rabbi Yochanan taught that all require consent except those lacking atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah could have used a general term 'sacrifices' but instead specified bird-offerings, indicating a special case of those lacking atonement (מחוסרי כפרה), who do not require consent.
Rabbi Yochanan states that all sacrifices require the owner's consent except those of people lacking atonement (מחוסרי כפרה), as proven by the verse 'זאת תורת הזב' applying to both adults and minors.

Rabbi Yochanan teaches that all offerings require the owner's consent except those lacking atonement, as a person may bring a korban (קרבן) for his minor children, based on the verse 'זאת תורת הזב' (this is the law of the zav) applying to both adult and child.

items.text: Objection: the verse about a woman who gave birth
items.text_en: Objection: the verse about a woman who gave birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's principle cannot apply to a woman who gave birth, as a minor cannot give birth, citing a baraita about three women who use a contraceptive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the verse 'זאת תורת היולדת' includes minors, it would contradict Rav Bibi's teaching before Rav Nachman that a minor girl cannot give birth and must use a contraceptive.
The Gemara asks rhetorically whether a minor girl is capable of giving birth, implying she is not.

sub.text: Supporting baraita cited by Rav Beivai before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita cited by Rav Beivai before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita taught by Rav Beivai before Rav Nachman, listing three women who use a contraceptive (מוך), including a minor girl (קטנה) because pregnancy could kill her, proving a minor cannot give birth.

items.text: Resolution: the verse includes a fool and a minor
items.text_en: Resolution: the verse includes a fool and a minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'this is the Torah of the one who gave birth' includes a fool and a minor, as a man may bring a sacrifice for his foolish wife, according to Rabbi Yehuda who says a man brings a rich person's sacrifice for his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת' (this is the Torah of the one who gave birth) includes both a competent woman and a fool, since a man may bring a sacrifice for his foolish wife.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a man brings a rich person's sacrifice for his wife and all the sacrifices she is obligated in.

sub.text: Supporting evidence from the marriage document
sub.text_en: Supporting evidence from the marriage document
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the husband writes in the marriage document that he accepts responsibility for her obligations from before their marriage, justifying his bringing sacrifices for her.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Abba's challenge from the metzora's sacrifice
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Abba's challenge from the metzora's sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Abba cites a baraita where a kohen who is a metzora may have his chatas and asham blood sprinkled for him, implying that the kohen acts as an agent for the metzora, not as a divine agent. This challenges the idea that kohanim are agents of Heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Abba cites a baraita where a kohen who is a metzora may have his chatas and asham blood sprinkled for him, implying that the kohen acts as an agent for the metzora, not as a divine agent.

items.text: Gemara's response from piggul in the Temple
items.text_en: Gemara's response from piggul in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna about kohanim who commit piggul intentionally or unintentionally. If kohanim were agents of the owners, then unintentional piggul should not be piggul, since the kohen could argue he was appointed only to fix, not to ruin. The Gemara answers that piggul is different because the verse says 'lo yeichashev lo' in any case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna stating that kohanim who commit piggul in the Temple are liable if intentional, but if unintentional they are exempt yet the piggul is still piggul.

The Gemara argues that if kohanim are agents of Heaven, the mishna is consistent, but if they are agents of the owners, then unintentional piggul should not be piggul, since the kohen could claim he was appointed only to fix, not to ruin.
The Gemara answers that piggul is different because the verse says 'לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב לוֹ' (it shall not be accounted to him) in any case, overriding the agent's limitation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and challenge from a friend's chatas
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and challenge from a friend's chatas
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all sacrifices require the owner's intent except for a mechusar kapparah, since a person can bring a korban for his minor children. The Gemara challenges: if so, a person should be able to bring a chatas for a friend, just as one brings for his insane wife according to Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Elazar says one cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all sacrifices require the owner's intent except for a mechusar kapparah, since a person can bring a korban for his minor children.
The Gemara challenges: if so, a person should be able to bring a chatas for a friend, just as one brings for his insane wife according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Elazar objects that one who sets aside a chatas for a friend has done nothing.

items.text: Analysis of the case of an insane wife
items.text_en: Analysis of the case of an insane wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the case of an insane wife: if she ate fat while insane, she is not liable for a korban; if she ate while sane and then became insane, Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan rules that the korban is invalid because it was pushed off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the case of an insane wife? If she ate fat while insane, she is not liable for a korban at all.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: if she ate while sane and then became insane, Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan rules that the korban is invalid because it was pushed off (נדחה).

items.text: Challenge from bringing a pesach for a friend
items.text_en: Challenge from bringing a pesach for a friend
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges further: a person can bring a pesach for his minor children, so why can't he bring a pesach for a friend? Rabbi Elazar says one cannot. Rabbi Zeira answers that the requirement of 'seh leveis avos' is not from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: since a person can bring a pesach for his minor children, why can't he bring a pesach for a friend, contradicting Rabbi Elazar's ruling that such an action is void.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the requirement of 'שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבֹת' (a lamb per paternal household) for the pesach is not from the Torah, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Proof from a mishna about the pesach
items.text_en: Proof from a mishna about the pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves Rabbi Zeira's point from a mishna where a father says he will slaughter the pesach for whichever son enters Jerusalem first. The first son acquires his portion and can share with his brothers. If 'seh leveis avos' were Torah law, the father could not allocate the pesach based on a race.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we know that 'seh leveis avos' is not Torah law? From a mishna where a father says he will slaughter the pesach for whichever son enters Jerusalem first, and the first son acquires his portion and shares with his brothers.
The Gemara objects: if 'seh leveis avos' were Torah law, how could the father allocate the pesach based on a race and thereby give a portion to the other sons?

The Gemara answers: the father's statement was only to encourage them in the מצוה (commandment), as a supporting baraita (תניא נמי הכי) recounts a story where daughters were zealous and sons were sluggish.

items.text: Transition to the next topic
items.text_en: Transition to the next topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins the next clause of the mishna regarding terumah, but does not develop it further in this segment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the next clause of the mishna, which discusses terumah, but does not develop it further.

items.text: Initial inquiry: does the donor need the owner's knowledge?
items.text_en: Initial inquiry: does the donor need the owner's knowledge?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: when one separates terumah from his own produce on behalf of his friend, does he need the friend's knowledge? The doubt is whether it is considered a benefit to the friend (so no knowledge needed) or a mitzvah of the donor (so he wants to do it himself).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: when one separates תרומה (priestly portion) from his own produce on behalf of his friend, does he need the friend's knowledge, or is it considered a benefit (זכות) that can be done without consent, versus a מצוה (commandment) of the donor who wants to perform it himself.

items.text: Attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the Mishnah that no knowledge is needed. It analyzes the phrase 'תּוֹרֵם אֶת תְּרוּמוֹתָיו לְדַעְתּוֹ' and concludes that it must refer to one who separates from his own on behalf of another, and since he benefits the owner, it implies no knowledge is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that no knowledge is needed, analyzing the phrase 'תּוֹרֵם אֶת תְּרוּמוֹתָיו לְדַעְתּוֹ' and considering whether it refers to the owner's knowledge.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must refer to one who separates from his own on behalf of another, and since he benefits the owner, it implies no knowledge is required.

items.text: Rejection: the Mishnah refers to a general permission
items.text_en: Rejection: the Mishnah refers to a general permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah deals with a case where the owner said 'whoever wishes to separate may come and separate,' so the donor acts with the owner's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the Mishnah deals with a case where the owner said 'whoever wishes to separate may come and separate,' so the donor acts with the owner's knowledge.

items.text: Second inquiry: who receives the benefit of the mitzvah?
items.text_en: Second inquiry: who receives the benefit of the mitzvah?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: when one separates terumah from his own on behalf of another, who receives the benefit (טובת הנאה)? Is it the donor, since without his produce the other's crop would not be fixed, or the owner, since without the owner's crop the donor's produce would not be terumah? Rabbi Zeira answers with a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: when one separates תרומה (priestly portion) from his own produce on behalf of another, who receives the benefit (טובת הנאה) — the donor or the owner?
Rabbi Zeira answers by citing the verse 'את כל תבואת זרעך... ונתת' (all the produce of your seed... and you shall give), implying the donor gives and thus retains the benefit.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: if the benefit belonged to the owner, the donor would be benefiting him without knowledge. It concludes that the benefit belongs to the donor, but the Mishnah is explained as referring to a case of general permission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: if the benefit belonged to the owner, the donor would be benefiting him without knowledge.
The Sages resolve that the Mishnah refers to a case where the owner gave general permission for anyone to separate terumah.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement of Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Avahu that explicitly states: one who separates terumah from his own on behalf of another — the benefit is his.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement of Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Avahu that explicitly states: one who separates תרומה (priestly portion) from his own on behalf of another — the benefit (טובת הנאה) is his.

items.text: Digression: teaching Torah for pay
items.text_en: Digression: teaching Torah for pay
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses why one may teach midrash and aggadah for pay but not Mikra, explaining that in places where teachers are paid for Mikra, the prohibition is due to benefiting the student, but midrash is allowed because no fee is taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may teach midrash, halachot, and aggadot for pay, but not Mikra.
The Gemara questions why Mikra is prohibited while midrash is permitted, since both involve benefiting the student.
Shmuel answers that in places where teachers are paid for Mikra but not for midrash, the prohibition is due to benefiting the student, but midrash is allowed because no fee is taken.
The Gemara asks what the practical ruling (פסק) is regarding this distinction.

items.text: Gemara's initial distinction between Scripture and Midrash
items.text_en: Gemara's initial distinction between Scripture and Midrash
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even where teachers are paid, one may accept payment for teaching Scripture but not for Midrash. It derives this from verses where Moses taught for free, implying all Torah teaching should be free, but then questions why Scripture is an exception.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even where teachers are paid, one may accept payment for teaching Scripture but not for Midrash.

The Gemara questions why Midrash is treated differently from Scripture, citing verses where Moses taught for free, implying all Torah teaching should be free, and then challenges why Scripture is an exception.

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan's explanations for the fee
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan's explanations for the fee
items.desc_en: Rav says the fee is for guarding the child, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is for teaching the cantillation (division of verses into accents). This sets up the debate for the rest of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the fee is for guarding the child, while Rabbi Yochanan states it is for teaching the cantillation (division of verses into accents).

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's ruling that a father cannot teach his son Scripture. According to Rabbi Yochanan (fee for cantillation), this makes sense because the father would be paying for teaching. But according to Rav (fee for guarding), a grown child does not need guarding, so the Mishnah must refer to a young child. The Gemara then resolves a contradiction in the Mishnah by emending it to distinguish between a young child and an adult.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a father cannot teach his son Scripture.
The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yochanan (fee for cantillation), the Mishnah's prohibition makes sense, but according to Rav (fee for guarding), why would a grown child need guarding?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to a young child who needs guarding.
The Gemara objects: If the Mishnah refers to a young child, how can the continuation say 'he may teach his sons' — a young child does not have sons.
The Gemara resolves by emending the Mishnah: it distinguishes between a young child (prohibited) and an adult (permitted to teach himself and his sons).

items.text: Objection from the law of teaching children on Shabbat
items.text_en: Objection from the law of teaching children on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: children do not begin reading on Shabbat but review what they already learned. According to Rabbi Yochanan (fee for cantillation), this is understandable because teaching new material involves cantillation which is forbidden on Shabbat. But according to Rav (fee for guarding), why would it be forbidden? There is no guarding fee on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about children not reading on Shabbat, arguing that according to Rav's view (fee for guarding), the prohibition is inexplicable since there is no guarding fee on Shabbat.

items.text: Refutation of the objection: cantillation is permitted on Shabbat
items.text_en: Refutation of the objection: cantillation is permitted on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the objection by arguing that even according to Rabbi Yochanan, cantillation is permitted on Shabbat because it is considered 'swallowing' (a natural act) and not a forbidden labor. It cites a baraita that a worker hired to guard a child on Shabbat does not receive Shabbat pay, implying guarding is permitted. Thus the objection is neutralized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to the view that the fee is for cantillation, is cantillation on Shabbat forbidden? It is merely 'swallowing' (הבלעה, a natural act), which is permitted.
The Gemara cites a baraita: one who hires a worker to guard a child, a cow, or seeds does not receive Shabbat pay, implying guarding is permitted on Shabbat.
The Gemara concludes: therefore, the objection is neutralized, as cantillation is permitted on Shabbat.

items.text: Mishnah: liability for lost scrolls
items.text_en: Mishnah: liability for lost scrolls
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a teacher hired by the week/month/year, who is paid for Shabbat and liable for loss, and one hired by the day, who is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a teacher hired by the day is not liable for lost scrolls, but one hired by the week, month, or year is paid for Shabbat and therefore liable for loss.

items.text: Gemara: reasons for not reading initially on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara: reasons for not reading initially on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that on Shabbat, people are occupied with the meal or feel heavy, so they do not read initially; it cites Shmuel's statement about change of routine causing illness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives the first reason why one does not read initially on Shabbat: because the fathers of the children are occupied with the Shabbat meal (מצותא דשבתא).
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: on Shabbat people eat and drink and feel heavy (יַקִּיר עֲלֵיהוֹן עָלְמָא), so they do not read initially.

The Gemara supports the second reason by citing Shmuel's statement that a change of routine (שינוי וסת) is the beginning of intestinal illness, implying that eating heavily on Shabbat makes people sluggish.

items.text: Debate: wage for punctuation vs. guarding
items.text_en: Debate: wage for punctuation vs. guarding
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says the wage is for punctuation does not say it is for guarding, and answers that daughters do not need guarding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says the wage is for punctuation does not say it is for guarding.
The answer explains that daughters do not need guarding, so the wage cannot be for guarding.

items.text: Debate: wage for guarding vs. punctuation
items.text_en: Debate: wage for guarding vs. punctuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says the wage is for guarding does not say it is for punctuation, and answers that punctuation is from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says the wage is for guarding does not say it is for punctuation.
The Gemara answers that punctuation (פיסוק טעמים) is from the Torah, so no wage is needed for it.

items.text: Proof from verse: punctuation is Torah
items.text_en: Proof from verse: punctuation is Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Avin quotes Rav Chananel quoting Rav that the verse in Nehemiah refers to punctuation, and some say it refers to the Masorah.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Avin quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Avin quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Avin cites a chain of tradition that the verse in Nehemiah refers to punctuation (פיסוק טעמים) as part of Torah.
An alternative interpretation is offered: the same verse refers to the Masorah (מסורות), the tradition of how to read and write the text.

items.text: Masoretic traditions: halacha l'Moshe miSinai
items.text_en: Masoretic traditions: halacha l'Moshe miSinai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak lists categories of Masoretic traditions (e.g., qere/ketiv) that are halacha l'Moshe miSinai, with examples for each.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak declares that four categories of Masoretic traditions (מקרא סופרים, עיטור סופרים, קריין ולא כתיבן, כתיבן ולא קריין) are all halacha l'Moshe miSinai (הלכה למשה מסיני).

The Gemara lists examples of the first category, מקרא סופרים (scribal readings): the words ארץ (land), שמים (heavens), and מצרים (Egypt) are read with a specific vocalization not reflected in the written text.

The Gemara lists examples of the second category, עיטור סופרים (scribal embellishments): five verses where an extra word is added in the reading but not in the written text, such as 'אחר תעבורו' (after you pass) and others.

The Gemara lists examples of the third category, קריין ולא כתיבן (read but not written): eight words that are pronounced in the reading but absent from the written text, such as 'פרת' in the verse 'בלכתו' and others.
The Gemara begins listing examples of the fourth category, כתיבן ולא קריין (written but not read): the word 'נא' in the verse 'יסלח' is written but not pronounced in the reading.

items.text: Opening statement on Torah scrolls
items.text_en: Opening statement on Torah scrolls
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists words in the Torah that are written but not read, establishing a pattern of textual anomalies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists words in the Torah that are written but not read, establishing a pattern of textual anomalies.

items.text: Division of a verse in the West
items.text_en: Division of a verse in the West
