items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda reports that in the West (Eretz Yisrael), they divide a particular verse into three verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda reports that in the West they divide a certain verse into three verses.

items.text: Moses' wealth from the tablets' chips
items.text_en: Moses' wealth from the tablets' chips
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says Moses became wealthy from the chips of the tablets, as God told him to hew the tablets and keep the chips. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that the Torah was given only to Moses and his descendants, but Moses generously gave it to Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that Moses became wealthy only from the chips of the tablets, citing the verse 'פסל לך' (hew for yourself) to imply the chips were his.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that the Torah was given only to Moses and his descendants, but Moses generously gave it to Israel, citing the verse 'טוב עין הוא יבורך' (a good eye will be blessed).

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding Torah transmission
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding Torah transmission
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects from verses showing Moses taught the Torah to Israel, implying it was not exclusively his. The Gemara resolves that the verses refer to the Torah itself, while the oral tradition (pilpula) was given to all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects by citing verses where Moses says God commanded him to teach the Torah to Israel, implying it was not exclusively for Moses and his descendants.
The Gemara resolves that the verse about writing the song refers only to the Torah itself, while the oral tradition (פילפולא) was given to all Israel.

items.text: Four attributes of Moses for the Divine Presence
items.text_en: Four attributes of Moses for the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Divine Presence rests only on one who is strong, wealthy, wise, and humble, all found in Moses. Proofs are given: strength from spreading the Tabernacle, wealth from the tablets' chips, wisdom from having all but one of the fifty gates of understanding, and humility from the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Divine Presence rests only on one who is strong, wealthy, wise, and humble, all found in Moses.

sub.text: Proof of strength from the Tabernacle
sub.text_en: Proof of strength from the Tabernacle
sub.desc_en: The gemara initially cites Moses spreading the Tabernacle as proof of strength, but questions whether it required mere height rather than strength.

sub.text: Alternative proof of strength from the tablets
sub.text_en: Alternative proof of strength from the tablets
sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves by citing Moses breaking the tablets, which were six by six by three handbreadths, as proof of his strength.

sub.text: Proof of wealth from the tablets' chips
sub.text_en: Proof of wealth from the tablets' chips
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse 'פסל לך' (hew for yourself) to show Moses became wealthy from the chips of the second tablets.

sub.text: Proof of wisdom from the fifty gates
sub.text_en: Proof of wisdom from the fifty gates
sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel state that all fifty gates of understanding were given to Moses except one, as per the verse 'ותחסרהו מעט מאלהים' (You have made him a little less than God).

sub.text: Proof of humility from the verse
sub.text_en: Proof of humility from the verse
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse 'והאיש משה ענו מאד' (and the man Moses was very humble) as proof of his humility.

items.text: All prophets were wealthy
items.text_en: All prophets were wealthy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that all prophets were wealthy, proven from Moses, Samuel, Amos, and Jonah. For Moses, the verse 'I have not taken one donkey from them' implies even for pay, and the chips show wealth. For Samuel, his house traveled with him. Rava notes Samuel's greatness exceeded Moses' in not even accepting a gift. Amos was a cattle owner, and Jonah paid the entire ship's fare of 4,000 gold dinars.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by asserting that all prophets were wealthy, citing Moses, Samuel, Amos, and Jonah as proof.
The gemara proves Moses' wealth from the verse 'I have not taken one donkey from them' — implying even for pay, and from the chips of the tablets.
The gemara proves Samuel's wealth from the verse 'whose donkey have I taken' — implying even for pay, and from Rava's statement that his house traveled with him.
Rava notes that Samuel's greatness exceeded Moses' in that he did not even accept a gift, while Moses only refused pay.
The gemara proves Amos' wealth from the verse 'I am a cattle owner and a dresser of sycamores', as translated by Rav Yosef.
The gemara proves Jonah's wealth from the verse 'he paid her fare', with Rabbi Yochanan stating he paid the entire ship's fare and Rabbi Romanus specifying it was 4,000 gold dinars.

items.text: Moses initially forgot Torah
items.text_en: Moses initially forgot Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Moses initially learned Torah and forgot it until it was given to him as a gift, as the verse states.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Moses initially learned Torah and forgot it until it was given to him as a gift, citing the verse 'וַיִּתֵּן אֶל מֹשֶׁה כְּכַלֹּתוֹ לְדַבֵּר אִתּוֹ' (and He gave to Moses when He finished speaking with him).

items.text: Mishnah on sustenance for family and animals
items.text_en: Mishnah on sustenance for family and animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may sustain his wife and children even if obligated, but not his animals. Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between impure and pure animals, arguing that pure animals' souls belong to Heaven and their bodies to the owner, while impure animals are entirely the owner's.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may feed his wife and children even though he is obligated for their sustenance, but he may not feed his animal, whether impure or pure.
Rabbi Eliezer says one may feed an impure animal but not a pure one.
The Sages ask Rabbi Eliezer what is the difference between an impure and a pure animal.
Rabbi Eliezer answers that a pure animal's soul is for Heaven and its body is his, while an impure animal's soul and body are both his.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a טמאה animal, its soul is for Heaven and its body belongs to the owner, since he can sell it to gentiles or feed it to dogs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for a טמאה (ritually impure) animal, its soul belongs to Heaven and its body to the owner, who may sell it to gentiles or feed it to dogs.

items.text: Gemara's initial ruling and question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial ruling and question
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one who is under a vow of benefit from another may marry off his daughter to him. Rabbi Zeira questions this, suggesting that if the father-in-law's property is forbidden to the groom, giving a maidservant for service would be a benefit.

sub.text: Rav Huna via Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya
sub.text_en: Rav Huna via Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one who is under a vow of benefit from another may marry off his daughter to that person.
Rabbi Zeira questions the ruling, arguing that if the father-in-law's property is forbidden to the groom, giving a maidservant for service would be a benefit.

items.text: Alternative scenario and objection
items.text_en: Alternative scenario and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that the case might be where the groom's property is forbidden to the father-in-law, but then a greater leniency would apply: one may support his wife and children even if obligated, so marrying off his daughter should certainly be permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the case is where the groom's property is forbidden to the father-in-law, then a greater leniency (supporting one's wife and children) would apply, so permitting the father to marry off his daughter is inconsistent.

items.text: Resolution and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Resolution and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where the father-in-law's property is forbidden, but the daughter is a בוגרת (adult) acting of her own accord. A baraita supports this: one may not marry off his daughter, but may marry off his adult daughter with her consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by specifying that the case involves a בוגרת (adult daughter) who acts of her own accord, so the father-in-law does not benefit from the marriage.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states: one may not marry off his daughter to a מודר הנאה (one forbidden by vow from benefit), but may marry off his adult daughter with her consent.

items.text: Permitted services for a son under vow
items.text_en: Permitted services for a son under vow
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov permits filling a barrel of water and lighting a lamp for a son who is under a vow from Torah study. Rabbi Yitzchak adds roasting a small fish. Rabbi Yirmeya quoting Rabbi Yochanan permits giving a cup of peace (identified as a cup for mourners or a bathhouse cup).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov rules that a father who vowed his son away from Torah study may still fill a barrel of water and light a lamp for him.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds that roasting a small fish for the son is also permitted.
Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan permits giving a cup of peace to one under vow, identified locally as a mourner's cup or in the West as a bathhouse cup.

items.text: Feeding animals vs. Canaanite slaves
items.text_en: Feeding animals vs. Canaanite slaves
items.desc_en: A baraita from Yehoshua of Uzza states that one may feed his Canaanite slaves but not his animals (whether טמאה or טהורה), because slaves are for service while animals are for fattening.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is מודר הנאה (forbidden benefit) from another may not feed his animals, whether טמאה (impure) or טהורה (pure).
A baraita from Yehoshua of Uzza supports the Mishnah, stating that one may feed his Canaanite slaves but not his animals, whether טמאה or טהורה.

The baraita explains the rationale: Canaanite slaves are for service (למנחרותא), so feeding them is not considered benefit to the owner, while animals are for fattening (לפיטומא), so feeding them directly benefits the owner.

items.text: Mishnah: Visiting and healing the sick
items.text_en: Mishnah: Visiting and healing the sick
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one under a vow may visit a sick person but must stand, not sit. He may provide medical care for the body (רפואת נפש) but not for monetary gain (רפואת ממון).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one under a vow may visit a sick person but must stand, not sit, and may provide medical care for the body (רפואת נפש) but not for monetary gain (רפואת ממון).

items.text: Gemara's initial question and Shmuel's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and Shmuel's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which case the Mishnah addresses: if the visitor's property is forbidden to the patient, even sitting should be allowed; if the patient's property is forbidden to the visitor, even standing should be forbidden. Shmuel answers that it deals with a place where payment is taken for sitting but not for standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which case the Mishnah addresses, presenting two logical possibilities: if the visitor's property is forbidden to the patient, even sitting should be permitted; if the patient's property is forbidden to the visitor, even standing should be forbidden.
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah deals with a place where payment is taken for sitting but not for standing, so sitting is forbidden while standing is permitted.

items.text: Two explanations for Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Two explanations for Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two interpretations: first, that Shmuel teaches that even where payment is taken, one must pay for sitting but not for standing; alternatively, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim, it is a decree lest the visitor linger while standing or sitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point Shmuel teaches, and offers the first explanation: that even where payment is taken, one must pay for sitting but not for standing.

sub.text: Alternative answer via Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
sub.text_en: Alternative answer via Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation following Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim: Shmuel's ruling is a decree lest the visitor linger while standing or sitting.

items.text: Ulla's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Ulla's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that the Mishnah deals with the case where the patient's property is forbidden to the visitor, and the visitor did not vow from the patient's livelihood. Even so, standing is possible, so sitting is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Ulla argues that the Mishnah deals with the case where the patient's property is forbidden to the visitor, and the visitor did not vow from the patient's livelihood; even so, standing is possible, so sitting is forbidden.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if the visitor himself is sick, he enters to visit; if his son is sick, he asks in the market. This supports Ulla but challenges Shmuel. Shmuel resolves that the Mishnah deals with the visitor's property being forbidden, while the baraita deals with the patient's property being forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if the visitor himself is sick, he enters to visit; if his son is sick, he asks in the market.
The gemara notes that the baraita fits Ulla's position that the patient's property is forbidden, and the visitor was not prohibited from benefiting from the patient during his lifetime.
The gemara challenges Shmuel: according to his view that the visitor's property is forbidden, why should there be a difference between the visitor himself being sick and his son being sick?
Shmuel resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah deals with the visitor's property being forbidden to the patient, while the baraita deals with the patient's property being forbidden to the visitor.

items.text: Rava's clarification of Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Rava's clarification of Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that Shmuel explicitly said the Mishnah deals with the visitor's property being forbidden to the patient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point (פסק) Shmuel's statement teaches.
Rava clarifies that Shmuel explicitly stated the Mishnah deals with the visitor's property being forbidden to the patient.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'standing but not sitting' regarding visiting the sick, inferring that the visitor's property is forbidden to the patient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'standing but not sitting', inferring that the visitor's property is forbidden to the patient.

items.text: Resh Lakish's biblical hint for visiting the sick
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's biblical hint for visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish derives a hint for visiting the sick from the Torah, citing the verse about Korach's rebellion, and Rava explains that if the rebels die like all people, who are sick and visited, then people will say God did not send Moses.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish derives a hint for visiting the sick from the Torah, citing the verse about Moses and Korah.
Rava explains that if the rebels die like all people, who are sick and visited, then people will say God did not send Moses.

items.text: Rava's homily on Gehinnom and the objection
items.text_en: Rava's homily on Gehinnom and the objection
items.desc_en: Rava interprets a verse to mean that if Gehinnom was already created, good; if not, God will create it. An objection is raised from a baraita listing seven things created before the world, including Gehinnom. The Gemara resolves that Rava meant the mouth of Gehinnom, and addresses the verse 'there is nothing new under the sun' by saying the mouth is brought near.

sub.desc_en: Rava interprets the verse 'אם בריאה יברא ה (if a creation the Lord creates)' to mean that if Gehinnom was already created, good; if not, God will create it.
The Gemara objects from a baraita listing seven things created before the world, including Gehinnom, contradicting Rava's suggestion that Gehinnom might not yet exist.
The Gemara resolves that Rava meant the mouth of Gehinnom, not Gehinnom itself, and addresses the verse 'אין כל חדש תחת השמש (there is nothing new under the sun)' by saying the mouth is brought near.

items.text: Rava or Rabbi Yitzchak's homily on the sun and moon
items.text_en: Rava or Rabbi Yitzchak's homily on the sun and moon
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yitzchak) explains a verse about the sun and moon standing in the celestial 'Zevul', teaching that they protested to God about doing justice for Moses, and God shot arrows at them, rebuking them for not protesting for His honor but for a mortal's.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yitzchak) interprets the verse about the sun and moon standing in the heavenly dwelling, describing how they threatened not to shine if God did not vindicate Moses, and God shot arrows at them for failing to protest His honor.

God rebukes the sun and moon for protesting for a mortal's honor but not for His own, and shoots arrows at them; nevertheless, they continue to shine daily, as the verse 'לְאוֹר חִצֶּיךָ יְהַלֵּכוּ' indicates.

items.text: The measure of visiting the sick
items.text_en: The measure of visiting the sick
items.desc_en: A baraita states that visiting the sick has no limit. Rav Yosef thought this meant no limit to its reward, but Abaye objects that all mitzvot have no limit to reward. Abaye explains it means even a great person visiting a small one; Rava says even a hundred times a day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'visiting the sick has no measure' means, and records Abaye's and Rava's interpretations: even a great person visiting a small one, or even a hundred times a day.
The gemara asks what 'no limit' means in this context.
Rav Yosef thought it meant no limit to its reward.
Abaye objects that all mitzvot have no limit to reward, citing a mishnah.
Abaye explains it means even a great person visiting a small one.
Rava says it means even a hundred visits a day.

items.text: The reward for visiting the sick
items.text_en: The reward for visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina says a visitor takes one-sixtieth of the patient's suffering. The Gemara objects that sixty visitors would remove all suffering. He answers it is like the tithe of Rabbi's house, and when the visitor is a contemporary. A supporting baraita about a daughter's tithe from Rabbi's estate is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina states that one who visits a sick person takes away one-sixtieth of the patient's suffering.
The Gemara objects that if each visitor takes one-sixtieth, then sixty visitors would remove all suffering, leaving the patient completely healed.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina answers that the one-sixtieth is like the tithe of Rabbi's house, and only applies when the visitor is a contemporary (בן גילו) of the patient.

A supporting baraita is cited: Rabbi rules that a daughter supported from brothers' estate takes a tithe of the property, illustrating the principle of a fixed portion that does not exhaust the whole.
The sages object to Rabbi that according to his rule, a man with ten daughters and one son would leave nothing for the son, since each daughter takes a tithe.

Rabbi resolves the objection by explaining that the first daughter takes a tithe of the entire estate, the second takes a tithe of what remains, and so on, and then they all divide the remainder equally.

items.text: Rabbi Chelbo's illness and Rav Kahana's announcement
items.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo's illness and Rav Kahana's announcement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rabbi Chelbo falling ill and Rav Kahana announcing it, but the segment ends abruptly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rav Chelbo fell ill and Rav Kahana went out to announce it.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva visiting a sick student
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva visiting a sick student
items.desc_en: Rav Chelbo is sick and no one comes to visit him. He tells the story of a student of Rabbi Akiva who was sick, and the sages did not visit him, but Rabbi Akiva did, and by cleaning and sweeping before him, the student recovered. Rabbi Akiva then taught that one who does not visit the sick is like a murderer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chelbo falls ill and no one comes to visit him.
Rav Chelbo recounts the story of Rabbi Akiva's sick student who recovered after Rabbi Akiva visited and cleaned for him.
Rabbi Akiva teaches that one who does not visit the sick is like a murderer.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of visiting the sick
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi teaches that visiting the sick causes them to live, and not visiting causes them to die. The Gemara questions this, clarifying that not visiting does not cause death, but rather one does not pray for them to live or die.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi states that visiting the sick causes them to live, and not visiting causes them to die.
The Gemara questions how not visiting could cause death, rejecting the notion that one would pray for the sick to die.
The Gemara clarifies that not visiting means one does not pray for the sick at all, neither for life nor for death.

items.text: Rava's practice regarding visiting the sick
items.text_en: Rava's practice regarding visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Rava instructs that on the first day of illness, no one should be told, so as not to worsen his fortune. Afterwards, he says to announce in the market so that his enemies will rejoice (and thus not be punished) and his friends will pray for him.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs that on the first day of illness, no one should be told so as not to worsen his fortune; afterwards, announce in the market so that enemies rejoice (and thus not be punished) and friends pray for him.

items.text: Rav's teaching on the reward for visiting the sick
items.text_en: Rav's teaching on the reward for visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that one who visits the sick is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom, as derived from verses where 'dal' refers to a sick person and 'ra'ah' refers to Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: Rav teaches that visiting the sick saves one from Gehinnom, deriving 'dal' as sick person and 'ra'ah' as Gehinnom from verses.

items.text: Additional reward for visiting the sick in this world
items.text_en: Additional reward for visiting the sick in this world
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the reward is in this world for visiting the sick, and answers with a verse: 'Hashem will preserve him and keep him alive, and he will be blessed in the land, and You will not deliver him to the soul of his enemies.' This is interpreted to mean protection from the evil inclination, from suffering, that all will honor him, and that he will have friends like Naaman who healed his leprosy, not like Rehoboam who divided his kingdom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional reward one receives for visiting the sick in this world, since the reward of being saved from Gehinnom was already stated.

The Gemara answers with a verse and its interpretation: the visitor is protected from the evil inclination, from suffering, honored by all, and given beneficial friends like Naaman rather than harmful ones like Rehoboam.

items.text: Baraita on listening to elders over children
items.text_en: Baraita on listening to elders over children
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that if children say 'build' and elders say 'destroy,' listen to the elders, because the building of children is destruction and the destruction of elders is building, with the example of Rehoboam.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches a baraita that when children say 'build' and elders say 'destroy,' one should listen to the elders, because the building of children is destruction and the destruction of elders is building, citing Rehoboam as an example.

items.text: Advice on when not to visit the sick
items.text_en: Advice on when not to visit the sick
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi teaches that one should not visit a sick person in the first three hours of the day or the last three hours, so as not to distract from prayer. In the first three hours, the sick person's mind is at ease, and in the last three, his weakness is strong.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi rules that one should not visit a sick person during the first three or last three hours of the day, to avoid distracting from prayer; the first three hours find the patient at ease, the last three find his weakness strong.

items.text: The Shekhinah above the sickbed
items.text_en: The Shekhinah above the sickbed
items.desc_en: Ravin in the name of Rav teaches that God sustains the sick and that the Shekhinah is above the sickbed, as derived from the verse 'Hashem will support him on the bed of suffering.' A baraita adds that one who visits the sick should not sit on the bed, bench, or chair, but should wrap himself and sit on the ground, because the Shekhinah is above the sickbed.

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Ravin in the name of Rav derives from the verse 'ה׳ יִסְעָדֶנּוּ עַל עֶרֶשׂ דְּוָי' (The Lord will support him upon the bed of suffering) that the Holy One, Blessed be He, sustains the sick person.

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Ravin in the name of Rav further derives from the same verse that the Divine Presence (שכינה) rests above the bed of the sick person.

A baraita supports this by ruling that one who visits the sick must not sit on the bed, bench, or chair, but must wrap himself and sit on the ground, because the Divine Presence is above the sickbed, as per the same verse.

items.text: A digression on rain and rivers
items.text_en: A digression on rain and rivers
items.desc_en: Ravin in the name of Rav says that rain in the west is attested by the great Euphrates. This disagrees with Shmuel, who says a river is blessed from its source, and also disagrees with another statement of Shmuel that water is not purified by flowing.

sub.desc_en: Ravin in the name of Rav states that rain in the West (Eretz Yisrael) is attested by the great Euphrates River.
The Gemara notes that Rav's statement disagrees with Shmuel, who says a river is blessed from its banks (tributaries), not from rain.
The Gemara further notes that Shmuel's statement disagrees with another statement of Shmuel, that water does not purify when flowing.

items.text: Statement about mikvaot in Tishrei
items.text_en: Statement about mikvaot in Tishrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the practice of making mikvaot is only during the days of Tishrei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the practice of making mikvaot (ritual baths) is only during the days of Tishrei.

items.text: Avuh deShmuel's practice
items.text_en: Avuh deShmuel's practice
items.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel made mikvaot for his daughters in Nisan and pools in Tishrei, illustrating a different practice.

sub.text: Stam's citation of Avuh deShmuel's practice
sub.text_en: Stam's citation of Avuh deShmuel's practice
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites Avuh deShmuel's practice of making mikvaot (ritual baths) for his daughters in Nisan and pools in Tishrei, illustrating a different approach to water usage.

items.text: Rabbi Ami quoting Rav on exile vessels
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami quoting Rav on exile vessels
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami quotes Rav interpreting the verse 'Make for yourself vessels of exile' as referring to a lamp and a bowl.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami in the name of Rav explains the verse 'Make for yourself vessels of exile' as referring to a lamp and a bowl.

items.text: Interpretations of 'lack of everything'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'lack of everything'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents multiple Amoraitic interpretations of what constitutes 'lack of everything' (בְּחֹסֶר כֹּל), including without a lamp, table, wife, servant, or knowledge. Abaye then summarizes that true poverty is lack of knowledge, and the Gemara elaborates on this idea.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi cites Rav interpreting 'lack of everything' as lacking a lamp and a table.
Rav Chisda interprets 'lack of everything' as lacking a wife.
Rav Sheshet interprets 'lack of everything' as lacking a servant.
Rav Nachman interprets 'lack of everything' as lacking knowledge.
A Tanna adds another interpretation: lacking salt and a vegetable (or seasoning).
Abaye summarizes the tradition: there is no poor person except one lacking knowledge.
The Western sages elaborate: one who has knowledge has everything; one who lacks it lacks everything.

items.text: Sickness and forgiveness of sins
items.text_en: Sickness and forgiveness of sins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri quotes Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that a sick person does not recover until all their sins are forgiven, citing Psalms 103:3. Rav Hamnuna adds that the sick person returns to their youth, citing Job 33:25. Rav Yosef interprets a verse to mean that illness causes one to forget their learning.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri in the name of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states that a sick person does not recover until all their sins are forgiven, citing Psalms 103:3.
Rav Hamnuna adds that the sick person returns to their youth, citing Job 33:25.
Rav Yosef interprets the verse 'כׇּל מִשְׁכָּבוֹ הָפַכְתָּ בְחׇלְיוֹ' to mean that illness causes one to forget their learning.

items.text: Rav Yosef's illness and the story of Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's illness and the story of Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef fell ill and forgot his learning, which Abaye restored to him. The Gemara then recounts how Rabbi taught thirteen versions of a halacha to Rabbi Chiya, but when Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Chiya forgot six of them. A weaver who had overheard Rabbi teaching helped restore the remaining seven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Yosef fell ill and forgot his learning, and Abaye restored it to him, as evidenced by Rav Yosef's later statements.

The Gemara tells how Rabbi taught thirteen versions of a halacha to Rabbi Chiya, but when Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Chiya forgot six; a weaver who had overheard Rabbi teaching helped restore the remaining seven, and Rabbi praised the weaver.

items.text: The miracle of healing is greater than the miracle of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
items.text_en: The miracle of healing is greater than the miracle of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri quotes Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that the miracle performed for a sick person is greater than that for Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, because their fire was human-made and could be extinguished, whereas the sick person's affliction is from Heaven and cannot be quenched.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri in the name of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba declares that the miracle of healing a sick person is greater than the miracle of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, because their fire was human-made and extinguishable, whereas the sick person's affliction is from Heaven and cannot be quenched.

items.text: When a person's time comes, all rule over him
items.text_en: When a person's time comes, all rule over him
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri quotes Rabbi Chiya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) that once a person's appointed time arrives, everyone rules over him, citing Cain's statement in Genesis 4:14. Rav cites a different verse from Psalms. The Gemara then brings two anecdotes: Rabbah bar Sheila's death from a fall, and Shmuel's observation of a scorpion killing a man.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Chiya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Chiya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri states in the name of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) that once a person's appointed time arrives, everyone rules over him, citing Cain's statement in Genesis 4:14.
Rav cites a different verse from Psalms (119:91) to support the same idea.
The Gemara relates an anecdote about Rabbah bar Sheila, who died from a fall and applied the same verse to himself.
The Gemara relates an anecdote about Shmuel observing a scorpion killing a man, and applying the same verse.

items.text: Who may be visited? The exception for certain illnesses
items.text_en: Who may be visited? The exception for certain illnesses
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one may only visit a sick person who has a fever, excluding those with eye or head ailments. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei ben Parta in the name of Rabbi Eliezer forbids visiting those with intestinal, eye, or head ailments. The reason for eye and head ailments is given by Rav Yehuda: speech is harmful to the eyes but beneficial for fever.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one may only visit a sick person who has a fever (חַמָּה).
The Gemara asks what Shmuel's statement excludes.
The Gemara answers that it excludes the baraita of Rabbi Yosei ben Parta in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, which forbids visiting those with intestinal, eye, or head ailments.
The Gemara notes that the reason for intestinal ailments is embarrassment, but asks what the reason is for eye and head ailments.
Rav Yehuda explains that speech is harmful to the eyes but beneficial for fever, so visiting is forbidden for eye and head ailments but permitted for fever.
Rava adds that fever, if not for the angel of death's permission slip, would be beneficial.

items.text: Remedies for the sick: חיזרא, תיריאקי, and ערסן
items.text_en: Remedies for the sick: חיזרא, תיריאקי, and ערסן
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the comparison of חיזרא to dates and תיריאקי to the body. Rabbah bar Yonatan quotes Rav Yechiel that ערסן is good for the sick, and Abaye specifies its cooking requirements.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that חיזרא (a type of date) is to palm trees as תיריאקי (an antidote) is to the body, implying a beneficial relationship.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the comparison, saying that neither חיזרא nor תיריאקי are truly effective.

items.text: Definition of ערסן and its preparation
items.text_en: Definition of ערסן and its preparation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan defines ערסן as old barley flour from the top of the sieve. Abaye states it requires cooking like beef. Rav Yosef offers a similar definition, and Abaye repeats the cooking requirement.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Yonatan quoting Rav Yechiel
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Yonatan quoting Rav Yechiel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Yonatan quotes Rav Yechiel that ערסן (a barley dish) is beneficial for the sick.
The gemara asks what exactly is meant by ערסן.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that ערסן is a dish made from old barley flour that is sifted from the top of the sieve.
Abaye adds that this barley dish requires cooking equivalent to the cooking of beef.
Rav Yosef defines ערסן as fine flour from old barley sifted from the top of the sieve.
Abaye reiterates that this dish requires cooking equivalent to beef.

items.text: The illness בורדם: no visiting or mentioning its name
items.text_en: The illness בורדם: no visiting or mentioning its name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that for בורדם, one does not visit or mention its name. Rabbi Elazar explains it is like a flowing spring, and that its name derives from that property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that regarding בורדם (a type of illness), one does not visit the sick nor mention its name.
The gemara asks for the reason behind this prohibition.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the reason is because the illness is like a flowing spring (i.e., it spreads easily).
Rabbi Elazar adds that the name בורדם itself indicates it is like a flowing spring.

items.text: Interpretation of 'healing the soul' vs. 'healing property'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'healing the soul' vs. 'healing property'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing: if healing the soul is free and healing property is for pay, it should say so. Rather, 'healing the soul' refers to his body, 'healing property' to his animal. Rav Zutra bar Toviah quotes Rav that one may advise which medicine is good or bad for the animal.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how the mishna should be understood regarding the distinction between healing the soul and healing property.
The gemara objects: if the mishna meant that healing the soul is free and healing property is for pay, it should have stated explicitly 'heals him for free but not for pay'.
The gemara resolves: rather, 'healing the soul' refers to his own body, and 'healing property' refers to his animal.

sub.text: Rabbi Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav that one may tell the owner which medicine is good or bad for the animal.

items.text: Mishnah: Bathing, sleeping, and eating with a נדר
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bathing, sleeping, and eating with a נדר
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits bathing with him in a large bath but not a small one, and sleeping in the same bed. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between summer and winter to avoid benefit. It also discusses reclining and eating from the same table but not from the same bowl, except a returning bowl.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may bathe with the vow-bound person in a large bath but not a small one, and may sleep in the same bed.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between summer (permitted) and winter (forbidden) for sleeping in the same bed, because in winter the bed-warmer provides benefit.
The Mishnah adds that one may recline with him on a couch and eat from the same table, but not from the same bowl, except a returning bowl.

items.text: Gemara: Tannaitic dispute on bathing and sleeping
items.text_en: Gemara: Tannaitic dispute on bathing and sleeping
items.desc_en: A baraisa records Rabbi Meir prohibiting bathing and sleeping in any bath or bed. Rabbi Yehuda permits a large bath in winter and a small one in summer. The baraisa also details reclining and eating, with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explaining the 'returning bowl' as one returned to the homeowner.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir forbids bathing with the sick person in any bath or sleeping in any bed, large or small.
Rabbi Yehuda permits a large bath in winter and a small bath in summer, and allows sweating with him in a small bath.
The baraita repeats the mishnaic rules about reclining, eating at the table, and the returning bowl.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the returning bowl (תמחוי החוזר) is one that is returned to the host.

items.text: Mishnah: Eating from the workers' trough and working together
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eating from the workers' trough and working together
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits eating from the workers' trough or working together with a נדר according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages permit working at a distance.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one may not eat with the sick person from the trough of workers or work with him in the same craft, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages permit working with him as long as he is at a distance.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about proximity in work
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about proximity in work
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that both agree working close is forbidden. The dispute is about working at a distance: Rabbi Meir decrees distance due to closeness, as it might lead to helping him; the Rabbis do not decree.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that both Rabbi Meir and the Sages agree that working close to the sick person is forbidden.
The gemara clarifies that the dispute is specifically about working at a distance.
Rabbi Meir holds that we decree a prohibition on distance work because of proximity, as he might relax his guard in front of the sick person.
The Sages hold that we do not decree a prohibition on distance work because of proximity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who forbids benefit from his friend before the Sabbatical year: the friend may not enter his field or eat from the overhanging branches. During the Sabbatical year, he may not enter but may eat from the overhanging branches. If he forbade only food, the rules differ.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who forbids benefit from his friend before the Sabbatical year, detailing the rules of entering the field and eating from overhanging branches, with distinctions for the Sabbatical year and for a vow limited to food.

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel interpret the Mishnah as referring to a case where the vow was 'these properties are upon you,' while Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish interpret it as 'my properties are upon you.' They disagree on whether the prohibition applies even after the Sabbatical year begins.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel state their interpretation of the Mishnah: the vow formula is 'נכסים אלו עליך' (these properties are upon you), and the prohibition persists even after the Sabbatical year begins.

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish give their alternative interpretation: the vow formula is 'נכסי עליך' (my properties are upon you), and once the Sabbatical year arrives, the prohibition on eating the fallen produce is lifted.

items.text: Gemara's proposed underlying principle
items.text_en: Gemara's proposed underlying principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute hinges on whether a person can forbid an object that is currently in his domain even for after it leaves his domain. Rav and Shmuel hold that he can, while Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish hold that he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel versus Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish hinges on whether a person can forbid something that is currently in his possession even for after it leaves his possession.

items.text: Objection to the proposed principle
items.text_en: Objection to the proposed principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is there anyone who holds that a person cannot forbid an object for after it leaves his domain? If so, the dispute should have been in the case of 'these properties' and certainly in 'my properties.' Furthermore, a Mishnah explicitly states that a person can forbid an object for after it leaves his domain, as in the case of one who says to his son 'Konam that you benefit from me' — after the father dies, the son inherits him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is there anyone who holds that a person cannot forbid an object for after it leaves his domain? If so, the dispute should have been in the case of 'these properties' and certainly in 'my properties.'

The Gemara further objects by citing a Mishnah that explicitly states a person can forbid an object for after it leaves his domain, as in the case of one who says to his son 'Konam that you benefit from me' — after the father dies, the son inherits him.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction from the earlier Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction from the earlier Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the phrase 'these properties' (נכסים אלו) and 'my properties' (נכסי). The case where the giver said 'in his life and in his death' is different, but the general principle is that the dispute is about the wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the case where the giver said 'in his life and in his death' from the general rule.

items.text: Refining the dispute
items.text_en: Refining the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between the Sages is specifically about the phrase 'my properties' (נכסי), while regarding 'these properties' (נכסים אלו) everyone agrees that one can prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the resolution and proposes that the dispute is about the wording 'these properties' vs. 'my properties'.
The Gemara resolves: regarding 'these properties' (נכסים אלו) all agree one can prohibit; the dispute is only over 'my properties' (נכסי).

items.text: Positions of Rav and Shmuel versus Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Positions of Rav and Shmuel versus Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel hold that there is no difference between 'these properties' and 'my properties' — one can prohibit. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish hold that with 'these properties' one can prohibit, but with 'my properties' one cannot prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the positions: Rav and Shmuel hold that both phrases forbid, while Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish distinguish between them.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: Is there anyone who says there is no difference? The Mishnah explicitly distinguishes between 'your house' (ביתך) and 'this house' (בית זה), showing that specific designation matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a Mishnah that shows a distinction between specific and general wording, challenging Rav and Shmuel's position.

items.text: Resolution: No actual dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: No actual dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there is no dispute: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish spoke about 'my properties' (נכסי), while Rav and Shmuel spoke about 'these properties' (נכסים אלו), so they do not disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish spoke about 'my properties' and Rav and Shmuel about 'these properties', so they do not actually disagree.

items.text: Question on the Sabbatical year ruling
items.text_en: Question on the Sabbatical year ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why in the Sabbatical year may one eat from the produce that grows spontaneously but not enter the field? The produce is ownerless, but the land too should be ownerless?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why in the Sabbatical year one may not enter his field to work but may eat the produce, asking why the land is not also considered ownerless.

items.text: Two answers regarding the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Two answers regarding the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: Ulla answers that the trees stand on the borders (so the land is not entirely ownerless). Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim answers that it is a decree lest one delay in standing (and come to work the land).

sub.desc_en: Ulla answers that the case involves trees standing on the borders, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim adds a decree lest one linger in standing.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim answers that it is a decree lest one delay in standing and come to work the land.

items.text: Mishnah: General laws of one who is forbidden to benefit from his fellow
items.text_en: Mishnah: General laws of one who is forbidden to benefit from his fellow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is forbidden to benefit from his fellow may not lend to him or borrow from him, nor sell to him or buy from him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is forbidden by vow from benefiting from another may not lend, borrow, sell, or buy from him.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's list of prohibitions: while lending to the other party is clearly a benefit, borrowing from him is not obviously a benefit. Similarly, borrowing and buying from him are benefits, but borrowing an item from him is not clearly a benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's list: lending to the other party is a benefit, but borrowing from him is not obviously a benefit; similarly, borrowing and buying are benefits, but borrowing an item is not clearly a benefit.

items.text: Two answers to the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Two answers to the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the case is where both parties vowed not to benefit from each other, so borrowing is a benefit. Abaye says it is a decree: borrowing is prohibited because it leads to lending.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that the case involves two people who each vowed not to benefit from the other.
Abaye answers that the prohibitions are a גזירה (rabbinic decree) — borrowing is forbidden because it leads to lending, and similarly for all other cases.

items.text: Mishnah: Case of borrowing a cow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Case of borrowing a cow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one person asks to borrow another's cow, and the owner refuses. The borrower then vows that his field, which he plows with that cow, is forbidden to him. If he normally plows, only he is forbidden; if not, both he and others are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites a case: one says 'Lend me your cow' and the other replies 'It is not available.'
The Mishnah rules: if the person normally plows, he is forbidden but others are permitted; if he does not normally plow, both he and others are forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Ways to circumvent the vow for food and labor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ways to circumvent the vow for food and labor
items.desc_en: If a person is forbidden to benefit from his friend and has nothing to eat, he can go to a storekeeper and hint that the friend is a vow-issue, and the storekeeper gives him food and collects from the friend. Similarly, for building or harvesting, he can hire workers who work and collect from the friend.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a person forbidden from benefit who has nothing to eat may hint to a storekeeper, who gives him food and collects from the friend.
The Mishnah adds a second case: for building, fencing, or harvesting, the forbidden person hires workers who work and collect their wages from the friend.

items.text: Mishnah: Travelers with no food and the dispute with Rabbi Yossi
items.text_en: Mishnah: Travelers with no food and the dispute with Rabbi Yossi
items.desc_en: If travelers are on the road and one has no food, he can give food to another as a gift, and the vow-bound person may eat it. If no one else is present, he can declare the food ownerless, and the vow-bound person may take and eat. Rabbi Yossi forbids this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: if they are walking and have nothing to eat, one gives food to another as a gift, and the other is permitted to eat it.
The Mishnah rules: if no one else is present, one declares the food הפקר (ownerless) on a rock or fence, and the other takes and eats.
Rabbi Yosei forbids this practice.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Yossi's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Yossi's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Yossi considers ownerless property like a gift: just as a gift requires transfer from the giver's domain to the receiver's, so too ownerless property requires that it come into the domain of the one who acquires it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks: what is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning?

Rabbi Yochanan explains: Rabbi Yosei holds that הפקר (ownerless property) is like a gift — just as a gift requires transfer from the giver's domain to the recipient's domain, so too הפקר requires transfer to the acquirer's domain.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Abba objects and cites Rabbi Yossi's own statement
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Abba objects and cites Rabbi Yossi's own statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects by citing the Mishnah's continuation where Rabbi Yossi says his ruling applies only when the vow preceded the declaration of ownerless property, implying that if the declaration came first, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'and the other takes and eats, and Rabbi Yosei forbids' — implying that Rabbi Yosei's position is stated without qualification.
Rabbi Yosei clarifies: the prohibition applies only when his vow preceded his declaration of הפקר (ownerless status).

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on hefker preceding a vow
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on hefker preceding a vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a vow does not take effect on property that was declared ownerless before the vow, and answers that a person who vows does not intend to include what they have already made hefker.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the ownerless declaration (הפקר) preceded the vow, the property is permitted, given the assumption that the vow takes effect only when the property enters the domain of a acquirer.
The Gemara answers that one who vows does not intend to include what he has already declared ownerless (הפקר).

items.text: Rava's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a Mishnah where if some of the produce went to the first person and all to the second, the first acquires but the second does not, implying that hefker can be acquired even after a vow.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a Mishnah: if some produce went to the first person and all to the second, the first acquires but the second does not, implying that hefker can be acquired even after a vow.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation for Rabbi Yosi's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation for Rabbi Yosi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the true reason for Rabbi Yosi's ruling is a decree due to the case of Beit Horon, where people would make hefker to circumvent vows.

sub.desc_en: Rava provides an alternative explanation for Rabbi Yosi's ruling, attributing it to a decree (גזירה) due to the case of Beit Horon (מתנת בית חורון), where people would make hefker (הפקר) to circumvent vows.

items.text: Baraita on the time limit for retracting hefker
items.text_en: Baraita on the time limit for retracting hefker
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who declares his field hefker can retract within three days, but after that cannot retract.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who declares his field hefker can retract within three days, but after that cannot retract.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one declares a field ownerless for a limited period, both he and another can retract before anyone takes possession, but after possession, neither can retract. The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause seems to follow the Rabbis (who hold that temporary hefker is valid), while the second clause follows Rabbi Yosei (who holds that temporary hefker is invalid).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of temporary ownerless property: before anyone takes possession, both the owner and another may retract; after possession, neither may retract.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause follows the Rabbis (who hold temporary hefker valid), while the second clause follows Rabbi Yosei (who holds it invalid).

items.text: Ulla's answer: Both clauses follow the Rabbis
items.text_en: Ulla's answer: Both clauses follow the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis. The reason the first clause allows retraction before possession is that a year or a septennate is uncommon, so the declaration is not considered a valid hefker until someone actually takes possession.

sub.desc_en: Ulla argues that the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis, and the reason the first clause allows retraction before possession is that a year or a septennate is uncommon, so the declaration is not considered a valid hefker until someone actually takes possession.

items.text: Reish Lakish's answer: Both clauses follow Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's answer: Both clauses follow Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei. The first clause allows retraction before possession because otherwise the institution of hefker would be undermined, as people would declare ownerless property and then retract.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish answers that both clauses follow Rabbi Yosei, explaining that the first clause allows retraction before possession only to prevent the institution of hefker (ownerless property) from being undermined by people who declare property ownerless and then retract.

items.text: Objection and Rabba's answer
items.text_en: Objection and Rabba's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the concern is that hefker would be undermined, then even from the first day the declaration should be valid. Rabba answers that the concern is specifically for deceivers who declare hefker and then retract, so the Rabbis instituted that temporary hefker is not valid until possession is taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the concern is that hefker would be undermined, then even from the first day the declaration should be valid.
Rabba answers that the concern is specifically for deceivers who declare hefker and then retract, so the Rabbis instituted that temporary hefker is not valid until possession is taken.

items.text: Question about Torah law
items.text_en: Question about Torah law
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, according to Torah law, such a temporary declaration is not considered hefker at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, according to Torah law, a temporary declaration of hefker is not considered hefker at all.

items.text: Gemara's response to the concern of improper tithing
items.text_en: Gemara's response to the concern of improper tithing
items.desc_en: The Gemara dismisses the concern that one might come to tithe from the obligated on the exempt or vice versa, stating that we instruct him to tithe from the produce itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the concern that one might come to tithe from the obligated produce on the exempt or vice versa.
The Gemara dismisses the concern by stating that we instruct him to tithe from the produce itself.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about one who consecrates his vineyard
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about one who consecrates his vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one who consecrates his vineyard and then harvests it is obligated in the gifts for the poor but exempt from tithes. This challenges Reish Lakish's view, as according to him the exemption should not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one who consecrates his vineyard and harvests it the next morning is obligated in the poor gifts but exempt from tithes.
The Gemara objects: according to Ulla the baraita is consistent, but according to Reish Lakish, why is the vineyard exempt from tithes?
Reish Lakish responds that his ruling applies only according to Rabbi Yosi, while this baraita reflects the view of the Rabbis.

items.text: Reish Lakish's resolution
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's resolution
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish responds that his statement was according to Rabbi Yosei, while this baraita follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish resolves the contradiction by stating that his own statement follows Rabbi Yosei, while the baraita follows the Rabbis.

items.text: First answer: distinction between two and three witnesses
items.text_en: First answer: distinction between two and three witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an answer to a previous question by distinguishing between cases: one where the owner declared hefker before two witnesses (invalid) and one before three (valid). It cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that hefker before three is valid, before two is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a distinction: if the owner declared hefker before two witnesses it is invalid, but before three it is valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that hefker before three is valid, before two is not.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's alternative position
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's alternative position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argues that by Torah law, hefker is valid even before one witness, but the Sages required three so that one can acquire the property and two can testify.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that by Torah law even one witness suffices for hefker, but the Sages required three so that one can acquire and two can testify.
He explains that the Sages required three witnesses so that one can acquire the property and two can testify to the act of hefker.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that partners who vowed not to benefit from each other are forbidden to enter the shared courtyard. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov offers a dissenting view: each may enter his own portion.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the general rule: partners who vowed not to benefit from each other are forbidden to enter the shared courtyard.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov offers a dissenting view: each partner may enter his own portion of the courtyard.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents laws of a shared courtyard when one partner is forbidden by vow from benefiting from the other. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits the non-vowed partner to enter claiming his own share, and the court forces the vower to sell his share. It also discusses a third party from the market who is under a vow with one of the partners, and cases of a bathhouse or olive press that are rented out.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule that both partners in a shared courtyard are forbidden to set up a mill, oven, or raise chickens.
The Tanna Kamma states that if one partner is under a vow forbidding benefit from the other, the vower may not enter the courtyard.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits the non-vowed partner to enter, claiming he enters only his own share.
The Mishnah adds that the court forces the vower to sell his share.
The Tanna Kamma rules that if a third party from the market is under a vow with one of the partners, that third party may not enter the courtyard.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits the third party to enter, claiming he enters only the other partner's share.
The Mishnah discusses a case where the vower has a rented bathhouse or olive press in the city: if he has a claim of possession (תפיסת יד) it is forbidden, otherwise it is permitted.
The Mishnah distinguishes between a vow that refers to the other's property (permitted after death or sale) and a vow that refers to the specific object (forbidden even after death or sale).

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Did the Sages dispute only when both partners voluntarily vowed (נדרו), but if one was forced by the other's vow (הדירו), do they agree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that it is like coercion? Or do they dispute even in the case of coercion?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: Did the Sages dispute only when both partners voluntarily vowed (נדרו), but if one was forced by the other's vow (הדירו), do they agree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that it is like coercion? Or do they dispute even in the case of coercion?

items.text: First attempted resolution from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First attempted resolution from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'one of them was under a vow of benefit from his fellow,' which implies the Sages disputed. However, the text is corrected to read 'vowed' (נדור) rather than 'was under a vow' (מודר), suggesting the dispute is only about voluntary vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the inquiry by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'one of them was forbidden (מודר) by vow from his fellow,' and notes that the baraita explicitly teaches 'vowed (נדור) from his fellow,' implying the dispute applies even when one was coerced by the other's vow.

items.text: Supporting proof from the Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Supporting proof from the Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah's statement 'they force the vower to sell his share' supports the interpretation that the dispute is about voluntary vows, because if it were a coerced vow, why would the court force him? He is already coerced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides logical support: the Mishnah's continuation states 'they force the one who vowed (הנודר) to sell his share,' which only makes sense if he voluntarily vowed; if he was coerced by the other's vow, why would they force him, since he is compelled?

items.text: Citation of a tradition from Rabbah and Ze'iri
items.text_en: Citation of a tradition from Rabbah and Ze'iri
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites Ze'iri, likely providing a definitive ruling or further clarification on the matter, though the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah begins to cite a statement in the name of Ze'iri, introducing further discussion.

items.text: Opening statement on the dispute
items.text_en: Opening statement on the dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when there is enough property to divide, there is a dispute; but when there is not enough, all agree it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: when there is enough property to divide, there is a dispute; when there is not enough, all agree it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges the Mishnah by citing the case of a synagogue, which is like something insufficient for division, yet the Mishnah rules both are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to the Mishnah's ruling by citing the case of a synagogue, which is like something insufficient for division, yet the Mishnah rules both are forbidden regarding a matter of that city.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution via Ze'iri
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution via Ze'iri
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by citing Ze'iri, who reverses the Mishnah's ruling: the dispute is when there is not enough to divide, but when there is enough, all agree it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by citing Ze'iri, who reverses the Mishnah's ruling: the dispute is when there is not enough to divide, but when there is enough, all agree it is forbidden.

items.text: Halakhic ruling in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Elazar both rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rabbi Elazar independently affirms that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: The case of a bathhouse and the extent of joint ownership
items.text_en: The case of a bathhouse and the extent of joint ownership
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of one who is forbidden from benefiting from a friend and has a share in a bathhouse. Rav Nachman defines the extent of ownership as half, third, or quarter, but less is permitted; Abaye argues that even less is forbidden, and explains when it is permitted—when he receives it as a tax.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah case of one who is forbidden from benefiting from a friend and has a share in a bathhouse.
The Gemara asks how much ownership share constitutes a significant holding in the bathhouse.
Rav Nachman defines the threshold as half, third, or quarter ownership; less than that is permitted.
Abaye argues that even less than a quarter share is forbidden.
Abaye explains that it is permitted only when he receives the bathhouse as a tax (טסקא), not as an owner.

items.text: Abimi's question about a vow on a house after sale or death
items.text_en: Abimi's question about a vow on a house after sale or death
items.desc_en: Abimi asks: if one says 'konam to this house that you enter' and the house is sold or the owner dies, does the vow still apply? The question is whether a person can forbid something that is currently in his domain from the time it leaves his domain.

sub.desc_en: Abimi asks whether a vow forbidding entry to a house remains effective after the house is sold or the owner dies, i.e., whether a person can forbid something currently in his domain from the time it leaves his domain.

items.text: Rava's proof from the Mishnah about a son inheriting
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the Mishnah about a son inheriting
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from a Mishnah: if a father says to his son 'konam that you benefit from me' and the father dies, the son inherits; but if he says 'in my life and after my death', the son does not inherit. This shows that a person can forbid something that is in his domain even for after it leaves his domain.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a father who forbids his son from benefiting from him: if the father dies, the son inherits unless the vow explicitly includes death, proving that a person can forbid something from the time it leaves his domain.
The Mishnah adds that if the father says 'in my life and after my death', the son does not inherit.
The Gemara concludes that this proves a person can forbid something that is in his domain even for after it leaves his domain.

items.text: Mishnah about forbidden produce and their substitutes
items.text_en: Mishnah about forbidden produce and their substitutes
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if one says 'konam these fruits upon me' or 'konam they are to my mouth', he is forbidden from their substitutes and their growths. This sets the stage for a new question about forbidding another person's produce.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if one vows 'konam these fruits upon me' or similar formulations, he is forbidden from their substitutes and growths, establishing a principle about vowing on future entities.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about forbidding another's produce
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about forbidding another's produce
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if one says 'konam these fruits upon so-and-so', are the substitutes forbidden? He distinguishes between one's own case, where a person can forbid another's fruits on himself, and another's case, where a person cannot forbid another's fruits on that other person. The question is whether this extends to things not yet in existence.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a vow forbidding specific fruits to another person applies to their substitutes, reasoning that since one can forbid another's fruits on himself, he might also forbid future entities on himself, but regarding another person, since one cannot forbid another's fruits on that other, future entities are also not forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's unresolved dilemma
items.text_en: Gemara's unresolved dilemma
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the unresolved question: whether exchanged items are considered like the original prohibited items, such that the prohibition applies to both the original and the exchanged item, or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the unresolved question: whether exchanged items are considered like the original prohibited items, such that the prohibition applies to both the original and the exchanged item, or not.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's attempted proof
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's attempted proof
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi brings a proof from a case where a husband prohibits his wife from benefiting from him, yet creditors can collect from him. He argues this shows that exchanged items are not like the original prohibited items, since the husband's property (which is exchanged for the loan) is not prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Minyomi cites a baraita about a husband who forbids his wife from benefiting from him, where creditors can collect from her, implying that exchanged items (the loan repayment) are not like the original prohibited item.

items.text: Rava's rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rava's rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: Rava rejects the proof, suggesting that the creditors' collection is only post-facto (דיעבד), not initially permitted (לכתחילה). Thus, the case does not prove that exchanged items are permitted ab initio.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the proof, suggesting that the baraita only permits creditors to collect בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard), leaving the dilemma unresolved.

items.text: Alternative proof from orlah
items.text_en: Alternative proof from orlah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another attempted proof from the laws of orlah: if one sells orlah fruit and uses the proceeds for betrothal, the betrothal is valid. This suggests that exchanged items are not like the original. However, the Gemara again rejects it, saying the same distinction applies: it is only post-facto.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about one who betroths with orlah fruit (ערלה) and then sells it and betroths with the proceeds, where the betrothal is valid, but Rava's same distinction applies: only בדיעבד (after the fact) is permitted.
The Gemara rejects the proof, applying the same distinction: the betrothal is only valid בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (a-priori).

items.text: Mishnah: Mutual vows of prohibition
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mutual vows of prohibition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new case: if one says 'I am hereby banned to you' or 'you are hereby banned to me', the one who is prohibited is bound. If both say it, both are prohibited, but both are permitted to use items dedicated to the Temple in Babylon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rules of one who declares another's property as חרם (dedicated property), specifying who is forbidden and who is permitted regarding items of עולי בבל (those who ascended from Babylonia).
The Mishnah continues: if one says 'You are hereby banned to me', the one who makes the vow (the speaker) is bound.
The Mishnah concludes: if both say 'I am banned to you and you are banned to me', both are prohibited, but both are permitted to use items dedicated to the Temple in Babylon.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Things belonging to עולי בבל and the town, and the rule of writing one's share to the Nasi
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Things belonging to עולי בבל and the town, and the rule of writing one's share to the Nasi
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines what constitutes property of עולי בבל (e.g., the Temple Mount, courtyards, the well on the road) and property of the town (e.g., the plaza, bathhouse, synagogue, ark, scrolls). It then states that one who vows not to benefit from townspeople may write his share to the Nasi. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between writing to the Nasi (no need for formal acquisition) and to a commoner (needs acquisition). The Sages say both require acquisition, and the mention of Nasi is only as a common case. Rabbi Yehuda adds that Galileans need not write because their ancestors already wrote on their behalf.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines property of עולי בבל (Temple Mount, courtyards, roadside well) and property of the town (plaza, bathhouse, synagogue, ark, scrolls), and states that one who vows not to benefit from townspeople may write his share to the Nasi.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between writing to the Nasi (no formal acquisition needed) and to a commoner (acquisition needed).
The Sages say both require acquisition, and the mention of Nasi is only as a common case.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that Galileans need not write because their ancestors already wrote on their behalf.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is it prohibited?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is it prohibited?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the property is prohibited to the vow-maker. Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah is actually stating the remedy: they should write their share to the Nasi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the property is prohibited to the vow-maker.
Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah is actually stating the remedy: they should write their share to the Nasi.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation about Galileans
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation about Galileans
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda explains that the Galileans were quarrelsome (קנטרנין) and would vow not to benefit from each other, so their ancestors wrote their shares to the Nasi. This clarifies the Mishnah's earlier statement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda explains that the Galileans were quarrelsome and would vow not to benefit from each other, so their ancestors wrote their shares to the Nasi.

items.text: Mishnah: Case of a son circumventing his father's vow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Case of a son circumventing his father's vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a son, whose father vowed not to benefit from him, gives a courtyard and meal to a friend as a gift, with the condition that the father may come and eat. The friend then declares the items consecrated, leading to a dispute. The Sages rule that any gift that cannot be consecrated is not a valid gift.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows not to benefit from a friend and has nothing to eat may give to another as a gift, and the recipient is permitted to give to the vow-maker.
The Mishnah recounts a story from Beit Choron where a father vowed not to benefit from his son, and the son gave a courtyard and meal to a friend with the condition that the father could join.
The friend objects that if the gift were truly his, he would dedicate it to Heaven, and the son clarifies the gift was conditional on the father's participation.
The Sages rule that any gift which cannot be freely dedicated to Heaven is not a valid gift.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the story seems to contradict the Mishnah's earlier ruling. It explains that the Mishnah is incomplete and should read: if the end proves the beginning, it is prohibited. The story from Beit Horon is an example where the end proved the beginning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the story contradicts the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: if the end proves the beginning, it is forbidden, and the story illustrates that case.
