items.text: Rava's distinction: Wording of the gift
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: Wording of the gift
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the prohibition applies only when the giver says 'and they are before you' (והינן לפניך), indicating the gift is conditional. But if he says 'they are before you' (הן לפניך) without the 'and', it is a valid gift. A second version states that even with 'הן לפניך' it is prohibited because the meal itself testifies to the intent.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes that the prohibition applies only when the giver says 'והינן לפניך' (and they are before you), indicating a conditional gift, but if he says 'שיהו לפניך' (they shall be before you), it is a valid gift given willingly.
A second version states that even if the giver says 'הן לפניך' (they are before you), it is still prohibited because the meal itself testifies to the conditional intent.

items.text: The case of the father and the son who steals flax bundles
items.text_en: The case of the father and the son who steals flax bundles
items.desc_en: A man whose son steals flax bundles vows his property away from him. When asked what if his grandson becomes a Torah scholar, he says the property should be acquired by the grandson. The Gemara asks: what is the halakhic status of this arrangement?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a man whose son steals flax bundles vows his property away from him, and when asked about a grandson who becomes a Torah scholar, he says the property should be acquired by the grandson; the Gemara asks what the halakhic status of this arrangement is.

items.text: Pumbedita's opinion: 'kinyan al menat lehaknot' does not acquire
items.text_en: Pumbedita's opinion: 'kinyan al menat lehaknot' does not acquire
items.desc_en: The Pumbedita scholars say this is a case of 'acquire on condition to transfer', and such an acquisition is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Pumbedita scholars rule that this is a case of 'acquire on condition to transfer' (קני על מנת להקנות), and such an acquisition is invalid.

items.text: Rav Nachman's opinion: it is valid, like a sudarium
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's opinion: it is valid, like a sudarium
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman argues that such an acquisition is valid, because a sudarium (used in kinyan sudar) is itself an acquisition on condition to transfer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman argues that such an acquisition is valid, because a sudarium (סודרא) used in kinyan sudar is itself an acquisition on condition to transfer (קני על מנת להקנות).

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection: the sudarium is different
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection: the sudarium is different
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rav Nachman: who says the sudarium is not truly acquired? Moreover, the sudarium is acquired immediately and then transferred, whereas here the acquisition is conditional on a future event, so the sudarium returns to its owner.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rav Nachman's analogy: the sudarium (סודרא) is acquired immediately and then transferred, whereas here the acquisition is conditional on a future event, so the sudarium returns to its owner.

items.text: Rava's challenge from the Beit Horon incident
items.text_en: Rava's challenge from the Beit Horon incident
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: the Beit Horon gift was also a 'kinyan al menat lehaknot', and it was not valid!

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman's position by citing the Beit Horon gift, which was also a 'קני על מנת להקנות' (acquisition on condition to transfer) and yet was not valid.

items.text: Two answers: due to the meal or Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Two answers: due to the meal or Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman gives two answers: sometimes he says the meal accompanying the gift proves intent, and sometimes he says it follows Rabbi Eliezer who prohibits even a trivial benefit for one who is forbidden to derive benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that sometimes the meal accompanying the gift proves the donor's intent to give a full gift.
Rav Nachman alternatively answers that the case follows Rabbi Eliezer, who prohibits even a trivial benefit (ויתור) for one who is forbidden to derive benefit.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah: 'all gifts that cannot be consecrated'
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah: 'all gifts that cannot be consecrated'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that any gift which, if consecrated, would not be consecrated, is not a valid gift. It asks whether this includes the case of the flax bundles, and answers that it refers to Rava's later statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that any gift which, if consecrated, would not be consecrated, is not a valid gift.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah's inclusive term 'all' comes to include.
The Gemara proposes that the inclusive term comes to include the case of the flax bundles discussed earlier.
The Gemara rejects the proposal and answers that the inclusive term refers to the latter version of Rava's statement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between one who vows from 'cooked' (מבושל) and one who vows from 'a cooked dish' (תבשיל), detailing what is permitted and forbidden in each case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rule: one who vows from 'cooked' (מבושל) is permitted roasted and boiled, but one who vows from 'a cooked dish' (תבשיל) is forbidden all pot-cooked items.

items.text: Gemara's discussion of Rabbi Yoshiyah's position
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of Rabbi Yoshiyah's position
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yoshiyah who forbids roasted meat to one who vows from 'cooked', citing a verse about cooking the Passover. The Gemara initially suggests a dispute over following Torah language vs. common parlance, but resolves that both follow common parlance, differing only by locale. The verse is merely a support, not a proof.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yoshiyah who forbids roasted meat to one who vowed from 'cooked', citing the verse 'וַיְבַשְּׁלוּ אֶת הַפֶּסַח בָּאֵשׁ' (they cooked the Passover in fire) as a support.
The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about whether to follow לשון תורה (Torah language) or לשון בני אדם (common parlance) in vows.

The Gemara rejects the proposal, stating that both follow common parlance, differing only by locale: in the Tanna's locale, roasted is called 'צָלִי' and cooked 'מְבוּשָּׁל', while in Rabbi Yoshiyah's locale, even roasted is called 'מְבוּשָּׁל'.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction of citing a verse, explaining it is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion), not a proof.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'cooked dish' and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'cooked dish' and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits certain items when one vows from 'cooked dish' (תבשיל), since they are indeed cooked dishes. Abaye explains that the Tanna calls anything eaten with bread a 'cooked dish', citing a baraita that includes soft gourds and the like.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah permits certain items despite the vow being from 'cooked dish' (תבשיל), since they are indeed cooked dishes.
Abaye explains that this Tanna (תנא) calls anything eaten with bread a 'cooked dish' (תבשיל), citing a baraita that includes soft gourds and the like.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yirmeya's story and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yirmeya's story and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's explanation with a story about Rabbi Yirmeya, where a doctor fled upon seeing a gourd (קרא) in his house, implying it is not a food for the sick. The Gemara resolves that soft gourds are different from hard ones, and Rava bar Ulla adds a distinction between the gourd itself and its inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Abaye's explanation by citing a story about Rabbi Yirmeya, where a doctor fled upon seeing a gourd (קרא) in his house, implying that gourds are not a food for the sick.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between soft gourds (בְּרַכִּיכֵי) and hard ones (בְּאַשּׁוּנֵי), and Rava bar Ulla adds a distinction between the gourd itself and its inside, citing Rav Yehuda's statement about the danger of eating gourd shoots with beets.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of 'cholim'
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of 'cholim'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that 'cholim' in the baraita refers to rabbis (רבנן), not ordinary sick people, consistent with his own view.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that 'חולין' (ordinary people) in the baraita refers to rabbis, consistent with his own view that rabbis eat gourds with bread.

items.text: Opening discussion on the Mishnah's terms
items.text_en: Opening discussion on the Mishnah's terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's terms 'קצירי' and 'מריעי' are interpreted according to Rabbi Yosi, where 'קצירי' refers to actual reapers and 'מריעי' to rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to whom do we pray for the reapers and the rabbis? — according to Rabbi Yosi.
The Gemara explains: from the fact that the Mishnah says 'קצירי' and 'מריעי', it implies that 'קצירי' means actual reapers and 'מריעי' means rabbis, consistent with Rabbi Yosi's view.

items.text: Mishnah's allowance of thick bread
items.text_en: Mishnah's allowance of thick bread
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling about being permitted to eat thick bread contradicts the practice of Babylonians, who eat bread with bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's allowance of thick bread contradicts the Babylonian practice of eating bread with bread, as stated by Rabbi Zeira.

items.text: Question about eating deisa
items.text_en: Question about eating deisa
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks the date-gatherers of Hutzal a question: should deisa made from wheat be eaten with wheat bread or barley bread, and vice versa?

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks the date-gatherers of Hutzal whether deisa (a dish) made from wheat should be eaten with wheat bread or barley bread, and vice versa.

items.text: Stories about eating deisa
items.text_en: Stories about eating deisa
items.desc_en: Rava ate deisa with חסיסי (a type of bread). Rabba bar Rav Huna saw Rav Huna eating deisa with his fingers and explained that eating with fingers is tastier. Rav instructed his son Chiyya and Rav Huna instructed his son Rabba that one should travel up to a parasang for deisa and up to three parasangs for beef, and that one should spit out anything before one's teacher except for kara and deisa, which are like an arrow of lead.

sub.desc_en: Rava ate deisa with חסיסי (a type of bread), demonstrating a specific way of eating it.

sub.text: Narrative: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna saw Rav Huna eating deisa with his fingers and explained that eating with fingers is tastier, and even more so with two or three fingers.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav's and Rav Huna's instructions to their sons
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav's and Rav Huna's instructions to their sons
sub.desc_en: Rav instructed his son Chiyya and Rav Huna instructed his son Rabba that one should travel up to a parasang for deisa and up to three parasangs for beef, and that one should spit out anything before one's teacher except for kara and deisa, which are like an arrow of lead.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda about eating deisa
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda about eating deisa
items.desc_en: One of them ate deisa with his fingers and the other with a thorn. The one eating with a thorn complained about eating the other's feces, while the one eating with his fingers complained about eating the other's saliva.

sub.desc_en: The stam describes a dispute between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda: one ate deisa with his fingers and the other with a thorn, and the finger-eater complained that the thorn-eater was feeding him his feces.
The finger-eater retorts to the thorn-eater: 'Until when will you feed me your saliva?'

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on blusfin
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on blusfin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ate blusfin (a type of food) while Rabbi Shimon did not, arguing that it does not leave the bowels at all. Rabbi Yehuda countered that this is all the more reason to rely on it for the next day.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces that blusfin (a type of food) was brought before Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon; Rabbi Yehuda ate it, but Rabbi Shimon did not.
Rabbi Yehuda asks Rabbi Shimon why he did not eat the blusfin.
Rabbi Shimon explains that blusfin do not leave the bowels at all, so eating them provides no benefit for the next day.
Rabbi Yehuda counters that since blusfin remain in the bowels, all the more reason to rely on them for the next day's sustenance.

items.text: Anecdotes about Rabbi Yehuda's appearance
items.text_en: Anecdotes about Rabbi Yehuda's appearance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon noted Rabbi Yehuda's yellow face, which he attributed to eating radishes without salt. A matronita accused him of being a drunkard, but he denied it, attributing his shining face to wisdom. A heretic said his face resembled that of a usurer or pig-breeder, but Rabbi Yehuda explained it was due to his many trips to the bathroom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon notes Rabbi Yehuda's yellow face, and Rabbi Yehuda explains it was from eating radishes without salt.
A matronita accuses Rabbi Yehuda of being a drunkard, but he denies it, attributing his shining face to wisdom.
A heretic says Rabbi Yehuda's face resembles that of a usurer or pig-breeder, but Rabbi Yehuda explains it is due to his many trips to the bathroom.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's practices and a story about a cloak
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's practices and a story about a cloak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon would carry tools to the study hall, praising labor. Rabbi Yehuda's wife made a cloak from wool, which they both used. When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel decreed a fast, Rabbi Yehuda did not attend because he lacked a cloak; when one was sent, he refused it.

sub.text: Narrative about Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Narrative about Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The narrative describes how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon would carry tools to the study hall, each praising labor as honoring its owner.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yehuda's wife and the cloak
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yehuda's wife and the cloak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda's wife made a fine wool cloak, which she wore in the market and Rabbi Yehuda wore for prayer, reciting a blessing for being wrapped in a garment.

sub.text: Story about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's fast
sub.text_en: Story about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's fast
sub.desc_en: When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel decreed a fast, Rabbi Yehuda did not attend because he lacked a cloak; when one was sent to him, he refused it.

items.text: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Akiva's poverty
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Akiva's poverty
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how Rabbi Akiva, while poor, would remove straw from his wife's hair and promise her a golden Jerusalem if he had means. Elijah appears as a beggar asking for straw, highlighting their destitution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an anecdote: Rabbi Akiva, while poor, removes straw from his wife's hair and promises her a golden Jerusalem; Elijah appears as a beggar asking for straw, highlighting their destitution.

items.text: Background: Kalba Savua's vow and the marriage
items.text_en: Background: Kalba Savua's vow and the marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Kalba Savua vowed to forbid his daughter from benefiting from his property after she married Rabbi Akiva, who was then unlearned. She married him anyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Akiva became engaged to the daughter of Kalba Savua, who took a vow prohibiting her from benefiting from his property, yet she married Rabbi Akiva despite this.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's poverty and his wife's encouragement
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's poverty and his wife's encouragement
items.desc_en: In winter, they slept in a straw hut; Rabbi Akiva picked straw from her hair. He promised her a golden Jerusalem. Elijah came as a beggar asking for straw, and Rabbi Akiva remarked that even straw is lacking for some.

sub.desc_en: The story continues during a winter when they slept in a straw hut; Rabbi Akiva removes straw from her hair and promises her a golden Jerusalem; Elijah appears as a beggar needing straw for his wife, and Rabbi Akiva comments on the man's poverty.
Rabbi Akiva promises his wife that if he could, he would give her a golden Jerusalem.
Elijah appears disguised as a beggar asking for straw for his wife who just gave birth, demonstrating that some lack even straw.
Rabbi Akiva points out to his wife that there is a man who lacks even straw, putting their own poverty in perspective.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's departure to study and his wife's patience
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's departure to study and his wife's patience
items.desc_en: His wife urged him to go study. He studied for twelve years before Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Upon returning, he overheard a wicked man mocking his wife, but she encouraged him to study another twelve years. He agreed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva's wife urges him to go study; he spends twelve years with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, returns home overhearing her wish for him to continue, and goes back for another twelve years.
Upon returning home, Rabbi Akiva overhears a wicked man mocking his wife's patience.
His wife encourages him to study another twelve years, and he agrees, returning for an additional twelve years of study.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's return with students and reconciliation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's return with students and reconciliation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva returned with 24,000 pairs of students. The whole town came out to greet him, including his wife. The wicked man mocked her, but she quoted Proverbs 12:10. The rabbis tried to push her away, but Rabbi Akiva declared that his and their Torah is hers. Kalba Savua then had his vow annulled.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva returns with 24,000 disciples; his wife comes to meet him, he declares that what is his and theirs is hers; Kalba Savua has his vow annulled and is permitted.
Rabbi Akiva's wife also rises to greet him, and the wicked man mocks her, asking where she thinks she is going.
She responds by quoting Proverbs 12:10, 'A righteous man knows the soul of his animal,' implying that Rabbi Akiva recognizes her worth.
When she comes to show herself to Rabbi Akiva, the rabbis try to push her away.
Rabbi Akiva declares that they should leave her alone, for his Torah and theirs is hers.
Kalba Savua hears of this, comes to have his vow annulled, and it is permitted.

items.text: Six sources of Rabbi Akiva's wealth
items.text_en: Six sources of Rabbi Akiva's wealth
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists six ways Rabbi Akiva became wealthy: from Kalba Savua, from a deer found on a ship, from a nut that was full of dinars, from a certain woman (serukita), and from a matron.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rabbi Akiva became wealthy from six sources, beginning with Kalba Savua.
The Gemara recounts the second source: a deer found on a ship, which the sailors had been using as a talisman and which Rabbi Akiva discovered when they forgot it on the shore.

The Gemara recounts the third source: a nut found on the shore that was full of dinars, and then lists the remaining three sources (a certain woman called serukita, and a matron) without further elaboration.

items.text: Opening continuation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening continuation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes its list of permitted items, mentioning the wife of Tornosrufus and Ketia bar Shalom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes its list of permitted items, mentioning two specific individuals, the wife of Tornosrufus and Ketia bar Shalom.

items.text: Story of Rav Gammada and the monkey
items.text_en: Story of Rav Gammada and the monkey
items.desc_en: Rav Gammada gave four zuz to merchants to buy something; they bought a monkey, which escaped into a hole, and they found it sitting on pearls, bringing all to him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav Gammada gave four zuz to merchants to buy something; they bought a monkey, which escaped into a hole, and they found it sitting on pearls, bringing all to him.

items.text: Dialogue between the Caesar's daughter and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.text_en: Dialogue between the Caesar's daughter and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.desc_en: The Caesar's daughter questions why the Torah is contained in an ugly vessel (the body). Rabbi Yehoshua uses a parable about storing wine in clay vessels to explain that the Torah is best preserved in humble people. He adds that if the sages were ugly, they would be even more learned.

sub.desc_en: The Caesar's daughter asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why the Torah, which is glorious, is contained in an ugly vessel (the body).
Rabbi Yehoshua responds with a parable: just as wine is stored in clay vessels, so too the Torah is preserved in humble people; the daughter's father stores wine in clay vessels, not silver or gold.
The daughter tests the parable by putting wine in silver and gold vessels, and it spoils; Rabbi Yehoshua confirms that the Torah is similarly preserved in humble vessels.
The daughter objects that there are handsome sages who are also learned, contradicting the idea that ugliness is necessary for Torah study.
Rabbi Yehoshua resolves that if those handsome sages were ugly, they would be even more learned.

items.text: Case before Rav Yehuda and the woman's insult
items.text_en: Case before Rav Yehuda and the woman's insult
items.desc_en: A woman who lost a case before Rav Yehuda from Nehardea insulted Shmuel by describing him as short and ugly. Rav Yehuda placed her under a ban, and she died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a woman came before Rav Yehuda of Nehardea for judgment and lost.
The woman challenges Rav Yehuda's ruling by insulting Shmuel, describing him as short, pot-bellied, black-skinned, and large-toothed.
Rav Yehuda places the woman under a ban (שמתא) for insulting Shmuel, and she dies as a result.

items.text: Definition of 'beitzah tormita'
items.text_en: Definition of 'beitzah tormita'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a 'beitzah tormita' is an egg prepared by a slave, worth a thousand dinar, boiled in hot and cold water a thousand times until it shrinks to be swallowed. It is used for diagnosis: if a patient has pain, the egg is rubbed on the body, and when it comes out, the doctor knows the remedy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of a 'beitzah tormita'.
Shmuel describes the intricate preparation of the 'beitzah tormita' and its diagnostic use.

items.text: Shmuel's medical self-test
items.text_en: Shmuel's medical self-test
items.desc_en: Shmuel would test himself with a kulkha (a type of gourd) until his household would tear their hair over him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara relates that Shmuel would test himself with a kulkha (a type of gourd) to the point that his household would tear their hair over him.

items.text: Mishnah about klufsin and bnot sheva
items.text_en: Mishnah about klufsin and bnot sheva
items.desc_en: A baraita states: If one eats klufsin, he should not eat bnot sheva, and vice versa. The Gemara defines klufsin as a type of fig used for making lafdei (cakes).

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule: one who eats klufsin should not eat bnot sheva, and vice versa.
The Gemara asks for the definition of 'klufsin'.
The Gemara explains that klufsin is a type of fig used for making lafdei (cakes).

items.text: Case of the slave and the lafdei
items.text_en: Case of the slave and the lafdei
items.desc_en: A man gave his slave to a friend to teach him a thousand types of lafdei (cakes), but he taught only eight hundred. They came before Rabbi for judgment, and Rabbi lamented that the earlier generations knew the good, but they did not even see it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man gave his slave to a friend to teach him a thousand types of lafdei (cakes).
The friend taught only eight hundred types, and they came before Rabbi for judgment.
Rabbi laments that earlier generations knew the good, but they did not even see it.

items.text: Rabbi's wedding for Rabbi Shimon and Bar Kappara's response
items.text_en: Rabbi's wedding for Rabbi Shimon and Bar Kappara's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi made a wedding for his son Rabbi Shimon, spending 24,000 myriad dinar, but did not invite Bar Kappara. Bar Kappara commented that if this is done for those who transgress His will, how much more for those who do His will. Rabbi then invited him, and Bar Kappara added that if this is for those who do His will in this world, how much more in the World to Come. The Gemara notes that on the day Rabbi laughed, calamity came to the world, so he told Bar Kappara not to make him laugh, and he would give him forty se'ah of wheat.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens: Rabbi made a wedding feast for his son Rabbi Shimon, spending 24,000 myriad dinar on the garden house, but did not invite Bar Kappara.
Bar Kappara objects to being excluded, remarking that if this feast is made for those who transgress God's will, how much more for those who do His will.

sub.text: Rabbi's invitation and Bar Kappara's second remark
sub.text_en: Rabbi's invitation and Bar Kappara's second remark
sub.desc_en: Rabbi then invites Bar Kappara, who adds that if this is for those who do His will in this world, how much more in the World to Come.
The Gemara notes that on the day Rabbi laughed, calamity came to the world, so he told Bar Kappara not to make him laugh.
Rabbi offers Bar Kappara forty se'ah of wheat if he refrains from making him laugh, and Bar Kappara responds with a request for Rabbi to see something.

items.text: Bar Kappara's first riddle and demand for wheat
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's first riddle and demand for wheat
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara approaches Rabbi with a riddle, claiming he is taking wheat that he taught him. Rabbi rebukes him for jesting, but Bar Kappara insists he is taking the wheat he taught.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara declares that he takes every griva of wheat he wants.
Bar Kappara takes a large basket, covers it with pitch, and places it on his head.
Bar Kappara asks Rabbi to give him forty griva of wheat that he taught him.
Rabbi rebukes Bar Kappara for jesting.
Bar Kappara insists he is taking the wheat he taught.

items.text: Bar Kappara's boast to Rabbi's daughter
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's boast to Rabbi's daughter
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara tells Rabbi's daughter that tomorrow they will drink wine at the dance of her father and the clapping of her mother. The narrative introduces Ben El'ashah, Rabbi's wealthy son-in-law, who was invited to the wedding feast of Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara tells Rabbi's daughter that tomorrow they will drink wine at the dance of her father and the clapping of her mother, introducing Ben El'ashah, Rabbi's wealthy son-in-law, who was invited to the wedding feast of Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi.

items.text: Bar Kappara interprets 'To'eva'
items.text_en: Bar Kappara interprets 'To'eva'
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi the meaning of 'To'eva'. When Rabbi gives an answer, Bar Kappara refutes it. Rabbi asks Bar Kappara to explain, and Bar Kappara demands that Rabbi's household throw him a cup. After receiving it, he tells Rabbi to dance for him, and then explains: 'To'eva' means 'you err in her' (to'eh atah bah).

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi the meaning of 'תּוֹעֵבָה' (abomination), and after Rabbi gives an answer, Bar Kappara refutes it.
Rabbi asks Bar Kappara to explain, Bar Kappara demands a cup and a dance from Rabbi, then explains that 'תּוֹעֵבָה' means 'תּוֹעֶה אַתָּה בָּהּ' (you err in her).

items.text: Bar Kappara interprets 'Tevel'
items.text_en: Bar Kappara interprets 'Tevel'
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi the meaning of 'Tevel'. Rabbi gives a similar answer, but Bar Kappara demands that Rabbi perform for him again. Bar Kappara then explains: 'Tevel' means 'there is a seasoning (tavlin) in it'. He then asks rhetorically: Is this intercourse different from all other forbidden acts?

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi the meaning of the word 'Tevel' (תֶּבֶל) in the context of forbidden intercourse.
Rabbi gives a similar answer to the previous one, but Bar Kappara demands that Rabbi perform for him again.
Bar Kappara explains that 'Tevel' means 'there is a seasoning (tavlin) in it', and then asks rhetorically whether this forbidden intercourse is different from all other forbidden acts.

items.text: Bar Kappara interprets 'Zimmah' and Ben El'ashah flees
items.text_en: Bar Kappara interprets 'Zimmah' and Ben El'ashah flees
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi the meaning of 'Zimmah'. Rabbi tells him to do as before. Bar Kappara performs and says 'This is what it is'. Ben El'ashah could not bear it, so he and his wife left the wedding feast.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi what the word 'Zimmah' means.
Rabbi tells Bar Kappara to perform the same action as before.
Bar Kappara performs the action and says 'This is what it is'.
Ben El'ashah could not bear it, so he and his wife left the wedding feast.

items.text: Explanation of Ben El'ashah and the High Priest's haircut
items.text_en: Explanation of Ben El'ashah and the High Priest's haircut
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the identity of Ben El'ashah: he was the one who scattered his money to demonstrate the High Priest's haircut style. The haircut is described as a 'lulyanit' (a single haircut), with Rava explaining that one head is next to the other's root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the identity of Ben El'ashah and cites a baraita explaining he scattered his money to demonstrate the High Priest's haircut.
The baraita cites a verse and describes the haircut as a 'lulyanit', with Rav Yehuda and Rava explaining it as a single haircut where one head is next to the other's root.

items.text: Interpretation of 'dala'at ha-remutzah'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'dala'at ha-remutzah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'dala'at ha-remutzah'. Shmuel says it is a 'kara karkuzai' (a type of gourd). Rav Ashi says it is a gourd hidden in embers. Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita where Rabbi Nehemya says the Egyptian gourd is kilayim with the Greek gourd and with the 'remutzah' gourd, which is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'dala'at ha-remutzah' (the pressed gourd) means.
Shmuel explains that it is a 'kara karkuzai' (a type of gourd).
Rav Ashi explains that it is a gourd hidden in embers (remetz).

Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing a baraita where Rabbi Nehemya states that the Egyptian gourd is kilayim (forbidden mixture) with the Greek gourd and with the 'remutzah' gourd, which is a refutation.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on vows regarding cooking vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on vows regarding cooking vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from 'ma'aseh kederah' is only forbidden from cooked dishes. If he says 'konam ha-yored lakederah', he is forbidden from everything cooked in a pot. The Gemara adds a baraita distinguishing between 'yored lakederah' and 'yored le'ilpas', and similarly for 'tanur'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: one who vows from 'ma'aseh kederah' is only forbidden from cooked dishes, and one who says 'konam ha-yored lakederah' is forbidden from everything cooked in a pot.

A baraita is cited that distinguishes between 'yored lakederah' and 'yored le'ilpas', ruling that one who vows from what goes into a pot is forbidden from what goes into a larger pot, but not vice versa, and similarly for what is made in each vessel.
The baraita adds a parallel case: one who vows from what goes into an oven is only forbidden from bread, but if he says 'all oven-made things on me', he is forbidden from everything made in an oven.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows using 'cooked' and 'salted'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows using 'cooked' and 'salted'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between vows that specify 'from the cooked' (limited to vegetable stew) and 'cooked that I taste' (all cooked foods), with a parallel distinction for 'salted'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by distinguishing between a vow using 'from the cooked' (limited to vegetable stew) and 'cooked that I taste' (all cooked foods), with a parallel distinction for 'salted'.

items.text: Gemara's question on ambiguous terms
items.text_en: Gemara's question on ambiguous terms
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of terms like 'dichvish' (pickled) and 'dishlik' (cooked) when used in vows, leaving the question unresolved.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi about the status of a vow using the Aramaic forms 'דִכְבִישׁ' (pickled) and 'דִשְׁלִיק' (cooked), leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows on roasted, salted, and fish
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows on roasted, salted, and fish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with distinctions for 'roasted' (limited to meat according to Rabbi Yehuda) and 'salted' (limited to fish), then details vows about fish, including exceptions for brine and fish sauce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a vow using 'roasted' only forbids roasted meat.
The Mishnah states that a vow using 'roasted that I taste' forbids all roasted items.
The Mishnah rules that a vow using 'salted' only forbids salted fish, while 'salted that I taste' forbids all salted items.
The Mishnah details that a vow using 'fish' forbids all fish, but permits טרית טרופה (chopped tuna) and brine.
The Mishnah rules that a vow from 'צחנה' (fish brine) forbids chopped tuna but permits brine and fish sauce.
The Mishnah concludes that a vow from chopped tuna forbids brine and fish sauce.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the meaning of 'dag' vs 'dagah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the meaning of 'dag' vs 'dagah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between 'dag' (large fish) and 'dagah' (small fish). Rav Pappa questions Abaye using biblical verses, concluding that in vows we follow common language, where 'dagah' can mean both large and small.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita distinguishes between 'דג' (large fish) and 'דגה' (small fish) in vows.
Rav Pappa questions Abaye, citing verses that seem to contradict the baraita's distinction between 'דג' and 'דגה'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'דגה' can mean both large and small, and in vows we follow common language.

items.text: Gemara: Question on 'tzichin'
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on 'tzichin'
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of 'tzichin' in a vow, leaving the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of a vow using the term 'צִיחִין' (a type of fish brine), leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows on milk, curd, and cheese
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows on milk, curd, and cheese
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses vows about milk (permitted in curd, but Rabbi Yosei forbids), curd (permitted in milk), and cheese (forbidden in all forms according to Abba Shaul).

sub.text: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Yosei, Abba Shaul)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma, Rabbi Yosei, Abba Shaul)
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new topic: one who vows from milk is permitted in קוֹם (whey), but Rabbi Yosei forbids it; one who vows from קוֹם is permitted in milk; Abba Shaul says one who vows from cheese is forbidden in both salted and unsalted cheese; and the Mishnah begins the rule for one who vows from meat.
The Mishnah states that one who vows from curd is permitted in milk.
Abba Shaul says that one who vows from cheese is forbidden in it, whether salted or unsalted.
The Mishnah begins the next clause about one who vows from meat, which is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from meat is permitted to eat the broth (רוטב) and the seasoning (קיפה), but Rabbi Yehuda forbids it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who vows from meat is permitted to eat the broth (רוטב) and the seasoning (קיפה), but Rabbi Yehuda forbids it.

Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent: Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs cooked with meat, and the Sages agreed that when one says 'this meat is forbidden to me,' anything that absorbs its taste (נותן טעם) is forbidden.

The Mishnah adds a parallel case: one who vows from wine is permitted in a dish that has wine taste, but if he said 'konam this wine that I taste' and it fell into a dish, if it imparts taste (נותן טעם) it is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's testimony and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's testimony and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent where Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs cooked with meat. The Sages qualify that this applies only when one says 'this meat is forbidden to me,' and if the mixture imparts a taste (נותן טעם), it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent that Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs cooked with meat.
The Sages affirm Rabbi Yehuda's precedent but qualify that it applies only when one says 'this meat is forbidden to me.'
The Sages establish the general principle: one who vows from a substance that then mixes with another, if it imparts a taste (נותן טעם), it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on wine
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that one who vows from wine is permitted to eat a dish that has the taste of wine. However, if one explicitly says 'this wine is forbidden to me' and it falls into a dish, if it imparts a taste, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general rule: one who vows from wine is permitted to eat a dish that has the taste of wine.
The Gemara adds that if one explicitly forbade this specific wine and it falls into a dish, if it imparts a taste, the dish is forbidden.

items.text: Resolving a contradiction about lentils and porridge
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction about lentils and porridge
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah (which permits porridge for one who vows from lentils) and a baraita where Rabbi Yossi permits it. It resolves the contradiction by explaining that in Rabbi Yossi's locale, porridge is called 'lentil porridge,' so it is considered a derivative of lentils.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says one who vows from lentils is forbidden in porridge, but a baraita has Rabbi Yossi permitting it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that in Rabbi Yossi's locale, porridge is called 'lentil porridge,' so it is considered a derivative of lentils.

items.text: Baraita on vows from milk, cheese, and broth
items.text_en: Baraita on vows from milk, cheese, and broth
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who vows from milk is permitted in curd (קום), and vice versa; similarly for cheese and milk, and for broth and its congealed fat (קיפה). However, if one says 'this meat is forbidden to me,' he is forbidden in the meat, its broth, and its fat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the rules of vows regarding milk, cheese, broth, and their derivatives, concluding that if one says 'this meat is forbidden to me,' he is forbidden in the meat, its broth, and its congealed fat.

items.text: Vows from wine and taste of wine
items.text_en: Vows from wine and taste of wine
items.desc_en: The baraita continues: one who vows from wine is permitted in a dish that has a taste of wine. But if he says 'konam this wine that I will not taste' and it falls into a dish, if it imparts a taste, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one who vows from wine is permitted in a dish with a taste of wine, but if he says 'konam this wine that I will not taste' and it falls into a dish with a taste, it is forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows from grapes and olives
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows from grapes and olives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who vows from grapes is permitted in wine; from olives, permitted in oil. But if he says 'konam these olives and grapes that I will not taste,' he is forbidden in them and in their derivatives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who vows from grapes is permitted in wine, from olives permitted in oil, but if he says 'konam these olives and grapes that I will not taste,' he is forbidden in them and their derivatives.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question: 'these' or 'that I will not taste'?
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question: 'these' or 'that I will not taste'?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that one is forbidden in derivatives depends on the word 'these' (אלו) or the phrase 'that I will not taste' (שאיני טועם). The Gemara suggests that if 'these' is decisive, the phrase 'that I will not taste' teaches that even with that phrase, only if he says 'these' is he forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that one is forbidden in derivatives depends on the word 'אלו' (these) or the phrase 'שאיני טועם' (that I will not taste).

The Gemara suggests that if 'אלו' (these) is decisive, the phrase 'שאיני טועם' (that I will not taste) teaches that even with that phrase, only if he says 'אלו' (these) is he forbidden, and if not, not.

items.text: Rava's first proof: 'these' forbids substitutes and growths
items.text_en: Rava's first proof: 'these' forbids substitutes and growths
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita: one who says 'konam these fruits upon me' is forbidden in their substitutes and growths, implying that derivatives (יוצא מהם) are permitted. The Gemara deflects, saying the baraita could mean even derivatives are forbidden, but it chose to teach that substitutes are like growths.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita: one who says 'konam these fruits upon me' is forbidden in substitutes and growths, implying that derivatives (יוצא מהם) are permitted.
The Gemara deflects: the baraita could mean even derivatives are forbidden, but it chose to teach that substitutes are like growths.

items.text: Second proof: 'that I will not eat' permits substitutes, implies derivatives forbidden
items.text_en: Second proof: 'that I will not eat' permits substitutes, implies derivatives forbidden
items.desc_en: Another baraita: one who says 'that I will not eat' or 'that I will not taste' is permitted in substitutes and growths, implying derivatives are forbidden. The Gemara deflects, saying the baraita simply didn't mention derivatives in either clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that permits substitutes and growths for one who says 'that I will not eat' or 'that I will not taste', implying that derivatives (יוצא מהן) are forbidden.
The Gemara deflects: the baraita simply did not mention derivatives in either clause, so no inference can be drawn.

items.text: Third proof: Rabbi Tarfon's case with eggs
items.text_en: Third proof: Rabbi Tarfon's case with eggs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda recounts that Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs cooked with meat when one said 'this meat upon me.' The Gemara clarifies that the question is only about 'that I will not taste' (שאיני טועם), not 'these' (אלו), which is clearly decisive.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda recounts that Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs cooked with meat when one said 'this meat upon me' (בשר זה עלי), establishing that a vow with 'these' (אלו) is decisive.
The Gemara clarifies that the case of 'אלו' (these) is not in question, but the question is whether 'שאיני טועם' (that I will not taste) is decisive (דווקא) or not.

items.text: Final proof: 'fish that I will not taste' forbids fish but permits brine
items.text_en: Final proof: 'fish that I will not taste' forbids fish but permits brine
items.desc_en: A baraita: one who says 'fish that I will not taste' is forbidden in all fish but permitted in brine and fish hash. Rava explains that this is because the brine has already left the fish, showing that 'that I will not taste' does not extend to derivatives.

sub.desc_en: The gemara brings a baraita: one who says 'fish that I will not taste' is forbidden in all fish but permitted in brine and fish hash, showing that 'that I will not taste' does not extend to derivatives.
Rava explains that the brine is permitted because it has already left the fish, resolving that 'that I will not taste' does not forbid derivatives.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows and Derivatives
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows and Derivatives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows against dates is permitted to eat date honey, and one who vows against winter grapes is permitted to eat their vinegar. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira argues that if the derivative shares the name of the original, it is forbidden, while the Sages permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who vows against dates is permitted to eat date honey.
The Mishnah adds that one who vows against winter grapes is permitted to eat their vinegar.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira argues that if the derivative shares the name of the original, one who vows from the original is forbidden in the derivative.
The Sages permit the derivative in all cases.

items.text: Gemara: Distinguishing the Sages from Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinguishing the Sages from Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Sages differ from the first Tanna. It cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that provides a general rule: if the primary item and its derivative are both typically eaten, a vow against one prohibits the other; if only the derivative is typically eaten, the vow only prohibits the derivative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Sages differ from the first Tanna (תנא קמא) in the Mishnah.

sub.text: Gemara's answer via baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that provides a general rule: when both the primary item and its derivative are typically eaten, a vow against one prohibits the other.

sub.text: Continuation of baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Continuation of baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The baraita adds the second case: when only the derivative is typically eaten, a vow against the primary item only prohibits the derivative, since the intent was only for the derivative.

items.text: Second Mishnah: More Vow Derivative Cases
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: More Vow Derivative Cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional cases: one who vows against wine is permitted apple wine; against oil is permitted sesame oil; against honey is permitted date honey; against vinegar is permitted winter grape vinegar; against leeks is permitted chives; against vegetables is permitted wild vegetables, since 'vegetable' is a borrowed name.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first case: one who vows against wine is permitted apple wine.
The Mishnah adds: one who vows against oil is permitted sesame oil.
The Mishnah adds: one who vows against honey is permitted date honey.
The Mishnah adds: one who vows against vinegar is permitted winter grape vinegar.
The Mishnah adds: one who vows against leeks is permitted chives.
The Mishnah concludes: one who vows against vegetables is permitted wild vegetables, because 'vegetable' is a borrowed name.

items.text: Gemara: Geographical Variation for Oil Vows
items.text_en: Gemara: Geographical Variation for Oil Vows
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who vows against oil in Eretz Yisrael is permitted sesame oil but forbidden olive oil; in Babylonia, the opposite applies. Where both are used, both are forbidden. The Gemara clarifies that even if the majority uses one type, the rule applies due to doubt in prohibitions being stringent.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited detailing the geographical variation for oil vows: in Eretz Yisrael sesame oil is permitted and olive oil forbidden; in Babylonia the reverse; where both are used, both are forbidden.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's ruling is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is necessary even where the majority uses one type, teaching that in cases of doubt regarding prohibitions we rule stringently (ספק איסורא לחומרא).

items.text: Gemara: Seasonal Distinction for Vegetable Vows
items.text_en: Gemara: Seasonal Distinction for Vegetable Vows
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who vows against vegetables in non-Sabbatical years is forbidden garden vegetables but permitted wild vegetables; in the Sabbatical year, the opposite applies. Rabbi Avahu cites Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel as the source.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who vows against vegetables in non-Sabbatical years is forbidden garden vegetables but permitted wild vegetables.
The baraita adds that in the Sabbatical year, the opposite applies: one is forbidden wild vegetables but permitted garden vegetables.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu attributes the baraita to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, identifying its source.

items.text: Gemara's qualification of the Mishnah's leniency
items.text_en: Gemara's qualification of the Mishnah's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara limits the earlier ruling that vegetables from outside the land are permitted: this only applies where vegetables are not imported from outside the land; where they are imported, they are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara limits the Mishnah's leniency: vegetables from outside the land are permitted only where such vegetables are not imported; where they are imported, they are forbidden.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on importing vegetables
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on importing vegetables
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the Sages forbid importing vegetables from outside the land, while Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel permits it. Rabbi Yirmeya explains the reason for the prohibition is due to gush (clods of earth that might contain impurity).

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a Tannaitic dispute: the Sages forbid importing vegetables from outside the land, while Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel permits it.
The Gemara asks: what is the reason of the one who says they do not bring vegetables from outside the land?
Rabbi Yirmeya answers: the prohibition is due to gush (clods of earth that might carry impurity from outside the land).

items.text: Mishnah: Vows on food pairs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows on food pairs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents rules for pairs of related foods: if one vows from cabbage, asparagus is forbidden; from asparagus, cabbage is permitted. Similar rules apply for grits and porridge, porridge and garlic, lentils and lentil cakes. Rabbi Yosei is lenient in certain cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: one who vows from cabbage is forbidden from asparagus, but from asparagus is permitted cabbage.

The Mishnah states: one who vows from grits is forbidden from porridge, but Rabbi Yosei permits; from porridge, grits is permitted; from porridge, garlic is forbidden, Rabbi Yosei permits; from garlic, porridge is permitted.
The Mishnah concludes: one who vows from lentils is forbidden from lentil cakes, Rabbi Yosei permits; from lentil cakes, lentils are permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows on wheat and grits in different forms
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows on wheat and grits in different forms
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows from 'wheat' or 'wheats', they are forbidden both as flour and bread. If one vows from 'grit' or 'grits', they are forbidden both raw and cooked. Rabbi Yehuda says that if one says 'konam grit or wheat that I taste', they are permitted to eat them raw.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows from 'wheat' or 'wheats', they are forbidden both as flour and bread; if one vows from 'grit' or 'grits', they are forbidden both raw and cooked.
Rabbi Yehuda says that if one says 'konam grit or wheat that I taste', they are permitted to eat them raw.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on the wording of vows for wheat and grits
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on the wording of vows for wheat and grits
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel elaborates: if one vows from 'wheat', they are forbidden to bake but permitted to eat raw; from 'wheats', forbidden to eat raw but permitted to bake; from 'wheat wheats', forbidden both. Similarly for 'grit', 'grits', and 'grit grits' regarding cooking and eating raw.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's baraita opens with the rule for a vow from 'wheat' (חִטָּה): forbidden to bake, permitted to eat raw.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: a vow from 'wheats' (חִטִּים) forbids eating raw but permits baking.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes the wheat section: a vow from 'wheat wheats' (חִטָּה חִטִּין) forbids both baking and eating raw.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.desc_en: The baraita now addresses grits: a vow from 'grit' (גְּרִיס) forbids cooking but permits eating raw.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (continued)
sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: a vow from 'grits' (גְּרִיסִין) forbids eating raw but permits cooking.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (conclusion)
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel (conclusion)
sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes: a vow from 'grit grits' (גְּרִיס גְּרִיסִין) forbids both cooking and eating raw.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from vegetables is permitted gourds, but Rabbi Akiva forbids them. The Sages challenge Rabbi Akiva by noting that a person might tell his messenger 'buy me vegetables' and the messenger says 'I only found gourds', implying gourds are not considered vegetables. Rabbi Akiva responds that the messenger could also say 'I only found legumes', yet legumes are not vegetables, so the analogy fails; he concludes that gourds are included in vegetables but legumes are not, and the vow also forbids fresh Egyptian beans but permits dry ones.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that one who vows from vegetables is permitted gourds, but Rabbi Akiva forbids them.
The Sages object to Rabbi Akiva by citing the common practice: a person tells his messenger to buy vegetables, and the messenger reports finding only gourds, implying gourds are not vegetables.

Rabbi Akiva responds that the analogy fails: the messenger could also say he found only legumes, yet legumes are not vegetables; he concludes that gourds are included in vegetables but legumes are not.
The Mishnah concludes that the vow also forbids fresh Egyptian beans but permits dry ones.

items.text: Gemara's question and Ulla's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Ulla's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since he vowed from vegetables, why are gourds permitted? Ulla answers that the case is where he said 'vegetables for a pot are upon me', and the Gemara clarifies that he said 'vegetables that are cooked in a pot are upon me', excluding gourds which are not typically cooked in a pot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: since he vowed from vegetables, why are gourds permitted?
Ulla answers that the case is where he said 'vegetables for a pot are upon me'.
The Gemara objects: perhaps he meant vegetables that are eaten in a pot (including gourds)?
The Gemara resolves: the case is where he said 'vegetables that are cooked in a pot are upon me', excluding gourds which are not typically cooked in a pot.

items.text: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Sages hold that anything about which a messenger must consult is not of the same kind, so gourds are not vegetables. Rabbi Akiva holds that anything about which a messenger consults is of the same kind, so gourds are vegetables. Abaye adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes that one does not receive lashes for eating gourds in this case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the fundamental point of dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara explains that the Sages hold: anything about which a messenger must consult is not of the same kind, so gourds are not vegetables.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds: anything about which a messenger consults is of the same kind, so gourds are vegetables.
Abaye adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes that one does not receive lashes for eating gourds in this case.

items.text: Support from a Mishnah on me'ilah
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah on me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a messenger who performs his mission versus one who does not, regarding misuse of consecrated property. Rav Chisda says this Mishnah is not like Rabbi Akiva, because if the messenger gave liver instead of meat, Rabbi Akiva would hold that the owner misuses the property, not the messenger, contradicting the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah from Me'ilah stating that if a messenger performed his mission, the owner misuses consecrated property; if not, the messenger misuses it.
The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of this Mishnah.

Rav Chisda says this Mishnah is not like Rabbi Akiva, because if a messenger gave liver instead of meat or vice versa, Rabbi Akiva would hold that the owner misuses the property, not the messenger, contradicting the Mishnah's ruling.

items.text: Abaye's defense of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Abaye's defense of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the Mishnah on me'ilah could be consistent, because the case there involves a clear deviation from the owner's instructions, not a matter of consultation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the Mishnah on me'ilah could be consistent, because the case there involves a clear deviation from the owner's instructions, not a matter of consultation.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva would admit that consultation (אימלוכי) is needed. The ruling was stated before Rava, who approved of Nachmani's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva would admit that consultation (אימלוכי) is needed.
The ruling was stated before Rava, who approved of Nachmani's statement.

items.text: Identifying the disputant: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Identifying the disputant: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva. It cites a baraita where the first Tanna prohibits all types of meat including poultry but permits fish and locusts, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits head, feet, etc., and adds that innards are not considered meat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna disagrees with Rabbi Akiva, and answers that it is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara cites a baraita where the first Tanna prohibits all types of meat including poultry but permits fish and locusts.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits head, feet, etc., and adds that innards are not considered meat, and those who eat them are not considered people.

items.text: Gemara's question on the distinction between poultry and fish
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the distinction between poultry and fish
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first Tanna prohibits poultry but permits fish, given that both could be brought by a messenger if meat is unavailable. The messenger would consult about fish as well, so they should also be prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first Tanna prohibits poultry but permits fish, given that both could be brought by a messenger if meat is unavailable.

items.text: Abaye's first answer: a case of bloodletting
items.text_en: Abaye's first answer: a case of bloodletting
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the case is where one has undergone bloodletting, and thus cannot eat fish. The Gemara objects that poultry is also harmful after bloodletting, citing Shmuel and a baraita. Abaye distinguishes that poultry can be eaten if boiled.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the case is where one has undergone bloodletting, and thus cannot eat fish.
The Gemara objects that if bloodletting is the reason, poultry should also be forbidden.
The Gemara cites Shmuel's statement that eating poultry after bloodletting causes heart palpitations and a baraita that prohibits bloodletting after eating fish, poultry, or salted meat.
The Gemara cites another baraita that after bloodletting one may not eat milk, cheese, eggs, fish, poultry, or salted meat.
Abaye resolves the objection by distinguishing that poultry can be eaten if boiled, whereas fish cannot be made safe after bloodletting.

items.text: Abaye's second answer: a case of eye pain
items.text_en: Abaye's second answer: a case of eye pain
items.desc_en: Abaye offers another scenario: where one's eyes hurt, and fish are harmful for the eyes. The Gemara objects that fish are actually beneficial for eyes, citing Shmuel. The Gemara resolves that this refers to a specific type of fish that is harmful at the end of a meal.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes a scenario where one's eyes hurt, and fish are harmful for the eyes.
The Gemara objects that fish are actually beneficial for eyes, citing Shmuel's statement that fish is a remedy for eyes.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement refers to a specific type of fish that is harmful at the end of a meal.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that one who vows from 'grain' (דגן) is forbidden even in Egyptian beans (dry), while the Sages limit the prohibition to the five species. Rabbi Meir further distinguishes between 'produce' (תבואה) and 'grain' (דגן).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's position: one who vows from 'grain' (דגן) is forbidden even in dry Egyptian beans.
The Sages counter that one who vows from 'grain' is forbidden only in the five species of grain.

Rabbi Meir further distinguishes: one who vows from 'produce' (תבואה) is forbidden only in the five species, but one who vows from 'grain' (דגן) is forbidden in everything except tree fruits and vegetables.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that 'grain' (דגן) means anything that is dried. Rav Yosef objects from a verse that lists דגן alongside תירוש ויצהר, implying it is a specific category. Abaye answers that the verse includes fruits of the tree and vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the term 'דגן' (grain) means anything that is dried (דמידגן).
Rav Yosef objects from a verse that lists 'דגן' alongside 'תירוש ויצהר' (wine and oil), implying it is a specific category, not a general term for dried produce.
Abaye answers that the verse includes fruits of the tree and vegetables, so 'דגן' still means dried produce generally.

items.text: Agreement on the term 'produce' (תבואה)
items.text_en: Agreement on the term 'produce' (תבואה)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all agree one who vows from 'produce' (תבואה) is only forbidden the five species. A baraita supports this, and the Gemara clarifies that this teaching is necessary lest one think תבואה includes everything.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's position that one who vows from תבואה (produce) is only forbidden the five species.
Rabbi Yochanan states that all agree one who vows from תבואה is only forbidden the five species.
A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's statement, saying the sages agree on this point.
The Gemara questions why this teaching is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the teaching is necessary lest one think תבואה includes everything, so it teaches that it does not.

items.text: Rav Yosef's second objection and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's second objection and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef again cites the verse, and Rava distinguishes between 'תבואה' alone and 'תבואת שדה' (produce of the field), implying the latter is broader.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing the verse that lists 'דגן' (grain) alongside 'תבואת שדה' (produce of the field), implying 'דגן' is not all that is gathered.
Rava distinguishes between 'תבואה' (produce) alone, which refers only to the five species, and 'תבואת שדה' (produce of the field), which is broader.

items.text: Story of Bar Mar Shmuel's gift and the meaning of 'עללתא'
items.text_en: Story of Bar Mar Shmuel's gift and the meaning of 'עללתא'
items.desc_en: Bar Mar Shmuel instructed that 13,000 zuz from the income of the Nahal Panya canal be given to Rava. Rava asked Rav Yosef what 'עללתא' (income) means. Rav Yosef cited the Mishnah that 'תבואה' is only the five species, but Abaye objected that 'עללתא' is broader.

sub.desc_en: Bar Mar Shmuel instructed that 13,000 zuz from the income (עללתא) of the Nahal Panya canal be given to Rava.
Rava sent a query to Rav Yosef asking how the term 'עללתא' (income) is defined.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's answer citing the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer citing the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answered by citing the Mishnah that one who vows from 'תבואה' (produce) is only forbidden from the five species.
Abaye objected that the cases are not comparable: 'תבואה' (produce) only means the five species, but 'עללתא' (income) implies everything.

items.text: Rava's real question and Rav Yosef's pique
items.text_en: Rava's real question and Rav Yosef's pique
items.desc_en: Rava clarified that he already knew 'עללתא' includes everything; his real question was whether rent from houses and ships (which depreciate) is considered income. The rabbis reported this to Rav Yosef, who was offended that Rava asked an unnecessary question.

sub.desc_en: Rava clarifies that his real question was not about the meaning of 'עללתא' (income), which he already knew includes everything, but whether rent from houses and ships (which depreciate) is considered income.

sub.text: Rabbis' report and Rav Yosef's reaction
sub.text_en: Rabbis' report and Rav Yosef's reaction
sub.desc_en: The rabbis report Rava's clarification to Rav Yosef, who becomes offended that Rava sent an unnecessary question.

items.text: Rava's visit to Rav Yosef and the homily on humility
items.text_en: Rava's visit to Rav Yosef and the homily on humility
items.desc_en: Rava visited Rav Yosef on Yom Kippur eve, served him wine, and asked for an explanation of a verse about the journey from Midbar to Bamot. Rav Yosef expounded that one who makes oneself like a desert (humble) receives the Torah as a gift, inherits it, and rises to greatness, but pride leads to being lowered.

sub.desc_en: Rava heard that Rav Yosef was upset, came to him on Yom Kippur eve, and served him wine, revealing his identity.
Rav Yosef demanded that Rava explain the verse about the journey from Midbar to Bamot before sitting down.
Rav Yosef expounded that one who makes oneself humble like a desert receives the Torah as a gift, inherits it, rises to greatness, but pride leads to being lowered.

items.text: Opening verse citation
items.text_en: Opening verse citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse (Isaiah 40:4) as a prooftext for the concept that a valley (gay) is lifted up, possibly related to the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse (Isaiah 40:4) 'every valley shall be lifted up' as a prooftext for the concept that a valley (gay) is elevated.

items.text: Baraita on vows from grain and produce
items.text_en: Baraita on vows from grain and produce
items.desc_en: A baraita details what is forbidden when one vows from grain (including dry Egyptian beans but not fresh, and excluding rice, etc.) and from produce of the year (excluding lambs, milk, eggs, etc., but including all if one says 'produce of the year upon me'). Another baraita covers vows from produce of the earth (including mushrooms and truffles, but excluding them if one says 'produce of the ground upon me').

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing what is forbidden and permitted when one vows from grain (דגן).
The baraita continues with the case of one who vows from produce of the year, specifying permitted items and the effect of the phrase 'growths of the year upon me'.
The baraita concludes with the case of one who vows from produce of the land, distinguishing between 'produce of the land' and 'growths of the ground'.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution on mushrooms
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution on mushrooms
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a beraita says one recites 'shehakol' over something that does not grow from the earth, yet another beraita includes mushrooms and truffles in that category. Abaye resolves that mushrooms and truffles grow from the earth but nurse from the air, so the beraita should be emended to say 'something that does not nurse from the earth'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a mishna says one recites 'shehakol' over something that does not grow from the earth, yet a baraita includes truffles and mushrooms in that category.
Abaye resolves that truffles and mushrooms grow from the earth but nurse from the air, not from the earth.
The Gemara objects: the mishna says 'something whose growth is not from the earth,' not 'something that does not nurse from the earth.'
The Gemara resolves by emending the mishna to read: 'something that does not nurse from the earth.'

items.text: Mishnah on vows from clothing
items.text_en: Mishnah on vows from clothing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from clothing is permitted sack, curtain, and cloak. If one says 'konam wool upon me,' he may cover himself with wool fleeces; if 'flax upon me,' he may cover himself with flax stalks. Rabbi Yehuda says all depends on the vower: if he was burdened and sweated and had a bad odor, saying 'konam wool and flax upon me' permits covering but forbids placing them behind him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches: one who vows from clothing is permitted in sack, curtain, and cloak; if he said 'konam wool upon me' he is permitted to cover himself with wool fleeces; if he said 'konam linen upon me' he is permitted to cover himself with linen fibers.

Rabbi Yehuda says: everything depends on the vower — if he was carrying wool and sweated and his smell was bad, and he said 'konam wool and linen upon me', he is permitted to cover himself but forbidden to drape them over his back.

items.text: Gemara's baraita on additional clothing items
items.text_en: Gemara's baraita on additional clothing items
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the Mishnah: one who vows from clothing is permitted sack, curtain, and cloak, but forbidden certain garments like פונדא, פסיקיא, etc. Rabba bar Chana explains that 'איסקורטי' is a shirt of felt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who vows from clothing is permitted in sack, curtain, and cloak, but forbidden in punda, piskiya, iskurtiya, katabulya, anpilya, plinya, trousers, and hat.
The Gemara asks: what is 'iskurtiya'?
Rabbah bar Chanah answers: it is a prayer shawl (כיתונא דצלא).

items.text: Baraita on going out with sack for rain
items.text_en: Baraita on going out with sack for rain
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses that one may go out with thick sack, thick sagum, curtain, and cloak because of rain, but not with a chest, basket, or mat. Shepherds go out with sacks, and the sages spoke of the common practice.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one may go out with thick sack, thick sagus, curtain, and cloak because of rain, but not with a box, basket, or mat because of rain; shepherds go out with sacks, and not only shepherds but all people, but the Sages spoke of the common practice.
The baraita continues: shepherds go out in sacks, and not only shepherds but all people, though the sages spoke of the common case.
The baraita notes that shepherds go out with sacks, and the sages spoke of the common practice, applying to all people.

items.text: Baraita explaining Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Baraita explaining Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita clarifies Rabbi Yehuda's statement: if one was wearing wool and was distressed, saying 'konam wool upon me,' he is forbidden to wear but permitted to carry; if he was carrying flax and sweated, saying 'konam flax upon me,' he is permitted to wear but forbidden to carry.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on Rabbi Yehuda's principle: if one was wearing wool and was distressed, and said 'konam wool upon me', he is forbidden to wear but permitted to carry; if he was carrying linen and sweated, and said 'konam linen upon me', he is permitted to wear but forbidden to carry.
The baraita continues: if one was carrying flax and sweated, and said 'flax upon me', he is permitted to wear but forbidden to carry.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows against a house or upper story
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows against a house or upper story
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from a house is permitted in the upper story according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say the upper story is included in the house. Similarly, one who vows from the upper story is permitted in the house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who vows from a house is permitted in the upper story according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say the upper story is included in the house; similarly, one who vows from the upper story is permitted in the house.

items.text: Gemara: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that the word 'בית' in the verse includes the upper story. Rav Chisda says it is Rabbi Meir, because the Sages already include the upper story in 'house' and would not need a verse. Abaye counters that even the Sages might need the verse, since one might think only a structure attached to the ground is called a house, not an upper story.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that the word 'בית' in the verse includes the upper story.
Rav Chisda answers that it is Rabbi Meir, because the Sages already include the upper story in 'house' and would not need a verse.

items.text: Support from Rav Huna bar Chiyya's statement
items.text_en: Support from Rav Huna bar Chiyya's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna bar Chiyya in the name of Ulla: if one says 'I am selling you a house in my house,' he shows him the upper story, but if he says 'house' without qualification, he does not show the upper story. The Gemara asks if this follows Rabbi Meir, and answers that even the Sages could agree, interpreting 'עלייה' as the choicest of houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by Rav Huna bar Chiyya in the name of Ulla, who said that if one says 'I am selling you a house in my house' he shows the upper story, but if he says 'a house' without specification, he does not show the upper story.
The Gemara answers that it could even be the Rabbis, because the term 'עֲלִיָּיה' (upper story) in that context means the choicest (מעולה) of the houses, not a separate structure.
The Gemara answers that even the Sages could agree, interpreting 'עלייה' (upper story) in this context as the choicest of houses (מעולה שבבתים), not a literal upper story.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Vows against a bed or couch
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Vows against a bed or couch
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from a bed is permitted in a couch (דרגש) according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say the couch is included in the bed. Similarly, one who vows from a couch is permitted in the bed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from a bed is permitted in a דרגש (dargesh, a type of couch) according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say the דרגש is included in the bed; similarly, one who vows from the דרגש is permitted in the bed.

items.text: Gemara: What is a דרגש?
items.text_en: Gemara: What is a דרגש?
items.desc_en: Ulla defines דרגש as a goat's cradle (ערסא דגדא). The Rabbis object based on a baraita about a mourner who sits on a דרגש while others sit on the ground, questioning why he would use it only then. Ravina deflects by comparing it to meat and wine which he may eat all year. The Gemara then raises a contradiction from another baraita about not tipping a דרגש but standing it up, and asks if it is a goat's cradle, why not tip it like other beds?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a דרגש (dargesh) is, and Ulla answers that it is a goat's cradle (ערסא דגדא).
The Rabbis object to Ulla's definition based on a baraita about a mourner who sits on a דרגש while others sit on the ground, questioning why he would use it only then if it is a goat's cradle.
Ravina deflects the objection by comparing it to meat and wine, which the mourner may eat all year but which we specifically give him on that day.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita about not tipping a דרגש but standing it up, and asks if it is a goat's cradle, why not tip it like other beds, but then dismisses the difficulty.

items.text: Clarifying the bed designated for vessels and the identity of dargesh
items.text_en: Clarifying the bed designated for vessels and the identity of dargesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the mishnah's ruling about a bed designated for vessels is based on a beraita. It then raises a difficulty from a beraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a dargesh is permitted by loosening its straps, implying it has straps, but a dargesh is a bed for a goat (arsa de-gada) which has no straps. Ravin resolves this by citing a tradition that dargesh is a bed for a fisherman (arsa de-tzala).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah's ruling about a bed designated for vessels is based on a beraita that states such a bed does not need to be overturned.
