The Gemara raises a difficulty from a beraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a dargesh is permitted by loosening its straps, but a dargesh is a bed for a goat (עַרְסָא דְגַדָּא) which has no straps.
Ravin resolves the difficulty by citing a tradition from Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva that dargesh is a bed for a fisherman (עַרְסָא דְצַלָּא), which does have straps.

items.text: Defining mita and dargesh by their construction
items.text_en: Defining mita and dargesh by their construction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya defines mita as having its weaving on top of its frame, while dargesh has its weaving within its frame. An objection is raised from a mishnah about wooden vessels that says a mita and arisa become susceptible to impurity after being smoothed with fish skin, implying both are woven within the frame. The Gemara resolves that both are woven within the frame, but mita is used for carrying items in a basket (bizyanei) and dargesh in a sack (avakta).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses the question: what distinguishes a mita from a dargesh?
Rabbi Yirmeya defines mita as having its weaving on top of its frame, while dargesh has its weaving within its frame.

The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah about wooden vessels: both mita and arisa become susceptible to impurity after being smoothed with fish skin, implying both are woven within the frame, contradicting Rabbi Yirmeya's definition.
The Gemara resolves that both are woven within the frame, but mita is used for carrying items in a basket (ביזיוני), while dargesh is used in a sack (אבקתא).

items.text: Ruling on a bed with protruding legs and halakha like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Ruling on a bed with protruding legs and halakha like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha quotes Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) that a bed whose legs protrude can be stood upright and suffices. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha reports in the name of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) that a bed whose legs protrude can be stood upright and suffices.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi states in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Mishnah: Vowing from a city or a house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vowing from a city or a house
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who vows from a city is permitted to enter its techum (Sabbath boundary) but forbidden to enter its ibur (outskirts). One who vows from a house is forbidden from the doorpost (agaf) inward.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that one who vows from a city may enter its techum but not its ibur, and one who vows from a house is forbidden from the doorpost inward.

items.text: Gemara: Proof that the ibur of a city is like the city
items.text_en: Gemara: Proof that the ibur of a city is like the city
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the ibur of a city is considered like the city. Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse about Joshua being in Jericho, which must refer to its ibur since Jericho was closed. The Gemara rejects that it could mean the techum, as the verse about the techum says 'outside the city'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the ibur (outskirts) of a city is considered like the city itself.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse about Joshua being in Jericho, arguing that since Jericho was closed, the verse must refer to its ibur (outskirts).
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse refers to the techum (Sabbath boundary) of the city, but rejects this because the verse about the techum explicitly says 'outside the city'.

items.text: Gemara: Defining the house for vows and a challenge from the metzora
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining the house for vows and a challenge from the metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one who vows from a house is only forbidden from the doorpost inward. Rav Mari challenges this from the law of the metzora, which requires the priest to go to the door of the house, but not inside. The Gemara resolves that the case of a house is different because the verse says 'from the house' until he leaves the entire house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from a house is only forbidden from the doorpost inward, but not from the doorpost outward.
Rav Mari challenges the Mishnah by citing the metzora (leper) law, where the priest must stand at the door but not inside, yet the verse 'from the house' requires him to leave entirely.
The Gemara resolves that the case of a house is different because the verse explicitly says 'from the house,' meaning until he leaves the entire house.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between 'konam' and 'that I eat/taste' for produce
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between 'konam' and 'that I eat/taste' for produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'konam these fruits upon me' or similar formulations, he is forbidden from their exchanges and growths. However, if he says 'that I eat' or 'that I taste', he is permitted exchanges and growths for items whose seed perishes, but for items whose seed does not perish, even the growths of growths are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a vow using the term 'קונם' (konam) forbids exchanges and growths of the produce, whereas a vow using 'שאני אוכל' (that I eat) or 'שאני טועם' (that I taste) permits exchanges and growths for items whose seed perishes, but for items whose seed does not perish, even the growths of growths are forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Same distinction applied to wife's handiwork
items.text_en: Mishnah: Same distinction applied to wife's handiwork
items.desc_en: The Mishnah applies the same rule to a man who says to his wife 'konam your handiwork upon me' or similar formulations, forbidding exchanges and growths. For 'that I eat' or 'that I taste', the same distinction between perishable and non-perishable items applies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a husband who forbids his wife's handiwork upon himself, applying the same distinction between perishable and non-perishable items as in the previous Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional vows with timeframes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional vows with timeframes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where a man says to his wife 'that which you make I will not eat until Passover' or similar. If she made it before Passover, he may eat or cover himself after Passover. But if he says 'that which you make until Passover I will not eat', and she made it before Passover, he is forbidden to eat or cover himself after Passover. It also discusses a conditional vow about going to her father's house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if a man says to his wife 'that which you make I will not eat until Passover', and she made it before Passover, he is permitted to eat or cover himself after Passover.
The Mishnah presents the second case: if he says 'that which you make until Passover I will not eat', and she made it before Passover, he is forbidden to eat or cover himself after Passover.
The Mishnah presents the third case: a conditional vow about going to her father's house before the festival, where if she went before Passover, she is forbidden to benefit from him until Passover.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman is forbidden to benefit from her husband until the festival if she goes to her father's house before Passover, but is permitted to go after Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman is forbidden to benefit from her husband until the festival if she goes to her father's house before Passover, but is permitted to go after Passover.

items.text: Gemara's question about growths canceling the root
items.text_en: Gemara's question about growths canceling the root
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of an onion from the Sabbatical year planted in the eighth year, where its permitted growths outnumber the forbidden root. Rabbi Ami did not have an answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a man who forbids his wife's handiwork on himself, and relates that Rabbi Yishmael of Kfar Yamma brought a question about a seventh-year onion planted in the eighth year, whose growth exceeded its original bulk, asking whether the permitted growth nullifies the forbidden original.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's answer from Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's answer from Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha answers from Rabbi Chanina citing Rabbi Yannai that an onion of terumah planted with growths outnumbering the root is permitted. Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the master leaves two opinions and follows one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha resolves the question from a ruling of Rabbi Chanina Terita'ah citing Rabbi Yannai: an onion of תרומה (priestly portion) that was planted and whose growth exceeded its original bulk is permitted.
Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Zerika) objects: why does the master abandon two authorities and follow one?

items.text: The two opposing opinions: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
items.text_en: The two opposing opinions: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the two opinions: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan rules that a young vine grafted onto an old one with fruit is forbidden even if it increased twofold; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan rules that an onion planted in a vineyard that was uprooted is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the two authorities whose opinions were referenced in the previous discussion.
Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that a young vine grafted onto an old one with fruit is forbidden even if it increased twofold.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan rules that an onion planted in a vineyard that was uprooted is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's answer from Rabbi Yitzchak and the objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's answer from Rabbi Yitzchak and the objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami answers from Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan that a litra of onions that was tithed and replanted is tithed according to the whole, implying growths nullify the root. The Gemara objects that perhaps it is different because it is stringent.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami answers the question by citing Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a litra of onions that was tithed and replanted is tithed according to the whole, proving that growths nullify the root.
The Gemara objects that the case of tithing may be different because it is stringent (לחומרא), so it does not prove that growths nullify the root for all purposes.

items.text: Alternative answer from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Alternative answer from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a different answer from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon states a ruling, implying that growths can nullify the root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara instead resolves the question from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon states a ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Principle of Matirin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Principle of Matirin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything which has matirin (a permitted alternative), such as tevel, ma'aser sheni, hekdesh, and chadash, has no fixed measure for prohibition. Conversely, anything without matirin, such as terumah, challah, orlah, and kil'ei hakerem, has a fixed measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle: anything with matirin (a permitted alternative) has no fixed measure for prohibition, while anything without matirin has a fixed measure.

items.text: Objection: Shevi'it as a Counterexample
items.text_en: Objection: Shevi'it as a Counterexample
items.desc_en: The students object that shevi'it (sabbatical year produce) has no matirin, yet the Sages did not give it a fixed measure, as taught in a baraita that shevi'it prohibits any amount of its own species. The teacher responds that he only meant this rule applies to bi'ur (removal), not to eating.

sub.desc_en: The students object that shevi'it (sabbatical year produce) has no matirin, yet the Sages did not give it a fixed measure, citing a baraita that shevi'it prohibits any amount of its own species.
The Tanna Kamma responds that he only meant the rule of no fixed measure applies to bi'ur (removal), not to eating.

items.text: Gemara's Question: Distinction for Stringency
items.text_en: Gemara's Question: Distinction for Stringency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether shevi'it might be different because it is stringent (lechumra), and thus the rule about matirin might still apply to eating. This is a brief query seeking clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether shevi'it might be different because it is stringent (לחומרא), and thus the rule about matirin might still apply to eating.

items.text: Proof from Onions and Giddulei Heter
items.text_en: Proof from Onions and Giddulei Heter
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a Mishnah about onions that grew in shevi'it: if their leaves are black (from the old bulb) they are forbidden, but if green (new growth) they are permitted. Rabbi Chananya ben Antignos adds that if the leaves can be pulled with the bulb, they are forbidden; after shevi'it, they are permitted. This shows that giddulei heter (permitted growths) can nullify the prohibition. The Gemara questions whether this applies only to crushed (meduknanin) onions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about onions that grew in shevi'it: if their leaves are black (from the old bulb) they are forbidden, but if green (new growth) they are permitted.
Rabbi Chananya ben Antignos adds that if the leaves can be pulled with the bulb, they are forbidden; after shevi'it, they are permitted.
The Gemara infers from this that גידולי היתר (permitted growths) can nullify the prohibition.
The Gemara questions whether this applies only to crushed (meduknanin) onions.

items.text: Alternative Proof from a Baraita
items.text_en: Alternative Proof from a Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another proof from a baraita (which is not fully quoted here) to resolve the issue, suggesting a different source for the principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative proof from a baraita to resolve the issue, suggesting a different source for the principle.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who weeds with a Cuthean in the beds of vegetables may eat from them casually, but must tithe them as definite produce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who weeds with a Cuthean in vegetable beds may eat casually but must tithe the produce as definite.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling and the Gemara's initial challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling and the Gemara's initial challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that if an Israelite is suspected of violating the Sabbatical year, after the Sabbatical year the produce is permitted. The Gemara questions whether this implies that permitted growths nullify the prohibition, and notes that the vegetables in question are those whose seeds perish, so the prohibition should not apply.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that if an Israelite is suspected of violating the Sabbatical year, after the Sabbatical year the produce is permitted.
The Gemara questions whether this implies that permitted growths nullify the prohibition.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the ruling applies only to a plant whose seeds perish, where the prohibition does not carry over.
A baraita is cited listing the vegetables in question as leeks, garlic, and onions, which are plants whose seeds perish.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the ruling applies only to crushed vegetables, not whole ones.
The Gemara rejects this by noting that the mishna explicitly says 'suspected of violating the Sabbatical year,' implying the produce is whole.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the ruling applies only to a mixture, not pure produce.
The Gemara rejects this by noting that the mishna says 'one who weeds,' implying the produce is pure and not a mixture.
The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan's position.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that the Sabbatical year is different because its prohibition comes through the land, so its nullification also comes through the land.
The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply to tithe, whose prohibition also comes through the land, yet its nullification does not come through the land.
A baraita is cited showing that a litra of untithed produce that was planted and grew to ten litras is still subject to tithe, proving that nullification does not occur through the land for tithe.

items.text: Gemara's further objections
items.text_en: Gemara's further objections
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises additional objections: perhaps the produce is crushed, or perhaps it is a mixture. But the Mishnah explicitly says 'suspected of the Sabbatical year' and 'weeds', so these possibilities are dismissed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the produce in the Mishnah is crushed (medukkanin), which would make it subject to different rules.
The Gemara rejects the objection: the Mishnah explicitly says 'suspected of the Sabbatical year', implying the produce is fresh, not crushed.
The Gemara raises another objection: perhaps the produce is a mixture (ta'arovet) of permitted and forbidden items.
The Gemara rejects this: the Mishnah says 'one who weeds' (hamenakesh), indicating the produce is still growing and not a mixture.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan
items.desc_en: The Gemara declares this a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan. Rabbi Yitzchak responds that the Sabbatical year is different because its prohibition comes through the ground, so its nullification also comes through the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the baraita constitutes a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan's position.
Rabbi Yitzchak responds that the Sabbatical year (שביעית) is different because its prohibition comes through the ground, so its nullification also comes through the ground.

items.text: Counterexample from tithe
items.text_en: Counterexample from tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tithe also has its prohibition through the ground, yet its nullification is not through the ground, as shown by a baraita: a litra of tevel that is sown and yields ten litras is liable for tithe and Sabbatical year, and one must tithe from elsewhere for the original litra.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that tithe (מעשר) also has its prohibition through the ground, yet its nullification is not through the ground, as shown by a baraita: a litra of tevel that is sown and yields ten litras is liable for tithe and Sabbatical year, and one must tithe from elsewhere for the original litra.

items.text: Gemara's initial statement
items.text_en: Gemara's initial statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that in the case of ma'aser, the improvement (digun) is what causes the prohibition, implying that the produce itself is not inherently forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that regarding ma'aser (tithe), the process of דיגון (improvement/arrangement) is what causes the prohibition, implying the produce itself is not inherently forbidden.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's objection from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's objection from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites a Mishnah about konamot (vows) that distinguishes between cases where the vow is phrased as 'konam' (forbidding the produce itself) and cases where it is phrased as 'she'ani ochel' (forbidding the act of eating). In the latter, exchanges and growths are permitted for items whose seed is consumed, but forbidden for items whose seed is not consumed.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects by citing a Mishnah about קונמות (vow-offerings), where the prohibition extends to exchanges and growths, implying that the produce itself is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's answer: Konamot are different
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's answer: Konamot are different
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba answers that konamot are different because one can ask a sage to dissolve them, making them an item that has a means of nullification (yesh lo matirin), and such items are not nullified in a majority.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba answers that קונמות (vow-offerings) are different because they can be annulled by a sage, making them a דבר שיש לו מתירין (an item with a permitted alternative), which does not nullify in a majority.

items.text: Objection from terumah
items.text_en: Objection from terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Terumah also can be dissolved by a sage, yet it is nullified in a majority, as taught in a Mishnah about a se'ah of impure terumah falling into less than 100 hullin. The Gemara answers that we are dealing with terumah in the hands of a kohen, who cannot dissolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: תרומה (priestly portion) can also be annulled, yet it nullifies in a majority, as per the Mishnah that a se'ah of impure terumah falling into less than 100 hullin rots, but into 100 it rises.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with terumah in the possession of a priest, who cannot annul it.

items.text: Refutation of the answer from the Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Refutation of the answer from the Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If so, consider the continuation of the Mishnah which says pure terumah is sold to a kohen. This implies the terumah is in the hands of an Israelite who inherited it from his mother's father, a kohen, and can dissolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, the latter clause says pure terumah is sold to a priest, implying an Israelite owner; the Gemara resolves that it deals with an Israelite who inherited from his priestly maternal grandfather.
The Gemara answers: Rather, we are dealing with an Israelite who inherited terumah from his mother's father, a kohen, and thus cannot dissolve it.

items.text: Further objection from the Mishnah's end
items.text_en: Further objection from the Mishnah's end
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: The Mishnah says 'sold to a kohen except for the value of that se'ah', indicating that the terumah is not nullified, contradicting the earlier answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further objects: the Mishnah says it is sold to a priest except for the value of that se'ah, implying the priest cannot use it, contradicting the previous resolution.

items.text: Final answer: Mitzvah to dissolve vows
items.text_en: Final answer: Mitzvah to dissolve vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: Konamot are different because there is a mitzvah to dissolve them, as per Rabbi Nathan who says a nazir is like building a high place, and fulfilling it is like offering incense. Terumah has no such mitzvah to dissolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: regarding קונמות (vow-offerings), there is a מצוה (commandment) to annul them due to Rabbi Natan's statement that a vow is like building a high place, but for terumah there is no such mitzvah to annul.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and Rav Chisda's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and Rav Chisda's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a litra of onions that was tithed and replanted, which is tithed in its entirety. Rav Chisda challenges: Where did the permitted part go? Rabba responds with a parallel case from a Mishnah about onions that sprouted from rain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a litra of onions that was fixed and replanted is tithed according to its entirety.
Rav Chisda objects to Rabba's teaching of Rabbi Yochanan's statement, asking where the original permitted status of the onions went.
Rabba answers by citing a parallel Mishnah about onions that sprouted from rain, implying the original status is lost.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about black leaves
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about black leaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why black leaves are forbidden, since the original permitted part is gone. It suggests that the Mishnah refers to the added growth, not the original root, and then asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds to the Tanna Kamma's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why black leaves are forbidden, since the original permitted part is gone.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the added growth (תוספת), not the original root.
The Gemara asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds to the Tanna Kamma's statement.
A baraita is cited: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that growth from a prohibited source is prohibited, and growth from a permitted source is permitted.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna Kamma already says the same thing.

items.text: Resolution: The entire Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Resolution: The entire Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah is taught according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that growth that required effort is nullified in the majority, but here the growth did not require effort.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the entire Mishnah is taught according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and until now we did not hear his view where he does not exert effort.
The Gemara resolves that where he does exert effort, the prohibited part is nullified by the majority (בטל ברוב).

items.text: Objection from the case of a litra of untithed produce
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a litra of untithed produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is it always true that effort nullifies? The case of a litra of tevel (untithed produce) requires effort to separate tithes, yet it is not nullified. The Gemara distinguishes: regarding tithes, the Torah permits planting the permitted part, but not the forbidden part.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with the case of a litra of tevel tithe, where exertion is involved yet the Mishnah says to tithe from elsewhere proportionally.
The Gemara distinguishes regarding tithe, because the verse 'עשר תעשר' indicates that permitted produce is commonly sown, but prohibited produce is not.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's statement about a terumah onion
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's statement about a terumah onion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement by Rabbi Chanina citing Rabbi Yannai: If a terumah onion was planted and its growths exceeded the original root, it is permitted. This introduces a new principle about nullification of prohibited growth.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina Tirtata'ah citing Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina Tirtata'ah citing Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina Tirtata'ah reports in the name of Rabbi Yannai: an onion of תרומה (priestly portion) that was planted and its growths exceeded its root is permitted.
The Gemara begins to question whether this implies that growths are considered separate.

items.text: Growth nullifying prohibition
items.text_en: Growth nullifying prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the growth of a forbidden item can elevate the prohibition, citing a mishnah that the growth of terumah is terumah. It distinguishes between first and second growth, and concludes that the teaching is about a case where the seed does not wither, and that the growths are permitted only if they outnumber the original.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether permitted growth can elevate the prohibition, citing a mishnah that the growth of תרומה (priestly portion) is itself תרומה.
The Gemara answers that the discussion is about second growth, and cites a baraita that second growth of תרומה is חולין (non-sacred).
The Gemara objects that the teaching implies even a plant whose seed does not wither is permitted, but a mishnah says only a plant whose seed withers has permitted growth.
The Gemara resolves that the teaching means only when the growths outnumber the original is it permitted.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'הדרן עלך הנודר מן הירק' (we return to you, the one who vows from vegetables).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: Time-based vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Time-based vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rules for vows that specify a time period: 'today' is only until nightfall, 'this Shabbat' includes the entire Shabbat and the previous Shabbat, 'this month' includes the entire month and the next Rosh Chodesh, 'this year' includes the entire year and the next Rosh Hashanah, 'this week' includes the entire week and the previous Shabbat. If one says 'one day', 'one Shabbat', etc., it is from day to day. For 'until Passover', it is until it arrives; 'until it is' is until it ends; 'until before Passover' is disputed between Rabbi Meir (until it arrives) and Rabbi Yosei (until it ends).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows 'קונם יין שאני טועם היום' (a vow that I taste wine today) is forbidden only until nightfall, while 'שבת זו' (this Sabbath) forbids the entire Sabbath and the past Sabbath, and 'חודש זה' (this month) forbids the entire month and the coming New Moon.
The Mishnah continues: 'שנה זו' (this year) forbids the entire year and the coming New Year, and 'שבוע זה' (this week) forbids the entire week and the past Sabbatical year.
The Mishnah rules that if one says 'יום אחד' (one day), 'שבת אחת' (one Sabbath), 'חודש אחד' (one month), 'שנה אחת' (one year), or 'שבוע אחד' (one week), he is forbidden from day to day.

The Mishnah concludes: 'עד הפסח' (until Passover) forbids until it arrives; 'עד שיהא' (until it is) forbids until it ends; regarding 'עד לפני הפסח' (until before Passover), Rabbi Meir says forbidden until it arrives, and Rabbi Yosei says forbidden until it ends.

items.text: Gemara: Need for release for 'today' vow
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for release for 'today' vow
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya states that when night falls, one who vowed 'today' needs a sage's release. Rav Yosef explains the reason: it is a decree to prevent confusion with a 'one day' vow, which lasts from day to day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya states that when night falls, one who vowed 'today' needs a חכם (sage) for absolution.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yirmeya's ruling.
Rav Yosef answers that it is a decree: the term 'היום' (today) is treated like 'יום אחד' (one day) to prevent confusion.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on 'one day' vs 'today'
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on 'one day' vs 'today'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not decree a prohibition for 'one day' due to confusion with 'today'. The answer is that 'today' might be confused with 'one day', but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not decree a prohibition for 'one day' (יוֹם אֶחָד) due to confusion with 'today' (הַיּוֹם).
The Gemara answers that 'today' might be confused with 'one day', but not vice versa, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Ravina cites Marimar on Rabbi Yosef's ruling aligning with Rabbi Nathan
items.text_en: Ravina cites Marimar on Rabbi Yosef's ruling aligning with Rabbi Nathan
items.desc_en: Ravina reports that Marimar said in the name of Rav Yosef that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's ruling follows Rabbi Nathan, who compares vowing to building a high place and fulfilling it to offering incense.

sub.desc_en: Ravina reports that Marimar told him a tradition in the name of Rav Yosef.
Rav Yosef identifies that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's ruling follows Rabbi Nathan, who compares vowing to building a high place and fulfilling it to offering incense.

items.text: Mishnah: 'this Shabbat' includes the entire Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: 'this Shabbat' includes the entire Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that 'this Shabbat' prohibits the entire Shabbat is obvious, but it teaches that one might think the speaker meant only the days of Shabbat, so it clarifies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one vows 'this Shabbat,' he is prohibited for the entire Shabbat.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that one might have thought the speaker meant only the days of Shabbat (Friday night and Saturday), so it clarifies that the entire Shabbat is included.

items.text: Mishnah: 'this month' includes the whole month and the following new moon
items.text_en: Mishnah: 'this month' includes the whole month and the following new moon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about 'this month' is needed for a deficient month, where one might think the new moon belongs to the past month and is not prohibited, but the Mishnah teaches that people call it 'new moon' and it is included.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one says 'this month,' he is forbidden for the entire month and the following new moon.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling is necessary, since it seems obvious, and explains that it is needed only for a deficient month.
The Gemara answers that without the Mishnah, one might think the new moon belongs to the past month and is not prohibited, but the Mishnah teaches that people call it 'new moon' and it is included.

items.text: Mishnah: 'this year' includes the entire year
items.text_en: Mishnah: 'this year' includes the entire year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'this year', he is prohibited for the entire year, setting up the following inquiry about an intercalated year.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'this year', he is prohibited for the entire year, setting up the following inquiry about an intercalated year.

items.text: Inquiry: 'day' without article — like 'today' or 'one day'?
items.text_en: Inquiry: 'day' without article — like 'today' or 'one day'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a vow using 'day' without the definite article: is it like 'today' (until nightfall) or 'one day' (24 hours)? It attempts to resolve from the Mishnah but finds contradictory evidence, concluding no proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about a vow using 'יום' (day) without the definite article: is it interpreted like 'היום' (today) or 'יום אחד' (one day)?
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that 'יום' without the article is like 'יום אחד' (one day), since the Mishnah distinguishes 'היום' (today) from 'יום אחד' (one day).

The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah's continuation: if one says 'יום אחד' (one day), he is forbidden from day to day, which would imply that 'יום' alone is like 'היום' (today); thus no proof can be derived from the Mishnah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inquiry: 'the year' with intercalation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inquiry: 'the year' with intercalation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a Mishnah about a vow using 'the year' where the year was intercalated: the person is prohibited during the year and its added month. The Gemara asks what the case is, setting up further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a Mishnah about a vow using 'the year' where the year was intercalated: the person is prohibited during the year and its added month. The Gemara asks what the case is, setting up further discussion.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of 'year' vs 'the year'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of 'year' vs 'the year'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that if one said 'year' it is like 'the year', but then rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah's case is where one said 'the year', and it teaches that we do not follow the majority of years regarding intercalation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah would need to state the case of 'the year' if it is obvious, and suggests that the Mishnah actually said 'year' (without the definite article), implying that 'year' is equivalent to 'the year' and the same logic applies to 'day'.

The Gemara rejects the initial assumption and explains that the Mishnah indeed said 'the year', and it teaches that we do not follow the majority of years regarding intercalation, contrary to what one might have thought.

items.text: Inquiry about 'Jubilee' in a vow
items.text_en: Inquiry about 'Jubilee' in a vow
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one says 'wine that I taste on the Jubilee', does the Jubilee year count as before the fiftieth year or after?

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an inquiry: if one vows 'wine that I taste on the Jubilee', does the Jubilee year count as before the fiftieth year (i.e., part of the preceding cycle) or after the fiftieth (i.e., the start of the next cycle)?

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on Jubilee counting
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on Jubilee counting
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis argue whether the Jubilee year is included in the count of the sabbatical cycle. The Rabbis cite a verse showing only five years of planting, but Rabbi Yehuda counters with another verse. The Gemara concludes that both can be reconciled by referring to other years of the cycle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita presenting the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding whether the Jubilee year is counted in the sabbatical cycle.
The Rabbis object to Rabbi Yehuda's position, citing the verse 'Six years you shall sow your field' (שמות כג:י), arguing that if Jubilee is counted, only five planting years remain in the cycle.

Rabbi Yehuda counters by citing the verse 'it shall yield produce for three years' (ויקרא כה:כא), arguing that according to the Rabbis' logic, there would be four years of produce, which is also problematic.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that both verses can be reconciled by referring to the other years of the sabbatical cycle, not the Jubilee year itself.

items.text: Beginning of a new Mishnah discussion on 'until Passover'
items.text_en: Beginning of a new Mishnah discussion on 'until Passover'
items.desc_en: The Gemara starts a new topic: the Mishnah's ruling that one who vows 'until Passover' is forbidden until Passover begins, and it questions whether Rabbi Meir holds that one does not include oneself in the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens a new discussion on the Mishnah's ruling that one who vows 'until Passover' is forbidden until Passover begins, and questions whether Rabbi Meir holds that one does not include oneself in the prohibition.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei on uncertainty in vows
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei on uncertainty in vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where a man has two sets of daughters and says he betrothed his eldest, but is uncertain which one. Rabbi Meir prohibits all except the youngest of the youngest, while Rabbi Yosei permits all except the eldest of the eldest. This illustrates their differing views on entering uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita about a man with two sets of daughters who is uncertain which daughter he betrothed, and presents Rabbi Meir's ruling that all are forbidden except the youngest of the youngest.
Rabbi Yosei responds that all are permitted except the eldest of the eldest, presenting his contrasting position on uncertainty in vows.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi's statement on the reversal of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi's statement on the reversal of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi says in the name of Rav that the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei are reversed in the context of fixed-time vows. He cites a baraita where for a fixed time, Rabbi Meir says 'until it leaves' and Rabbi Yosei says 'until it arrives'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Abdimi states in the name of Rav that the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei are reversed in the context of fixed-time vows.

A baraita is cited establishing the general rule: for a fixed-time vow using 'עד לפני' (until before), Rabbi Meir says 'until it leaves' and Rabbi Yosei says 'until it arrives', confirming the reversal.

items.text: Mishnah: General rule for fixed and non-fixed time vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: General rule for fixed and non-fixed time vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for fixed-time events like harvest or vintage, if one says 'until it arrives' he is prohibited only until it arrives, but if he says 'until it will be' he is prohibited until it ends. For non-fixed times, both phrases mean only until it arrives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that for fixed-time events like harvest, vintage, and olive-gathering, a vow using 'until it arrives' prohibits only until the event arrives.
The Mishnah states the general principle: for a fixed-time event, saying 'until it arrives' prohibits until it arrives, but saying 'until it will be' prohibits until it ends.
The Mishnah concludes that for non-fixed-time events, both phrases prohibit only until the event arrives.

items.text: Mishnah: Definition of 'summer' in vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definition of 'summer' in vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines that if one says 'until summer' or 'until summer will be', he is prohibited until people begin to bring in baskets. If he says 'until summer passes', he is prohibited until the corners are folded.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one vows 'until summer' or 'until summer will be', he is prohibited until people begin to bring in baskets.
The Mishnah rules that if one vows 'until summer passes', he is prohibited until the corners are folded.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on the meaning of 'baskets' and 'summer fruits'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on the meaning of 'baskets' and 'summer fruits'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'basket' refers to a basket of figs, not grapes. A baraita states that one who vows from summer fruits is only prohibited from figs. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel includes grapes with figs. The Tanna Kamma holds that figs are picked by hand, grapes are not, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that when grapes are soft, they are also picked by hand.

sub.desc_en: A baraita clarifies that the term 'basket' (כלכלה) in the Mishnah refers specifically to a basket of figs, not grapes.
Another baraita states that one who vows from 'summer fruits' (פירות הקיץ) is only prohibited from figs.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disputes the baraita, ruling that grapes are included with figs in the vow.
The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of the Tanna Kamma (first Tanna) who excludes grapes?
The Gemara explains: The Tanna Kamma holds that figs are picked by hand (a summer fruit), while grapes are not picked by hand.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that when grapes become soft (מירדדן), they are also picked by hand, thus included in 'summer fruits'.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of 'until summer passes'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of 'until summer passes'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'until the corners are folded' means until the majority of corners are folded, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'until summer passes' means until the corners are folded.
A baraita clarifies that the condition is fulfilled when the majority of corners are folded.

items.text: Opening Tanna: ruling on הוקפלו רוב המקצועות
items.text_en: Opening Tanna: ruling on הוקפלו רוב המקצועות
items.desc_en: The Tanna states that when most of the bundles have been removed, the remaining produce is permitted from the perspective of theft and exempt from tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna rules that when most bundles have been removed, the remaining produce is permitted from theft and exempt from tithes.

items.text: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda visited a place where most bundles had been removed; Rabbi ate, but Rabbi Yosei refrained, suspecting the owner's statement was due to animosity.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda visit a place where most bundles were removed; Rabbi eats but Rabbi Yosei refrains, suspecting the owner's permission was insincere.
The owner arrives and asks why the rabbis are not eating, asserting that most bundles have been removed.
Despite the owner's statement, Rabbi Yosei still refrained, suspecting the owner spoke out of animosity.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina ate from the produce but his attendant did not; he instructed his attendant to eat, citing a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei in the name of his father that such produce is permitted.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina eats and instructs his attendant to eat, citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's ruling that when most bundles are removed, the produce is permitted and exempt from tithes.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's instruction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's instruction
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina instructed his attendant to eat, citing a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei in the name of his father that such produce is permitted from theft and exempt from tithes.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Tarfon and the grape thief
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Tarfon and the grape thief
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon found a man eating during the time of הוקפלו המקצועות, put him in a sack to throw him into a river, but the man cried out, and Rabbi Tarfon released him. Rabbi Tarfon later regretted using his Torah knowledge for personal benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon is seized by a man who mistakes him for a thief, but is released when the man fears him; Rabbi Tarfon later regrets having used his Torah knowledge for personal benefit.
The man cried out 'Woe to Tarfon who this man kills him!', and Rabbi Tarfon released him and fled.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports in the name of Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel that Rabbi Tarfon regretted his entire life for using his Torah knowledge for personal benefit, saying 'Woe is me that I used the crown of Torah.'

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana: punishment for using Torah crown
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana: punishment for using Torah crown
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who uses the crown of Torah is uprooted from the world, with a kal vachomer from Belshazzar who used holy vessels that became profane.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one who uses the crown of Torah is uprooted from the world, as derived from Belshazzar's fate for using sacred vessels.

The gemara presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if Belshazzar, who used holy vessels that had become profane, was uprooted from the world, then one who uses the eternal crown of Torah is certainly uprooted.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Tarfon's distress
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Tarfon's distress
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rabbi Tarfon was distressed: the man was a habitual thief, and Rabbi Tarfon could have appeased him with money since he was wealthy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon was distressed by the man's accusation, since he was eating permitted produce.
The Gemara explains that the man had been robbed of grapes all year and suspected Rabbi Tarfon was the thief.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon still distressed himself, since he was innocent.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Tarfon was very wealthy and could have appeased the man with money, avoiding the need to use his Torah status.

items.text: Baraita: learning Torah for love, not for honor
items.text_en: Baraita: learning Torah for love, not for honor
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not study Torah for the sake of being called 'wise' or 'rabbi', but rather learn from love, and honor will come. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok adds that one should act for the sake of the act itself, not for personal gain.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'לְאַהֲבָה אֶת ה׳' and warns against studying Torah for the sake of being called 'wise' or 'rabbi'.
The baraita resolves that one should learn from love, and honor will come, citing verses about the pleasantness of Torah.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok adds that one should act for the sake of the act itself, not for personal gain, and supports this with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from Belshazzar.

items.text: Rava: when one may reveal his piety
items.text_en: Rava: when one may reveal his piety
items.desc_en: Rava rules that one may reveal his piety in a place where he is unknown, citing the verse 'Your servant fears the Lord from his youth', but resolves the contradiction with 'Let a stranger praise you' by distinguishing between known and unknown places.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one may reveal his piety in a place where he is unknown, citing the verse 'Your servant fears the Lord from his youth', but then raises the difficulty of Rabbi Tarfon's case, explaining that Rabbi Tarfon was wealthy and could have appeased the owner with money.

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction between the verse 'Your servant fears the Lord from his youth' and the verse 'Let a stranger praise you' by distinguishing between a place where one is known (where one should not praise himself) and a place where one is unknown (where one may reveal his piety).

items.text: Rava: a Torah scholar may claim precedence in judgment
items.text_en: Rava: a Torah scholar may claim precedence in judgment
items.desc_en: Rava states that a Torah scholar may say 'I am a Torah scholar, give my case precedence', deriving from the verse that the sons of David were priests, and just as a priest takes precedence, so does a Torah scholar.

sub.text: Rava's ruling on Torah scholar's priority
sub.text_en: Rava's ruling on Torah scholar's priority
sub.desc_en: Rava permits a Torah scholar to say 'I am a Torah scholar, give me priority in my lawsuit', deriving from the verse about priests who take precedence, as the priest is sanctified for all matters of holiness.
Rava cites the verse that David's sons were priests, drawing a קל וחומר (a fortiori) that just as a priest takes precedence, so does a Torah scholar.
The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'וקדשתו' (and you shall sanctify him) that the priest is given precedence in all matters of sanctity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three honors given to a Torah scholar: opening first, blessing first, and taking a good portion first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three honors given to a Torah scholar: opening first, blessing first, and taking a good portion first.

items.text: Rava's rulings on tax exemption for a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on tax exemption for a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rava permits a Torah scholar to say he will not pay the tax, citing a verse about the exemption of priests and Levites. He also permits saying he is a fire-worshiper's servant to avoid the tax, as this is merely to ward off danger.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits a Torah scholar to say he will not pay the tax, citing the verse that exempts priests and Levites from tribute.
Rabbi Yehuda explains the three terms in the verse: מנדה (tribute), בלו (poll tax), and הלך (land tax).
Rava permits a Torah scholar to say he is a fire-worshiper's servant to avoid the tax.
The gemara explains that the scholar says this only to ward off danger (like fleeing a lion), not to actually convert.

items.text: Selling wood to a fire temple
items.text_en: Selling wood to a fire temple
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi sold a tree to a fire temple. Ravina objects based on the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind. Rav Ashi responds that most wood is used for heating, not idolatry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi sells a tree to a fire temple (בית נורא), setting up the halachic problem.
Ravina objects that selling wood to a fire temple violates the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind (לפני עור לא תתן מכשול), since the wood will be used for idolatry.
Rav Ashi responds that most wood (רוב עצים) is given for heating, not for idolatry, so the sale is permitted because the majority use is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows tied to harvest and rains
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows tied to harvest and rains
items.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that a vow 'until the harvest' is interpreted according to the local harvest season. For 'until the rains', it means until the second rainfall. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda debate the precise timing for 'until the rains cease'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining the vow 'until the harvest' as until the people begin harvesting wheat, varying by location.
The Mishnah defines 'until the rains' as until the second rainfall, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offering an alternative view.
Rabbi Meir states that 'until the rains cease' means until the entire month of Nisan has passed.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'until the rains cease' means until Passover has passed.

items.text: Gemara: Local interpretation of 'summer' and 'rains'
items.text_en: Gemara: Local interpretation of 'summer' and 'rains'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who vows 'until summer' in the Galilee is bound until summer arrives there, even if it has already come in the valleys. Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between 'until the rains' (plural) and 'until the rain' (singular), the latter meaning until the rainy season.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who vows 'until summer' in the Galilee is bound until summer arrives there, even if it has already come in the valleys.
Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between 'until the rains' (plural), where the dispute applies, and 'until the rain' (singular), which means until the rainy season.

items.text: Baraita on the timing of rain-based fasts
items.text_en: Baraita on the timing of rain-based fasts
items.desc_en: The baraita cites a dispute among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei about the intervals for the third (rain) fast in a drought. Rabbi Yosei adds that individuals do not begin fasting until Kislev arrives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that opens with the question of the timing of the third rain (רביעה), and presents Rabbi Meir's position: the early rain is at three intervals, the intermediate at seven, and the late at twenty-three.
Rabbi Yehuda gives his own set of intervals: at seven, seventeen, and twenty-three.
Rabbi Yosei gives his intervals: at seventeen, twenty-three, and the month of Kislev, and adds that individuals do not begin fasting until the arrival of the month of Kislev.

items.text: Gemara's question on the purpose of the second fast
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the purpose of the second fast
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the first fast is for prayer, the third for fasting, but what is the second for? Rabbi Zeira answers: for making vows (to donate charity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted the first fast is for prayer and the third for fasting, but what is the second fast for?
Rabbi Zeira answers: the second fast is for making vows (to donate charity).

items.text: Gemara identifies the baraita's author
items.text_en: Gemara identifies the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, which counts seven consecutive rainy days as the first and second fasts, aligns with Rabbi Yosei's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by the baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding counting seven consecutive rainy days as the first and second fasts.
The Gemara answers that the baraita aligns with Rabbi Yosei's view, as it counts the seven days as both the first and second fasts.

items.text: Transition to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A brief line introduces the Mishnah about a vow referring to 'until the rains'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to the Mishnah by referencing a case where one vowed 'until the rains'.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows tied to Adar in a leap year
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows tied to Adar in a leap year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules: if one vows to abstain from wine for a year and the year is intercalated, he is forbidden for the extra month. If he vows 'until Adar' or 'until the end of Adar', it refers to the first Adar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules: if one vows 'wine I will not taste for a year' and the year is intercalated, he is forbidden during the year and its added month; if he says 'until Adar' or 'until the end of Adar', it refers to the first Adar.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the Mishnah treats 'Adar' by default as the first Adar.

items.text: Debate: Does the Mishnah follow Rabbi Yehuda?
items.text_en: Debate: Does the Mishnah follow Rabbi Yehuda?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the first Adar is written 'Adar' without specification. Abaye counters that even Rabbi Meir would agree if the person knew it was a leap year; the Mishnah's case is where he did not know.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita.
Abaye counters that even Rabbi Meir would agree in the Mishnah's case, distinguishing between when the person knew it was a leap year and when he did not.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the baraita about Adar in a leap year
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the baraita about Adar in a leap year
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between a vow until the first Adar and until the second Adar in a leap year, implying the first clause deals with a known leap year and the second with an unknown one. This resolves the earlier ambiguity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between a vow until the first Adar and until the second Adar in a leap year.
The Gemara infers that the first clause deals with a known leap year and the second with an unknown one, resolving the earlier ambiguity.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows referring to Passover, fast, and Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows referring to Passover, fast, and Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who vows not to taste wine until Passover means only until the night of Passover, and similarly for meat until the night of a fast. Rabbi Yose his son rules that one who vows not to taste garlic until Shabbat means only until the night of Shabbat, all based on the time people typically consume those items.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who vows not to taste wine until Passover means only until the night of Passover, the time people typically drink wine.
Rabbi Yehuda similarly rules that one who vows not to taste meat until a fast means only until the night of the fast, the time people typically eat meat.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yose his son's ruling
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yose his son's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose his son rules that one who vows not to taste garlic until Shabbat means only until the night of Shabbat, the time people typically eat garlic.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional vow to benefit a friend can be annulled without a sage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional vow to benefit a friend can be annulled without a sage
items.desc_en: If one says to another, 'I forbid myself benefit from you unless you come and take a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine for your sons,' the vower can annul his own vow by saying, 'Didn't I say it only for my honor? This is my honor.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a person vows to forbid benefit from a friend unless the friend takes a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine for his sons, and rules that the vower can annul his own vow without a sage by declaring that his honor is satisfied.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about a conditional vow to give to the vower's son
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about a conditional vow to give to the vower's son
items.desc_en: Similarly, if one says to another, 'You are forbidden to benefit from me unless you give my son a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine,' Rabbi Meir says he is forbidden until the gift is given, but the Sages say he can annul the vow by saying, 'I am as if I have been received.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a case where one says to another, 'You are forbidden to benefit from me unless you give my son a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine.'
Rabbi Meir rules that the vower is forbidden until the gift is actually given.
The Sages rule that the vower can annul his vow without a sage by saying, 'I am as if I have been received.'

items.text: Mishnah: Vows made under marital pressure are permitted
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows made under marital pressure are permitted
items.desc_en: If one refuses to marry his niece and vows that she never benefit from him, or divorces his wife and vows that she never benefit from him, they are permitted to benefit from him because he only intended the vow for the sake of marriage (i.e., to prevent the relationship, not to permanently forbid benefit).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a vow made under marital pressure, such as refusing to marry one's niece or divorcing one's wife, is permitted because the intent was only for the sake of marriage.

items.text: Mishnah: Vow to avoid a friend's hospitality is permitted
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vow to avoid a friend's hospitality is permitted
items.desc_en: If one refuses a friend's invitation and vows not to enter his house or taste his cold drink, he is permitted to enter and drink, because he only intended the vow for the sake of the meal (i.e., to avoid the meal, not to permanently forbid the house or drink).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one refuses a friend's invitation and vows not to enter his house or taste his cold drink, he is permitted to enter and drink, because the vow was only intended to avoid the meal.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about opening vows with parental honor
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about opening vows with parental honor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer permits opening a vow for a person based on the honor of his father and mother, while the Sages prohibit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer permits opening a vow based on the honor of one's father and mother, while the Sages prohibit it.

items.text: Rabbi Tzadok's objection and the Sages' concession
items.text_en: Rabbi Tzadok's objection and the Sages' concession
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tzadok argues that if one can open with parental honor, one could also open with divine honor, nullifying all vows. The Sages concede to Rabbi Eliezer only in matters between the person and his parents.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tzadok objects: if one can open a vow by invoking the honor of father and mother, one might as well open by invoking the honor of God — if so, no vows would ever be binding.
The Gemara resolves: the Sages concede to Rabbi Eliezer in a matter between a person and his father and mother, where opening based on parental honor is permitted.

items.text: Dispute about opening vows based on new circumstances (nolad)
items.text_en: Dispute about opening vows based on new circumstances (nolad)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer further permits opening a vow based on a new development (nolad), such as a person becoming a scribe or his son getting married, while the Sages prohibit it. Examples are given of a vow against benefiting from someone who later becomes a scribe, or against entering a house that becomes a synagogue.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that one may open a vow based on a new development (נולד), while the Sages prohibit it.

sub.text: Mishnah: Example of a person becoming a scribe
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Example of a person becoming a scribe
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah gives an example: one vowed not to benefit from a certain person, and that person later became a scribe or married off his son; the vower says he would not have vowed had he known.

sub.text: Mishnah: Example of a house becoming a synagogue
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Example of a house becoming a synagogue
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah gives another example: one vowed not to enter a house, and it later became a synagogue; Rabbi Eliezer permits opening the vow, and the Sages prohibit it.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Tzadok meant by 'there would be no vows,' and Abaye explains that if that were the case, vows would not be properly dissolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does the phrase 'אֵין נְדָרִים' (no vows) mean in Rabbi Tzadok's statement?
Abaye answers: if so, vows would not be properly dissolved (אֵין נְדָרִים נִיתָּרִין יָפֶה).

items.text: Rava's statement
items.text_en: Rava's statement
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if a sage cannot open a vow with the birth of a child, then no vows would be opened for a sage at all.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if a sage cannot open a vow with the birth of a child, then no vows would be opened for a sage at all.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rava from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rava from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that one may open a vow with the honor of parents. It questions Rava's view, since the person has already been embarrassed. The answer is that since all vows require a sage, here too they open with this reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that one may open a vow with the honor of parents, and questions Rava's view, since the person has already been embarrassed.
The Gemara answers that since all vows require a sage, here too they open with this reason.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on opening with nold
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on opening with nold
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason for Rabbi Eliezer's view that one may open a vow with a new event (nold). Rav Chisda answers that it is derived from the verse 'for all the men are dead', which is a new event.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one may open a vow with a new event (נולד).

Rav Chisda answers that Rabbi Eliezer derives the principle from the verse 'כִּי מֵתוּ כׇּל הָאֲנָשִׁים' (for all the men are dead), which is a new event (נולד), teaching that one may open with a new event.

items.text: The Sages' reason and Reish Lakish's explanation
items.text_en: The Sages' reason and Reish Lakish's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason of the Sages who disagree. It first suggests that they think those men did not die, citing Rabbi Yochanan that 'nitzim' and 'nitzavim' always refer to Datan and Aviram. Reish Lakish explains that they became impoverished, which is considered like death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason of the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer.

The Gemara objects that those men (Datan and Aviram) did not die, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that wherever 'nitzim' and 'nitzavim' appear they refer only to Datan and Aviram.
Reish Lakish explains that the Sages interpret 'death' as impoverishment, meaning those men became impoverished, which is considered like death.

items.text: Four who are considered as dead
items.text_en: Four who are considered as dead
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one without children is considered dead. A baraisa lists four who are considered dead: a poor person, a leper, a blind person, and one without children, each with a prooftext.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that a person without children is considered as dead, citing the verse 'הָבָה לִּי בָנִים וְאִם אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי' (Give me children, and if not, I am dead).
A baraisa lists four categories of people considered as dead—a poor person, a leper, a blind person, and one without children—each supported by a biblical prooftext.

items.text: Baraita on dissolving a vow in the presence of the vow-maker
items.text_en: Baraita on dissolving a vow in the presence of the vow-maker
items.desc_en: The baraita states that one who is forbidden by vow from benefiting from a friend may only have the vow dissolved in his presence. Rav Nachman derives this from the verse where God tells Moshe in Midian to return to Egypt, implying that since Moshe vowed in Midian, he must dissolve the vow there. The Gemara explains that 'alah' refers to an oath, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who is forbidden by vow from benefiting from a friend may only have the vow dissolved in his presence.
The Gemara asks: from where are these words derived?
Rav Nachman answers by citing the verse where God tells Moshe in Midian to return to Egypt, implying that since Moshe vowed in Midian, he must dissolve the vow there.
The Gemara explains that 'וַיּוֹאֶל' (vayo'el) implies an oath, as 'אָלָה' (alah) refers to a שבועה (oath), citing a verse.

items.text: Story of Tzidkiyahu's oath and the Sanhedrin's failure
items.text_en: Story of Tzidkiyahu's oath and the Sanhedrin's failure
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Tzidkiyahu swore to Nebuchadnezzar not to reveal that he ate a live rabbit. Later, Tzidkiyahu sought absolution for his oath and revealed it. Nebuchadnezzar brought the Sanhedrin and Tzidkiyahu, asking if an oath can be dissolved. They said yes, and when asked if it must be in the presence of the oath-maker, they said yes. Nebuchadnezzar then rebuked them for not telling Tzidkiyahu earlier, leading to their punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of King Zedekiah's rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, who had sworn him by God, and describes how Zedekiah swore not to reveal Nebuchadnezzar's eating of a live rabbit.
Zedekiah later suffered physically, had his oath dissolved, and revealed the secret.
Nebuchadnezzar, hearing he was being disgraced, summoned the Sanhedrin and Zedekiah, and asked them: did Zedekiah not swear by Heaven not to reveal?
Zedekiah answered that he had his oath dissolved.
Nebuchadnezzar asked the Sanhedrin: can oaths be dissolved? And if so, in the presence of the oath-taker or even not in his presence?
The Sanhedrin answered: yes, oaths can be dissolved, and only in the presence of the oath-taker.
Nebuchadnezzar rebuked the Sanhedrin for not telling Zedekiah this law, and they were punished by having their cushions removed, as per Rabbi Yitzchak.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Meir's cases of 'like a born event but not'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Meir's cases of 'like a born event but not'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's opinion that there are cases which are like a 'born' event (a change of circumstances that would nullify a vow) but are not considered such, and the Sages disagree. Examples include vowing not to marry a woman because her father is bad, and later the father dies or repents, or vowing not to enter a house because of a dangerous dog or snake, and later the animal dies or is killed. These are considered like a born event but not, and the Sages do not agree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Meir's opinion that there are matters which are like a נולד (new circumstance) but not exactly, and the Sages disagree.
The Mishnah gives an example: one who vows not to marry a certain woman because her father is evil, and then the father dies or repents.
Another example: one who vows not to enter a house because of a dangerous dog or snake, and then the animal dies or is killed — this is like a נולד but not exactly.
The Mishnah concludes that the Sages do not agree with Rabbi Meir's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question and answers on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: In the case of the dog or snake dying, that is a 'born' event (a change of circumstances)! Rav Huna answers that it is considered as if he made his vow dependent on the thing (the dog or snake), so its death is not a new event but a fulfillment of the condition. Rabbi Yochanan says that they told him that the dog or snake was already dead or had already repented at the time of the vow, so it is not a new development.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: the death of the animal is a נולד (new circumstance), so why does Rabbi Meir treat it differently?
Rav Huna answers: it is considered as if he made his vow conditional on a circumstance, so the change is not a true נולד.
Rabbi Yochanan answers: they told him that the dog had already died or the father had already repented, so it is not a new circumstance.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from a baraita on mistaken vows
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from a baraita on mistaken vows
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises a baraita about a mistaken vow where the vow is annulled because it was based on a false premise. The Gemara questions how this fits with the views of Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the need for multiple teachings of 'mistaken vow'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises a baraita about a mistaken vow (נדר טעות) where the vow is annulled because the premise was false.
The Gemara explains that for Rav Huna, who holds that a vow can be treated as dependent on a condition, the baraita fits as one of two teachings: one for a conditional vow and one for a mistaken vow.
The Gemara objects that for Rabbi Yochanan, who already derives the law of mistaken vows from other cases, the baraita's redundant teaching of 'mistaken vow' is problematic.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening a vow with Torah verses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening a vow with Torah verses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's opinion that one may open a vow by citing Torah prohibitions against revenge, bearing a grudge, hatred, and the commandment to love one's neighbor and support the poor. If the person says they would not have vowed had they known, the vow is annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir permits opening for the vow with Torah verses about revenge, hatred, and loving one's neighbor, and the obligation to support a poor brother.
If the person says he would not have vowed had he known, the vow is permitted.
If the vower says 'Had I known, I would not have vowed,' he is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Discussion on supporting the poor
items.text_en: Gemara: Discussion on supporting the poor
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina suggests that one might say they are not obligated to support a particular poor person, but the Sages respond that anyone who falls into poverty first comes to the community fund collector.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina asks the rabbis: can we say that anyone who is poor does not fall on me, and I will support my relative along with everyone else?
The rabbis answer that anyone who falls into poverty does not fall first to the charity collector, implying a personal obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening a vow through the wife's ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening a vow through the wife's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may open a vow for a person based on his wife's ketubah. A story is told of a man who vowed not to benefit from his wife, and Rabbi Akiva compelled him to pay her ketubah of 400 dinars. When the man argued that his inheritance was only 800 dinars and his brother took half, Rabbi Akiva insisted he must pay even if he sells his hair. The man then regretted his vow and Rabbi Akiva annulled it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that one may open a vow for a person based on his wife's ketubah.
The Mishnah introduces a story of a man who vowed not to benefit from his wife, whose ketubah was 400 dinars.
The man came before Rabbi Akiva, who compelled him to pay her ketubah.
The man argued that his inheritance was only 800 dinars, his brother took half, and the wife should not take more than 200.
Rabbi Akiva insisted that even if the man sells his hair, he must pay the full ketubah.
The man expressed regret, and Rabbi Akiva annulled the vow.

items.text: Gemara: Question on movables and ketubah
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on movables and ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether movables are liened for the ketubah, citing the story where Rabbi Akiva said 'even if you sell the hair of your head.' Abaye answers that the land was worth 800 dinars, and the statement about hair means selling it for food, not for the ketubah payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: do movable property (מטלטלי) become liened to the marriage contract?
Abaye answers that the property was land worth 800 dinars, not movable goods.
The Gemara objects: but the Mishnah says 'hair of his head,' and hair is movable property!
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Akiva meant 'even if you sell the hair of your head and eat' — i.e., to sustain yourself, not to pay the debt directly.

items.text: Gemara: Question on siddur for a creditor
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on siddur for a creditor
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that there is no siddur (order of assets) for a creditor, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to address this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the story that we do not arrange assets for a creditor (i.e., leave him with basic necessities).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to respond (the continuation is cut off in the source).
