items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: A brief statement that one does not tear a ketubah document, likely concluding a prior discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that one does not tear a ketubah document.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening vows based on holidays and partial permission
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening vows based on holidays and partial permission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that originally, if one vowed not to benefit from others and was permitted regarding some days, only those days were permitted. Rabbi Akiva ruled that if a vow is partially permitted, it is entirely permitted. Examples follow: if one says 'konam I benefit from all of you' and one is permitted, all are permitted; if one says 'I benefit from this one and that one', the permission depends on which one is released. Additional cases involve vows about wine or onions based on mistaken health beliefs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that originally, when opening vows based on holidays and Sabbaths, only those days were permitted, until Rabbi Akiva taught that a vow partially permitted is entirely permitted.
The Mishnah gives the first example: if one says 'konam I benefit from all of you' and one is permitted, all are permitted.

The Mishnah gives the second example: if one says 'I benefit from this one and that one', the permission depends on which one is released — first releases all, last releases only itself, middle releases those below but not above.
The Mishnah gives the third example: if one says 'I benefit from this one as a korban and from that one as a korban', each requires a separate opening.
The Mishnah gives examples of mistaken vows about wine and onions based on health beliefs, concluding with a story where Rabbi Meir permitted all onions.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling on the last one
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling on the last one
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who is the Tanna behind the ruling that if the last one is permitted, only the last is permitted. Rava answers that it is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one must say 'shevuah' to each individually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of the Mishnah's ruling that if the last person is released from the vow, only the last is permitted.
Rava answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one must explicitly say 'shevuah' to each individual for them to be bound separately.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the wine and onion cases
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the wine and onion cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the person did not realize that wine is not harmful. Rabbi Abba explains that the Mishnah states 'good' (yafeh) for the stomach, implying the person thought it was bad, but it was actually good, so the vow was based on a mistake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the person did not realize that wine is not harmful, which would have dissolved the vow.
Rabbi Abba explains that the Mishnah states 'good' (yafeh) for the stomach, implying the person thought it was bad, but it was actually good, so the vow was based on a mistake.
The Gemara asks the same question regarding the onion case: why did the person not realize that kuferi onions are not harmful?
Rabbi Abba again explains that the Mishnah states 'good' (yafeh) for the heart, indicating the vow was mistaken.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening vows based on personal and family honor, and the story of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening vows based on personal and family honor, and the story of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that we open a vow for a person based on his own honor and his children's honor, e.g., if he would not have vowed knowing that people would say he divorces his wives or that his daughters are daughters of divorcees. Another case: if one vowed not to marry a woman because she is ugly, but she is actually beautiful, the vow is a mistake and permitted. The story is told of a man who vowed against his niece; Rabbi Yishmael had her beautified and asked if he vowed from this one; he said no, and Rabbi Yishmael permitted it. Rabbi Yishmael wept, saying that Jewish women are beautiful but poverty disfigures them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that we open a vow for a person based on his own honor and his children's honor, e.g., if he would not have vowed knowing that people would say he divorces his wives or that his daughters are daughters of divorcees.
The Mishnah gives another case: if one vowed not to marry a woman because she is ugly, but she is actually beautiful, the vow is a mistake and permitted.
The Mishnah relates a story of a man who vowed against his niece; Rabbi Yishmael had her beautified and asked if he vowed from this one; he said no, and Rabbi Yishmael permitted it.
Rabbi Yishmael wept, saying that Jewish women are beautiful but poverty disfigures them, and the Mishnah notes the lamentation for him upon his death.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah first says the vow is permitted only if the woman was actually beautiful all along, but then tells a story where she was made beautiful. It resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: Rabbi Yishmael says even if she was ugly and made beautiful, etc., and then the story follows.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: does the story contradict the earlier ruling?
The gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: Rabbi Yishmael says even if she was ugly and became beautiful, etc., and then the story follows.

items.text: Opening story about Rabbi Yishmael's golden tooth
items.text_en: Opening story about Rabbi Yishmael's golden tooth
items.desc_en: A tannaitic source recounts that Rabbi Yishmael made a golden tooth for a woman, and upon his death, a eulogizer praised him for beautifying the daughters of Israel.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna reports that a woman had a false tooth and Rabbi Yishmael made her a golden tooth from his own funds.
Upon Rabbi Yishmael's death, a eulogizer praised him for beautifying the daughters of Israel, citing the verse 'who clothes you'.

items.text: Story of the husband who vowed his wife taste her dish to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Story of the husband who vowed his wife taste her dish to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she fed her dish to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yehuda ate, reasoning by a fortiori argument from the bitter waters, while Rabbi Shimon refused, citing concern for the widow's sons and to prevent her from becoming accustomed to vowing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story about a man who vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she fed her dish to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehuda ate the dish, reasoning by a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the bitter waters where God's name is erased for marital peace, so he certainly should eat to make peace.
Rabbi Shimon refused to eat, declaring that all the widow's sons should die rather than he move from his place.
Rabbi Shimon added a second reason: to prevent the wife from becoming accustomed to vowing (מינדר).

items.text: Story of the woman who spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Story of the woman who spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: A man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. She did so, and Rav Acha from Difti questioned whether this was intended as humiliation, but was told that spitting on his garment is a great humiliation.

sub.desc_en: A man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she spat on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rav Acha from Difti asked Ravina whether the husband intended humiliation by making his wife spit on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Ravina answered that spitting on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's garment is a great humiliation, so the husband's intent was fulfilled.

items.text: Story of the woman who must show her fairest blemish to Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Story of the woman who must show her fairest blemish to Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: A man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she showed her fairest blemish to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Yishmael asked about each feature, and was told they were all ugly, and her name was 'Lichluchit' (filthy). He declared that she is appropriately named and released her from the vow.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story: a man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him until she showed her fairest blemish to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yishmael asks the people about each of the woman's features, starting with her head and ending with her name.
The people respond that every feature is ugly, and her name is Lichluchit (filthy).
Rabbi Yishmael declares that she is appropriately named Lichluchit because she is filthy with blemishes, and he releases her from the vow.

items.text: Story of the Babylonian who married a woman in the Land of Israel
items.text_en: Story of the Babylonian who married a woman in the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: A Babylonian man married a woman and gave her confusing instructions: first asking for two 'talpei' (which she understood as two legs of an animal), then for a 'griya' (a measure), then for two 'butzinei' (which she brought as two lamps). He then told her to break them on the head of 'Bava', and she broke them on the head of Bava ben Buta, who was judging a case. Bava ben Buta blessed her that God should give her two sons like him.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: a Babylonian man married a woman in the Land of Israel, and after a series of confusing commands (two 'talpei', a 'griya', two 'butzinei'), she brought him two lamps.
The husband tells her to break the lamps on the head of 'Bava'; she breaks them on the head of Bava ben Buta, who is judging a case, and he blesses her that God should give her two sons like him.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and opening of the next
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and opening of the next
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the standard formula for completing a chapter ('Hadran alach Rabbi Eliezer') and the opening words of the next Mishnah about a betrothed young woman whose father and husband annul her vows.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Rabbi Eliezer' (we return to you, Rabbi Eliezer).
The mishnah opens the next chapter: 'A betrothed young woman — her father and her husband annul her vows.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the father annulled a vow but the husband did not, or vice versa, the vow is not annulled. It adds that it is unnecessary to say that if one of them confirmed the vow, it is not annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the father annulled a vow but the husband did not, or vice versa, the vow is not annulled, and it is unnecessary to say that if one of them confirmed the vow, it is not annulled.

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: This is the same as the earlier Mishnah (Nedarim 66b) which says 'her father and her husband annul her vows'? It suggests that one might think the earlier Mishnah meant 'either her father or her husband', so this Mishnah teaches that both must act together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this is identical to the earlier Mishnah (Nedarim 10:1) which already states that her father and husband jointly annul her vows.

The Gemara answers: the Mishnah teaches that even if only one of them annulled, the vow is not annulled, countering a possible assumption that the earlier Mishnah meant 'either the father or the husband' annuls.

items.text: Question on the extra clause
items.text_en: Question on the extra clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah adds 'it is unnecessary to say that if one confirmed it'. If annulment by one alone is ineffective, certainly confirmation by one alone is ineffective. It asks why this needs to be taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why is it necessary to teach the clause 'it is unnecessary to say that if one of them confirmed the vow'?
The Gemara objects: if annulment by one alone is ineffective, then confirmation by one alone is obviously ineffective, so why state it?
The Gemara answers: the clause is indeed necessary for a specific case.

items.text: Answer: case of retracted confirmation
items.text_en: Answer: case of retracted confirmation
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: It is necessary for a case where one annulled and one confirmed, and then the one who confirmed later sought absolution from his confirmation. One might think the confirmation is retroactively nullified, so the Mishnah teaches that both must annul simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains: the clause is needed for a case where one annulled and one confirmed, and then the one who confirmed later asked a sage to dissolve his confirmation.
The Gemara raises a possible assumption: one might think that since the confirmer retracted, the confirmation is nullified and the annulment alone should suffice.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah teaches that both must annul simultaneously for the vow to be annulled, even if the confirmation was later dissolved.

items.text: Derivation of joint annulment from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of joint annulment from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a betrothed maiden's father and husband annul her vows. Rabba cites the verse 'And if she be to a husband and her vows are upon her' (Numbers 30:7). An objection is raised that this verse refers to a married woman. The Gemara responds that another verse (Numbers 30:11) also refers to a married woman, and both are needed to teach that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a betrothed maiden's father and husband jointly annul her vows.
Rabba cites the verse 'And if she be to a husband and her vows are upon her' (Numbers 30:7) as the source for joint annulment.
The Gemara objects that this verse refers to a married woman, not a betrothed maiden.
The Gemara responds that another verse (Numbers 30:11) also refers to a married woman, and both are needed to teach that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that a father and arus annul together is not self-evident from the verse, implying a partnership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that a father and an arus annul together is not self-evident from the verse, implying a partnership.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the verse teaches that the betrothal itself is effective for the arus to annul.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the father alone annuls, and the verse 'וְאָסְרָה אִסָּר בֵּית אָבִיהָ' would be superfluous if the father could annul even without the arus.
The Gemara objects further: perhaps the arus alone annuls, and the father's mention is only to teach that if he ratified the vow, it stands.
The Gemara objects: if the arus alone annuls, why is the verse 'בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה' needed, since a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) would show that the arus annuls even without the father.
The Gemara answers: the verse 'בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה' teaches that the husband does not annul vows made before betrothal.
From this, the Gemara infers that the arus does annul vows made before betrothal.
The Gemara concludes: rather, the Mishnah's ruling must be because of the father's partnership in annulment.

items.text: First answer: the verse implies betrothal
items.text_en: First answer: the verse implies betrothal
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse might be teaching that betrothal (kiddushin) is effective, not that the father and arus annul together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the verse teaches that betrothal (קידושין) is effective, not that the father and arus annul together.

items.text: Rejection: father alone cannot annul
items.text_en: Rejection: father alone cannot annul
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the father annuls alone, arguing that if so, the verse 'her father's house' would be superfluous, as it would be obvious that the father annuls even without the arus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the father alone could annul, the verse 'her father's house' would be superfluous, as it would be obvious that the father annuls even without the arus.

items.text: Second alternative: arus annuls alone
items.text_en: Second alternative: arus annuls alone
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the arus annuls alone, and the father's mention is only to teach that if he ratified the vow, it is ratified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the arus annuls alone, and the father's mention in the verse is only to teach that if he ratified the vow, it is ratified.

items.text: Rejection: superfluity of 'her husband's house'
items.text_en: Rejection: superfluity of 'her husband's house'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the arus annuls alone, the verse 'in her husband's house' is unnecessary, as a kal vachomer would prove that the arus annuls even without the father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the arus annuls alone, the verse 'in her husband's house' is superfluous, as a kal vachomer would prove the arus annuls even without the father.

items.text: Third alternative: arus cannot annul pre-existing vows
items.text_en: Third alternative: arus cannot annul pre-existing vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse teaches that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage, and from this it is inferred that an arus can annul pre-existing vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the verse 'if she vowed in her husband's house' teaches that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage.
From this, the Gemara infers that an arus (betrothed man) can annul pre-existing vows.

items.text: Conclusion: partnership is the reason
items.text_en: Conclusion: partnership is the reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the only consistent interpretation is that the father and arus annul together due to their partnership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the only consistent interpretation is that the father and the arus annul together due to their partnership.

items.text: Source for joint annulment and its interpretation
items.text_en: Source for joint annulment and its interpretation
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'between a man and his wife, between a father and his daughter' that a betrothed girl's father and husband jointly annul her vows. The Gemara asks what the school does with the verse 'if she be to a man', and answers that it is used for Rava's other derivation. Rava then asks what the school does with its own verse, and answers that it teaches that the husband annuls vows that are between him and her.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'between a man and his wife, between a father and his daughter' that a betrothed girl's father and husband jointly annul her vows.
The Gemara asks what the school of Rabbi Yishmael does with the verse 'if she be to a man'.
The Gemara answers that the verse is used for Rava's other derivation.
Rava asks what the school of Rabbi Yishmael does with its own verse.
Rava answers that the verse teaches that the husband annuls vows that are between him and her.

items.text: Inquiry: Does the husband cut or weaken the vow?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does the husband cut or weaken the vow?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: when the husband annuls a vow, does he cut it off entirely (so that violating it incurs lashes) or merely weaken it (so that only a prohibition remains)? The case is where the betrothed girl vowed two olives, the husband heard and annulled, and she ate them. If he cuts, she is liable for lashes; if he weakens, it is merely a prohibition. The Gemara leaves the question open.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: does the husband cut off the vow entirely or merely weaken it, illustrated by the case of a betrothed girl who vowed two olives, the husband heard and annulled, and she ate them.
The Gemara explains the two possibilities: if the husband cuts, she is liable for lashes; if he weakens, it is merely a prohibition, and the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Attempted resolution from a mishnah
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from a mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah: When does the husband's death return authority to the father? When the husband did not hear the vow before dying, or heard and was silent, or heard and annulled and died on the same day. This is the rule: the husband died, authority returns to the father. This is brought as a possible proof for the inquiry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah as a possible proof for the inquiry about whether the husband's annulment is a complete severance or a mere weakening.

items.text: Opening ruling: cases where the husband cannot annul
items.text_en: Opening ruling: cases where the husband cannot annul
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the husband heard and upheld the vow, or heard and remained silent and died the next day, he cannot annul it.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the husband heard and upheld the vow, or heard and remained silent and died the next day, he cannot annul it.

items.text: Two cases: father dies before husband hears, husband dies before father hears
items.text_en: Two cases: father dies before husband hears, husband dies before father hears
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents two scenarios: if the father heard and annulled, but the husband died before hearing, the husband's authority is not transferred to the father; if the husband heard and annulled, but the father died before hearing, the father's authority is transferred to the husband.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents two scenarios: if the father heard and annulled but the husband died before hearing, the husband's authority is not transferred to the father; if the husband heard and annulled but the father died before hearing, the father's authority is transferred to the husband.

items.text: Third case: husband annuls before father hears, then father dies
items.text_en: Third case: husband annuls before father hears, then father dies
items.desc_en: The mishnah rules that if the husband heard and annulled, but the father died before hearing, the husband cannot annul again, because a husband can only annul in partnership with the father.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that if the husband heard and annulled, but the father died before hearing, the husband cannot annul again, because a husband can only annul in partnership with the father.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a father heard his daughter's vow and annulled it, but the husband died before hearing it, the father can annul the husband's portion. Rabbi Nathan notes that this is the view of Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel says the father cannot annul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case: a father heard his daughter's vow and annulled it, but the husband died before hearing it, so the father can annul the husband's portion.
Rabbi Nathan notes that this ruling is the view of Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel holds that the father cannot annul.

items.text: Gemara's inference about the nature of annulment
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about the nature of annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that according to Beit Shammai, the husband's annulment completely severs the vow (migaz gayez), while according to Beit Hillel, it only weakens it (miklash kalesh). This is confirmed as a conclusive inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that for Beit Shammai the husband's annulment completely severs (מיגָּז גָּיֵיז) the vow, while for Beit Hillel it merely weakens (מִקְלָשׁ קָלֵישׁ) it.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about she'elah for ratification and annulment
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about she'elah for ratification and annulment
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether one can seek retroactive nullification (she'elah) for ratification (hakam), and if so, whether one can also seek it for annulment (hafar).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether there is a possibility of retroactive nullification (שְׁאֵלָה) for a husband's ratification (הָקֵם) of a vow, and if so, whether the same applies to annulment (הָפֵר).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on she'elah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on she'elah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Rabbi Yochanan, who states that one can seek she'elah for ratification but not for annulment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting statement from Rabbi Yochanan that one may seek retroactive nullification for ratification (הָקֵם) but not for annulment (הָפֵר).

items.text: Rabba's inquiry about sequential ratifications
items.text_en: Rabba's inquiry about sequential ratifications
items.desc_en: Rabba asks: if one said 'I ratify you, I ratify you' and then sought she'elah on the first ratification, what is the status of the second ratification?

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks about a case where a husband said 'I ratify you, I ratify you' twice and then sought nullification of the first ratification.

items.text: Rava's answer and Rabba's further inquiry
items.text_en: Rava's answer and Rabba's further inquiry
items.desc_en: Rava answers that if one sought she'elah on the first ratification, the second ratification takes effect. Rabba then asks about a case where one said 'I ratify you, and it is annulled for you, and the ratification should not take effect unless the annulment takes effect'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rava's ruling that if the husband sought nullification of the first ratification, the second ratification takes effect.
Rabbah asks about a case where the husband said 'I ratify you and it is annulled for you' — whether the annulment can take effect only if the ratification has already taken effect.

items.text: Proof from the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Proof from the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a substitute offering designated with two names, where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree. The Gemara argues that even Rabbi Meir would agree here that the annulment takes effect, because the husband said 'this ratification shall not take effect unless this annulment takes effect,' which is a conditional statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to bring a proof from the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei regarding a substitute offering designated with two names, citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Meir holds the substitute is for the first name and Rabbi Yosei holds that if he intended both from the start, his words stand.

The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Meir would agree here that the annulment takes effect, because the husband said 'this ratification shall not take effect unless this annulment takes effect,' which is a conditional statement, unlike the Mishnah case where no such condition was stated.

items.text: Rabba's inquiry: simultaneous ratification and annulment
items.text_en: Rabba's inquiry: simultaneous ratification and annulment
items.desc_en: Rabba asks: if one says 'ratified and annulled to you' simultaneously, what is the law? He then cites his own principle: anything that cannot take effect sequentially cannot take effect simultaneously either.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks: if the husband says 'ratified and annulled for you' simultaneously (בבת אחת), what is the halacha?

Rabbah answers by citing his own principle: anything that cannot be done sequentially (זה אחר זה) cannot be done simultaneously (בבת אחת), implying that since ratification and annulment cannot be done one after the other, they also cannot be done together.

items.text: Rabba's inquiry: time-limited ratification
items.text_en: Rabba's inquiry: time-limited ratification
items.desc_en: Rabba asks: if one says 'ratified to you today,' what is the law? Is it considered as if he said 'annulled to you tomorrow,' or not?

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks: if the husband says 'ratified for you today,' what is the halacha?

The Gemara clarifies the two possibilities: do we say that saying 'today' is like saying 'annulled for you tomorrow' (implying the ratification is temporary and annulment takes effect later), or perhaps he did not say anything about annulment at all?

items.text: First hypothetical: annulment stated for tomorrow after silence today
items.text_en: First hypothetical: annulment stated for tomorrow after silence today
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a case where the husband did not explicitly ratify the vow today but said 'It is annulled for you tomorrow.' The question is whether this is effective because he did not say 'ratified for you today,' or ineffective because he already ratified it by his silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a hypothetical: if the husband did not explicitly ratify the vow today but said 'It is annulled for you tomorrow,' is it effective because he did not say 'ratified for you today,' or ineffective because his silence today constitutes ratification?

items.text: Second hypothetical: ratification for an hour
items.text_en: Second hypothetical: ratification for an hour
items.desc_en: Assuming the previous case is ineffective, the Gemara asks: if the husband said 'It is ratified for you for an hour,' does this count as a full ratification that prevents later annulment, or is it like saying 'annulled after an hour'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the husband said 'It is ratified for you for an hour,' does this count as a full ratification that prevents later annulment, or is it like saying 'annulled after an hour'?

items.text: Third hypothetical: annulment after an hour
items.text_en: Third hypothetical: annulment after an hour
items.desc_en: Assuming the previous case is ineffective, the Gemara asks: if the husband said 'It is annulled for you after an hour,' does the ratification stand because he ratified it, or can he still annul later since the entire day is valid for both ratification and annulment?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the husband said 'It is annulled for you after an hour,' does the ratification stand because he ratified it, or can he still annul later since the entire day is valid for both ratification and annulment?

items.text: Proof from a Nazirite case
items.text_en: Proof from a Nazirite case
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof: a woman declared herself a Nazirite, and her husband said 'And I' (becoming a Nazirite himself). He cannot annul her vow. The Gemara suggests this is because once he ratified it, it stands. But it rejects this, explaining that 'And I' is like saying 'ratified for you forever.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as proof: a woman declared herself a Nazirite, her husband said 'And I' (becoming a Nazirite himself), and he cannot annul her vow.
The Gemara questions why the husband cannot annul her vow after the hour, since his 'And I' was a personal Nazirite vow, not a ratification of hers.
The Gemara suggests that the reason is because once he ratified it (by saying 'And I'), it stands permanently.
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that 'And I' is considered like saying 'ratified for you forever,' so it is not a case of simple ratification.

items.text: Mishnah: transfer of authority upon death
items.text_en: Mishnah: transfer of authority upon death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if the father dies, authority does not transfer to the husband; if the husband dies, authority transfers to the father. In this respect the father's power is greater. In another respect the husband's power is greater: he can annul vows of an adult woman (bogeret), while the father cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: upon the father's death, authority does not transfer to the husband; upon the husband's death, authority transfers to the father; the father's power is greater in this respect, while the husband's power is greater in that he can annul vows of an adult woman (בוגרת), which the father cannot.

items.text: Gemara: source for father's authority in her youth
items.text_en: Gemara: source for father's authority in her youth
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the rule that the father's authority applies only during her youth, citing the verse 'in her youth, in her father's house.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the rule that the father's authority applies only during her youth, citing the verse 'in her youth, in her father's house.'

items.text: Source for transfer to father upon husband's death
items.text_en: Source for transfer to father upon husband's death
items.desc_en: Rabbah derives from the verse 'And if she be to a husband, and her vows are upon her' that when the husband dies, authority returns to the father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that when the husband dies, authority over the daughter's vows returns to the father?
Rabbah answers by citing the verse 'And if she be to a husband, and her vows are upon her' (Bamidbar 30:7), implying that when the husband is no longer, authority reverts to the father.

items.text: Gemara's analogy between first and second betrothal
items.text_en: Gemara's analogy between first and second betrothal
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws an analogy between the first betrothal (when the father alone annuls) and the second betrothal (after marriage), arguing that in the second case too the father alone should annul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara draws an analogy between the period before the second betrothal and before the first betrothal, concluding that in both cases the father alone annuls.

items.text: Objection: distinction between vows seen and unseen by the groom
items.text_en: Objection: distinction between vows seen and unseen by the groom
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the father's sole annulment applies only to vows not seen by the groom, but for vows seen by the groom, the father cannot annul alone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the father's sole annulment applies only to vows not seen by the groom, but for vows seen by the groom, the father cannot annul alone.

items.text: Gemara's response: the case is already covered by the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's response: the case is already covered by the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara counters that if the Mishnah refers to vows unseen by the groom, it is already derived from the verse 'in her youth in her father's house', making the Mishnah redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's case refers to vows unseen by the groom, the law is already derived from the verse 'בנעוריה בית אביה' (in her youth in her father's house), making the Mishnah redundant.

items.text: Question about the Mishnah's phrase 'In this the father's power is greater'
items.text_en: Question about the Mishnah's phrase 'In this the father's power is greater'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's statement 'In this the father's power is greater than the husband's power', seeking the specific case it refers to.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's phrase 'In this the father's power is greater than the husband's power', seeking the specific case it refers to.

items.text: First suggestion: betrothal as a na'arah who then becomes a bogeret
items.text_en: First suggestion: betrothal as a na'arah who then becomes a bogeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is where he betrothed her as a na'arah and she became a bogeret, but rejects it because just as death removes the father's authority without transferring it to the husband, so too does bagrut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is where he betrothed her as a na'arah and she became a bogeret.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion by analogy: just as death removes the father's authority without transferring it to the husband, so too does bagrut.

items.text: Second suggestion: betrothal as a bogeret
items.text_en: Second suggestion: betrothal as a bogeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is where he betrothed her as a bogeret, but objects that this is already taught in the Mishnah about a bogeret who waited twelve months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's case is where he betrothed her when she was already a בוגרת (an adult woman past maidenhood).
The Gemara objects that this case is already taught in the Mishnah about a בוגרת who waited twelve months, so it would be redundant.

items.text: Internal difficulty in the Mishnah about the bogeret
items.text_en: Internal difficulty in the Mishnah about the bogeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: why would a bogeret need twelve months? She only needs thirty days. It resolves by explaining the Mishnah says 'a bogeret who waited twelve months'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an internal difficulty: why would the Mishnah mention a bogeret (a young woman who has reached physical maturity) needing twelve months, when she only requires thirty days?
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah actually teaches about a bogeret who waited twelve months, meaning the twelve-month period is stated in a different context.

items.text: Two resolutions for the remaining difficulty
items.text_en: Two resolutions for the remaining difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative resolutions: either the Mishnah here is precise and the other Mishnah mentions bogeret because of Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, or the other Mishnah is precise and the term 'bazeh' is used in both clauses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the difficulty remains unresolved despite the previous discussion.
First resolution: the Mishnah here is precise, and the other Mishnah mentions bogeret only because of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages.
Second resolution: the other Mishnah is precise, and the term 'bazeh' is used in both clauses for stylistic consistency.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a betrothed girl made vows, was divorced on the same day, and then re-engaged even a hundred times, her father and the latest husband annul her vows. The rule is that as long as she has not entered her own domain for even one hour, the father and the latest husband annul her vows.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that a betrothed girl's father and latest husband jointly annul her vows, even if she was divorced and re-engaged multiple times on the same day, as long as she never entered her own domain.

items.text: Gemara's derivation from a verse
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation from a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the latest husband annuls vows that were seen by the first husband. Shmuel cites the verse "And if she be to a man and her vows are upon her" — vows that were already upon her. The Gemara objects that this might only apply to vows not seen by the first husband, but Shmuel answers that the word "upon her" is an extra verse, implying all vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the latest husband annuls vows that were seen by the first husband.

Shmuel cites the verse 'וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ וּנְדָרֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ' (and if she be to a man and her vows are upon her), interpreting 'עָלֶיהָ' (upon her) to mean vows that were already upon her before the new marriage.
The Gemara objects that the verse might only apply to vows not seen by the first husband, but for vows seen by the first husband, the latest husband cannot annul them.
Shmuel resolves that the word 'עָלֶיהָ' (upon her) is an extra verse, implying all vows, including those seen by the first husband.

items.text: Supporting Tosefta
items.text_en: Supporting Tosefta
items.desc_en: A Tosefta supports Shmuel: If a betrothed girl's father heard and annulled, but the husband died before hearing, and she was re-engaged that same day, the father and the latest husband annul. If the husband heard and annulled, but the father did not hear before the husband died, the father returns and annuls the husband's portion.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta supports Shmuel's position by presenting two cases: when the father heard and annulled before the husband died, the father and the latest husband annul; when the husband heard and annulled before dying, the father returns and annuls the husband's portion.
Rabbi Natan notes that the Tosefta's ruling aligns with Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel disagree and hold that the father cannot annul the husband's portion, and the gemara asks what they dispute.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan reports that these are the words of Beit Shammai, but Beit Hillel say the father cannot annul the husband's portion. The Gemara asks: What is the basis of their dispute?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan reports that the cited baraita represents the view of Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel hold that the father cannot annul the husband's portion.
The Gemara asks: What is the basis of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel?

items.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the father's and husband's authority
items.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the father's and husband's authority
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai holds that vows suitable for the betrothed revert entirely to the father's authority, while Beit Hillel holds that the father and the last husband jointly annul vows.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai holds that vows suitable for the betrothed revert entirely to the father's authority, and the husband's authority is completely severed.
Beit Hillel holds that the father and the last husband jointly annul her vows, and the husband's authority is not completely severed.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: divorce as silence or ratification?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: divorce as silence or ratification?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a divorce after hearing a vow is like silence (allowing later annulment) or like ratification (preventing annulment). The practical case is a woman who vowed, her husband heard, divorced her, and remarried her the same day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: are divorces (in the context of vow annulment) analogous to silence or to ratification?

The Gemara clarifies the practical difference: if a woman vowed, her husband heard, divorced her, and remarried her the same day — if divorce is like silence, he can still annul; if like ratification, he cannot.

items.text: First proof attempt: divorce is like ratification
items.text_en: First proof attempt: divorce is like ratification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that lists cases where the father regains authority after the husband's death, but does not include divorce. If divorce were like silence, the Mishnah should have listed it. Since it does not, divorce must be like ratification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing cases where the father regains authority after the husband's death, and argues that if divorce were like silence (שתיקה), the Mishnah should have included divorce; since it does not, divorce must be like ratification (הקמה).

The Gemara raises a counter-argument from the latter clause of the same Mishnah: if divorce were like ratification, the Mishnah should have listed it there; since it does not, divorce must be like silence.
The Gemara rejects both proofs, explaining that the Mishnah's phrasing is not decisive because the first clause might be precise and the second clause follows from it, or vice versa.

items.text: Counter-proof from the same Mishnah's end
items.text_en: Counter-proof from the same Mishnah's end
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the end of the same Mishnah, which lists cases where the husband cannot annul. If divorce were like ratification, the Mishnah should have listed divorce there. Since it does not, divorce must be like silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the end of the Mishnah, which lists cases where the husband cannot annul, and argues that if divorce were like ratification (הקמה), the Mishnah should have listed divorce there; since it does not, divorce must be like silence (שתיקה).

items.text: Rejection of both proofs from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rejection of both proofs from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects both proofs, arguing that the Mishnah's phrasing may be imprecise: the first clause might be precise and the second clause is inferred from it, or vice versa. Thus no conclusion can be drawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects both proofs from the Mishnah, arguing that the phrasing may be imprecise: either the first clause is precise and the second is inferred from it, or vice versa, so no conclusion can be drawn.

items.text: Second proof attempt: divorce is like silence
items.text_en: Second proof attempt: divorce is like silence
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a betrothed woman who was divorced and re-betrothed on the same day has her vows annulled by her father and the last husband. If divorce were like ratification, the first husband's ratification would prevent the second from annulling. Since the second can annul, divorce must be like silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a betrothed woman who was divorced and re-betrothed on the same day has her vows annulled by her father and the last husband, implying divorce is like silence (שתיקה), not like ratification (הקמה).

items.text: Rejection of the baraita: case of an unheard first husband
items.text_en: Rejection of the baraita: case of an unheard first husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the first husband never heard the vow. The Gemara then questions why the baraita specifies 'on the same day' if the first husband never heard, and answers that it refers to a case where the father heard but the husband did not, so the father's ability to annul is limited to that day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the first husband never heard the vow.
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies 'on the same day' if the first husband never heard, implying the father could annul at any time.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to a case where the father heard the vow but the husband did not, so the father's ability to annul is limited to that day.

items.text: Third proof attempt: divorce is like ratification
items.text_en: Third proof attempt: divorce is like ratification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: a woman who vowed on the same day, was divorced and remarried on the same day, cannot have her vow annulled. This implies that divorce is like ratification, preventing later annulment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a woman who vowed, was divorced and remarried on the same day cannot have her vow annulled, implying that divorce is like ratification (הקמה).

The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a married woman (נשואה), and the reason she cannot annul is that a husband does not annul vows that preceded the marriage, not because divorce is like ratification.

items.text: Rejection: the baraita deals with a married woman
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita deals with a married woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita deals with a married woman, not a betrothed one. The reason she cannot annul is that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage (אין הבעל מיפר בקודמין), not because divorce is like ratification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita deals with a married woman (נשואה), not a betrothed one, and the reason the husband cannot annul is the principle that a husband cannot annul vows made before marriage (אין הבעל מיפר בקודמין), not because divorce is like ratification.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the practice of a father or husband annulling a woman's vows before she enters his domain, establishing that after she enters, he cannot annul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the practice of a father or husband annulling a woman's vows before she enters his domain, after which he cannot annul.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a husband can annul vows without hearing them, questioning if the verse "וְשָׁמַע אִישָׁהּ" is essential or not.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a husband can annul vows without hearing them, questioning if the verse 'וְשָׁמַע אִישָׁהּ' (and her husband heard) is essential or not.

items.text: Rava's attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava tries to prove that hearing is not required from the Mishnah's case where the father annuls before hearing, but the Gemara deflects by saying the father only annuls upon later hearing, and the Mishnah merely teaches proper conduct for a scholar.

sub.desc_en: Rava attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a husband can annul without hearing, citing the father's advance annulment before hearing his daughter's vows.
The Gemara deflects by explaining that the father only annuls upon later hearing, and the Mishnah merely teaches proper conduct for a scholar to avoid suspicion.

items.text: Attempted proof from the husband's case in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the husband's case in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the husband's parallel case in the Mishnah that hearing is not required, but it is rejected by positing that the husband also says he will annul upon hearing.

sub.text: Gemara's second proof from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.text_en: Gemara's second proof from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another proof from the Mishnah's continuation about the husband, but the Gemara deflects that the husband also speaks conditionally.
The Gemara rejects the proof by positing that the husband's declaration is conditional on hearing, i.e., he says 'when I hear'.

items.text: Attempted proof from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says a husband can annul future vows without hearing, but the Gemara deflects by saying he meant upon hearing, and explains the practical need for advance annulment due to potential distraction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining that Rabbi Eliezer's case is where the husband said 'when I hear,' and the practical need for advance annulment is due to concern that at the moment of hearing he might be distracted and forget to annul.

items.text: Debate about an agent for annulment
items.text_en: Debate about an agent for annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines whether a husband can appoint an agent to annul vows, citing Rabbi Yoshiyah who derives from the verse that only the husband can annul, and Rabbi Yonatan who argues that an agent is generally valid, with the Gemara noting that even Rabbi Yoshiyah's position is based on a scriptural decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a husband appoints an agent to annul his wife's vows, and Rabbi Yoshiyah derives from the verse 'אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ' that only the husband himself can annul, not an agent.
Rabbi Yonatan objects that throughout the Torah, a person's agent is considered like the person himself, so an agent should be valid for annulment.

The Gemara explains that even Rabbi Yoshiyah only rejects the agent due to a scriptural decree ('אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ'), but otherwise agrees that an agent is like the person himself.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case where a husband says 'when I hear' refers to a situation where he fears he might be distracted and forget to annul, not that he intends to delay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case where a husband says 'when I hear' refers to his fear of distraction, not intentional delay.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inquiry: can a deaf husband annul?
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inquiry: can a deaf husband annul?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a deaf man can annul his wife's vows. Rava brings a proof from the verse 'and her husband heard' which excludes the wife of a deaf man, implying he cannot annul. The Gemara concludes that this is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a deaf husband can annul his wife's vows, considering the possibility that hearing is not essential.
Rabbi Zeira's principle about the waving ceremony (בילּה) is cited as a parallel: what is fit for the act does not require it, but what is unfit requires it.
Rava resolves the question by citing the verse 'וְשָׁמַע אִישָׁהּ' (and her husband heard), which excludes a deaf husband, proving hearing is essential.

items.text: Inquiry: can a husband annul for two wives simultaneously?
items.text_en: Inquiry: can a husband annul for two wives simultaneously?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the word 'her' (אותה) in the verse implies that a husband can annul only one wife at a time. Ravina attempts to prove from the law of the suspected adulteress (sotah) that two women cannot be dealt with together, but Rabbi Yehuda objects that the reason there is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband may annul the vows of two wives simultaneously, questioning if 'אוֹתָהּ' (her) is exclusive.
Ravina cites a baraita that two suspected adulteresses (סוטות) are not made to drink together, implying a parallel restriction for simultaneous annulment.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that the reason for not drinking together is the verse 'וְהִשְׁקָהּ' (and he made her drink), which implies 'her alone', not the concern about a light heart.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a betrothed woman who has waited the prescribed time (12 months for a virgin, 30 days for a widow) is under her husband's authority to annul vows because he is liable for her sustenance; the Sages say he cannot annul until she enters his domain (i.e., the marriage is consummated).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer rules that a betrothed woman who has waited the prescribed time is under her husband's authority to annul vows because he is liable for her sustenance, while the Sages say he cannot annul until she enters his domain.

items.text: Rabbah's comparison to the first Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbah's comparison to the first Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that Rabbi Eliezer and the first Mishnah (about terumah) agree: just as the first Mishnah says a betrothed woman eats terumah after 12 months, so too Rabbi Eliezer allows vow annulment. The first Mishnah states that a virgin is given 12 months to prepare, and after that she eats from her husband's produce and terumah, but a yavam does not feed her terumah. Various scenarios are given for partial time with the husband or yavam.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that Rabbi Eliezer and the first Mishnah (about terumah) agree: just as the first Mishnah says a betrothed woman eats terumah after 12 months, so too Rabbi Eliezer allows vow annulment.

The gemara cites the first Mishnah: a virgin is given 12 months to prepare, after which she eats from her husband's produce and terumah, but a yavam does not feed her terumah; various scenarios for partial time with the husband or yavam are given.
The later court ruled that a woman does not eat terumah until she enters the wedding canopy.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: perhaps the first Mishnah only permits eating terumah (a rabbinic law), but vows are Torah law, so Rabbi Eliezer's leniency may not follow. The Gemara counters that Rabbi Eliezer's position on vows is based on a principle from Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: a woman who vows does so dependent on her husband's will, which is a Torah-based reason, so the comparison holds.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the first Mishnah's permission to eat תרומה (priestly portion) is only a rabbinic law, whereas vows are Torah law, so Rabbi Eliezer's leniency may not apply.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters that Rabbi Eliezer's position on vows is based on the principle that a woman vows dependent on her husband's will, which is a Torah-based reason, so the comparison to the first Mishnah holds; regarding תרומה (priestly portion), Rabbi Eliezer would not permit eating even rabbinically.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on yavam's annulment of vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on yavam's annulment of vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a shomeret yavam, whether for one or two yevamin. Rabbi Eliezer rules the yavam can annul, Rabbi Yehoshua limits it to one yavam, and Rabbi Akiva denies annulment entirely. The Tannaim then debate using a kal vachomer argument and a distinction about shared authority.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a shomeret yavam and the three Tannaic positions: Rabbi Eliezer permits annulment, Rabbi Yehoshua limits it to one yavam, and Rabbi Akiva denies it entirely.
Rabbi Eliezer argues by kal vachomer (a fortiori): if a man can annul the vows of a woman he acquired for himself, surely he can annul those of a woman acquired for him from Heaven.
Rabbi Akiva objects that the kal vachomer fails because a woman acquired for himself has no other authority, but a shomeret yavam has others with authority over her.
Rabbi Yehoshua distinguishes: Rabbi Akiva's objection applies only to two yevamin, but for one yavam the annulment is valid, though the yevamah is not fully acquired like an arusah.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva holds 'ein zikah' (no bond) and Rabbi Yehoshua holds 'yesh zikah' (there is a bond), but questions Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: if he holds yesh zikah, then there is no bererah (retroactive clarification) to allow annulment for two yevamin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Eliezer's position: if he holds that there is a bond (יש זיקה) like Rabbi Yehoshua, then retroactive clarification (ברירה) cannot apply to allow annulment for two yevamin.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's answer: Ma'amar and Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's answer: Ma'amar and Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami explains that Rabbi Eliezer's case involves a yavam who performed ma'amar (a formal betrothal-like act), and he follows Beit Shammai who hold that ma'amar acquires a complete acquisition, thus granting full annulment rights.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami answers that Rabbi Eliezer's case involves a yavam who performed ma'amar (a formal betrothal-like act), and he follows Beit Shammai who hold that ma'amar acquires a complete acquisition, thus granting full annulment rights.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's distinction and Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's distinction and Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes to Rabbi Eliezer for one yavam but not for two, since a second yavam could later forbid her through intercourse or a get, making annulment impossible. Rabbi Akiva holds ein zikah entirely.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehoshua's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehoshua's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes to Rabbi Eliezer for one yavam (יָבָם) but not for two, because a second yavam could later forbid her through intercourse or a גט (bill of divorce), making annulment impossible.

sub.text: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Akiva's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Akiva's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva holds the principle of אין זיקה (no bond of levirate connection), so he denies annulment entirely.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar and resolution via Rav Pinchas
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar and resolution via Rav Pinchas
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from Rabbi Elazar, who holds that ma'amar for Beit Shammai only serves to push off a rival wife. The Gemara resolves that the case is where the yavam stood in court and was obligated to support her, as per Rav Pinchas citing Rava: a woman who vows does so on the condition of her husband's (or supporter's) consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that ma'amar (formal betrothal) for Beit Shammai only serves to push off a rival wife (צרה), what can be said to explain Rabbi Eliezer's position in the Mishnah?

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Pinchas citing Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Pinchas citing Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the case is where the yavam stood in court and was obligated to support her, and as per Rav Pinchas citing Rava, any woman who vows does so on the condition of her husband's (or supporter's) consent.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer for a yavam
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer for a yavam
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if a man who acquires a woman for himself (through marriage) can annul her vows, then a yavam, who acquires a yevamah through Heaven (yibum), should certainly be able to annul her vows. The Gemara notes that if he made ma'amar, he has acquired her for himself, and the acquisition is through Heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if a man who acquires a woman for himself can annul her vows, a yavam who acquires a yevamah through Heaven should certainly be able to annul her vows; the Gemara notes that if he made ma'amar, he has acquired her for himself, and the acquisition is through Heaven.

items.text: Resolving Rabbah's question about ma'amar
items.text_en: Resolving Rabbah's question about ma'amar
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that this resolves Rabbah's question: according to Beit Shammai, does ma'amar effect betrothal or marriage? It would seem to effect marriage, because if it only effected betrothal, the Mishnah states that a betrothed maiden's father and husband annul her vows together, contradicting Rabbi Eliezer's claim that the yavam alone annuls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether we can resolve Rabba's question about whether ma'amar according to Beit Shammai is like betrothal or marriage, since if it were like betrothal, the father and husband would jointly annul her vows, but the Mishnah says otherwise.

The Gemara suggests resolving that ma'amar effects marriage, because if it only effected betrothal, the Mishnah's rule that a betrothed maiden's father and husband annul together would contradict Rabbi Eliezer's position.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reinterprets the word 'yafeir' in Rabbi Eliezer's statement to mean that the yavam annuls in partnership (with the father), not alone, thus avoiding the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Mishnah's 'annul' means annul in partnership (with the father), so it does not resolve Rabba's question.

items.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Ami's version
items.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Ami's version
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Ami's version: a shomeret yavam, whether one or two yevamim, is debated by Rabbi Eliezer (who says the yavam annuls), Rabbi Yehoshua (who says one yavam annuls but not two), and Rabbi Akiva (who says neither annuls).

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Ami's view, recording the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a yavam can annul, Rabbi Yehoshua says only for one yavam, and Rabbi Akiva says for neither.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that the yavam annuls the vows of a shomeret yavam, whether there is one yavam or two.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua rules that one yavam annuls, but two yevamim do not.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva rules that neither one yavam nor two yevamim annul the vows.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's second kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's second kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer presents another kal vachomer: if a woman in whom he has no share before she enters his domain becomes fully his after she enters, then a yevamah, in whom he has a share even before she enters his domain, should certainly become fully his after she enters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if a woman in whom he had no share before she entered his domain becomes entirely his, then a yevamah in whom he had a share (through the brother's marriage) should certainly become entirely his.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's rebuttal
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva rejects the kal vachomer: in the case of a woman he acquires for himself, no one else has a share in her, but in the case of a yevamah, others (other yevamim) also have a share, so the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva rejects the argument: in a regular marriage, no one else has a share, but in yibum, others (other brothers) may have a share, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's challenge and Rabbi Akiva's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's challenge and Rabbi Akiva's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua challenges Rabbi Akiva: your argument applies to two yevamim, but what about a single yavam? Rabbi Akiva responds that they never distinguished between one and two yevamim regarding ma'amar or no ma'amar, and the same applies to vows.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's objection to Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's objection to Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua challenges Rabbi Akiva: your argument applies only to two yevamim, but what about a single yavam? Rabbi Akiva responds that the distinction between one and two yevamim applies equally whether or not ma'amar was made, and so it applies to vows as well.
Rabbi Akiva responds that the dispute applies equally to one or two yevamim, and just as in other matters, so too with vows.

items.text: Ben Azzai's lament and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's lament and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai laments that he did not serve Rabbi Akiva, and the Gemara begins a new inquiry (ma'i) about the implications of the debate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks 'what?' (מאי) to introduce a new inquiry about the implications of the debate.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Ami
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Ami
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that seems to support Rabbi Ami's position, stating that whether or not the husband performed ma'amar (a formal betrothal act for a yevama), the yevama is fully acquired. The Gemara questions that if he did not sanctify her, what does 'fully acquired' mean? It concludes that it must refer to a case where he performed ma'amar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to support Rabbi Ami, stating that whether or not the husband performed ma'amar (a formal betrothal act for a yevama), the yevama is fully acquired.
The Gemara questions that if the husband did not sanctify her, what does 'fully acquired' mean?
The Gemara resolves that the baraita must refer to a case where he performed ma'amar.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava explains the baraita's phrase 'and similarly with vows' by rephrasing it: 'Do you not admit that she is not liable to stoning, like a betrothed maiden?' This clarifies the comparison between a yevama and an arusa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by the phrase 'and similarly with vows'.
Rava explains that the baraita means: 'Do you not admit that she is not liable to stoning, like a betrothed maiden?'

items.text: Rav Ashi's support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah itself supports the view that a yevama is not fully acquired like an arusa, as it states: 'A yevama is not fully acquired for her husband as an arusa is fully acquired for her husband.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah itself supports the view that a yevama is not fully acquired like an arusa, as it states: 'A yevama is not fully acquired for her husband as an arusa is fully acquired for her husband.'

items.text: Mishnah: Annulling future vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Annulling future vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a husband says to his wife that all vows she will make until he returns are upheld or annulled. If he says they are upheld, nothing happens. If he says they are annulled, Rabbi Eliezer says they are annulled, but the Sages disagree. Rabbi Eliezer argues by kal vachomer: if he can annul vows that have already taken effect, surely he can annul those that have not yet taken effect. The Sages respond with a verse: only a vow that has come into the realm of being upheld can come into the realm of being annulled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a husband who says to his wife that all vows she makes until he returns are upheld, in which case nothing happens.
The Mishnah presents the second case where the husband says the vows are annulled, and records the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says they are annulled, while the Sages say they are not.
Rabbi Eliezer argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if he can annul vows that have already taken effect, surely he can annul those that have not yet taken effect.
The Sages respond with a verse: only a vow that has come into the realm of being upheld can come into the realm of being annulled.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: according to Rabbi Eliezer, do the vows take effect and then get annulled, or do they never take effect at all? The practical difference is explored.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether according to Rabbi Eliezer the vows take effect and are then annulled, or never take effect at all, and inquires about the practical difference.

items.text: Opening question about vow taking effect
items.text_en: Opening question about vow taking effect
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a scenario where another person is bound by a vow, and asks whether the vow takes effect if one says 'it is unconsecrated' or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a scenario where another person is bound by a vow, and asks whether the vow takes effect if one says 'it is unconsecrated' or not.

items.text: First proof from Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.text_en: First proof from Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a husband cannot annul vows that have already taken effect, implying that vows not yet in effect cannot be annulled. The Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'that have not come' means they have not yet come, not that they cannot come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Rabbi Eliezer's statement that a husband cannot annul vows that have already taken effect, implying that vows not yet in effect cannot be annulled.
The Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'that have not come' means they have not yet come, not that they cannot come, thus rejecting the proof.

items.text: Second proof from Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.text_en: Second proof from Rabbi Eliezer's analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues from a kal vachomer: if a man cannot annul his own vows after they take effect but can before, then for his wife, where he can annul after, he should certainly be able to annul before. The Gemara questions whether the analogy holds regarding the vow taking effect, and distinguishes between the two cases.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's argument
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's argument
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a second proof: Rabbi Eliezer argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if a man cannot annul his own vows after they take effect but can before, then for his wife, where he can annul after she vows, he should certainly be able to annul before she vows.
The Gemara asks: does the analogy require that the wife's vows, like the man's own, do not take effect before the vow is made?

The Gemara answers: no, the two cases are distinct — each stands on its own terms, and the analogy does not force the conclusion that the wife's pre-vow annulment involves vows that have not taken effect.

items.text: Third proof from the mikveh analogy
items.text_en: Third proof from the mikveh analogy
items.desc_en: The Sages counter Rabbi Eliezer with an analogy: just as a mikveh, which purifies the impure, cannot prevent the pure from becoming impure, so a husband, who cannot purify the impure, cannot prevent his wife's vow from taking effect. The Gemara concludes that this proves vows do not take effect before they are uttered.

sub.desc_en: The Sages present an analogy: just as a מִקְוֶה (ritual bath) that purifies the impure cannot prevent the pure from becoming impure, so a husband who cannot purify the impure cannot prevent his wife's vow from taking effect.
The Gemara concludes from this analogy that vows do not take effect (לָא חָיְילִין) before they are uttered.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Sages' question to Rabbi Eliezer: if immersion purifies a vessel that is already impure, can it also purify a vessel that will become impure in the future? This implies that conditional vows do take effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Sages' question to Rabbi Eliezer: if immersion purifies a vessel that is already impure, can it also purify a vessel that will become impure in the future? This implies that conditional vows do take effect.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the Sages' argument
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Sages' argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages did not fully grasp Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning. They presented a dilemma: if Rabbi Eliezer holds that conditional vows take effect and then are nullified, his vessel analogy is refuted; if he holds they do not take effect, his mikveh analogy is refuted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages did not understand Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning, so they posed a dilemma: if he holds that conditional vows take effect and then are annulled, the vessel analogy refutes him; if he holds they do not take effect, the mikveh analogy refutes him.

The Sages present a dilemma: if Rabbi Eliezer holds that conditional vows take effect and then are nullified, his vessel analogy is refuted; if he holds they do not take effect, his mikveh analogy is refuted.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's a fortiori argument
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's a fortiori argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds with a kal vachomer: if impure seeds become pure when planted in the ground, then surely a vessel that is already pure should remain pure when immersed. This implies that conditional vows do not take effect.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if impure seeds become pure once planted in the ground, then seeds already planted and standing are certainly pure; this implies that conditional vows do not take effect.
The Gemara concludes from Rabbi Eliezer's argument that conditional vows do not take effect (לא חיילן).

items.text: Objection: Do the Sages reject a fortiori reasoning?
items.text_en: Objection: Do the Sages reject a fortiori reasoning?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sages truly reject kal vachomer, citing a baraita where a kal vachomer is used regarding selling one's daughter as a maidservant. This challenges the assumption that the Sages would dismiss Rabbi Eliezer's argument outright.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: do the Sages not employ קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning)? It cites a baraita where a קל וחומר is used regarding selling a daughter, showing that the Sages do use such reasoning.
The Gemara cites a baraita where the Rabbis use a kal vachomer regarding selling one's daughter, proving they do employ such arguments.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'her husband shall confirm it and her husband shall annul it' teaches that only a vow that can be confirmed can be annulled, using a kal vahomer argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'her husband shall confirm it and her husband shall annul it' teaches a kal vahomer (a fortiori) argument: only a vow that can be confirmed can be annulled.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Annulment all day
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Annulment all day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vow annulment can be done all day, with leniencies and stringencies. Examples are given: if she vowed on Friday night, he can annul until dark; if she vowed at dusk, he must annul before dark.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that vow annulment can be performed all day, with both leniencies and stringencies.
The Mishnah provides examples: if she vowed on Friday night, he can annul until dark; if she vowed at dusk, he must annul before dark, otherwise he cannot annul.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei/Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei/Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: A beraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon say annulment is from time to time (24 hours). The Tanna Kamma derives 'all day' from the verse 'on the day he hears', while the other rabbis derive from 'from day to day'.

sub.desc_en: A beraita is cited stating that annulment of vows is all day, with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon arguing it is from time to time (24 hours).
