The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Tanna Kamma, and answers that he derives 'all day' from the verse 'on the day he hears'.
The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the other rabbis (Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar), and answers that they derive 'from time to time' from the verse 'from day to day'.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verses
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both verses are needed: 'on the day he hears' alone might exclude nights, so 'from day to day' includes them; 'from day to day' alone might imply a full week, so 'on the day he hears' limits it to the same day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the first Tanna (תנא קמא) why the verse 'מיום אל יום' (from day to day) is needed, since 'ביום שמעו' (on the day he hears) alone might exclude nights, so 'מיום אל יום' includes them.
The Gemara answers that 'מיום אל יום' (from day to day) is necessary to include nights, which would otherwise be excluded by 'ביום שמעו' (on the day he hears).

items.text: Ruling against the minority opinion
items.text_en: Ruling against the minority opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha does not follow that pair (Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar). Levi wanted to act like them, but Rav said 'my friend said there is no halakha like that pair'. Chiyya bar Rav and Rabbah bar Rav Huna tested this.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the הלכה (binding law) does not follow the pair (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon).

sub.text: Narrative: Levi's intention and Rav's response
sub.text_en: Narrative: Levi's intention and Rav's response
sub.desc_en: Levi intended to act according to those Tannaim (the pair), but Rav told him that his friend (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) said the הלכה does not follow that pair.

sub.text: Narrative: Chiyya bar Rav and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's actions
sub.text_en: Narrative: Chiyya bar Rav and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's actions
sub.desc_en: Chiyya bar Rav shot arrows and checked (to test the ruling), while Rabbah bar Rav Huna sat and stood (in a demonstrative manner), showing their adherence to the majority view.

items.text: Opening question on annulling vows on Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening question on annulling vows on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that vows may be annulled on Shabbat and raises a question: is this only for Shabbat needs or even without such need?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that vows may be annulled on Shabbat and raises a question: is this only for Shabbat needs or even without such need?

items.text: Attempted resolution and refutation
items.text_en: Attempted resolution and refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Zutei's baraita states that vows are only annulled for Shabbat needs. Rav Ashi refutes this by noting the Mishnah's case of a vow made at nightfall, implying that without need, annulment would be impossible even during the day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zutei's baraita is cited as evidence that vows are only annulled for Shabbat needs.
Rav Ashi refutes the baraita by pointing out that the Mishnah's case of a vow made at nightfall implies that without need, annulment would be impossible even during the day.

items.text: Reconciliation via Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Reconciliation via Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to Tannaim: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon hold that annulment is only for Shabbat needs, while the Sages hold it is all day and thus even without need.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the dispute to Tannaim: one view holds annulment is all day, the other limits it to 24 hours.

The Gemara explains the practical halachic outcome: according to the view that annulment is all day, even unnecessary annulment is permitted; according to the view that it is 24 hours, only Shabbat-needs annulment is permitted.

items.text: Question on seeking absolution for vows on Shabbat
items.text_en: Question on seeking absolution for vows on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's permission to seek absolution for vows on Shabbat applies only when there was no time beforehand or even when there was time. A story about the son of Rav Zutra shows that the Rabbis attended to him even for vows that could have been addressed earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's permission to seek absolution for vows on Shabbat applies only when there was no time beforehand or even when there was time.
A story about the son of Rav Zutra shows that the Rabbis attended to him even for vows that could have been addressed earlier.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proposal and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proposal and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef thought that seeking absolution on Shabbat is only permitted with an expert individual, not with three laymen, due to appearance of judgment. Abaye objects that since we permit standing, relatives, and night, it does not appear as judgment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef proposes that seeking absolution for vows on Shabbat is permitted only with an expert individual (יחיד מומחה), not with three laymen (שלושה הדיוטות), because the latter would appear as a court judgment (דין).

Abaye objects that since we already permit vow annulment while standing, with relatives, and at night — all of which would normally be disallowed in a court setting — it does not appear as judgment (דין), so even three laymen should be permitted.

items.text: Rav's ruling on night absolution
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on night absolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav that the halakha permits annulling vows at night, but the Gemara notes this is obvious from the Mishnah, so it must refer to seeking absolution at night.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one may annul vows at night.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah already teaches that a husband may annul a vow made on Friday night, making Rav's ruling obvious.
The Gemara corrects Rav's statement: the halakha is that one may seek absolution from a sage at night, not annulment.

items.text: Clarification of Rav's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba questions Rav Huna about Rav's exact words, and Rav Huna's ambiguous response leads to further inquiry. Rav Ika bar Avin reports that Rav attended to Rabba for absolution at night.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether Rav actually said that one may annul vows at night, and Rav Huna remains silent.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether his silence means he is silent (affirming) or he is drunk (unreliable).
Rav Ika bar Avin reports that Rav attended to Rabba for absolution at night, confirming the practice.

items.text: Opening statement about dissolving vows
items.text_en: Opening statement about dissolving vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a statement from the school of Rav that vows may be dissolved while standing, alone, and at night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition from the school of Rav that vows may be dissolved while standing, alone, and at night.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on dissolving vows
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on dissolving vows
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that vows may be dissolved while standing, alone, at night, on Shabbat, and among relatives, even if there was time during the day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports in the name of Rav Nachman that the הלכה (binding law) is that vows may be dissolved while standing, alone, at night, on שבת (Sabbath), even with relatives present, and even if there was free time during the day.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Gamliel's practice
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Gamliel's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's ruling about standing, citing that Rabban Gamliel sat when dissolving a vow. It explains that Rabban Gamliel required sitting because he opened with regret, while Rav Nachman holds that one does not open with regret, so even standing is fine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the permissibility of dissolving vows while standing, citing a baraita where רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) dismounted from his donkey, wrapped himself, sat down, and then dissolved a vow.
The Gemara explains that Rabban Gamliel held that one opens with חרטה (regret) and needs to examine the vow, so he sat; Rav Nachman holds that one does not open with חרטה, so even standing is fine.

items.text: Story about dissolving a vow and the sin of vowing
items.text_en: Story about dissolving a vow and the sin of vowing
items.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Nachman about a sage who dissolved a vow for Rav Huna bar Avin's son, telling him to seek mercy for sinning. Rav Dimi teaches that one who vows is called a sinner, and Rav Zevid cites a verse: if you do not refrain from vowing, there is sin.

sub.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Nachman about a sage from the West who dissolved a vow for Rav Huna bar Avin's son and told him to seek mercy for sinning, citing a baraita that one who vows is called a sinner, with Rav Zevid citing the verse 'וכי תחדל לנדר לא יהיה בך חטא' (and if you refrain from vowing, there will be no sin in you).

sub.text: The sages' instruction to the son
sub.text_en: The sages' instruction to the son
sub.desc_en: The sages told the son to seek mercy for having sinned by vowing.
Rav Dimi teaches that anyone who vows, even if they fulfill it, is called a sinner.
Rav Zevid cites the verse 'וְכִי תֶחְדַּל לִנְדֹּר לֹא יִהְיֶה בְךָ חֵטְא' to prove that one who does not refrain from vowing incurs sin.

items.text: Tannaitic ruling on a husband's response to his wife's vows
items.text_en: Tannaitic ruling on a husband's response to his wife's vows
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a husband says to his wife 'I do not want any vows you make' or 'This is not a vow', his words are void. But if he says 'You did well', 'There is none like you', or 'If you had not vowed, I would have made you vow', his words are binding.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a husband says to his wife 'I do not want you to vow' or 'this is not a vow', his words are void; but if he says 'well done', 'there is none like you', or 'if you had not vowed I would have made you vow', his words take effect.
The baraita continues by stating that if the husband says 'You did well', 'There is none like you', or 'If you had not vowed, I would have made you vow', his words are binding.

items.text: Procedure for annulling vows on Shabbat
items.text_en: Procedure for annulling vows on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita states that on Shabbat, a husband should not say 'It is annulled for you' as on a weekday, but rather say 'Take and eat' or 'Take and drink', and the vow is automatically annulled. Rabbi Yochanan adds that he must annul it in his heart.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that on שבת (Sabbath) a husband should not say 'מופר ליכי' (it is dissolved for you) or 'בטיל ליכי' (it is void for you) as on a weekday, but rather say 'טלי ואכלי' (take and eat) and 'טלי ושתי' (take and drink), and the vow is automatically void.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the husband must also annul the vow in his heart.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai says: on Shabbat, annul in the heart; on a weekday, verbalize. Beit Hillel says: in both cases, annul in the heart and need not verbalize.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records that בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) say on שבת (Sabbath) one annuls in the heart and on a weekday one expresses with the lips, while בית הלל (Beit Hillel) say in both cases one annuls in the heart and need not express with the lips.

items.text: Distinction between sage and husband in annulment
items.text_en: Distinction between sage and husband in annulment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a sage speaks in the language of a husband (annulling) or a husband in the language of a sage (permitting), his words are void. This is derived from a baraita: 'This is the matter' — a sage permits, a husband does not permit. Even though a husband can annul, he cannot permit, as the verse teaches.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a sage speaks in the language of a husband (annulling) or a husband in the language of a sage (permitting), his words are void.

A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'זה הדבר' (this is the matter) that a sage permits but a husband does not permit, rejecting a possible a fortiori argument that a husband should also be able to permit.

items.text: Derivation from 'this is the word' regarding sage and husband
items.text_en: Derivation from 'this is the word' regarding sage and husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'this is the word' that a sage may permit (annul) vows but a husband may not, and a husband may nullify vows but a sage may not. It then presents a logical argument that a sage, who can permit, should also be able to nullify, but the verse restricts nullification to the husband.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from 'זה הדבר' (this is the word) that a sage may permit vows but a husband may not, and a husband may nullify vows but a sage may not, rejecting a logical argument that a sage should also nullify.

items.text: Gezerah shavah between vows and slaughtered outside
items.text_en: Gezerah shavah between vows and slaughtered outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws a gezerah shavah from 'this is the word' used in the portion of vows and in the portion of slaughtered outside (the Temple). It derives that just as in slaughtered outside the verse includes Aaron, his sons, and all Israel, so too in the portion of vows it includes them. Conversely, just as here 'heads of the tribes' is mentioned, so too there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'זה הדבר' here and in the section of slaughtering outside the Temple, equating the participants (Aaron, his sons, all Israel) and the requirement of 'ראשי המטות' (heads of tribes).

items.text: Purpose of 'heads of the tribes' in the portion of vows
items.text_en: Purpose of 'heads of the tribes' in the portion of vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what halakhic purpose 'heads of the tribes' serves in the portion of vows. Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that it qualifies three laymen (to serve as a court for annulment). The Gemara objects that it says 'heads of the tribes', implying experts, so Rav Chisda (or Rabbi Yochanan) explains it refers to a single expert judge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what halachic purpose the 'ראשי המטות' requirement serves in the vows section, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that it qualifies three laymen (הדיוטות) to serve as a court for permitting vows.
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'ראשי המטות' (heads of tribes), implying experts, not laymen; Rav Chisda (or Rabbi Yochanan) answers that it refers to a single expert (יחיד מומחה).
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'heads of the tribes', implying experts, not laymen.
Rav Chisda (or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan) explains that the phrase refers to a single expert judge, not three laymen.

items.text: Purpose of 'heads of the tribes' in slaughtered outside
items.text_en: Purpose of 'heads of the tribes' in slaughtered outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what halakhic purpose 'heads of the tribes' serves in the portion of slaughtered outside. Rav Sheshet answers that it teaches that there is a possibility of asking (for annulment) regarding consecrated items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose 'ראשי המטות' serves in the slaughtering outside section, and Rav Sheshet answers that it teaches that there is a possibility of asking for permission (שאלה) regarding consecrated property.
Rav Sheshet answers that it teaches that there is a possibility of asking for annulment regarding consecrated items.

items.text: Beit Shammai's view on the gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's view on the gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Beit Shammai, who say there is no possibility of asking regarding consecrated items, the 'heads of the tribes' written in slaughtered outside serves no purpose because Beit Shammai do not accept the gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Beit Shammai, who deny the possibility of asking about consecrated property and reject the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), the 'ראשי המטות' in the slaughtering section serves no purpose.
The Gemara answers: Beit Shammai do not accept the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) at all, so the phrase serves no purpose for them.

items.text: Purpose of 'this is the word' in both portions
items.text_en: Purpose of 'this is the word' in both portions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the purpose of 'this is the word' in the portion of vows: to teach that a sage permits but a husband does not, and a husband nullifies but a sage does not. In the portion of slaughtered outside, it teaches that one is liable for slaughtering but not for pinching (melikah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what purpose the phrase 'this is the word' is written in the portion of vows.
The Gemara answers that it teaches that a sage permits but a husband does not, and a husband nullifies but a sage does not.
The Gemara asks for what purpose 'this is the word' is written in the portion of slaughtered outside.
The Gemara answers that it teaches one is liable for slaughtering but not for pinching (melikah).

items.text: Source for three laymen according to Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Source for three laymen according to Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai derive that three laymen are qualified (for annulment of vows). It answers that they derive it from a teaching of Rav Asi bar Natan, who cites a baraita about the order of 'mo'adim' (festivals) and the exclusion of Shabbat and the portion of vows. Rav Asi bar Natan challenges the baraita, and Rav Sheshet explains the correct version.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai derive that three laymen are qualified for annulment of vows.
The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai derive it from a teaching of Rav Asi bar Natan.

sub.text: Baraita cited by Rav Asi bar Natan
sub.text_en: Baraita cited by Rav Asi bar Natan
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Natan cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Ben Azzai debate the exclusion of Shabbat and the portion of vows from the festivals.
Rav Asi bar Natan challenges the baraita, noting that Shabbat and the portion of vows are actually written alongside the festivals.
Rav Sheshet explains the correct version of the baraita to resolve the challenge.

items.text: Opening comparison: Festivals vs. Vows
items.text_en: Opening comparison: Festivals vs. Vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts festivals, which require court sanctification, with the section on vows, which does not require an expert court, only a lay court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by contrasting festivals, which require court sanctification and an expert court, with the section on vows, which requires only a lay court.

items.text: Objection and resolution: 'Heads of the tribes'
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: 'Heads of the tribes'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'heads of the tribes' implies experts, but Rav Chisda (or Rabbi Yochanan) answers that this applies only to an individual expert, not a court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'heads of the tribes' (ראשי המטות) implies that experts (מומחה) are required for the section of vows, contradicting the earlier statement.
Rav Chisda (or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan) answers that the requirement of a מומחה (expert) applies only to an individual expert (יחיד מומחה), not to a court of laymen.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that one who is silent with intent to nullify can nullify even after ten days. Rava challenges this from a Mishnah that distinguishes between hearing and silence, and the Gemara clarifies that the silence must be without intent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that one who is silent with intent to nullify (שותק על מנת למיקט) can nullify even after ten days.
Rava challenges Rabbi Chanina from a Mishnah that distinguishes between hearing and silence, implying that silence without immediate nullification is ineffective.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's silence refers to one who is silent with intent to nullify (שותק על מנת למיקט).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to one who is silent with intent to confirm (שותק על מנת לקיים), not to nullify.
The Gemara objects that if so, this case is identical to the Mishnah's category of 'heard and confirmed' (שמע וקיים).
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to one who is silent without any specific intent (שותק סתם), distinguishing it from both intent to nullify and intent to confirm.

items.text: Rav Chisda's challenge: Stringencies of ratification and nullification
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge: Stringencies of ratification and nullification
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins to cite a baraita about the relative stringencies of ratifying and nullifying vows, which will be analyzed further.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins to cite a baraita about the relative stringencies of ratifying and nullifying vows.

items.text: Gemara's question on silence and intent
items.text_en: Gemara's question on silence and intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that silence ratifies but does not annul. It asks whether this refers to silence with intent to annul, and concludes it refers to silence without specific intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's statement that silence ratifies refers to silence with intent to annul.
The Gemara first answers that it refers to silence with intent to ratify, but objects that this is identical to ratification in the heart.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to silence without specific intent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between ratification and annulment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between ratification and annulment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one may seek absolution for ratification but not for annulment, highlighting a stringency in annulment over ratification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found a stringency in ratification over annulment, but from where do we derive a stringency in annulment over ratification?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: one may seek absolution for ratification but not for annulment, establishing a stringency in annulment.

items.text: Rav Kahana's challenge from the verse
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's challenge from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing the verse 'If her husband remains silent' (Numbers 30:15), arguing that it refers to silence with intent to annul. The Gemara concludes this is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing the verse 'If her husband remains silent' (Numbers 30:15), arguing that it refers to silence with intent to annul, and poses a dilemma whether the verse speaks of silence for annulment or for confirmation.

The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing the parallel verse 'כי החריש לה' (for he remained silent to her), which refers to silence for confirmation, leaving the original verse to refer to silence for annulment, and concludes this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the verses
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that one verse refers to silence with intent to ratify, another to silence without specific intent, and the verses are redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by assigning one verse to silence with intent to ratify and the other to silence without specific intent, explaining that the verses are redundant.

items.text: Rava's challenge from the case of nightfall
items.text_en: Rava's challenge from the case of nightfall
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the principle by citing a case where a husband cannot annul after nightfall, even though his silence might be with intent to annul. The Gemara declares this a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the principle by citing a case where a woman vowed at nightfall and the husband cannot annul after dark, even though his silence might be with intent to annul.
The Gemara asks why this case does not count as silence with intent to annul, which would permit annulment after the fact.
The Gemara declares this a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of the principle that silence with intent to annul is effective.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge from ignorance of annulment
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge from ignorance of annulment
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges with a case where a husband is ignorant of the power to annul; Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether he can annul. The Gemara questions why this is not considered silence with intent to annul, and concludes it is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a Mishnah where a husband ignorant of annulment power can annul, but Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute a case where he is ignorant that this is a vow; the Gemara will question why this is not considered silence with intent to annul.
The Gemara objects: why is this not considered silence with intent to annul, given the husband's ignorance?
The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of the earlier position.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and opening of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and opening of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The chapter concludes with 'Hadran' (we return to you), and the next Mishnah lists vows that a husband can annul, specifically those involving affliction of the soul.

sub.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the formula 'Hadran alach' (we return to you) addressed to the Mishnah of the betrothed young woman.
The next Mishnah lists vows that a husband can annul, specifically those involving עינוי נפש (affliction of the soul), with examples of bathing and adorning oneself.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yosei's classification of vows
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yosei's classification of vows
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that certain vows are not considered vows of affliction, and he lists examples. He distinguishes between vows that can be annulled because they cause affliction and those that cannot, unless the husband's livelihood depends on the prohibited item.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens by stating that certain vows are not considered vows of affliction, then lists examples and the rule for annulment.

items.text: Gemara's first question: contradiction from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: contradiction from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that only vows of affliction can be annulled, citing a baraita that teaches a husband can annul vows that are 'between him and her' (things that affect their relationship), even if not afflictive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that only vows of affliction can be annulled, citing a baraita that teaches a husband can annul vows that are 'between him and her' (things that affect their relationship), even if not afflictive.

items.text: First answer: distinction between permanent and conditional annulment
items.text_en: First answer: distinction between permanent and conditional annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that both types of vows can be annulled, but with a difference: for vows of affliction, the annulment is permanent; for other vows, the annulment only lasts while she is under him, but if he divorces her, the vow takes effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that both types of vows are annulled, but for afflictive vows the annulment is permanent, while for non-afflictive vows between them the annulment only lasts while she is under his authority; if he divorces her, the vow takes effect.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous answer by citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says a husband must annul such vows because he might divorce her and she would be forbidden to him, implying that annulment is effective even after divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that the husband annuls such vows precisely because he might divorce her and she would be forbidden to him, implying that the annulment is effective even after divorce.

items.text: Second answer: distinction between annulment for oneself and for others
items.text_en: Second answer: distinction between annulment for oneself and for others
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a new answer: both types of vows are annulled permanently, but the difference is that for vows of affliction, the husband can annul both for himself and for others (i.e., to prevent her from being prohibited to others), while for other vows, he can only annul for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that both types of vows are effectively annulled, but the distinction is that afflictive vows are annulled both for himself and for others, while non-afflictive vows are annulled only for himself, not for others.

items.text: Analysis of a conditional vow: 'If I wash'
items.text_en: Analysis of a conditional vow: 'If I wash'
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a case where a woman vows that produce is forbidden to her if she washes, questioning why annulment is needed and how Rabbi Yosei could say it is not a vow of affliction, since if she washes, the vow takes effect and causes affliction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the conditional vow 'If I wash' is formulated, suggesting that if she said 'produce is forbidden to me if I wash', no annulment is needed because she can simply avoid washing.
The Gemara further objects that Rabbi Yosei could not call this a non-afflictive vow, since if she washes, the produce becomes forbidden and causes affliction.

items.text: First proposed scenario: indefinite prohibition
items.text_en: First proposed scenario: indefinite prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's case is where the wife says 'Konam if I bathe, bathing is forbidden to me forever.' If she bathes, she is prohibited; if she does not, she becomes repulsive. Rabbi Yosei holds that she can avoid bathing and we do not worry about repulsiveness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's case is where the wife says 'Konam if I bathe, bathing is forbidden to me forever,' and explains that Rabbi Yosei holds she can avoid bathing and we do not worry about repulsiveness.

items.text: Objection to the first scenario
items.text_en: Objection to the first scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if that is the case, the Mishnah should have stated explicitly that Rabbi Yosei says this condition does not involve affliction of the soul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yosei's reasoning were as suggested, the Mishnah should have explicitly stated that this condition does not involve עינוי נפש (affliction of the soul).

items.text: Second proposed scenario: one-day prohibition
items.text_en: Second proposed scenario: one-day prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara instead proposes that the wife says 'Bathing is forbidden to me forever if I bathe today.' Rabbi Yosei holds that one day's repulsiveness is not considered repulsiveness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a revised scenario where the wife's vow prohibits bathing forever if she bathes today, and explains that Rabbi Yosei holds that one day's repulsiveness is not considered repulsiveness.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's cases of 'if I do not bathe' and 'if I do not adorn'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's cases of 'if I do not bathe' and 'if I do not adorn'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of 'if I do not bathe', suggesting that if the woman simply vowed not to bathe today, she could just bathe. Rav Yehuda explains that she vowed not to bathe in מי משׁרה (tanning fluid), which is not a normal bath. Similarly, the case of 'if I do not adorn' refers to not adorning with נפט (a type of oil), which is actually a stain. Rav Yehuda then offers an alternative explanation: she made both a vow and a swear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of 'if I do not bathe', arguing that if the woman vowed not to bathe today, she could simply bathe, so why would the husband need to annul?
Rav Yehuda explains that the woman vowed not to bathe in מי משׁרה (tanning fluid), which is not a normal bath, so the husband must annul.
The Gemara objects that the parallel case of 'if I do not adorn' would refer to not adorning with נפט (a type of oil), which is actually a stain, not an adornment.
Rav Yehuda offers an alternative explanation: the woman made both a vow (to forbid benefit if she bathes/adorns today) and a swear (not to bathe/adorn), so the husband must annul both.

items.text: Ravina's objection and resolution: the Mishnah should say 'these are vows and oaths'
items.text_en: Ravina's objection and resolution: the Mishnah should say 'these are vows and oaths'
items.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that the Mishnah should have been titled 'these are vows and oaths' since it includes oaths. Rav Ashi responds that one can teach it as such, or alternatively, oaths are included in vows as per the Tosefta that 'vows of the wicked' include nazirite, sacrifice, and oath.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that the Mishnah should have been titled 'these are vows and oaths' since it includes oaths.
Rav Ashi responds that one can simply teach the Mishnah as 'these are vows and oaths'.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: oaths are included in vows, as per the Tosefta that 'vows of the wicked' include nazirite, sacrifice, and oath.

items.text: Contradiction on whether bathing is affliction, and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction on whether bathing is affliction, and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies that not bathing is affliction, but a baraita on Yom Kippur states that only eating, drinking, and work carry karet, implying bathing is not affliction. Rava resolves this by distinguishing between the contexts: regarding Yom Kippur, the verse speaks of something that is currently known as affliction (bathing is not), but regarding vows, the verse speaks of something that can lead to affliction (not bathing can lead to affliction).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies that not bathing is affliction, but a baraita on Yom Kippur states that only eating, drinking, and work carry karet, implying bathing is not affliction.

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the contexts: regarding Yom Kippur, the verse speaks of something currently known as affliction (bathing is not), but regarding vows, the verse speaks of something that can lead to affliction (not bathing can lead to affliction).

items.text: Contradiction within Rabbi Yossi's statements on laundry versus life
items.text_en: Contradiction within Rabbi Yossi's statements on laundry versus life
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the first Tanna says that one's own laundry takes precedence over others' laundry, but others' lives take precedence over one's own laundry. Rabbi Yossi says that one's own laundry takes precedence over others' lives. This seems to contradict another statement of Rabbi Yossi that laundry involves suffering, implying it is not a trivial matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yossi by citing a baraita where the first Tanna prioritizes others' lives over one's own laundry, while Rabbi Yossi prioritizes one's own laundry over others' lives.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yossi's statement that laundry takes precedence over others' lives contradicts his earlier statement that laundry involves suffering, implying it is not a trivial matter.

items.text: The severity of neglect according to Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: The severity of neglect according to Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Yosei, washing clothes is more stringent than saving a life, as neglect of clothes leads to mold, neglect of the body leads to boils and sores, and neglect of the head leads to blindness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if neglect of the head causes blindness, then neglect of the entire body should certainly cause even worse conditions.

The Gemara answers: yes, but for Rabbi Yosei, washing clothes is more stringent than saving a life, as Shmuel taught that neglect of the head leads to blindness, neglect of clothes leads to mold, and neglect of the body leads to boils and sores.

items.text: Warning about neglect and the poor
items.text_en: Warning about neglect and the poor
items.desc_en: A message is sent from the academy: beware of neglect, beware of company, and beware of the children of the poor, for from them Torah will emerge, as it is written: 'Water shall flow from his branches.'

sub.desc_en: The academy sends a warning to beware of neglect, company, and the children of the poor, from whom Torah will emerge.

items.text: Why Torah scholars' children often do not become scholars
items.text_en: Why Torah scholars' children often do not become scholars
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim offer reasons: Rav Yosef says so that they do not think Torah is an inheritance; Rav Sheshet says so that they do not become arrogant over the community; Mar Zutra says because they dominate the community; Rav Ashi says because they call people 'donkeys'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Torah scholars' children are not commonly found to become Torah scholars themselves.
Rav Yosef answers: so that people should not say that Torah is an inheritance for them.
Rav Sheshet answers: so that they should not become arrogant over the community.
Mar Zutra answers: because they dominate the community.
Rav Ashi answers: because they call people 'donkeys'.

items.text: The reason: not blessing the Torah first
items.text_en: The reason: not blessing the Torah first
items.desc_en: Ravina says it is because they do not recite a blessing over the Torah first. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the verse 'Who is the wise man who will understand this?' was asked of the sages and prophets but not explained until God Himself explained it: 'Because they forsook My Torah' – this refers to not reciting a blessing over the Torah first.

sub.desc_en: Ravina states that the reason Torah scholars do not produce scholarly sons is because they do not recite a blessing over the Torah first.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav introduces the verse 'Who is the wise man who will understand this?' and notes that sages and prophets could not explain it.
The Gemara relates that God Himself explained the verse, citing 'Because they forsook My Torah'.
The Gemara objects that the phrases 'have not obeyed My voice' and 'nor walked therein' seem redundant.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves the objection by explaining that 'nor walked therein' means they did not recite a blessing over the Torah first.

items.text: The source for Rabbi Yosei's ruling on washing clothes
items.text_en: The source for Rabbi Yosei's ruling on washing clothes
items.desc_en: Isi bar Yehuda did not attend Rabbi Yosei's academy for three days. Vardimus bar Rabbi Yosei asked him why, and Isi explained he did not know the reason for Rabbi Yosei's ruling that washing clothes takes precedence over saving others' lives. Vardimus then derived the source from the verse about the Levites' cities: 'and their open land shall be for their cattle' – 'chayyatam' refers to life itself, implying washing clothes due to the pain of neglect.

sub.desc_en: Isi bar Yehuda missed Rabbi Yosei's academy for three days; Vardimus bar Rabbi Yosei asked why, and Isi explained he did not know the reason for Rabbi Yosei's ruling that washing clothes takes precedence over saving others' lives.
Vardimus derived the source from the verse about the Levites' cities: 'chayyatam' refers to life itself, implying washing clothes due to the pain of neglect.

items.text: Debate: Can Rabbi Yosei annul vows for matters between him and her?
items.text_en: Debate: Can Rabbi Yosei annul vows for matters between him and her?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yosei, can a husband annul vows that are not for self-affliction but involve matters between him and his wife? The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosei's statement 'These are not vows of self-affliction' implies that matters between him and her are considered vows. However, it is possible he was speaking to his disputants, saying that for himself even those are not vows, but for them who consider these as self-affliction, he concedes they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's statement that these are not vows of self-affliction and asks whether he can annul them for matters between him and her.
The Gemara proposes a proof: Rabbi Yosei's statement implies that matters between him and her are considered vows.

The Gemara rejects the proof: Rabbi Yosei may have been speaking to his disputants, conceding that for them these are not vows of self-affliction, but for himself even matters between him and her are not vows.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Adda and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Adda and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rav Adda bar Ahava says the husband may annul, while Rav Huna says he may not annul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav Adda bar Ahava rules the husband may annul, while Rav Huna rules he may not annul.

items.text: Opening aphorism
items.text_en: Opening aphorism
items.desc_en: A brief statement that we never find a fox that died in the dust of a pit, likely a proverbial remark.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a proverbial statement that we never find a fox that died in the dust of a pit.

items.text: Baraita on annulment of vows
items.text_en: Baraita on annulment of vows
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Adda bar Ahava's view: vows that involve affliction of the soul are annulled by the husband, whether they affect him or others; vows without such affliction are annulled only if between him and her. Examples are given, and Rabban Gamliel adds that a sage cannot annul his own vows, citing the verse 'lo yachel devaro'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: vows with affliction of the soul are annulled by the husband regardless of whom they affect; vows without such affliction are annulled only if between him and her.
The baraita gives examples: a vow against fruits is annulled; vows against doing things for others or providing for animals are not annulled.
The baraita rules that vows about cosmetics and marital relations are annulled as matters between husband and wife.
The baraita rules that vows about domestic service to the husband do not require annulment.
Rabban Gamliel argues that such vows are annulled, and derives from the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' that a sage cannot annul his own vows.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna for cosmetics
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna for cosmetics
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the view that vows about cosmetics are matters between him and her is that of Rabbi Yosei, and the baraita rules that he annuls them for that reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that vows about cosmetics (not applying kohl or rouge) are matters between him and her, and identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita rules that the husband annuls such vows because they are matters between him and her, consistent with Rabbi Yosei's view.

items.text: Analysis of the vow about marital intimacy
items.text_en: Analysis of the vow about marital intimacy
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the case of a vow not to use the marital bed. If she says 'my intimacy is forbidden to you', no annulment is needed because she is obligated to him. If she says 'your intimacy is forbidden to me', he must annul it, as per Rav Kahana's principle that one cannot be fed something forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that a vow not to use the marital bed is annulled because it is a matter between husband and wife.
The Gemara asks what the specific case is.
The Gemara objects that if she said 'my intimacy is forbidden to you', no annulment is needed because she is obligated to him.
The Gemara answers that the case is when she says 'your intimacy is forbidden to me', and it follows Rav Kahana's principle.

Rav Kahana rules that if she says 'my intimacy is forbidden to you', he may force her to serve him, but if she says 'your intimacy is forbidden to me', he must annul it because one cannot be fed something forbidden.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna for the baraita on permitted matters
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna for the baraita on permitted matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna of a baraita that says one may not permit what others treat as forbidden, citing 'lo yachel devaro', and that a Torah scholar cannot annul his own vows. It concludes that this is Rabban Gamliel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that forbids permitting what others treat as forbidden, citing the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' (he shall not profane his word).
The baraita adds a second interpretation of the verse, deriving that a Torah scholar cannot annul his own vows.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows the view of Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about marital intimacy
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about marital intimacy
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether marital intimacy is considered affliction of the soul or matters between him and her. Rav Nachman responds that they have already learned this from the mishnah: 'And I am removed from the Jews'.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether marital intimacy (תשמיש המיטה) is classified as עינוי נפש (affliction of the soul) or as matters between him and her.
Rav Nachman responds that they have already learned this from the mishnah: 'ונטולה אני מן היהודים' (and I am removed from the Jews).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'she shall be removed from the Jews'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'she shall be removed from the Jews'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that if a woman vows to be 'removed from the Jews', the husband annuls his portion and she may serve him. It argues that if this is a vow of affliction, why would she be removed from the Jews? It concludes that such vows are matters between husband and wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'she shall be removed from the Jews', arguing that if this were a vow of affliction (נדר עינוי נפש), the husband could not annul it, so it must be a matter between husband and wife.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the Rabbis, the case of 'removed from the Jews' is a matter between husband and wife, but the Mishnah is taught by Rabbi Yosei, as Rav Huna said the entire chapter is Rabbi Yosei's. The proof is that since Rabbi Yosei already said these are not vows of affliction, why teach 'this one annuls' again? Hence the rest is Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis, the case of 'removed from the Jews' is a matter between husband and wife, but the Mishnah is taught by Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Huna states that the entire chapter is Rabbi Yosei's.
The Gemara proves that since Rabbi Yosei already said these are not vows of affliction, the rest of the Mishnah must be his.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on annulling vows regarding benefit from a specific person
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on annulling vows regarding benefit from a specific person
items.desc_en: Shmuel says in the name of Levi that a husband can annul all his wife's vows except 'my benefit from so-and-so', which he cannot annul. But if she says 'so-and-so's benefit from me', he can annul.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules in the name of Levi that a husband can annul all his wife's vows except 'my benefit from so-and-so', but if she says 'so-and-so's benefit from me', he can annul.

items.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of the Mishnah's case of produce from a specific region
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of the Mishnah's case of produce from a specific region
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says if a woman vows 'produce of this region is upon me', the husband brings her from another region. Rav Yosef explains that she meant 'that she bring' (i.e., she will bring it herself), so the husband can provide from elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman vows 'produce of this region is upon me', the husband brings her from another region.
Rav Yosef explains that the woman meant 'that she bring' (i.e., she will bring it herself), so the husband can provide from elsewhere.

items.text: Gemara's attempted proof from the case of a specific storekeeper
items.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from the case of a specific storekeeper
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah: if a woman vows 'produce of this storekeeper is upon me', the husband cannot annul. It suggests that here too she meant 'that you bring' (i.e., the husband brings), but the Gemara does not conclude.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a woman vows 'produce of this storekeeper is upon me' and the husband cannot annul, suggesting that here too she meant 'that you bring' (i.e., the husband brings), but the Gemara does not conclude.

items.text: Refutation from the case where the husband's livelihood depends on that storekeeper
items.text_en: Refutation from the case where the husband's livelihood depends on that storekeeper
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: if his livelihood is only from that storekeeper, he can annul. The Gemara argues: if she meant 'that you bring', why can he annul? Rather, from the latter clause where the husband does not bring, the first clause is where she brings herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the wife said 'that you bring,' why can the husband annul when his livelihood depends on that storekeeper?
The Gemara resolves: from the latter clause where the husband does not bring, the first clause is where she brings herself.

items.text: Conclusion: distinction between the two clauses
items.text_en: Conclusion: distinction between the two clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: in the first clause (specific storekeeper) he cannot annul because she brings herself; in the second clause (where his livelihood is from him) he can annul because she meant 'that you bring'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the two clauses: in the first clause (specific storekeeper) the husband cannot annul because she brings the produce herself, while in the second clause (where his livelihood is from him) he can annul because she meant 'that you bring'.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Yosi's view
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Yosi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah is in accordance with Rabbi Yosi, who holds that a husband cannot annul vows of עינוי נפש, but can annul other vows between him and her. The phrase 'cannot annul' refers only to עינוי נפש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yosi's view.
Rav Huna states that the entire chapter follows Rabbi Yosi's position.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'cannot annul' refers only to vows of עינוי נפש (affliction of the soul), but he can annul other vows between him and her.

items.text: Dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan on mixed vows
items.text_en: Dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan on mixed vows
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: if a woman vowed two loaves, one involving fasting (עינוי נפש) and one not, the husband annuls the entire vow because he can annul the fasting part. Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: he annuls only the fasting part, not the non-fasting part.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: if a woman vowed two loaves, one involving fasting (עינוי נפש) and one not, the husband annuls the entire vow because he can annul the fasting part.
Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: he annuls only the fasting part, not the non-fasting part.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Asi's inquiry
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Asi's inquiry
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan directly about the case of two loaves, and Rabbi Yochanan answered that he annuls only the fasting part.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan directly about the case of two loaves, and Rabbi Yochanan answered that he annuls only the fasting part.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a nazirite vow
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a nazirite vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and then drank wine and became impure to the dead — the implication challenges the previous ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and then drank wine and became impure to the dead, challenging the previous ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman vowed to be a nazirite and her husband annulled the vow without her knowledge, and she drank wine or became impure, she does not receive lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman vowed to be a nazirite and her husband annulled the vow without her knowledge, and she drank wine or became impure, she does not receive lashes.

items.text: Gemara's question on partial annulment
items.text_en: Gemara's question on partial annulment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the husband can annul only the part of the vow that causes suffering (wine) but not the part that does not (grapes and pits), which would still require lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the husband can annul only the part of the vow that causes suffering (wine) but not the part that does not (grapes and pits), which would still require lashes.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye's principle
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Abaye's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that there is no partial naziriteship. Abaye objects that the sacrifice would still be partial, and concludes that there is no partial naziriteship and no partial sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that there is no partial naziriteship (אֵין נְזִירוּת לַחֲצָאִין), meaning the husband's partial annulment is impossible.
Abaye objects that even if there is no partial naziriteship, the sacrifice would still be partial, so the principle must also apply to the sacrifice.
Abaye concludes that there is no partial naziriteship and no partial sacrifice (אֵין נְזִירוּת לַחֲצָאִין, וְאֵין קׇרְבָּן לַחֲצָאִין), resolving the objection.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that seems to require a bird sin-offering for partial naziriteship, contradicting Abaye. The Gemara resolves that the bird sin-offering is brought due to uncertainty, not as a partial nazirite sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a woman who vowed to be a nazirite and set aside an animal, then her husband annulled the vow, brings a bird sin-offering — implying a sacrifice for partial naziriteship, contradicting Abaye's principle that there is no sacrifice for partial naziriteship.

The Gemara resolves that the bird sin-offering is brought not as a sacrifice for partial naziriteship, but because it is a חטאת על הספק (sin-offering for uncertainty), thereby preserving Abaye's principle.

items.text: Second objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Second objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Another baraita is cited where a woman who became impure after her vow was annulled brings a bird sin-offering, challenging the principle that the husband only annuls for suffering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a woman who became impure after her husband annulled her nazirite vow brings a bird sin-offering, challenging the principle that the husband only annuls for suffering.

items.text: Question about annulling vows of impurity
items.text_en: Question about annulling vows of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a husband can annul his wife's vow regarding impurity from a corpse, since it causes no pain, unlike wine. It answers that even such impurity causes pain, citing Rabbi Meir's teaching about the living taking lessons from death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a husband annuls a wife's vow of impurity from a corpse, since it causes no pain, unlike wine.
The Gemara answers that even impurity from a corpse causes pain, citing Rabbi Meir's teaching that the living take lessons from death.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows forbidding benefit from people
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows forbidding benefit from people
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a woman vows not to benefit from "beriyot" (people), her husband cannot annul it, and she may benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah. If she vows that priests or Levites may not benefit from her, they take against her will; if she specifies certain priests or Levites, others take.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who vows not to benefit from 'beriyot' (people), stating that her husband cannot annul it and she may benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.
The Mishnah adds that if she vows that priests or Levites may not benefit from her, they take against her will; but if she specifies certain priests or Levites, others take.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction about husband's inclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction about husband's inclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah implies the husband is not included in "beriyot" (since she can benefit from him), but the ruling that she can only eat from gleanings etc. implies he is included (since she cannot eat from him).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the Mishnah's first clause implies the husband is not included in 'beriyot' (since she can benefit from him), but the second clause implies he is included (since she cannot eat from him).
Ulla resolves that the husband is never included in 'beriyot', and the reason he cannot annul is that she can sustain herself from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field.

Rava resolves that the husband is always included in 'beriyot', and the Mishnah means: 'What is the reason he cannot annul? Because she can benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field.'

Rav Nachman resolves that the husband is never included in 'beriyot', and the Mishnah actually means: 'If she is divorced, she can benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field.'

items.text: Ulla's resolution: husband not included
items.text_en: Ulla's resolution: husband not included
items.desc_en: Ulla resolves that the husband is never included in "beriyot", and the reason he cannot annul is because she can still benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: Ulla resolves that the husband is never included in 'beriyot', and the reason he cannot annul is because she can still benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

items.text: Rava's resolution: husband included
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: husband included
items.desc_en: Rava resolves that the husband is always included in "beriyot", and the Mishnah means: why can't he annul? Because she can benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the husband is always included in 'beriyot', and the Mishnah's statement that he cannot annul is explained by the reason that she can benefit from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: husband not included, Mishnah refers to divorce
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: husband not included, Mishnah refers to divorce
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves that the husband is never included in "beriyot", and the Mishnah's statement about gleanings etc. refers to after she is divorced.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves that the husband is never included in 'בריות' (people), and the Mishnah's allowance of gleanings etc. refers to after she is divorced.

items.text: Rava's challenge to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's challenge to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava cites a mishnah where a woman vows 'removed from Jews' and the husband can only nullify his portion, not the entire vow. If the husband were not included in 'creatures', argues Rava, he could nullify the entire vow since it is a vow of affliction.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing a mishnah where a woman vows 'removed from Jews' and the husband can only nullify his portion, implying the husband is included in the category 'creatures'.
Rava argues that if the husband were not included in 'creatures', the vow would be one of affliction and the husband could nullify it entirely, contradicting Rav Nachman's position.
Rav Nachman answers that the case is different because the woman's intent is clearly to forbid herself from permitted relations, not from the husband as a creature.
The gemara notes that the mishnah lists gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner of the field as permitted to the woman, but omits poor tithe, raising a contradiction with a baraita.

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Eliezer and the baraita to the rabbis, citing a dispute about whether one must designate a name for poor tithe of doubtfully tithed produce.

items.text: Gemara's answer: distinguishing the case
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: distinguishing the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that this case is different because it is evident that she is prohibiting herself based on permitted things (i.e., she intends to forbid herself from her husband's benefit, not from all Jews).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that this case is different because it is evident that she is prohibiting herself based on permitted things (i.e., she intends to forbid herself from her husband's benefit, not from all Jews).

items.text: Contradiction regarding ma'aser ani
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding ma'aser ani
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the mishnah says a poor person can benefit from leket, shikh'ha, and pe'ah but does not mention ma'aser ani, yet a baraita includes ma'aser ani.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the mishnah allows benefit from leket, shikh'ha, and pe'ah but omits ma'aser ani, while a baraita includes ma'aser ani.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one need not designate a name on ma'aser ani of demai, and the baraita to the Sages.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one need not designate a name on מעשר עני של דמאי (the poor man's tithe of doubtfully tithed produce), and the baraita to the Sages.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's ruling that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis hinges on whether doubtful produce requires immersion (tevila) and whether the kohen has a right to benefit (tovat hana'ah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis hinges on whether doubtful produce requires immersion (טבילה) and whether the kohen has a right to benefit (טובת הנאה).

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that everyone agrees doubtful produce requires immersion, and the real dispute is whether amei ha'aretz are suspected of violating ma'aser ani. Rabbi Eliezer holds they are not suspected, while the Rabbis hold they are.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts that all agree doubtful produce requires immersion, and the dispute is whether amei ha'aretz are suspected of violating ma'aser ani; Rabbi Eliezer holds they are not suspected because one could abandon property and become poor.
Abaye explains that the Rabbis hold that a person does not abandon his property, so amei ha'aretz are suspected of violating ma'aser ani.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding ma'aser ani
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding ma'aser ani
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes between ma'aser ani distributed within the house (where a 'giving' verse applies, making benefit forbidden) and that distributed at the threshing floors (where a 'leaving' verse applies, permitting benefit).

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by distinguishing ma'aser ani distributed within the house, where a 'giving' verse applies, making benefit forbidden.
Rava completes the distinction: ma'aser ani distributed at the threshing floors, where a 'leaving' verse applies, permits benefit.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah about kohanim and Levi'im
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah about kohanim and Levi'im
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a person says 'kohanim and Levi'im may benefit from me'—the first clause implies tovat hana'ah is not money, but the latter clause implies it is money, creating a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the first clause of a Mishnah where one says 'kohanim and Levi'im may benefit from me' and they take, implying that טובת הנאה (the right to designate the recipient) is not considered money.
The Gemara objects by citing the latter clause of the same Mishnah, where specifying 'these kohanim and these Levi'im' excludes them, implying that טובת הנאה is money.

items.text: Resolution by Rav Hoshaya
items.text_en: Resolution by Rav Hoshaya
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya resolves the contradiction by attributing the two clauses to different Tanna'im: Rabbi holds tovat hana'ah is money, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya resolves the contradiction by attributing the first clause to Rabbi and the second to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree about whether טובת הנאה (the benefit of directing the gift) is considered money.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute in the baraita is indeed about whether טובת הנאה (the benefit of directing the gift) is considered money.

items.text: Initial question on טובת הנאה
items.text_en: Initial question on טובת הנאה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda hinges on whether טובת הנאה is considered money (ממון).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda hinges on whether טובת הנאה (the right to designate the recipient) is considered ממון (money).

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the premise, asserting that all agree טובת הנאה is not money; the dispute is about gifts that have not been separated (מתנות שלא הורמו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the premise that the dispute is about טובת הנאה (the right to designate the recipient), asserting that all agree it is not money; rather, the dispute is about gifts that have not been separated (מתנות שלא הורמו).

items.text: Objection to the alternative
items.text_en: Objection to the alternative
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if טובת הנאה is not money, what difference does it make whether the gifts were separated or not?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if טובת הנאה (the right to designate the recipient) is not money, then what difference does it make whether the gifts were separated or not?

items.text: Revised explanation: Rabbinic penalty
items.text_en: Revised explanation: Rabbinic penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises: Rabbi holds the Sages penalized the thief to deter theft, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds they penalized the homeowner to prevent delay in tithing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the dispute: Rabbi holds the Sages penalized the thief to deter theft, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds they penalized the homeowner to prevent delay in tithing.

items.text: Rava's alternative reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's alternative reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different explanation: terumah is unique because it is only fit for priests, so when the thief tries to prohibit it to them, it is considered mere dust.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that terumah is different because it is only fit for priests, so when the thief tries to prohibit it to them, it is considered mere dust.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows not to work for father or husband
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows not to work for father or husband
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a wife vows not to work for her father, her husband's father, her brother, or her husband's brother — the husband cannot annul. If she vows not to work for her husband, he need not annul. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argue that he should annul due to potential consequences.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with cases where a wife vows not to work for her father, her husband's father, her brother, or her husband's brother — the husband cannot annul; if she vows not to work for her husband, he need not annul.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the husband should annul the vow, lest she do more work for him than is proper.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that the husband should annul, lest he divorce her and she become forbidden to him.

items.text: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling and question on consecrating future objects
items.text_en: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling and question on consecrating future objects
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, prompting the Gemara to ask whether Shmuel holds that one can consecrate something not yet in existence, and a contradiction is raised from a Mishnah about consecrating his wife's handiwork.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.
The Gemara infers from Shmuel's ruling that he holds one can consecrate something not yet in existence (דבר שלא בא לעולם).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Mishnah about one who consecrates his wife's handiwork, which implies that one cannot consecrate future objects.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה ופסק שמואל
items.text_en: Mishnah and Samuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says surplus produce is consecrated, Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar says it is unconsecrated. Samuel rules like Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, implying that one cannot consecrate something not yet in existence.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהאשה עושה ואוכלת, והמותר – מחלוקת: ר' מאיר אומר הקדש, ר' יוחנן הסנדלר אומר חולין. שמואל פוסק כר' יוחנן הסנדלר, ומכאן שאין אדם מקדיש דבר שלא בא לעולם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says surplus produce is consecrated, Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar says it is unconsecrated.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת: האשה עושה ואוכלת במעשה ידיה, והמותר ליכא.

sub.desc_en: Samuel rules like Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, implying that one cannot consecrate something not yet in existence.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת: האשה עושה ואוכלת במעשה ידיה, והמותר ליכא.

items.text: דחיית האפשרות ששמואל פסק על העדפה
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Samuel's ruling might refer to a different dispute (Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri) about surplus, not the general principle. It argues that Samuel should have specified which opinion he follows.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות ששמואל התכוון לפסוק כר' יוחנן בן נורי רק בהעדפה, שהרי היה צריך לומר זאת במפורש. כמו כן, לא ייתכן שפסק כתנא קמא או כר' עקיבא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Samuel's ruling might refer to the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about surplus (העדפה), not the general principle of sanctifying something not yet in existence.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה אפשרות ששמואל התכוון לפסוק כרבי יוחנן בן נורי רק לעניין העדפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Samuel should have specified his position explicitly, either as following Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri on surplus, the first Tanna, or Rabbi Akiva.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה אפשרות זו, שכן היה על שמואל לומר במפורש 'הלכה כרבי יוחנן בן נורי בהעדפה', או לפסוק כתנא קמא או כרבי עקיבא.

items.text: תירוץ רב יוסף: שאני קונמות
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: Nedarim are different
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the case of vows (konamot) is different because a person can forbid another's produce on himself, so he can also forbid something not yet in existence.
items.desc: רב יוסף מתרץ שקונמות שאני, כי אדם אוסר פירות חברו על עצמו, ולכן יכול לאסור גם דבר שלא בא לעולם על עצמו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that vows (קונמות) are different because a person can forbid another's produce on himself, so he can also forbid something not yet in existence.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מתרץ שקונמות שאני, כי אדם אוסר פירות חברו על עצמו, ולכן יכול לאסור גם דבר שלא בא לעולם על עצמו.

items.text: קושיית אביי על רב יוסף
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: while one can forbid another's produce on himself (since he can forbid his own produce on another), one cannot forbid something not yet in existence on another, as one cannot forbid another's produce on that other.
items.desc: אביי מקשה על רב יוסף: אמנם אדם אוסר פירות חברו על עצמו, אבל אינו אוסר דבר שלא בא לעולם על חברו, שהרי אין אדם אוסר פירות חברו על חברו.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's reasoning: while one can forbid another's produce on oneself (since one can forbid one's own produce on another), one cannot forbid something not yet in existence on another, because one cannot forbid another's produce on that other person.
sub.desc: אביי מקשה על רב יוסף: אמנם אדם אוסר פירות חברו על עצמו, שהרי אדם אוסר פירותיו על חברו, אבל כיצד יאסור דבר שלא בא לעולם על חברו, שהרי אין אדם אוסר פירות חברו על חברו.

items.text: תירוץ רב הונא: יקדשו ידי לעושיהן
items.text_en: Rav Huna's answer: Hands are already in existence
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the case involves a woman who says 'my hands shall be consecrated to their Maker,' and hands already exist in the world, so the principle does not apply.
items.desc: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע מתרץ שהאשה אומרת 'יקדשו ידי לעושיהן', והידיים כבר בעולם, ולכן ההקדש חל עליהן.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the case involves a woman who says 'my hands shall be consecrated to their Maker,' and hands already exist in the world, so the principle that one cannot consecrate something not yet in existence does not apply.
sub.desc: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע מתרץ שהאשה אומרת 'יקדשו ידי לעושיהן', והידיים כבר בעולם, ולכן ההקדש חל עליהן.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על תירוץ רב הונא
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Hands are liened to the husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how her statement can take effect, since her hands are already liened to her husband for labor. It suggests she might mean 'when she is divorced,' but currently she is not divorced, so how does the vow work?
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: וכי כשאמרה כך חל הקדש? הרי ידיה משועבדות לבעל! ומתרצת: כשאומרת 'לכי מגורשה' – אך כעת אינה מגורשת, ומה מועיל?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges how her statement 'let my hands be consecrated' can take effect, since her hands are already liened to her husband for labor.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: וכי כשאמרה 'לכי מגורשה' חל ההקדש? הרי ידיה משועבדות לבעל, ומה מועיל האומדנא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests she might mean the vow applies 'when she is divorced,' but notes that currently she is not divorced.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: וכי כשאמרה 'לכי מגורשה' חל ההקדש? הרי ידיה משועבדות לבעל, ומה מועיל האומדנא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the vow can take effect at all if it is contingent on a future event that has not yet occurred.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: וכי כשאמרה 'לכי מגורשה' חל ההקדש? הרי ידיה משועבדות לבעל, ומה מועיל האומדנא?

items.text: הקושיה הראשונה של רבי אילא
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila's initial analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila argues that if one says to another, 'This field that I am selling to you, when I take it back from you, let it be consecrated,' it would be consecrated. So too, a woman's vow to consecrate her future earnings should be valid.
items.desc: רבי אילא מקיש את דין האשה המקדישה מעשה ידיה לדין המוכר שדה ומקדישה לאחר שתחזור אליו, וטוען שגם שם ההקדש חל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila argues by analogy: if one says to another, 'This field that I am selling to you, when I take it back from you, let it be consecrated,' it would be consecrated; so too a woman's vow to consecrate her future earnings should be valid.
sub.desc: רבי אילא מביא דימוי: כשם שאדם יכול להקדיש שדה לאחר שמכרה, כך אשה יכולה להקדיש מעשה ידיה לאחר שתתגרש.

items.text: דחיית רבי ירמיה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and revised analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the field is currently in the seller's possession, whereas a woman does not have control over her earnings to consecrate them now. He proposes a better analogy: one who says, 'This field that I sold to you, when I take it back from you, let it be consecrated' — would it be consecrated?
items.desc: רבי ירמיה דוחה את ההקיש: במוכר השדה בידו להקדישה עכשיו, אבל האשה אינה יכולה להקדיש מעשה ידיה שעתידים לבוא. הוא משווה למכר שכבר נגמר, שם ההקדש לא חל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the analogy is flawed because the field is currently in the seller's possession, whereas a woman does not have control over her earnings to consecrate them now.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי: אשה אינה יכולה להקדיש מעשה ידיה בעודה נשואה, כשם ששדה שנמכרה אינה יכולה להתקדש על ידי המוכר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya proposes a better analogy: one who says, 'This field that I sold to you, when I take it back from you, let it be consecrated' — would it be consecrated?
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי: אשה אינה יכולה להקדיש מעשה ידיה בעודה נשואה, כשם ששדה שנמכרה אינה יכולה להתקדש על ידי המוכר.

items.text: דחיית רב פפא
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and revised analogy
