items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that in a sale the matter is finalized, but with a woman the matter is not finalized (she might not earn). He proposes an analogy to a mortgaged field: one who says, 'This field that I mortgaged to you, when I redeem it from you, let it be consecrated' — would it not be consecrated?
items.desc: רב פפא דוחה את ההשוואה למכר שכבר נגמר, כי במכר הדבר נפסק סופית, אבל באשה אין הדבר נפסק (היא עלולה לחזור בה). הוא משווה למשכון, שם ההקדש חל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that the sale analogy is flawed because in a sale the matter is finalized, but with a woman the matter is not finalized (she might not earn).
sub.desc: רב פפא מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי של שדה ממושכנת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes an analogy to a mortgaged field: one who says, 'This field that I mortgaged to you, when I redeem it from you, let it be consecrated' — would it not be consecrated?
sub.desc: רב פפא מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי של שדה ממושכנת.

items.text: דחיית רב שישא
items.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection and revised analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that the field owner can redeem it at will, but a woman cannot divorce herself at will. He proposes an analogy to a field mortgaged for a fixed term of ten years: one who says, 'When I redeem it from you, let it be consecrated' — would it not be consecrated?
items.desc: רב שישא דוחה את ההשוואה למשכון: השדה בידו לפדותה, אבל האשה אינה בידה להתגרש. הוא משווה למשכון לזמן קצוב, שם ההקדש חל.

sub.text: קושיית רב שישא בריה דרב אידי
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that the analogy to a sold field fails because the field owner can redeem it at will, but a woman cannot divorce herself at will.
sub.desc: רב שישא מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי של שדה ממושכנת לזמן קצוב.

sub.text: קושיית רב שישא בריה דרב אידי
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's revised analogy
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi proposes a revised analogy: a field mortgaged for a fixed term of ten years, where the owner says 'When I redeem it from you, let it be consecrated' — would it not be consecrated?
sub.desc: רב שישא מקשה על הדימוי הקודם, ומציע דימוי חלופי של שדה ממושכנת לזמן קצוב.

items.text: דחיית רב אשי
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's final objection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that in the case of a fixed-term mortgage, there is a definite end, but for a woman, there is no fixed term for her marriage. Thus the analogy fails, and the woman's vow remains invalid.
items.desc: רב אשי דוחה את ההשוואה למשכון לזמן קצוב: שם יש קצבה, אבל לאשה אין קצבה לגירושין, ולכן ההקדש לא חל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the analogy to a fixed-term mortgage fails because a woman's marriage has no fixed term, so her vow remains invalid.
sub.desc: רב אשי מקשה על הדימוי: לשדה יש קץ קצוב, אך לאשה אין קץ לגירושין, ולכן הקושיה נותרת ללא מענה.

items.text: תירוץ רב אשי: קונמות מפקיעות מידי שעבוד
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution using Rava's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that konamot (vows of prohibition) are different because they are like sanctity of the body, and cites Rava's principle that consecration, leaven, and manumission override liens.
items.desc: רב אשי מחדש שקונמות, בהיותן כקדושת הגוף, מפקיעות מידי שעבוד, ומביא ראיה מדברי רבא לגבי הקדש, חמץ ושחרור.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by asserting that konamot (vows of prohibition) are different because they are like sanctity of the body.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שקונמות דומות לקדושת הגוף ולכן מפקיעות מידי שעבוד.

sub.text_en: Rava's principle cited by Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports his resolution by citing Rava's principle that consecration (הקדש), leaven (חמץ), and manumission (שחרור) override liens.
sub.desc: רב אשי מביא ראיה מדברי רבא שהקדש, חמץ ושחרור מפקיעים מידי שעבוד.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא ותירוצה
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the earlier statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier source said 'lest he divorce her' if the vow is already annulled, and answers that the text should read 'and furthermore, lest he divorce her'.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם קונמות מפקיעות מידי שעבוד, מדוע נחוץ החשש שמא יגרשנה? ועונה: התנא אומר 'ועוד שמא יגרשנה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier source includes the phrase 'lest he divorce her' if the vow is already annulled by the husband's death.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם קונמות מפקיעות מידי שעבוד, מדוע נחוץ החשש שמא יגרשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the text should read 'and furthermore, lest he divorce her', indicating an additional concern rather than a primary one.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם קונמות מפקיעות מידי שעבוד, מדוע נחוץ החשש שמא יגרשנה?

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: טעות בנדרי אשה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of mistaken vow revocation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a husband mistakenly thought his wife vowed about one thing but she actually vowed about another, and rules that he must revoke the vow again.
items.desc: המשנה מביאה מקרים שבהם הבעל טעה בזיהוי הנודרת או בפרטי הנדר, וקובעת שעליו לחזור ולהפר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of mistaken identity in vow revocation, where a husband or father mistakenly thought a different person or type of vow was involved.
sub.desc: מתחיל את המשנה במקרה הראשון של טעות בזהות הנודרת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that in all such cases of mistaken revocation, the husband or father must revoke the vow again.
sub.desc: מתחיל את המשנה במקרה הראשון של טעות בזהות הנודרת.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על דיוק המשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah implies that the phrase 'he shall revoke her' (יָנִיא אוֹתָהּ) is precise, meaning he must revoke specifically the vow she actually made.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם מכך שהמשנה דורשת 'יחזור ויפר' משמע שההפרה תלויה דווקא באיתו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling implies that the phrase 'יָנִיא אוֹתָהּ' (he shall revoke her) is precise, meaning that only a proper revocation is effective.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם מדיוק הלשון 'יניא אותה' במשנה משמע שההפרה תלויה דווקא באיתו?

items.text: Initial contradiction from keri'ah
items.text_en: Initial contradiction from keri'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: regarding keri'ah, the verse uses 'upon' twice, and a baraita states that if one was told 'your father died' and tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he fulfilled his obligation. This seems to conflict with the principle that a mistaken action is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: regarding keri'ah (rending garments), the verse uses 'עַל' (upon) twice, and a baraita states that if one was told 'your father died' and tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he fulfilled his obligation — seemingly conflicting with the principle that a mistaken action is invalid.

The Gemara resolves: the first baraita refers to a case where the informant spoke in general terms (סתם), while the second baraita refers to a case where the informant specified the relationship (מפרש).

The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita: if they said 'your father died' and he tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he did NOT fulfill his obligation; but if they said 'a relative died' and he thought it was his father and tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he did fulfill his obligation.

Rav Ashi resolves: the case where he fulfilled his obligation is when the discovery occurred within תוך כדי דיבור (within the time of speech), while the case where he did not fulfill his obligation is after that time.

sub.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who had a sick person at home who fainted and he mistakenly tore, and then the person died — he did not fulfill his obligation; Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara explains that this applies only if the death occurred after תוך כדי דיבור, but within that time it is considered as if spoken.
The Gemara rules: תוך כדי דיבור (within the time of speech) is considered as speech, except for blasphemy, idolatry, betrothal, and divorce.

items.text: First resolution: general vs. specific
items.text_en: First resolution: general vs. specific
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the contradiction is not difficult: one case is where the statement was general (e.g., 'a dead person'), and the other where it was specific (e.g., 'your father').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a general statement (סתם) and a specific one (מפרש).

items.text: Contradictory baraita
items.text_en: Contradictory baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita that seems to contradict the first: if one was told 'your father died' and tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he did not fulfill his obligation. But if he was told 'a dead person died' and thought it was his father, and then it turned out to be his son, he did fulfill it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a contradictory baraita: if one was told 'your father died' and tore, and then it turned out to be his son, he did not fulfill his obligation; but if he was told 'a dead person died' and thought it was his father, and then it turned out to be his son, he did fulfill it.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: within vs. after speech
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: within vs. after speech
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between within 'tokh kedei dibbur' (the time it takes to say a short phrase) and after that time. If the son was found within that time, the tearing is valid; if after, it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between within 'tokh kedei dibbur' (the time it takes to say a short phrase) and after that time.
Rav Ashi explains that the case where he fulfilled the obligation refers to when the son was found within 'tokh kedei dibbur', and the case where he did not refers to after that time.

items.text: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's statement
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's statement
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about one who had a sick person who fainted, and he tore, and then the person died. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara: this only applies if the death occurred after 'tokh kedei dibbur', but within that time, it is considered as speech.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who had a sick person who fainted, and he tore his garment thinking he died, and then the person died later, has not fulfilled the obligation of tearing.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi states in the name of Bar Kappara: the baraita's ruling applies only if the death occurred after תוך כדי דיבור (the time required for speaking a short phrase), but if within that time, the tearing is considered as if done at the moment of death.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on 'tokh kedei dibbur'
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on 'tokh kedei dibbur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the halakha: within 'tokh kedei dibbur' is considered as speech, except for blasphemy, idolatry, betrothal, and divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues a final halakhic ruling: within תוך כדי דיבור (the time it takes to utter a short phrase) is considered as speech, except for blasphemy, idolatry, betrothal, and divorce.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara's identification of the Tanna
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara's identification of the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a woman who vows not to taste figs and grapes, and the husband's partial ratification or nullification. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yishmael, who derives from the verse that partial ratification is effective but partial nullification is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a woman who vows not to taste figs and grapes together, where partial ratification or nullification has specific effects; and a woman who vows separately on figs and grapes, which are treated as two independent vows.
The Gemara asks which Tanna's opinion is reflected in the Mishnah.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ' (her husband may uphold it, or her husband may nullify it) that partial ratification upholds the entire vow, while partial nullification is ineffective.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on partial annulment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on partial annulment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael holds that annulling only part of a vow (e.g., figs but not grapes) is ineffective, while Rabbi Akiva argues that annulment, like ratification, applies to the specific item mentioned. The Gemara then questions Rabbi Yishmael's logic.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yishmael's position: annulling only part of a vow (e.g., figs but not grapes) is ineffective until the husband annuls the entire vow.
Rabbi Akiva argues from the verse 'אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ' that annulment, like ratification, applies only to the specific item mentioned.
The Gemara objects: does the verse actually write 'יָפֵר מִמֶּנּוּ' (annul from it) to support Rabbi Akiva's analogy?
Rabbi Akiva responds that he derives the rule by a היקש (analogy) comparing annulment to ratification: just as ratification applies only to the specific item, so too annulment.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition: Sages' view on partial ratification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition: Sages' view on partial ratification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan, stating that the Sages disagree with both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. The Sages analogize ratification to annulment: just as partial annulment is valid, so too partial ratification is valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan notes that the Mishnah's dispute is only between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages hold a different view.
The Sages reverse the analogy: they compare ratification to annulment, so that ratification, like annulment, applies only to the specific item mentioned.

items.text: Rava's identification of the Mishnah with Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rava's identification of the Mishnah with Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the Mishnah's case (a woman vowing 'konam figs') as following Rabbi Shimon's view, who requires specifying 'shevuah' for each item to be bound.

sub.desc_en: Rava identifies that the Mishnah's case (a woman saying 'קונם תאנה') follows Rabbi Shimon's view.
Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon requires a separate oath for each item, analogous to the need for separate annulment for each item in the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Ignorance of annulment laws
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ignorance of annulment laws
items.desc_en: A new Mishnah discusses a husband who knows about vows but not about annulment, or knows about annulment but not that a particular statement is a vow. Rabbi Meir prohibits annulment in the latter case, while the Sages permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband knows vows exist but does not know annulment exists, he may still annul.
The Mishnah presents a second case: if the husband knows annulment exists but does not know this is a vow, Rabbi Meir says he may not annul.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir and hold that the husband may annul even if he does not know this is a vow.
The Sages rule that in the second case the husband may annul.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction from a baraita on a blind person
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction from a baraita on a blind person
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that 'without seeing' excludes a blind person (Rabbi Yehuda), while Rabbi Meir includes the blind person. This challenges the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that the phrase 'בְּלֹא רְאוֹת' (without seeing) excludes a blind person from the law of vows.
The baraita attributes this exclusion to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Meir disagrees and holds that the phrase includes the blind person, not excludes him.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rava explains that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir derive their positions from the context of the verse. Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'without seeing' excludes a blind person, while Rabbi Meir holds that it includes a blind person, each using different parts of the verse to support their view.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir derive their positions from the context of the verse, and explains Rabbi Yehuda's view that the verse about a murderer mentions entering a forest, which includes a blind person, so the phrase 'without seeing' must exclude a blind person.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's conclusion
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's conclusion
sub.desc_en: Rava concludes that Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'without seeing' excludes a blind person, since otherwise the inclusion would already be derived from the word 'forest'.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Meir's view
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Meir's view
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Meir holds that the verse says 'without knowledge', which excludes a blind person from the category of knowledge, so the phrase 'without seeing' must include a blind person.
Rava concludes that Rabbi Meir holds that 'without seeing' includes a blind person, since otherwise the exclusion would already be derived from the word 'without knowledge'.

items.text: Mishnah: Father giving money to his daughter while her husband is forbidden from benefit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Father giving money to his daughter while her husband is forbidden from benefit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a father forbids his son-in-law from benefit, but wants to give money to his daughter. He can give it as a gift with the condition that the husband has no rights to it, only what she puts into her mouth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a father who forbids his son-in-law from benefit but wishes to give money to his daughter, instructing her that it is a gift on condition that the husband has no rights except what she puts into her mouth.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the husband's acquisition
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the husband's acquisition
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the husband acquires the money only if the father says 'what you put into your mouth', but if he says 'do whatever you want', the husband acquires it. Shmuel disagrees, holding that even if he says 'do whatever you want', the husband does not acquire it. Rabbi Zeira raises an objection.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the husband acquires the money only if the father says 'מה שאת נותנת בפיך' (what you put into your mouth), but if he says 'מה שתרצי עשי' (do whatever you want), the husband acquires it.
Shmuel disagrees, holding that even if the father says 'מה שתרצי עשי' (do whatever you want), the husband does not acquire the money.
Rabbi Zeira raises an objection against the positions of Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Identifying Rav's ruling with Rabbi Meir's principle
items.text_en: Identifying Rav's ruling with Rabbi Meir's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Meir, who says a woman's hand is like her husband's hand, meaning she cannot acquire property independently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rav's ruling as aligning with Rabbi Meir's principle that a woman's hand is like her husband's hand.

items.text: Contradiction from the baraita on partnership in an alleyway
items.text_en: Contradiction from the baraita on partnership in an alleyway
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that one can establish a partnership in an alleyway through his wife, implying she can acquire for others. But if her hand is like her husband's, the eiruv would not leave his domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that lists the wife among those through whom one can establish a partnership in an alleyway, implying she can acquire for others.
The Gemara objects that if the husband acquires the eiruv from his wife, the eiruv would not leave his domain, contradicting the baraita's implication.
Rava answers that Rabbi Meir concedes regarding partnership (שיתוף) that since the wife acts to benefit others, she acquires from her husband's hand.
Ravina objects by citing a baraita that explicitly lists the wife among those through whom one cannot acquire, contradicting Rava's answer.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah deals with a case where the wife has her own courtyard in the alleyway, so she acquires for herself and then for others.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Meir concedes for the sake of benefiting others
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Meir concedes for the sake of benefiting others
items.desc_en: Rava answers that even Rabbi Meir concedes that regarding partnership (shittuf), since the intent is to benefit others, the wife can acquire for them from her husband's hand.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by stating that Rabbi Meir concedes regarding partnership (שיתוף), since the intent is to benefit others, the wife can acquire for them from her husband's hand.

items.text: Ravina's objection from the Mishnah of those who can acquire
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from the Mishnah of those who can acquire
items.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rava's answer by citing a Mishnah that lists those who can acquire for others: adult sons and daughters, and Hebrew slaves, but explicitly excludes a wife.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi by citing a Mishnah that lists those who can acquire for others, explicitly excluding a wife, contradicting the idea that a wife can acquire for others.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: the case involves her own courtyard
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: the case involves her own courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the wife has her own courtyard in that alleyway; since she can acquire for herself, she can also acquire for others.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah deals with a wife who has her own courtyard in the alleyway, so she can acquire for herself and thereby acquire for others.

items.text: Mishnah: The vow of a widow or divorcee stands
items.text_en: Mishnah: The vow of a widow or divorcee stands
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new topic: the vow of a widow or divorcee, stating that if she says 'I am a nazirite after thirty days' and marries within that time, her husband cannot annul it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the rule that the vow of a widow or divorcee stands, giving the example of a woman who says she will be a nazirite after thirty days and marries within that time — her husband cannot annul it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows before marriage or divorce
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows before marriage or divorce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman vows while under her husband's authority, he can annul it. If she says 'I am a nazirite after thirty days' and is widowed or divorced within that time, the vow is annulled. However, if she vows and is divorced on the same day, then remarried, he cannot annul. The rule: any time she is independent for even one hour, he cannot annul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a husband can annul his wife's vows made while under his authority, but if she becomes independent for even one hour, he cannot annul.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita presents two cases: a widow or divorcee who says 'I am a nazirite when I marry' and then marries, and a married woman who says 'I am a nazirite when I am divorced' and then divorces. Rabbi Yishmael rules that the husband can annul in the first case but not the second, while Rabbi Akiva rules the opposite. Their reasoning is based on different interpretations of the verse: Rabbi Yishmael requires the vow to be made during widowhood/divorce, while Rabbi Akiva requires the prohibition of the vow to take effect during that time.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents two cases: a widow or divorcee who vows to be a nazirite when she marries, and a married woman who vows to be a nazirite when she divorces, with Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva disputing the husband's ability to annul in each case.
Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'וְנֵדֶר אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה' to require that the vow itself be made during widowhood or divorce for the husband to annul.
Rabbi Akiva cites the verse 'כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָסְרָה עַל נַפְשָׁהּ' to require that the prohibition of the vow take effect during widowhood or divorce for the husband to annul.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and reconciling with the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and reconciling with the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva. Abaye counters that even if it follows Rabbi Yishmael, the Mishnah's case (vow tied to days) differs from the baraita's (vow tied to marriage/divorce). The Mishnah's case involves a vow contingent on a time period, not on a marital event.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva's position.
Abaye counters that even if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, it is reconcilable because the Mishnah's vow is tied to days (יומי) while the baraita's vow is tied to marriage/divorce (נישואין).

items.text: Clarification of 'This is the rule' regarding a betrothed young woman
items.text_en: Clarification of 'This is the rule' regarding a betrothed young woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the rule stated in the Mishnah regarding a betrothed young woman (in the earlier chapter) comes to include a case where the father goes with the husband's agents or the father's agents go with the husband's agents, meaning that both the father and husband can annul her vows.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of 'זה הכלל' in the betrothed maiden section
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of 'זה הכלל' in the betrothed maiden section
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the 'זה הכלל' (this is the rule) stated in the betrothed maiden section includes the case where the father went with the husband's agents or the father's agents went with the husband's agents, regarding a betrothed maiden whose father and husband annul her vows.

items.text: Clarification of 'This is the rule' regarding 'These are the vows'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'This is the rule' regarding 'These are the vows'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the rule stated in the Mishnah regarding 'These are the vows' (in the previous chapter) comes to include a case where the father hands over the daughter to the husband's agents or the father's agents hand her over to the husband's agents, meaning that the husband cannot annul vows made before she entered his authority.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of 'זה הכלל' in the 'These are the vows' section
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of 'זה הכלל' in the 'These are the vows' section
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the 'זה הכלל' stated in the 'These are the vows' section includes the case where the father handed the daughter to the husband's agents or the father's agents handed her to the husband's agents, establishing that the husband cannot annul vows made beforehand.

items.text: Mishnah: Nine young women whose vows are valid
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nine young women whose vows are valid
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists nine young women whose vows are valid (not subject to annulment by a father or husband): a bogeret (mature) who is an orphan, and a na'arah (young woman) who is a bogeret and an orphan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the nine types of young women whose vows are valid and cannot be annulled, beginning with a בוגרת (mature maiden) who is an orphan, and a נערה (young maiden) who has matured and is an orphan.

items.text: Mishnah: Categories of young women for vow annulment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Categories of young women for vow annulment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various categories of a young woman (na'arah) based on whether she is a minor, a bogeret, an orphan, or has a living father, and includes Rabbi Yehuda's additional case of a daughter who remarried and returned to her father.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories of a young woman (na'arah) regarding vow annulment, including cases of orphanhood, majority, and a living father, with Rabbi Yehuda adding the case of a daughter who remarried and returned to her father.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Yehuda's clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Yehuda's clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the Mishnah reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view, but the Sages hold that only three types of young women have their vows upheld: a bogeret, an orphan, and an orphan during the father's lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that the Mishnah's list reflects only Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
The Sages hold that only three categories of young women have their vows upheld: a bogeret, an orphan, and an orphan during the father's lifetime.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional vows and annulment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional vows and annulment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a woman vows not to benefit from her father or her husband's father if she acts according to her husband's will, or vows not to benefit from her husband if she acts according to her father's will, and rules that the husband can annul such vows.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman vows not to benefit from her father or her husband's father if she acts according to her husband's will, and rules that the husband may annul it.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Nathan and the Sages on conditional vows
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Nathan and the Sages on conditional vows
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Nathan says the husband does not annul a vow where the woman says she will not benefit from her father or her husband's father if she acts according to her husband's will, while the Sages say he does annul.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites a similar vow formulation.
Rabbi Natan rules that the husband does not annul this vow.
The Sages rule that the husband does annul this vow.

items.text: Gemara: Another dispute on a similar vow
items.text_en: Gemara: Another dispute on a similar vow
items.desc_en: A second baraita presents a case where a woman says she is removed from Jews if she serves her husband; Rabbi Nathan says the husband does not annul, while the Sages say he does annul.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents another vow formulation: 'I am removed from the Jews if I serve you.'
Rabbi Natan rules that the husband does not annul this vow.
The Sages rule that the husband does annul this vow.

items.text: Story: A man who vowed not to marry until he learned a halakha
items.text_en: Story: A man who vowed not to marry until he learned a halakha
items.desc_en: A story is told of a man who forbade all worldly benefit on himself if he married before learning a certain halakha; he struggled to learn it until Rav Acha bar Rav Huna confused him, and he eventually married.

sub.desc_en: A man vowed that all worldly benefit would be forbidden to him if he married a woman before he finished learning a halachic tradition, and he struggled to learn it.
Rav Acha bar Rav Huna came and confused him (about the tradition), and he married a woman.

items.text: Rava's praise and initial position
items.text_en: Rava's praise and initial position
items.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Acha bar Rav Huna for his clever action, asserting that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Natan regarding annulment applies equally to dissolution of vows.

sub.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Acha bar Rav Huna for his clever action, asserting that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Natan regarding annulment (הפרה) applies equally to dissolution (שאלה) of vows.

items.text: Rav Papi's distinction between annulment and dissolution
items.text_en: Rav Papi's distinction between annulment and dissolution
items.desc_en: Rav Papi argues that the dispute between Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis is only regarding annulment, where Rabbi Natan requires the vow to have taken effect. However, regarding dissolution, all agree that a sage cannot permit a vow unless it has taken effect, based on the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papi rejects Rava's analogy, explaining that the dispute is only in annulment (הפרה) because of conflicting verses, but in dissolution (שאלה) all agree that a sage may only dissolve a vow that has already taken effect, based on the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.
Rav Papi concludes that regarding dissolution (שאלה), all agree that a sage cannot permit a vow unless it has taken effect, based on the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

items.text: First attempted support for Rav Papi
items.text_en: First attempted support for Rav Papi
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Papi from a mishnah about a vow conditional on seeking dissolution, but questions whether the order is fixed or optional, leaving the support inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to bring a supporting baraita about a vow conditioned on dissolution, but questions whether the order of dissolution is known, implying the vow must have taken effect.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah's order may be merely conventional, not mandatory, since the person does not know which vow was made first, leaving the support inconclusive.

items.text: Second attempted support and resolution
items.text_en: Second attempted support and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another mishnah about a nazirite vow conditional on dissolution, which seems to show a fixed order. The Gemara concludes that this supports Rabbi Natan's view, not Rav Papi's, as Rabbi Natan holds that dissolution requires the vow to have taken effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a different baraita about a vow and a nazirite vow conditioned on dissolution, and concludes that the ruling follows Rabbi Natan's position that dissolution requires the vow to have taken effect.
The Gemara objects that if dissolution could occur before the vow takes effect, the order would be arbitrary, contradicting the mishnah's fixed sequence.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah aligns with Rabbi Natan's view, who holds that dissolution requires the vow to have taken effect, not with Rav Papi's view.

items.text: Rav Papi's revised position via Marimar
items.text_en: Rav Papi's revised position via Marimar
items.desc_en: Ravina reports in the name of Marimar quoting Rav Papi's father that the dispute is only regarding annulment, but regarding dissolution, all agree that a sage may permit even a vow that has not yet taken effect, based on the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

sub.text: Ravina citing Marimar citing Avuh citing Rav Papi
sub.text_en: Ravina citing Marimar citing Avuh citing Rav Papi
sub.desc_en: Ravina reports in the name of Rav Papi that the dispute is only in annulment (הפרה), but in dissolution (שאלה) all agree that a husband may annul even before the vow takes effect, citing the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

items.text: Challenges to the principle of order in vow nullification
items.text_en: Challenges to the principle of order in vow nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially asserts that the order of nullification does not matter, but is challenged by a baraita about a vow that specifies 'first' and 'second' persons, and another about a vow and a nazirite vow. The Gemara attempts to answer but is refuted, concluding with a תיוּבְתָּא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the order of nullification does not matter, implying no practical consequence.
A baraita is cited that requires nullifying the vow for the 'first' person before the 'second', challenging the assertion that order is irrelevant.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to a case where the identity of 'first' and 'second' is unknown, so the order is forced.
Another baraita is cited that requires nullifying the vow before the nazirite vow, again challenging the assertion that order is irrelevant.
The Gemara concludes that the initial assertion is refuted (תיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Mishnah: Three women who leave with their ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three women who leave with their ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the earlier ruling that three women—one who says 'I am impure to you,' 'Heaven is between me and you,' and 'I am removed from the Jews'—leave and receive their ketubah. The later ruling restricts this to prevent women from scheming, requiring proof for the first, a request for the second, and partial annulment for the third.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the original ruling: three women go out and receive their ketubah: one who says 'I am impure to you', 'Heaven is between me and you', or 'I am removed from the Jews'.
The Mishnah states the earlier ruling that three women—one who says 'I am impure to you,' 'Heaven is between me and you,' and 'I am removed from the Jews'—leave and receive their ketubah.

The Mishnah then presents the revised ruling: to prevent a woman from setting her eyes on another and undermining her husband, the first case requires proof, the second requires a request, and the third requires partial nullification.

items.text: Gemara: Does a woman who says 'I am impure' eat terumah?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does a woman who says 'I am impure' eat terumah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman who tells her husband 'I am impure' may eat terumah. Rav Sheshet says she may, to avoid slander against her children. Rava says she may not, as she can eat non-sacred food.

items.text: Rava's qualification: If she becomes widowed or divorced
items.text_en: Rava's qualification: If she becomes widowed or divorced
items.desc_en: Rava notes that Rav Sheshet agrees that if the woman becomes widowed or divorced, she may not eat terumah, because the concern for slander about her children no longer applies.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Rav Sheshet agrees that if the woman becomes widowed or divorced, she may not eat terumah.
Rava explains that the only reason Rav Sheshet permitted eating terumah was to prevent slander about her children.
Rava concludes that once she is widowed or divorced, people say she is now a non-priest's wife, so the concern for slander no longer applies and she is forbidden to eat terumah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's inquiry: Does an raped wife of a priest receive a ketubah?
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inquiry: Does an raped wife of a priest receive a ketubah?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Rava asked whether the wife of a priest who was raped receives a ketubah. The question is whether rape for a priest is like consent for an Israelite (so no ketubah) or whether she can claim she was unaware.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's report of Rava's question
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's report of Rava's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Rava tested them: does a kohen's wife who was raped have a ketubah or not, considering whether rape for a kohen is like consent for an Israelite, or she can claim she saw something.
Rav Pappa presents the alternative possibility that the woman can claim she was unaware of the rape, thereby retaining her right to a ketubah.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a woman who says 'I am defiled to you' has a ketubah. It considers whether she is an Israelite woman or a priest's wife, and whether the case is consensual or forced, concluding it must be a priest's wife who was raped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's case of a woman who says 'I am defiled to you' and has a ketubah.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah is dealing with, considering whether she is an Israelite woman or a priest's wife, and whether the act was consensual or forced.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must be speaking of a priest's wife who was raped, as only then does she have a ketubah.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's proof regarding 'You divorced me'
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's proof regarding 'You divorced me'
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna attempts to prove from the Mishnah's later version (where she is not believed) that a woman who says 'You divorced me' is believed, because she would not brazenly lie to her husband who knows the truth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if a woman says to her husband 'You divorced me,' what is the law regarding her credibility?

Rav Hamnuna attempts to prove from the Mishnah's later version (where she is not believed regarding 'I am impure to you') that a woman who says 'You divorced me' is believed, because she would not brazenly lie to her husband who knows the truth.

items.text: Rava's counter-proof
items.text_en: Rava's counter-proof
items.desc_en: Rava argues the opposite: even in the Mishnah's first version where she is believed, that is because she would not degrade herself. But here, she might brazenly lie because she is angry at her husband.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues the opposite: even in the Mishnah's first version where she is believed, that is because she would not degrade herself. But here, she might brazenly lie because she is angry at her husband.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's objection to Rava
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's objection to Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rava from the Mishnah's first version: the case of 'Heaven is between me and you' where she has no shame, yet she is believed. Rava explains that there she would not say it unless it were true, because she cannot avoid the claim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rava from the Mishnah's first version: the case of 'Heaven is between me and you' where she has no shame, yet she is believed.
Rava explains that there she would not say it unless it were true, because she cannot avoid the claim that 'he does not shoot like an arrow'.

items.text: Objection to Rav Hamnuna and his response
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Hamnuna and his response
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya also objects to Rav Hamnuna from the later Mishnah's 'Heaven is between me and you' case, where she is not believed despite the husband knowing. Rav Hamnuna explains that there she might lie because the husband does not know about the specific detail of 'shooting like an arrow'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rav Hamnuna from the later Mishnah's 'Heaven is between me and you' case, where the wife is not believed despite the husband knowing about the matter.
Rav Hamnuna explains that in that case the wife might lie because the husband does not know about the specific detail of 'shooting like an arrow' (יורה כחץ).

items.text: A story about a suspicious woman
items.text_en: A story about a suspicious woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a woman who always washed her husband's hands before intercourse, but one day did not, leading to suspicion of infidelity with a gentile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a woman who always washed her husband's hands before intercourse, but one day did not, leading to suspicion of infidelity with a gentile.

items.text: First case: woman claims strangers were present
items.text_en: First case: woman claims strangers were present
items.desc_en: A woman tells her husband that strangers were present, implying she was forced. Rav Nachman dismisses her claim, saying she has set her eyes on another and her words have no substance.

sub.desc_en: The woman tells her husband that strangers were present, implying that one of them may have forced her.
Rav Nachman dismisses her claim, stating she has set her eyes on another and her words have no substance.
The Gemara recounts a similar case where a woman, unhappy with her husband, made a comparable claim about strangers.
Rav Nachman rules that the court should not heed her, as she has set her eyes on another man.

items.text: Second case: adulterer flees through window
items.text_en: Second case: adulterer flees through window
items.desc_en: A man and woman are locked in a house; the adulterer flees when the husband arrives. Rava rules the woman is permitted to her husband, reasoning that if she had committed a sin, she would have been flustered.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: a man and woman were locked in a house, and when the husband arrived, the adulterer fled through a window.
Rava rules the woman is permitted to her husband, reasoning that if she had committed a sin, she would have been flustered and unable to act calmly.

items.text: Third case: adulterer warns about poisoned food
items.text_en: Third case: adulterer warns about poisoned food
items.desc_en: An adulterer hides in the house and warns the husband not to eat poisoned food. Rava rules the woman is permitted, because if she had sinned, she would have wanted the husband to die, as it is written 'for they have committed adultery and blood is in their hands.'

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a case where an adulterer entered a woman's house, hid when the husband arrived, and warned the husband not to eat poisoned vegetables.

Rava rules the woman is permitted to her husband, reasoning that if she had sinned, she would have wanted the husband to die, as the verse says 'for they have committed adultery and blood is in their hands.'

items.text: Gemara's clarification: why not assume the opposite?
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: why not assume the opposite?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this is obvious, and suggests that one might think the adulterer warned the husband because he wants the wife to be available for him, citing 'stolen waters are sweet.' The Gemara concludes that the ruling teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that Rava's ruling is obvious, and raises the possibility that the adulterer warned the husband because he wanted the woman as his wife, citing the verse 'stolen waters are sweet.'
The gemara concludes that Rava's ruling teaches us that the adulterer's warning is not motivated by desire for the woman, but rather indicates he did not commit adultery.
